review_text:
This is easily the best third person shooter of the past 5 years.

Naturally being a sniper elite game, it has solid sniping, but you can also just run around with a trench shotgun if you prefer. I'm pretty sure you could beat the game with an SMG if you modified it right, although that's not a knock against the game, it has a high flexibility of playstyles (unlike Doom Eternal) and you can be as sneaky or as loud as you want.
The game also has the multiplayer "invasion" mode where you can join other people's singleplayer games and hunt them down (thankfully this is togglable if you don't want to be invaded).
It also has a survival wave mode which is neat.
Although the "shoot Hitler" level is a DLC and not base game. So unfortunately you have to pay to detonate Hitler's left nut with a derringer.

9/10, nearly perfect game.

Is not bad, decent to buy on sale though only a hard maybe at full price(I would not). I like the weapon customization and it is a huge plus over previous games. Axis invasion is interesting and I am glad I can just disable EAA and not have to deal with it as well. The maps are best they have ever been, they look stunning, have pretty good sniping angles. In general the colors and visuals are great. The smgs and pistols really benefit so much from the new ADS options as it makes smgs and pistols actual worthwhile options in more scenarios than in previous games.

The downsides: 
The tanks, they use king tigers which makes no sense, AP small arms can pen their rear which, also, makes no sense, and somehow their AI is just 10x worse than in 4, god knows why. They should have kept the same tanks but maybe made them like the Panzer 4G, with occassional heavier panthers and tiger1s and maybe a singular king tiger on the last mission, each being harder to kill with the last requiring panzerfausts. 
The AI is absolutely awful, that may be overstating it but the AI can be really wonky at times, with the worst being when they are alert as they act so nonsensically, but otherwise they are pretty decent in combat or stealth. But there are usually just so few of them as well, really should have placed more, but they also can see you from farther so idk.
The actual sniping is something, it's not really a hard negative but it just feels so much less satisfying than it did in 4, the icon itself just isn't as clean as the older one, the x-ray somehow feels off and I am not sure why, and the focus takes time to now even create the wind and drop. Spotting now just requires hovering over which is stupid since I can no longer decide specifically what to spot and takes way longer to just mark people who exist.
Small thing but a really big gripe, the removal of proper weakspots from most vehicles pisses me off. It's most likely there to force the usage of AP ammunition, but the lack of weakspots makes the sniping aspect of the game weaker.

Overall it's not bad, and I prefer 4, but if I could get the same feel of sniping of 4 and return of regular weakspots here I would probably prefer this one.

review_text:
Did anyone on the team behind Sniper Elite 5 actually play their own game?

The movement feels unbelievably stiff — Karl handles like he’s pushing 80 instead of being a trained WWII operative. Reloading a pistol takes what feels like three full seconds. With that kind of “fitness” and reaction time, how is this guy supposed to survive a battlefield?

And the traversal makes even less sense. Why can’t you just drop down from a low wall? We’re talking about something under two meters, and somehow this elite agent is completely stuck unless the game explicitly allows it. It’s clunky, restrictive, and honestly embarrassing for a modern game.

Then there’s the enemy AI. Their patrol and detection logic is absurd — they act like they’ve all got built-in radar in their heads. There’s no nuance, no believable behavior, just instant awareness that kills any sense of stealth or immersion.

And honestly, if you had bothered to replay Sniper Elite 4, the difference would be painfully obvious. Just a few minutes of comparison would show how much worse the handling feels now — it’s genuinely unpleasant.

On top of all that, there are countless little issues that make playing this game feel unnecessarily frustrating — like everything is working against you instead of with you.

Overall, it’s a clunky, awkward experience that feels far more irritating than it should be.

I would still give the game 5/5 in terms of a stealthy shooter. Peak content here, no question. 

My gripes come in the sense that many things have been made very much easier on the hardest difficulty settings. For example:

- your position and orientation are shown on the map screen
- you have an embedded wind meter on every gun when you ADS
- you have an embedded projectile falloff meter on every scoped weapon when you ADS
- these meters automatically adjust to whatever is at the centre of your crosshairs
- your character has psychic powers and will always let you know when an enemy has discovered his position; "Time to move", "They'll find me if I stay here"

These things would be fairly easy to make a toggle for in the difficulty menu. It would add a lot of value for those that like a challenge, and give the term "Authentic" a lot more truth. Force me to use my brain a little more. Binoculars to find range, scope on gun to zero that range, feeling and judgement to make up the difference. Having a persistent wind meter makes sense on a scoped weapon, but at least give us the option to turn off all these HUD elements if we want to? This is a barely positive review for me, and strictly if you acquire the game with a 60%+ discount.

The game has two main issues for me. The first thing is AI's behavior, which makes zero sense. The moment they start investigate something and deviate from their strict up-and-down path, they lose it and run around like brainless chickens. Impossible to predict, and it completely breaks the immersion. The AI animations also feel out of sync, and they usually "snap" from one state to the other, instead of transitioning seamlessly.

Secondly are the levels/maps. They feel more like Hitman maps rather than Sniper Elite maps. It feels like the game drags you to go on foot and kill everybody with your little silenced pistol, rather than finding a sniper's nest. Opportunity wise, sniping also gets a smaller piece of the pie as well. It's just weird that the devs went that way, it doesn't fit that much the older style of games (e.g SE3), and it did bother me a little.

On the good side, the graphics are gorgeous. Story is generic nazi vs americans ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but it's good enough, since nobody plays this for the story anyway. The maps even though they are not as "Sniper Elite like" they are nice and they are structured in such a way as to allow you multiple entries to the map as well as different exfill locations. Finally, you get more of those great killcams that this game is known for, so yeah, I'll add that to the list too.

Overall, if you get it for 15-25 bucks max, I believe it's a buy, especially if you like the style of Sniper Elite games and want some more of it!

I enjoyed SE4 and finally bought Sniper Elite 5, which immediately went into my personal top 100.

10/10. It’s taken all the best parts of Fallout 4 and left out all that other junk. The gunplay in it is so entertaining that you sometimes forget the game has a whole kit of other magic tricks included. As soon as I remember to use mines, people just start dropping like flies. In some trench labyrinth, I remembered: oh yeah! Mines. Then I started dropping them there, and some enemy found a body, so they started rushing all over that trench and the screen just filled with text: "infantry kill, infantry kill..."

This is like a puzzle game that you solve with a gun. Except for the tanks, which take some serious work since they don't want to go to pieces no matter what you do. First drop a mine so they stop, then a Panzerfaust to the rear, then some satchel charge and a couple more TNTs, then maybe it finally blows up. And when there are two of them at the same time, oh man, it gets interesting.

The weakest part of this is the perks or upgrades, of which about three are useful. Then when you get to the end of the perk tree, there are just ones where you're like, "why would anyone want to use this?" But they are only weak because the core gameplay is so excellent. Now when I level up, it’s just like, ugh, really? Well, I guess I’ll check them through, then I scroll for a minute and don’t actually want any of them.

Good. Damn good.

review_text:
Sniper Elite 5 delivers exactly what the series is known for: tactical sniping, large sandbox maps, and brutally satisfying kill cams. It doesn’t reinvent the formula, but it refines it enough to make it one of the stronger entries in the franchise.

 What It Does Well

The sniping mechanics are the highlight. Bullet drop, wind, heart rate, and distance all matter, making long-range shots feel earned and incredibly satisfying. The signature X-ray kill cam is more detailed than ever and never gets old.

The missions are large and open-ended, encouraging different playstyles. You can ghost through objectives in full stealth, set traps and manipulate enemy patrols, or go loud if things fall apart. There’s real freedom in how you approach each mission.

Weapon customization is deeper this time around, allowing meaningful tweaks to fit your preferred playstyle. The Invasion Mode is also a standout feature — being invaded by another player (or invading someone else’s campaign) adds tension and unpredictability.

Performance on PC is solid overall, with good optimization and plenty of graphical options.

 Where It Falls Short

The story is serviceable but forgettable. It mostly acts as a backdrop for the missions rather than something emotionally engaging.

Enemy AI can be inconsistent. Sometimes they react well to sound and movement; other times they feel predictable or slow to adapt. Close-quarters combat and some animations also feel a bit dated compared to modern shooters.

While environments are detailed, certain textures and character models don’t always match current AAA standards.

Final Verdict

Sniper Elite 5 is a strong tactical shooter that rewards patience and precision. If you enjoy methodical gameplay, planning your shots, and clearing large maps at your own pace, you’ll have a great time.

It doesn’t revolutionize the series, but it delivers a polished and satisfying sniping experience.

Sniper Elite 5 is an excellent sniping game for both 2‑player co‑op and competitive 1v1‑style multiplayer, as long as you’re okay with it being online‑only. The core campaign can be played fully in co‑op with a friend, and that’s where the game feels most satisfying: you can share ammo, heal each other, and coordinate long‑range takedowns over big, detailed maps that encourage stealth and teamwork. Splitting roles sniper in the back, scout/enforcer up close makes missions feel fresh and tactical, and the classic X‑Ray kill cam is even more fun to watch with a partner.

The 2‑player co‑op campaign is very polished: you can “request assistance” anytime, and hosting a session lets both players progress through the same story beats. Survival mode is also great in co‑op, where you and up to three others defend hot‑zones against waves of enemies, making good use of the larger maps and layered objectives. Strategy, communication, and reviving each other turn what could be a grind into a fun, replayable co‑op shooter.
​

For 1v1 / adversarial play, Sniper Elite 5 offers more traditional multiplayer modes, including team and squad matches where you compete for kills or objectives. The sniper‑focused design means you have to think like a real marksman: accounting for wind, distance, and that tell‑tale rifle glint others can see. Invasion mode adds a cat‑and‑mouse twist, letting you invade a friend’s campaign as an Axis sniper and hunt them during their mission, which feels like a tense 1v1‑style challenge embedded in the PvE world.
​

Overall, Sniper Elite 5 is a strong pick if you love tactical sniping and want to play with a friend. The co‑op campaign and Survival mode are the highlights, while the competitive and Invasion modes give you extra 1v1‑style tension and variety. It’s a satisfying, well‑built sniping game that shines brightest when you’re playing with someone else or hunting them.

[b]To be quite honest with you, this game sucks.[/b]

The movement is clunky, there are invisible barriers everywhere (that are implemented in the laziest way I have ever seen), the AI is laughably bad and the general gameplay loop gets repetetive very quickly.

When playing this game, you will soon realise that freedom of movement and engagement are just illusions. Don't be fooled by how open the map looks, because I guarantee you that you'll encounter 101 invisible barriers in your attempt to traverse the terrain in any way that is even slightly conducive to how you might expect a trained sniper to. Seriously though, you have barriers that are plonked down meters from the nearest set of rocks or foliage, you have barriers preventing you from leaping down from a rock wall that is no higher than 1.5 meters, and you have barriers that actively prevent you from attempting to take an alternate path towards the main objective area. 

Despite all such barriers, even the movement that you CAN make in the game (without being severely limited) is just god-awful. General movement is horrifically clunky, and terrain traversal (like climbing, vaulting, dropping etc.) is just as bad. I just cannot fathom the fact that you're supposed to be playing as a world-class sniper when your movement is akin to a child learning to walk & climb for the first time.

I'm not even going to expand on the AI, because you can experience that for yourself. But otherwise, this game and the implementation of all the mechanics is genuinely embarrassing. It's almost as if all the time & effort went into making the X-Ray Shots impressive and they then subsequently rushed everything else.

I don't feel like a world class sniper,
I don't enjoy navigating the terrain in any capacity,
The enemies are not satisfying to kill - and they're Nazi's, so this should be a damn given,
The story has not been expanded in any significant way from the previous games,
And somehow, a game from 2022 feels like it was released in 2008 (and looks like it at times).

It's an embarrassing excuse for a Sniper game, and due to the fact that I've only been able to enjoy the game through Axis Invasion, I simply cannot recommend it unless you get it for ridiculously cheap (and you're expecting the clunkiness of this title). There are indie developers who could make a better sniper game with less time & money, and it's a real shame that this game is as expensive as it is.

Pros:

Level Design: Massive, non-linear maps that reward reconnaissance and creative pathfinding.

Invasion Mode: Adds a necessary layer of human unpredictability to an otherwise predictable AI loop.

Weapon Customization: Deep, stats-driven modification system that actually impacts ballistics and handling.

Technical Polish: High-fidelity X-ray kill cams provide a visceral visual feedback.

Cons:

The story is WW2 sniper kills everyone.

Incremental Innovation: If you’ve played Sniper Elite 4, the core loop will feel like a refined expansion rather than a sequel.

AI is inconsistent: Enemies oscillate wildly in their ability to detect me.

Bottom Line: A reliable, high-performing tactical tool for your library. Recommended for the gameplay loop, not the story.

review_text:
Sniper Elite stands as one of the most refined and satisfying tactical shooter series in gaming, delivering an experience where precision, patience, and strategy are just as important as firepower. From the moment you raise your rifle and let a well-aimed shot fly, Sniper Elite delivers the visceral thrill that sniping aficionados have long craved.

What truly defines Sniper Elite is its unparalleled ballistics simulation. Every shot feels weighty and realistic — from wind influence and bullet drop to heart-pounding moments as you scope in on distant targets. This attention to detail elevates every encounter into a calculated challenge that rewards careful planning and skillful execution. Long-range engagements don’t just feel tactical; they feel personal.

The series’ iconic X-Ray Kill Cam continues to be one of its most memorable features — a visceral, slow-motion depiction of bullet impact that blends satisfying feedback with dramatic flair. It’s not just a cosmetic spectacle; it’s a testament to the game’s uncompromising commitment to making every shot count.

Beyond the shooting mechanics, Sniper Elite thrives as a stealth-oriented tactical adventure. Levels are cleverly designed with multiple paths, verticality, and environmental interplay that allow you to chart your own approach. Whether you’re silently eliminating sentries, avoiding patrols through careful timing, or using traps and distractions to thin enemy numbers, every mission feels like a carefully crafted sandbox where creativity is rewarded.

Visually and aurally, the game captures the era and tone with authenticity. Atmospheric lighting, detailed environments, and period-accurate sound design put you right in the heart of WWII theaters or other conflict zones, making every mission feel immersive and high-stakes.

Co-op and competitive modes add extra layers of replayability, allowing friends (or rivals) to team up or test their sharpshooting skills against each other. And with a wide array of weapons, upgrades, and customization options, Sniper Elite offers depth for both newcomers and hardened tactical gamers.

In summary, Sniper Elite isn’t just about pulling the trigger — it’s about mastering the art of the shot. It delivers an exceptional blend of strategy, simulation, and action that stands out in a genre filled with fast-paced shooters.

Rating: 9/10 – A deeply satisfying tactical shooter that redefines precision gameplay and rewards mastery.

In addition to this, you have an ocular implant that upon holding your breath, shows you where the bullet may hit, useful for extra long distance or windy shots.

I played Sniper Elite V2 quite a lot when I was a kid but haven't touched the franchise since, so I was happy when I picked up Sniper Elite 5 to see that it still scratches that same itch the old one did. The starting mission is a bit slow-paced, but once you get used to the play style it's quite good. 
Despite only having 8 main campaign missions (plus a mini-mission at the very end), there's quite a lot of content. I had a stealth-focused playthrough, which lead to missions lasting a little over an hour and a half as I would wait for patrols to pass or knock out guards one-by-one. In total it took me just shy of 20hrs to finish the game. If you took a louder or more lethal approach, missions would probably take a bit less time. I spent quite a lot of time exploring the map, so I did get many but not all side objectives or intel.
Regarding the gameplay itself, I loved it. Stealth and sniper combat is well-balanced with only a few minor nitpicks that really don't detract from the gameplay. Scouting in the game gives you small snippets of info about (almost!) every soldier you meet and I found myself scouting enemy soldiers just to learn info about them. Of course, I also used that info to determine whether they got shot or left to live for another day; soldier who terrorized the locals = dead, guy worried about his family back in Berlin = spared. It's the little bits of RP that you're able to do that really cement this as a great game. If the game is on sale I'd say it is close to a must-buy, if it is full-price buy if you love stealth shooters.

The developers didn't think about this so much when they made the game.
Thus, I have to say I do not recommend.

review_text:
Review: Sniper Elite 5 
Score: 8.8 / 10 

Sniper Elite 5 is a tactical stealth shooter that rewards patience, 
planning, and precision. 
Set during World War II, the game places the player in large, open-ended levels where reconnaissance, positioning, and timing are just as important as marksmanship. 
After investing over 100 hours into the game, it becomes clear that Sniper Elite 5 is both highly engaging and genuinely enjoyable on multiple levels.

 The core gameplay is exceptionally addictive. The maps are well designed, offering multiple approaches to objectives, and the overall pacing encourages thoughtful play rather than constant action. 
The game succeeds in creating tension and satisfaction through long-range engagements, careful movement, and strategic elimination of enemies. 

The most significant drawback, however, is the lack of thorough playtesting prior to release. The game frequently feels as though it was not fully polished. Numerous bugs are present, including instances where the player character clips into level geometry, becomes partially immobile while animations continue, or carries bodies in a broken state where the corpse appears invisible and cannot be dropped. These issues occur often enough to be noticeable and immersion-breaking. 

There are also smaller but unfortunate inconsistencies in narrative and presentation. For example, characters with established backgrounds implying fluency in German occasionally pronounce German names incorrectly, defaulting to English pronunciation. While minor in isolation, these details stand out in a game that otherwise strives for authenticity. 

Difficulty balance is another area with curious inconsistencies. The most enjoyable difficulty mode is Authentic, which offers a slower, more methodical experience. Ironically, lower difficulties such as Civilian (Very Easy) often feel more chaotic, with aggressive enemy AI attacking from all directions, while Authentic allows for calmer and more controlled encounters. Additionally, realism sometimes stretches credibility, as surviving direct hits from heavy weaponry undermines the intended authenticity of the mode. 

This evaluation is intentionally limited to the single-player experience. Multiplayer and cooperative modes are excluded, as their performance and perceived quality are strongly affected by external factors such as network conditions, server stability, and latency. These variables fall outside the scope of the game’s core design and would not provide a consistent or objective basis for assessment within this review. 

Despite these flaws, the game remains highly enjoyable. It is absolutely worth playing, provided one does not allow minor technical issues to overshadow the experience. That said, perfectionist players may find certain collectible challenges frustrating. Some Stone Eagles are hidden in such extreme and unintuitive locations that finding them without external assistance can take hours or even days, significantly harming motivation. 

Overall, Sniper Elite 5 delivers a satisfying and memorable experience. The negative aspects stem almost exclusively from insufficient testing and rushed polishing rather than from flawed design. Having participated personally in multiple testing phases for games prior to release, it is evident that this title would have benefited from additional quality assurance time. 

Conclusion Sniper Elite 5 is an excellent and highly engaging game that offers deep tactical gameplay and rewarding stealth mechanics. While technical issues and uneven difficulty balance detract from an otherwise strong experience, the game remains well worth playing. Its shortcomings are the result of rushed testing rather than poor design, making it a strong title that narrowly misses true excellence. 

For reference, I have uploaded screenshots to my profile showcasing multiple bugs and engine-related issues observed during gameplay.

I am a fan of this franchise and played every part except Resistance and the first one maybe a couple hours, V2 I don't have on steam. So when it was on sale for just five Euros I naturally bought it.
I had some expectations for this one and - oh, boy - am I disappointed. My theory is that Rebellion learned from the best. Unfortunately only the worst things.
This game is barely a new one, I rather call it an update to Sniper Elite 4. There is some changes but I dare you to call it improvements.
Yes, the maps are bigger and you have many options to fulfill a mission objective. But don't get fooled by the "open world". You cannnot go anywhere you want because there are restrictions. And some of them kill the immersion to me.
For instance the character (I have played the story mode and some Surivial so far) is not able to get over a step or a stone or even a muddy hill which is no higher than his feet. WTF? And in some places where it looks like it would be of no difficulty to climb it is not possible. The other way around is where you can hang you cannot drop down even it wouldn't be a problem to do so. Of course it's no Assasin's Creed, but come on!
The next thing is the motion mechanics in general. When in one mission I tried to climb a ladder up a church, I needed three attempts in a row! Why? Karl Fairburne behaves like a drunk and missed the ladder even I straight went towards it. That bugs me out. And that is not even everything that is not working as expected regarding this issue.
What also bugs me out is the way the mode Axis Invasion was executed. So poorly. When some mates of mine and I wanted to play it, it didn't work of course. Why should it? There is just no intuitive UI. So I had to do some research on the internet to find out how that mode works. You cannot just join a campaign and play as Axis Sniper, no! You'll need a code to join. But you cannot just be easily invited to this mode either. So I just had the menu to look at. Turns out,  your mates first have to fulfill a mission objective before you could join. Why, though? Why can't it just as easy by invite or joining my mates?
The game is essentially the same as Sniper Elite 4 Italy. Reusing the same assets would proove my point.

Hopefully SE5 will not land on my pile of shame (of unfinished games).
Another issue is that the game at start always wants me to connect my Epicgames account. No, I do NOT want that, leave me alone!

So, as I said, Rebellion learned the worst things from the best there is. Publish a "new" game with barely updates but charging full price (EA?). Also the DLC policy is annoying. Not only for this IP. But publish DLC charging also nearly for a full price game and providing almost nothing new is a shame (Starbreeze, is that you?).
It's sad to see what Rebellion has become. Shame on you! Rename yourself into "One of them", because I see no Rebellion here.
Please, put some more effort into your games.

I once planned to try their new game "Atomfall". But I guess I shouldn't.
If you never played Sniper Elite wait for a big discount on this one or buy SE3 or SE4 instead.

review_text:
As an unconditional fan of the Sniper Elite franchise, I must analyze the fifth installment, which undoubtedly has its highs and lows.

To begin with, this fifth installment is essentially identical to the fourth in terms of mission structure and gameplay formula. This is generally not a bad thing, since, gameplay-wise, Sniper Elite 4 is a very good game. Possibly, one of the few aspects I liked the most is the atmosphere and the well-crafted levels.

And here comes the negative part. Rebellion, the developer, has brought us the same story for the third time: We are in the area, we investigate a Nazi superweapon, we destroy it, and finally we kill the mastermind behind it all. I know for many the story isn't important, but the same premise is getting tiresome.

Regarding enemies, we basically have the same as in the fourth, but without the Italian troops, so we basically see the same troops throughout the entire game. Possibly the worst aspect I see in this game is the weapons, since the base game includes very few. As an example of this lack of variety, we didn't even have a secondary shotgun, which was added later as free DLC. A rifle like the Lee Enfield was also added as free DLC, but weapons like the Mosin Nagant, the PPSh, the Mauser C96 pistol, or the Grease submachine gun are behind a paywall—weapons that were in the base game of previous installments.

But the worst part is that these weapons were already made in Zombie Army 4, a game that came out a year earlier and uses the same graphics engine as Sniper Elite 5. Basically, they copied and pasted them and are selling them separately. However, this problematic DLC issue has been evident since the third installment.

The question is, do I recommend Sniper Elite 5? If you liked the fourth installment, I recommend this one, but only when it's on sale, especially now that the price has dropped quite a bit with the latest discounts.

- Sniping is satisfying as usual, it is not much of a challenge in terms of actually shooting, but it is not straight forward enough to make it a bit more interesting than just point and shoot.

- Map restrictions are extremely frustrating, I get that you don't want the player to find exploits or make areas of interest too easy to access via climbing, but some areas are inaccessible for no reason at all or, things that look climbable are not and vice-versa. 🎯 Sniper Elite 5: A Masterclass in Precision Carnage 🎯

⭐ 9/10 – Stealthy Symphony of Bullets and Boom
Hey gamers, let me tell you about Sniper Elite 5 – the game that turned me into a ghost in the fog of WWII France. From the moment I scoped in on my first long-range shot, I was hooked. This isn't just another shooter; it's a tense, tactical ballet of death where every heartbeat matters, and every bullet tells a story. Developed by Rebellion, it dropped in 2022 and still feels fresh in 2026. If you crave that perfect blend of stealth, strategy, and gloriously gruesome kill cams, this is your jam.

✅ The Hits: What Makes It Elite

Sniper Mechanics on Steroids 💥
Ballistics are chef's kiss realistic – wind, gravity, heartbeat, bullet drop? All in play. One-shotting a Nazi officer from 500m feels like poetry in motion.
X-Ray Kill Cams: Pure Ecstasy 🩸
Those slow-mo dissections of hearts, lungs, and spines? Satisfying doesn't cover it. It's gore porn for tacticians – I replayed kills just to admire the physics.
Massive, Freedom-Filled Maps 🗺️
Levels are huge playgrounds with rooftops, sewers, chateaus, and forests. Multiple entry points, side objectives, and rat-traps galore. Freedom to play your way.
Invasion Mode: Chaos Unleashed ⚔️
Jump into someone else's campaign as an enemy sniper? Genius multiplayer twist. Heart-pounding cat-and-mouse that elevates solo play to legendary status.
Audio and Atmosphere: Immersive AF 🎧
Pinpoint sound design – footsteps crunch, bullets whiz, bodies thud. Paired with stunning visuals (ray-tracing on PC? Drool-worthy), it's a sensory feast.

❌ The Misses: Room for a Reload

Story? Meh, It's Filler 📖
The plot is a forgettable spy thriller. Leo and Sophie are fine, but it's just an excuse for the action. Don't expect Hearts of Iron depth.
Stealth Can Be Punishing 😤
AI is smart (too smart sometimes), spotting you from afar or through walls. One wrong move, and it's alarm city. Frustrating for casual sneaks.
Repetition Creeps In 🔄
Missions follow a formula: infiltrate, snipe, sabotage, exfil. After 10 hours, it feels samey without more variety.
Performance Hiccups (Console Woes) 🐛
On last-gen hardware, frame drops and pop-in mar the beauty. PC masters it better, but optimize your rig.

Final Scope: Worth the Shot?
Sniper Elite 5 is a love letter to snipers – thrilling, replayable, and brutally rewarding. It's not perfect, but the highs (those impossible shots!) eclipse the lows. If you're into Hitman stealth with Battlefield destruction, grab it now. I've sunk 50+ hours and still crave more.
Play it. Scope it. Own it.
– Your friendly neighborhood ghost shooter 👻

- Visuals: This is pretty obvious, so I won't go into further detail.
- Varied maps and an interesting storyline: I didn't feel like I was playing the same level twice; there was always something new or different compared to the previous mission.

Things I disliked about SE5:
- Excessive DLC: A lot of content should have been included in the Deluxe Edition. The additional DLC feels like a cash grab and highlights the developers' greed.
- Survival Mode: It’s interesting at first but gets boring quickly. This isn't because of the "wave defense" mechanic, but because the maps are unnecessarily long. The fact that enemies are randomly getting close to you (not instantly after a round starts) doesn't help either.

 Final thoughts:
I enjoyed SE5 more than I expected and I am hopeful for the next title, I mean SE6, not Resistance, since Karl Fairburne is not the protagonist of that one. You won't regret purchasing this game unless you expect an extensive campaign or captivating alternative game modes.

review_text:
Sniper Elite 5 is a slow-burn stealth sandbox that’s at its best when you treat every mission like a puzzle you’re solving at your own pace. The story is mostly an excuse to drop you into occupied France, but the moment-to-moment experience—scouting, planning angles, and choosing when to take the shot—carries the whole game.

The level design is the big upgrade here. Each map is wide, layered, and packed with routes, vantage points, and little side objectives that naturally pull you off the “main path.” You can play it clean and quiet, or you can turn it into a messy firefight, and the game usually supports both without feeling like you’re doing it wrong.

Sniping still feels great. Leading shots, accounting for distance, and using sound cover (generators, planes, artillery, etc.) makes kills feel earned, and the X-ray cam is as over-the-top as ever. It’s not the most realistic sniper sim, but it nails that satisfying rhythm of patience → setup → payoff.

On the ground, the stealth and gunplay are solid but a bit uneven. Suppressed play, tagging enemies, and slipping through restricted areas works well, yet the AI can be inconsistent—sometimes sharp, sometimes weirdly clueless—and going loud can feel less interesting than the careful stealth approach. When the game gets chaotic, it’s fun, but it’s clearly built to reward methodical play.

The extra modes add a lot, especially Axis Invasion. Being hunted (or doing the hunting) changes the entire mood of a mission: suddenly every open field is risky, every tower is suspicious, and you start thinking like another human is watching your habits. Co-op also fits the campaign nicely, because splitting roles—spotter and shooter—makes the missions feel even more tactical.

Customization is deep enough to matter without turning into pure spreadsheet work. Ammo types, weapon attachments, and loadout choices let you tailor a build for stealth, range, or flexibility, and difficulty options can push it toward either a relaxed power fantasy or a tense “one mistake hurts” experience.

Overall, Sniper Elite 5 is easy to recommend if you like stealth sandboxes and the specific satisfaction of lining up perfect shots. It’s not a story-driven masterpiece, and it has some jank and AI quirks, but the missions, sniping mechanics, and invasion/co-op options make it a game you can sink a lot of time into—especially if you enjoy replaying maps with different approaches.

[h1]Sniper Elite 5[/h1]

Motion sickness sucks and I have a hard time with it when playing games. SE5 pushed my limits a bit but I managed to soldier through (pun intended). Because the camera is often still or movement is slow and it's just far enough over the shoulder, I can play it though I feel a bit woozy afterwards. In this case, the effort and discomfort were worth it. 

I don't get to play those games very often and the last one I played was Sniper Elite 2 so this felt fairly new and fresh. The graphics are great and you just have to love the slo-mo bullet impacts. The maps are huge and I loved looking for shots that were 200m or more (I think my longest was somewhere around 400m). It generally rewards patience and, unlike SE2, I didn't notice "enemy spawn" where you completed part of the mission and all of a sudden new enemies popped up in places where they weren't before. The open maps allowed me a lot of freedom to tackle issues as I thought best with few bottlenecks and the map variety was really awesome - factories, villas, castles, rural, bombed out ruins, etc.

If there is any downside to the game, it's the AI. The enemy is dumb. They'll walk past dead comrades sometimes without noticing. They'll expose themselves unnecessarily to sniper fire. They can't see me from 5 feet away in daylight if I'm in the tall grass. All of this one the "normal" difficulty level (whatever it's called) and so it made the game a bit less challenging than desired at times. 

To be fair there are still great challenges as some situations require some well-thought out approaches (or blind luck) and vehicles can spot you quite well. Taking out a tank is a pretty epic endeavor. And if I do play it again, I'll ramp the difficulty on both the enemies and the shooting as on the normal difficulty I'd rarely miss a shot.  I also enjoy the recaps at the end where it shows the style in how you played - lethal or not (they're Nazis, I'm killing everyone I see) and stealthy or not. I had a couple of maps where I played more of a run-and-gun style and others where I was a sneak.

It took me about 28 hours to complete the base game. Not a bad value considering I paid $4 from GMG. Also, I experienced absolutely no bugs, crashes or other issues. 

Note that I didn't buy any of the DLC. Maybe it's good and maybe it's not but this is a game where you absolutely don't need it to enjoy the game. I'll return to this title in the future to either look for some of the stuff I missed and/or start in the different locations but I also bought the deluxe version of SE4 from GMG for like $7 because I had so much fun with this one.

So given what it costs on sale, this is one of the better bargains I've played in recent years. Thumbs up.

Sniper Elite 5 is just like Sniper Elite 4 and so on. There's less noise than #4, so sniping is harder, plus you tend to move around more. It's a lot of fun.

So if you shoot them, they kind of stagger and if you keep shooting, you'll empty a clip of bullets and then the enemy suddenly recovers and starts shooting at you again. So you have to reload and get shot a few times.

Also, it's a pain sometimes when you go to search a body, but there's also a weapon nearby and the key to pick it up is the same as search, so you pick it up even though you didn't want it.

Edit: I have since found that you can pick up new guns, but they are only temporary. It's good and bad.

The save function is okay. It respawns you close-ish, but sometimes you have to re-do parts of it.

Killing Nazis is always a guaranteed winner, and it's fitting that the in-game character of Moller looks suspiciously like an old Elon Musk. Clearly the devs went all in on the Nazi angle, and I'm all for it.

This game is just enjoyable enough to recommend, but on the whole it is eye-rollingly 'MURCA!
The PC looks like he has 10,000 years of German ancestry trying to leap out of his face, and every chance he gets is "Nazi" this and "German" that, I found it quite funny.
The voice acting is fine, I guess, but the directing choice for the PC's voice is abysmal. The guy sounds like after the war he went on to voice Ford commercials. And he sounds like that ALL THE TIME. There isn't an ounce of dynamics in his performance at any moment. 
You're a sniper, it's a stealth game (optional?) but here goes the big bad American(TM) hero sneaking up behind some dirty nazi and some tall grass catches his eye and he feels forces he can't understand compel him to blurt out in his V8 truck of the year growl "LONG GRASS, COULD BE GOOD FOR STAYING HIDDEN-" *springs from behind a desk and winds up with the worlds longest, most telegraphed, least respectful to any martial art style haymaker cinema has ever SEEN before cold cocking this poor grunt who thought the nazis had a moon base.
First off, like dude, I am 85% of the way done this entire game, I've brought down entire compounds by myself //through you//, why does this feel like you've never left the tutorial?
Second of all, why do all of your lines need to be voiced at the same projection level/volume as every other one of your speaking lines? This 100% makes be believe you are actually speaking these lines out loud, made especially bad as you seem like you must have been that kid in school who someone had cranked the volume of their voice up to 9 and ripped the knob off.
Best part though was honestly just how much it paid off to think the game was cheese.
PC interacts with a few people during cut scenes. Mostly women who at the very least are friendly with him and at the most are being professional but want to bang. I recall one guy he speaks with as a recurring character and it's just the most predictable relationship arc. They don't like each other, begrudgingly do so, one proves himself to the other, the other does it off screen (I guess), and they shake hands LIKE MEN at the end, which you know would have been a dap if they were wise to the ways.

Germans this, French that, English the other thing, but it's gotta be an American named The Shadow to singlehandedly change the tide in the occupation of France. But wait - there's more, and possibly the best twist you definitely see coming - the Nazis' real plan is to attack the east coast of AMERICA. This was never a plan IRL. This is a choice for the game because SAVING FRANCE wasn't a good enough wrap on the thing, the American has to SAVE AMERICA. Of course. 

I played this on "Sharpshooter" which is their medium, default, middle of the road difficulty but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, there were a lot of moments it felt too easy - the enemies have zero awareness. You can dance around them, beside them, hidden by a box with your shoulders and up showing and they won't see a thing. They could trip over the 5 foot long extended barrel of your rifle with a suppressor on it and think it was just the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ wind, I swear to god. 
However, it being a little too easy encouraged me to make it more difficult by trying to be the least lethal as possible, using only non-lethal ammunition or "pacifying" them with a little CTE before stuffing them in a crate which maybe someone will find them. 
I found tagging as many people as I could before engaging with anyone to be a lot of fun actually, and reading the little personal blurbs for each one. The ones who didn't agree with what they were doing, just wanted the war to end, hoped their family was okay, just wanted to see their wife again, etc, I went out of my way to really spare and prop them up in as respectful a manner as the ragdoll physics would allow. The ones who was super pro war might have woken up in a fire, who's to say.

The graphics are great, I really enjoyed the maps! I wish there was more, and since I'm playing strictly singleplayer I wish I could explore them a bit more freely. There were a few that I could do so after neutralizing everyone but that's a hell of a lot of work. 
The hitboxes of the landscape though needs some work. At no point should you assume that just because you leaped over, or mantled, or climbed, or interacted in anyway with one thing does that mean you should expect to be able to do the same with any other of those things you encounter, or even things which look smaller or easier to do those actions with than the ones you previously had success with. 
There is a jump mechanic. 
Why?
You'll have to let me know when you figure that out. I think it came into use exactly twice, and I think each time I found a workaround after the fact, so it wasn't necessary. The third time it popped up as an action was while crossing over an extra wide box on I think it was Rubble and Ruin. Since it's not an option you always have, I wanted to see what it would proc my little hero boy to jump to, and I then got to witness this big softy launch himself off this box as far as he could (which, I guess was a respectable distance but absolutely not a long jump by any standards) and land... on the ground. 
There was nothing dodged, nothing avoided, absolutely nothing, no reason for that jump. I went back and forth a few times with and without jumping. Can't for the life of me think of why that was there. 
A permanent jump mechanic and some more interesting landscape to interact with would be awesome. 
It'll never happen, but would be nice. 

More guns are locked behind DLC. There are not a lot of options to begin with, you unlock more as you play, so in the beginning there's really not much, and as you go you will probably settle into a loadout which you won't really change for the second half of the game. You unlock guns by killing certain people certain ways, completing missions, finding certain things in the missions, etc. 
The skill tree doesn't really matter, you will fill the entire thing out by the end so there's no real uniqueness to your build. 

I was actually super let down by the Loose Ends final mission/cut scene. There's not really any emotional attachment in this game for the player to feel like "NOOOO, THE GAME CAN'T END WITHOUT ME KILLING THIS ONE BAD GUYYYY!!!!1!" So including an entire map (which looks really neat!) just for you to make one shot (which pales in comparison to the shooting range distances (honestly, why allow you to practice shots up to 1000 meters when in game you won't often reach more than 350?)) just felt powerfully dumb. I figured there must be some achievements hidden in that level somewhere, so I replayed it maybe 40 times. 
First go was a headshot - achievement for killing him that way. Shot his car up, he runs to another, can't shoot that one up before he gets in it because it's hidden.  Tried running down there to storm the level and you're restricted to the sniper post. Lameeee. I tried taking out all the other guys before the big bad, impossible. He will run and there is just not enough time (not even close) to take everyone out before he skedaddles. 

I really wish there was more sniper vs sniper action in these levels. I would enjoy having to creep around and play the waiting game with someone who could take me out in a shot as well. Instead these elite snipers are in watch towers that might as well have a big flag that say SNIPER HERE and have ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ flashlights mounted to their guns so when they aim at the PC you get to see the "lens reflection" from 300 meters away as though it's a magnesium flare

If it's dirt cheap, if you've got memory just falling out of you like a senator, and if what I've just described above sounds like something you'd tell your wife "not tonight, honey" in order to push through, then by all means, I recommend this game to you.

[h1]First time into Sniper Elite series[/h1]

You can't see there are different ways to reach the objectives at first---you only figure it out after disastrous attempts. Then the real fun starts.

Getting creative rewards as the game progresses. While I tend to sneak and wait---the singleplayer campaign can be played in 4 styles; from "non-lethal" (no kills), to "lethal" which can be noisy. I have an impatient friend that usually plays Rambo; that's the 3rd style, "assault." 

To get your style better, you can evolve Karl's skills into three segments: combat, equipment and body. Can also equip or man temporary guns or mod yours in workbenches.

Moving like a shadow I land in the 4th style: "stealth," but since class can combine, I'm also fall into lethal. If I have to blow a bunker because the silent option is FUBAR, I'd bobby-trap possible reinforcement routes or sabotage proxy installations. Can wait for external sounds to pull the trigger and mask the boom. 

Sometimes I'm non-lethal to avoid alarming the scorn about my presence, even though blowing fascists into smithereens is very tempting.

Campaign story is ok but cutscenes are just generic body-capture. Maybe fans of the series still want to know about whatever happened to their characters. The only thing I know is that you'd be working behind France's liberation via Atlantic Wall behind of the lines, providing covert-ops---quite like Splinter Cell used to do. Game is unusually doing that in the 40s era.

Voice acting is formidable though. Main character Karl is voiced by Tom Clarke Hill (from Tony the tiger cornflakes), and the man is very good at it. Lois Chimimba voices Charlie, instantly removing the boring cliche of "damsel" straight to a bad-ass girl. The list goes.

There is a co-op mode (it's more fun with friends), counter-coop or player invasion (if you allow it) and there is a survival mode and classic multiplayer. Expect a lot of DLC trying to cash-in after your buy, but none are really that needed unless you want to extend the game's shelve life and play some more.

I expected to be more impressed with the graphics. At least sound effects and music are great and enjoyable.

[code]HISTORICAL ACCURACY SCORE: 5/10[/code]

The devs used "Photogrammetry" of objects and locations to make it realistic. However... expect some WW2 fantasy here and there. Some aren't exactly false, such as secret technologies like the "subsonic ammo" (that won't whistle as much) or TNT packed like C-4, certain vehicles and other prototype equipment back in the 1944s. A few inaccurate or disarranged things, but it won't cross as much as Wolfenstein does. 

It's just Hollywood, Gamewood. I'm reporting this in case people still wonder about the era.

[h1]Be advised before embarking[/h1]

A game about elite precision got some faulty bits. You might need to give it a chance.

Stealth won't always keep the stance if you're toggled into it. When crouching, Karl stands up when activating something like when opening a door. It can get to be a nuisance after some time. Should be opening doors slowly when crouching, like Splinter Cell used to do.

You'll see cutscenes with Karl holding a specific gun you're not equipped with, in positions the cutscenes never moves to, then resuming gameplay out of it. Lack of polishing maybe, or just not very good a that I don't know. After I presume to be a glitch, special ammo disappeared and I had to relocate it back to my SREM-1 rifle... bad for a tactical game where every little move you do can mean victory or defeat.

When playing harder difficulty I stressed the game and saw some AI bugs and other glitches. Had to reload the game to get rid of it.

[b]2) Too modern on HUD, alerts, challenges and screen related[/b]

The very idea of bullet cams (showing the bullet path and penetration) and cinematic takedowns is awesome, but also too modern for something playing 1944. But... You can turn it off in the options---also the useless x-ray deaths. Despise that effect, enemy models won't be all blown up. There is no actual gore out of the x-ray.

I nicknamed gaming as "outward" and "inward" to define the world focus when reviewing Watch Dogs 2 years ago.

Games like Tomb Raider 2013 got attention to details closer to a center, so the world might look harder to reach and the main character more detailed. That's the "inward" type.

The "outward" types are usually games wider to the sides. They tend to lose details around the character, focusing in the open world and making it lighter. Some games mixes both, such as GTA V that leans more to outward than GTA IV so the world was a bit easier to reach. RDR2 is the only one that had the guts to mix extremes, mega detailed and inward in a wide open world.

review_text:
Compared to its predecessor, Sniper Elite 5 takes some steps forward but also some steps back.

The sniping gameplay we all love from the franchise is back. Shooting from a distance while staying hidden and managing your ammo types feels great, now with even more improvements. For instance, you don't get "suppressed rounds" as early, forcing you to get used to other ammo types first. Even when you do get them, their silence depends on your gun's specific range. Measuring that distance becomes a vital tactical component. To help with this, there is now a HUD notification showing if an enemy is within range to hear your shot. Just like in Sniper Elite 4, the enemy AI is unironic a masterpiece in how they engage you as a team. I also liked the new X-ray kills with more detailed muscle tissue.

However, my biggest complaint is how enemies are distributed across the maps. They are often concentrated in specific areas, making it extremely hard to kill everyone stealthily. I even suspect they keep respawning, which sucks if you like to fully clear an area.

There is also a flaw in the new Axis Invasion mode. Don't get me wrong: letting another player infiltrate your level to hunt you down creates some awesome, tense moments. The problem is that if you eliminate an invader, instead of the mode ending, another player can immediately join your session. If this happens repeatedly, it completely ruins your stealth run. Ultimately, the constant interruptions become annoying, which is a shame for such a great idea. That’s why I ended up disabling the mode after the first encounter in every mission.

Aside from the campaign, there are match-based PvP modes, which I personally didn't like because the core elements of Sniper Elite don't translate well there. However, beside the main story mode, the Survival mode is a highlight. It feels more rewarding to complete a map on the first try now, while still remaining challenging.

In the end, if you liked Sniper Elite 4, can enjoy the levels without needing to kill every single enemy, and want to test the new Axis mode, you'll like this one too.

review_text:
Short Version:
This game is a heavily watered down experience compared to previous entries. If you are looking at getting into Sniper Elite as a franchise do not start with this. Start with V2, 3, or 4. They only get better as you go on from V2. I really hope they cook hard for Sniper Elite 6 when/if it comes out. This game is a pretty heavy departure in style from the previous entries and that is, in my opinion, to it's detriment.

Long Version:
This game feels like an overall regression for the series. 

The 5 biggest issues are:

1. Map Size/Enemy Population
2. Overall Level Design (and lack of sniping as a result)
3. Mechanical Regression (items, movement, etc.)
4. Non-Lethal Options
5. Extremely lacking difficulty options

The maps are far too big with far too little enemies. I found myself out loud questioning "only X number of guards here?" or "where are the enemies?" during missions. I'm to believe this is the height of the occupation of France during WW2 but it feels like the Germans just left some stragglers behind for me to pick off. This severely hampers the experience even on the hardest difficulties and ruins believability of the setting. Many have thrown around that this is to improve the performance on previous gen consoles. Screw previous gen consoles, maps should not be 150% the size of Sniper Elite 4's maps with 50% of it's population. And they also boasted that the maps are recreations of real life locations in France, which leads into my next point...

The level design has regressed. There are really only two standout maps, and all the rest feel worse than Sniper Elite 4 and even Sniper Elite 3. V2 can't really be compared with it's very linear nature. The maps were "faithful recreations" of real French locations during occupation. This does not mean they function well as video game levels. There are tons of invisible walls, random blocks to seemingly clear routes, and terrain that looks to be climbable but isn't for some reason. They had the formula down for the previous entry, where you make a good level first and then make it looks like it could really exists afterwards. The main detriment of all of this is the severe lack of long range sniping in most levels. The previous games had strong sniping positions (often called Sniper Nests or power positions) all throughout the levels with clear sight lines and advantages like sound masking and cover. This game has some but they very rarely give you good sight lines or just straight up block half the map with trees and bushes to prevent you from getting more than maybe 4 or 5 kills. This forces very pistol/secondary-heavy close range gameplay which really should not be the focus. 

In that same vein the mechanical complexity just feels dumbed down. Weapon customization is cool, map tools like bolt cutters and crowbars are neat, and new ammo types are fun, But they also removed a lot. Various mines were removed, rocks were replaced with inferior bottles, the skill point system is very dumb, and the biggest downgrade is movement. Movement feels clunkier, and I don't know how they did it but maybe it's the engine? Button prompts are often delayed when interacting with things, the player character frequently gets out of sneak mode when interacting or finishing interacting with thing, and they removed crouch sprinting. Why would you remove the ability to sneak a bit faster when your maps are 150% bigger. I know it sounds like a nitpick but it's such a downgrade in practical gameplay. Also binocular tagging is just annoying now, where instead of clicking what you want to tag you have to hold over it for a little bit. This is annoying and results in both accidental tags, which you can't remove unlike previous games, and constant missed tags. It used to be if I sniped an officer I could mark his corpse to find later for that sweet Duty Roster, but don't worry they also removed Duty Rosters too. I don't care about the invasion mode they added. I'm not about PVP, nor about harming people trying to do single player content. And I am ESPECIALLY not about playing as a Nazi. I play these games to kill Nazis, not be one. Speaking of which...

They added non-lethal options. This should be self explanatory. Your enemies are Nazis. I don't care if they have funny little info popups when you tag them, or if they're humans just like you and me. They are Nazis. I don't think there is a more universal enemy possible, it's practically family friendly fun to kill them. This is not Metal Gear Solid, you are not gonna be haunted by ghosts or grow devil horns. They are Nazis, kill them. Schu mines are dumb, wooden bullets are ESPECIALLY dumb, and when enemies are injured and laying on the ground dying of blood loss they should "BLEED OUT" like every previous entry and not be "INCAPACITATED" like in this one. Don't gimme a chart at the end and act like I'm a good little sniper for "sparing" some enemies on the map. If I saw em, if I knew they were breathing, I'd have killed them without a second damn thought. Kill Nazis. End of story. 

Lastly this is a minor point for me personally, but some dedicated members of the community really care about it. Difficulty options are lacking compared to previous entries. Beyond having too few enemies they are also less diverse and less difficult. And they also removed Authentic Plus. Why? I don't personally do super hard challenges, but for the significant part of the community that does this is a major detriment. Authentic overall is much easier too according to said part of the community. Bring it back or at least add custom difficulty sliders for people. 

Overall, if you want to get into this series please don't start with this one. I really tried my best to like this game, and it's still *fine* as a game, but when compared to it's predecessors it falls flat. If you still want to try it for yourself please get it at a discount somehow.

Well, let me give a thumbs up on a thumbs flat game, just because it doesn't deserve a thumbs down. You who have played other SE games know the drill: the old recipe where a single man saves the world. When it comes to plot, that's it, and nothing more. 
It's not an open world game neither a linear one, I'd say it's a linear open world, cause you can't go from A to B following the path you choose, as you won't pass through certain obstacles, even if they are a simple hedge or similar, thus you are forced to follow this or that path to achieve areas of interest, but are free to complete objectives in any order. 
But gameplay is good. Indeed. You find yourself immersed, for sure, with beautiful graphics, good sound and satisfying kills or stealth knock outs. Despite being repetitive (like 99% of games I've played in my long, long life), it's rewarding to stop, think and tackle that objective without being noticed, or sabotage a generator to mask your rifle noise and perform kills from a long distance. Moreover, it's very well optimized, without a single frame drop and no crashes.
As I never play anything multiplayer anymore, cause I'm an old man who can't compete with the kids, can't say anything about this part of the game. 
Have a good one, you all.

[h1] Sniper Elite 5: Changing for Changes Sake [/h1]

[i] "For every one step forward, it takes 15 back" [/i]

Its not the worst game ever played, but the longer I played it,
 the less and less it felt like a sniper elite game, 
and I yearned for some of the action from the 4th game.

        Let's start off with the pricing.  Which is a slight recurring issue with this title.
On sale, that's not a bad price for the base game,
but I wouldn't recommend this game for full sale price due to all the shady DLC practices.
So if you are wanting to try this game, definitely get it on sale!

       Graphically speaking, the game ain't too shabby, 
but my biggest issues have to be the U.I.
the game models and the sniping hud.

Something about Karls re-design just seems . ..  off.
Its mainly his facial features and head proportions.
He looks like he's aged 20 years LESS than the previous installment.
Like he's a fresh recruit straight out of training, but due to his unfortunate character design he looks to be in his late 40s at the same time.

The reason this is off putting a bit is because it's jarring to see the great voice actor for 'em
not fit the character model. Which begs the question, 

Why change it?

I get updating a model for  a new engine is to be considered, but tampering with the design like this doesn't paint a good look.

As for the U.I mentioned earlier, I'm getting sub-familiar battlefield 1 vibes, which isn't
ideal considering we are playing a SNIPER ELITE game and not a DICE game.
The old U.I. was fine, maybe polish a few corners here n' there, but this is just kinda meh.

The sniper scope hud, however,  has to be the biggest offender here by far.
The handling on the scope feels very snappy, like it's a fast paced tactical FPS multiplayer instead of a strategic, calculated sniper shot.

The breath holding mechanic has been tampered to adhere to this "snappiness" so it suffers just as much.

Add in that they misled the enemy tagging function from before, and it plays out more like a frantic paranoia-filled game of hit or miss whats shootin at you from a bush (or 2 feet away from you) instead of a clean, decisive sniper kill.

These tweaks don't really improve anything from the last title, instead, they change 'em' almost as if they could. This also has the added negative of souring the games artstyle.

The previous title was  [b] VIBRANT! [/b]
Lush, green forests, haunting corridors, beaming sunny Italian countryside and villages.

Here? Dark, mute, cold, rainy rainy, dark/cold, rainy-rainy. 
 Ive never seen a wet environment  that left me so dry.


Speaking of environments  . . .


What is going on here? What can I jump over? What can I [u] NOT [/u]  jump over?
With the previous title, scalable boundaries and obstacles were fairly imperative.
Right of the bat, sniper elite 4 clearly tells you what is and isn't on the table to climb.

In  SE5, because the maps are over-detailed with fluff, the high quality texture models may look neat, but it doesn't do anything for gameplay reinforcement.
It would be like modeling the notre-dame for a video game to insane detail, but forget to add proper attention to the players pertinent interaction with it.

Why make a playground that I cant play on?

This becomes more of an issue with arguably the most important selling point of this game: 

[b] THE ACTUAL SNIPING! [/b]

Masking is another reason, mainly the lack of masking your sniper shots and more importantly, where you can mask them as well.

elite 4 dropped implied yet [u] subtle  [/u] hints on areas where you could snipe and how to go about it masked. Not to mention the very easy to understand masking U.I. that gave the quick heads up that your shots where being masked and its distinguishable sounds.
Obvious things like Explosive traps, crates, engines, grenades, barrels, trucks, could all be used in creative ways  for a clever undetected chain kill like a michael bay/ mona lisa amalgamation, 

but there were also little interesting random masks like the planes flying overhead or cannons firing in the background to spice things up where you could utilize it for an on-the-spot kill if you were versatile enough.  

Not here, the masking mechanic is poorly explained and implemented in SE5 so half the time I  kinda just gave up using it! Out of all the levels I played, I really only truly did a good sniping run about 3-5 times give or take, whereas most of the time I kinda just had to lightly skirmish ducked behind a box for cover.


     For the weapons, the choice isn't terrible, 
but there's alot going on here that raises some concerns.

For starters, why cant Karl pickup ammo for guns he picks up? Hell, why cant he KEEP the guns he picks up or even choose them in the start menu?!
Seriously, why change this mechanic that worked fine as it was in the previous title?
If it was for "historical accuracy" (which is laughable given what I'm soon to bring up next)
given the main protagonist's reputation and previous  experience [b] it feels like they just changed it just cause they could. [/b]

[h1] Also, WHY THE F*CK WOULD I WANT TO USE NON-LETHAL AMMO ON NAZIS?[/h1],

The result? You're forced to stick to a [i] verrrry [/i] slim selection of base weapons and the lack of ammo retention drives out interest in trying out new guns, 
[b] because you kinda cant! [/b]

Call me crazy, but if I was  a game dev, I'd want to encourage my players to try out and experiment with all the cool weapons I added instead of  . . . putting. . . them  . . . behind a paywall---[i] OOoooooooh [/i] 

aaaaaand [b]thats[/b] why you shouldn't pay full price for this game, 
because alot of the content is locked behind a paywall for DLC.



      Now, when it comes to the weapon mod system in this game, its . . . fine.

The minor problems lies in the execution of it in terms of it being kinda dry due to limited and minuet, poignant attachment selections.

Major issue? 

[h3] HISTORICAL INACCURACY ! [/h3]

Im not even a major WW2 spoof, but dear god, they didn't try with alot of this crap.
The game as a whole has this problem, but the guns suffer most from this because the modifications are so far stretched and egrigious its very hard to take the game seriously even remotely because of how outlandish it is.

The final product just feels contrived and forced in.


Collectibles suffer too in this installment for a variety of reasons.

Things like replacing the rock  with a bottle, for distractions
which  have to be restocked. 
Why? 
Again, the character in this franchise knows how to pick up a F*cking rock for christ's sake, did he just forget?
Alot of the misled mechanics suffer from this reoccurring  issue and it's kinda off putting,
even if you are new to this series, cause it logically doesnt make sense lol.

ALL Items have to be manually picked up now too, which doesn't sound too bad, but its a slight irk considering the previous title understood you'd want as much munitions and items as possible because there no need to manage it.
Maybe [i] meticulously [/i] picking up each and every item YOU KNOW YOU NEED is more enjoyable?

For some games, this makes sense, there may be an item you don't wanna bother with, but for a game like this where inventory management is unnecessary ,
 its rather useless.  [b] It feels like they changed it just cause they could [/b] 

[h2] OVERALL VERDICT [/h2]

Once its all put together, or the lack thereof, the feeling I get boils down to;

I'm playing a worse version of sniper elite 4.

If Rebellion was just trying to stick to their bread and butter, just make another 
[u] improved [/u] version of sniper elite 4.

[i]OR[/i]

Do something different with this installment and not a rehash of other franchises.
Don't screw with the old and poorly implement the new and 
serve me your EXACT same formula that's slightyworse than the last.

If you are new to this franchise, I highly recommend sniper elite 4 instead.
You'll have a much better time in my opinion.

I've never been the biggest Sniper/Shooters enthusiast growing up, but after being a little burnt from my very long first playthrough of BG3, I fancied diving into new territory. I first started with Sniper Elite 4, and I had such a wonderful time with that game. And then proceeded to buy Sniper Elite 5 straight after. 

I know the general consensus is that Sniper Elite 5 isn't held as high as the previous entry, but I'm actually on the opposite spectrum. SE5 has kept me glued consistently from start to finish across 3 seperate runs. Currently nearing the end of my Authentic run, and this game has to be the most rewarding Sniper/stealth games I've played. 

Rebellion has nailed the formula for the series, with a few minor step backs here eg No trip mines, no crouch sprint and less varied map design, but some of the more enhanced gameplay improvements make up for it. Gun customisation is here, stealth is improved, and even 2nd or 3rd primary weapons feel punchier and satisfying than ever. 

For anyone starting a first run, I'd highly recommend going Sniper Elite difficulty first and turning empty lung assist to minimal to remove the red diamond aid. This game will having you coming back once you start to slowly master your shots and gauging winds and bullet drop.

review_text:
Overall it's still a fun entry, but feels somewhat confused. SE4 still felt like a Sniper Elite game that also happened to improve enough of the stealth mechanics to be played like a stealth game as a bonus. Comparatively, 5 feels like a stealth game that just happens to have Sniper Elite mechanics. That may not sound like a bad thing on paper, but it means I was looking at the stealth mechanics with more scrutiny and a lot of them feel very frivolous. Like, Rebellion just looked at a bunch of other stealth games over the past few years and went, "Oh yeah, add that in there," for the sake of it (MGSV probably being the biggest one).

The inclusion of a non-lethal playstyle sort of embodies the feeling of adding mechanics for the sake of having them. I'm usually not one to balk at more player choice in a stealth game, but in here it mechanically does not serve a purpose. You get LESS XP for knocking somebody out than using a lethal takedown (unless you intend to kill the enemy right after), both takedown types are quiet, you don't have to worry about something like a blood trail coming out of a corpse if relocating a body, and a patrolling enemy finding a body unconscious is identical to finding them dead (they'll check the body and become partially alerted). There are a lot of opportunities Rebellion could've taken to make non-lethal an actual ideal option depending on enemy layouts (have enemies immediately go for an alarm if they see a dead body, make lethal takedowns loud, etc.) and they took none of them. And of course narratively speaking (I know, it's Sniper Elite, who cares, shut up), it just doesn't make much sense at all because 5 takes place after 3 and 4. Karl has a corpse pile of god knows how many Nazis and fascists under his belt at this point in the war, why would he care now?

Also the levels in 5 are much larger than 4 which isn't a bad thing on its own, but it just makes it stick out incredibly hard when Karl is incapable of moving through invisible walls portrayed by bushes or a wall he should be very capable of mantling, because the developers wanted the player to go through more intended routes.

Still, at the end of the day, it's more Sniper Elite fun, if diluted a little ironically because of them attempting to add new features. The new Invasion mode at the very least is an actual fun inclusion that adds newfound tension that normally wouldn't be in the game otherwise.

Well this was a really pleasant surprise. This is the most fun I’ve had in a stealth/action game for years. It reminded me a lot of Hidden & Dangerous 2 for some reason, but without the bugs.

As far as I can recall, I’ve only played the 1st one and can’t quite remember if I ended up completing it, but remember really liking it at the time, which is why I picked this one up on a recent sale (I just realised that I also purchased SE3 on a sale in 2017 but never played it for some reason).

The graphics in the game are absolutely stunning, with the developers delivering an outstanding job on the environments. Each area you encounter is visually distinct, offering a lot of variety as you progress. Although there are only eight main missions, most of them are very large and provide a great deal of gameplay flexibility, allowing for different approaches and tactics. There are also optional and hidden objectives, and there are numerous paths available through each map, which will probably be ideal for subsequent plays.

I played most of the game using stealth, blackjacking/stabbing enemies and snipering key enemies from afar. It wasn't until mid game or so that I started experimenting more with the various tools and equipment, targeting groups of enemies, environmental hazards, and vehicles. During these moments, some limitations of the game’s AI became apparent. While the AI is generally solid and has clearly been adjusted to be forgiving (making stealth more enjoyable without requiring constant save-scumming) they can remain on high alert for an extended period after being triggered. Sometimes, the alert status persists almost indefinitely, especially if a soldier discovers a new dead body or another suspicious event, which can prolong the alert phase even further.

The story is a standard WW2 plot, adequate but not memorable, so I skipped most cutscenes.

Sniper Elite 5 is a powerful, methodical, meticulously crafted stealth shooter that confronts the player not with routine firefights, but with sweeping trials of character. There’s something here of Barry Pepper’s icy sprint in Saving Private Ryan, and something of that predatory silence in the ruins of Stalingrad from Enemy at the Gates—moments when the very landscape becomes an adversary. This is a game that refuses to let you relax, even for a heartbeat.

Each mission unfolds like a new act in a grand wartime production, staged with an almost documentary devotion to the era. The locations are unique, diverse, and unforgiving in their own elegant ways.

You’ll navigate coastal fortifications where the wind claws sound into shreds, and where every fold of terrain turns into a natural rampart or trap.
You’ll move through French manors with shaded avenues and cold stone walls, behind which patrols, spotlights, and hidden routes are woven into a dark, intricate tapestry.
You’ll infiltrate industrial districts where metal sings at the touch of the wind, and where the maze of warehouses and workshops operates like a multi-layered chessboard—one in which verticality matters as much as the horizontal plane.
You’ll descend into ancient fortresses wrapped in heavy historical silence, where each corridor resembles the throat of a beast, and the shadows whisper of those who walked there before you.
You’ll operate within coastal towns where promenades echo with distant footsteps, and where wealthy homes and narrow alleyways form a geometry of risk, refuge, and endless tactical permutations.

This is a world where the horizon is layered, where each hill is an opportunity, every tower a point of power, and every sound a potential fuse to your undoing.

In Sniper Elite 5, missions are not tasks—they are wide, branching meadows of decisions.
Your entry point, your exit route, your elevation, pacing, distance—everything belongs to you. The game seems to whisper, “Choose your path. Choose your rhythm. See how far you’re willing to go.”
They’re vast as a river in flood, yet precise and clockwork in their internal logic.

Playing on the highest difficulty becomes its own form of self-awareness.
Distance turns into a philosophical variable.
Wind becomes a fluctuation of fate.
A bullet becomes your signature under a decision you cannot retract.
Any step may be your last—yet it’s this fragility that creates the sense of truth. You feel every second, every breath, as if you were not in a game but in someone else’s war, compelled to see it through.

Sniper Elite 5 possesses a rare quality: it fuses you with your character.
With every mission you begin to feel the weight of the rifle, the cold edge of the scope beneath your fingers, the dry crackle of grass beneath your elbow. You start breathing in sync with this world—its winds, its echoes, its danger. And at some point, almost imperceptibly, you realize: you are no longer just playing.
You’ve stepped onto that terrible page of history where everything—absolutely everything—hinges on a single, solitary shot.
