Rating: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (9/10)

🎨 A Sharpshooter’s Evolution
Sniper Elite 5 feels like the point where the series finally steps into its prime. Rebellion takes everything that’s worked across the franchise — the tension, the open-ended missions, the glorious X-ray kills — and elevates it into one of the most polished sniping experiences to date. It’s not just another entry; it’s the series hitting a confident stride, refined and razor-sharp.

🎮 Gameplay
Core Experience:
Every mission feels like a sandbox built specifically for creativity. Multiple infiltration routes, detailed maps, and dynamic enemy patrols give you the freedom to play like a ghost in the shadows or a long-range executioner perched hundreds of meters away. And when that bullet leaves the barrel? The impact is still unmatched. The X-ray cam remains brutal, cinematic, and endlessly satisfying.

Mechanics & Feel:
Movement is smoother, stealth feels more flexible, and weapon customization adds a depth that earlier games only hinted at. Compared to Sniper Ghost Warrior or older Sniper Elite titles, the AI is smarter and the levels feel alive. Every adjustment — wind, distance, timing — contributes to that perfect shot, and the game makes each one feel worth the setup.

❤️ For Fans of the Long Shot
Having played Sniper Elite games, Sniper Ghost Warrior, and even Zombie Army, this one feels like a culmination of everything I’ve loved across those series. The precision of Ghost Warrior, the creativity of Zombie Army’s action moments, and the classic Elite tactical charm all show up here — but more polished, more ambitious, and more confident. It’s familiar in the best way, yet fresh enough to stand out.

📊 A Beautiful, Brutal Battlefield
The environments are some of the best the series has seen — lush countryside, fortified bunkers, sprawling villages — all crafted with detail and purpose. Performance is steady, the sound design pops with tension, and the soundtrack walks the line between subtle and dramatic. It all supports the core fantasy: being a lone marksman shaping the battlefield from afar.

Final Verdict:
Sniper Elite 5 is an awesome game — a near-perfect blend of stealth, tactical shooting, and satisfying sniping. It raises the bar for the series, delivering both nostalgia and innovation in a single clean shot. For anyone who’s followed sniping games over the years, this one feels like the reward for sticking with the genre.

I wasn’t expecting it to be as good as it is. As a long time Hitman fan, this was superb. I had never played the fourth entry before, though I went through the first three, which were solid but lacked the incredible environmental design found here. Some of these missions have the best layouts I’ve ever played, and the third mission genuinely stunned me. It hooked me the same way Hitman does making me want to revisit each location to explore it more thoroughly, since I usually don’t the first time around. The level layouts make sense, and the scale is absolutely impressive. The freedom to approach objectives in multiple ways really enhances the experience, making each mission unique which was awesome might I add and coming from the third game that surprised me.

The gunplay is excellent the sniping feels impactful, and the iconic kill cam is as satisfying as ever. Its just the medium range that lacks finesse so usually the best option is either close up or long range which suits the game and guns ablazing is possible but not without the right loadout. The ability to customize weapons is always appreciated and my god are there a lot of options available to you, even a testing range to try out your combinations, and you will want to replay missions to unlock new weapons since only a limited amount of armaments are available from the beginning. However, it’s not without flaws. The story is your usual fan fare and characters aren’t particularly strong they mostly serve as background for the gameplay. The AI can be inconsistent, sometimes reacting unrealistically, and there are moments where close quarters combat overshadows the sniping focus. All in all, it’s much better than I expected, and I’d wholeheartedly recommend everyone give it a try especially since it’s often available at a steep discount.

[b]Intro[/b]

Sniper Elite 5 is a third person shooter in which you explore medium-large sized locations and kill fascists. You can be stealthy, shooty or anything in between.

For comparison: [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/anarchistica/recommended/312660?snr=1_5_9__402]my review of Sniper Elite 4[/url].

- Shoot Nazis, steal the letters they wrote for their families.

- The best "kill Hitler" mission so far.
- Really nice locations.
- Bigger and better maps.
- Improved weapon unlock system, no more "kill X over Y meters with a SMG" stuff.
- Still the same goofy stuff about Wunderwaffles.
- Amusing special ways to deal with kill list targets.
- Expanded skill system is a big improvement.

[b]The Bad[/b]

- They should've made it so XP can be used for weapon unlocks.
- Selling a single pistol as DLC for €4 is gross.
- A few cosmetics locked behind PVP.

[b]Conclusion[/b]

SE5 isn't as big a leap forward as previous games but honestly, there isn't that much they could do better. If you like brutally murdering Nazis you'll love this.

review_text:
At the 5th instalment of the series, they've really nailed this one — it's EXCELLENT! Each new version slightly refines their formula! From the signature slo-mo snipe kill cam, to the fine-grained and customizable control set up, to the audio and visuals... This is easily the best Sniper Elite yet. And yes, I've played them all. For a laid back sneaky "dad" shooter it ticks all the boxes.

The maps are gorgeous, the guns feel great and the replayability is good with the invasion mode where you can (optionally) let a single human opponent play against you as a counter sniper. Very clever.

The biggest criticism I have is really that the game on the easy side. If you are even a little bit familiar with shooters, my tip for you is to play on AUTHENTIC difficulty right from the start which removes some of the most egregious assists (cheats). Like overly accurate sniping assists which takes the challenge out of sniping by making it too easy; and 'focus mode' which is basically wall hacking where you can see enemies through walls. It's a third person shooter which already lets you corner peek by design. So even without the x-ray vision it's still easy to sneak around. If you liked the previous games, you will probably like this one. I enjoyed SE4, so I am enjoying SE5. 

That said, For a game that is supposed to be all about being a sniper, this game seems to discourage actually sniping. More so than the previous game.

But the way levels are designed in this game so far (I am doing 4th mission at the moment) you do not get many opportunities to actually play a sniper. It feels a lot easier and more natural to play close combat stealth style where you crawl around, hide around corners and backstab people or use a silenced pistol.

There are mechanics in game intended to make sniping easier, like sabotaging cars and generators to make noise to cover your shots. But these feel both contrived and inconvenient. Using them feels like a waste of time and breaks suspension of disbelief more than it should.

Like sure, I could rig a car to start making noise. Then run away and wait for the enemy investigation to be over. Watch the enemies fiddle with the car and then go away without shutting it down or fixing it. Then come back to the car and take a few shots using the noise for cover. But it is a whole lot quicker and easier to just go full stealth mode and just knife everyone.

In the last game most levels involved large open spaces where you could always find some remote and elevated position where you could then carefully pick your shots and clear up a lot of enemies the way a sniper character would. In this game, so far, pretty much every level involves narrow streets and enclosed spaces and too many enemies to use your sniper rifle safely. 

Still, I like stealth games and as far as stealth games go this one is not bad. Just don't feel like a sniper most of the time.

[h1]🎯 Sniper Elite 5 — Friends, Foes & The Art of the Perfect Headshot[/h1]  

There’s something special about *Sniper Elite 5*. It’s not just the x-ray kill cams (though let’s be honest — they’re still disgustingly satisfying). It’s the way this game manages to be both a tactical sandbox and a social experiment in friendship.  

[h2]🎮 Co-op: Two Snipers, One Brain[/h2]  
Playing with a friend is pure joy. Coordinating shots, silently clearing out enemy outposts, or accidentally alerting the entire Wehrmacht because someone “thought it was a silencer” — it’s chaos in the best possible way. Every mission feels like a co-op puzzle that rewards patience and teamwork, but still leaves room for those perfect moments of panic and laughter.  

[h2]💀 The Invasion Mode: Friendship... Terminated[/h2]  
Then there’s *Invasion Mode*. You sneak into someone else’s campaign as the enemy sniper — their personal nemesis. Maybe they’re strangers. Maybe they’re “friends.” Either way, you get to test how strong that friendship really is as you patiently stalk them from the shadows, waiting for that one shot that will make them scream “NOOO!” in voice chat. It’s cruel, thrilling, and absurdly fun.  

[h2]⚙️ The Gameplay Feel[/h2]  
Gunplay feels weighty and satisfying, and the level design is fantastic — open, detailed, and full of opportunities to improvise. Sometimes it’s stealth perfection, other times it’s chaos incarnate. Either way, it never gets old hearing that slow-motion *crack* of a successful shot echo through the French countryside.  

[h2]🏁 Verdict[/h2]  
Sniper Elite 5 nails the mix of precision, tension, and humor. It’s great solo, amazing in co-op, and absolutely *evil* when you’re invading. Whether you’re a tactical perfectionist or an agent of chaos, this game gives you endless ways to make memories — or end friendships.  

[b]8.5/10 — A headshot to the heart.[/b]

Sniper Elite 5 is easily one of the most satisfying tactical shooters I’ve played in years. Rebellion really nailed the formula this time, it’s not just about pulling off slow-mo headshots (though those are as brutal and cinematic as ever), but about the freedom and creativity in how you approach every mission.

The maps are absolutely massive and beautifully detailed. Each location feels alive and encourages exploration, whether you’re sneaking through the French countryside, sabotaging enemy lines, or setting up the perfect sniping perch. The open-ended design means you can tackle objectives in countless ways: stealthy infiltration, loud assaults, or clever traps. It’s up to you.

The gunplay feels fantastic. Every shot carries weight, and watching that iconic X-Ray kill cam never gets old, especially when you pull off a 300-meter headshot through the wind. Weapon customization is also deeper than before, letting you tune your rifles exactly to your playstyle.

Co-op and invasion modes add a ton of replayability. Playing through the campaign with a friend is a blast, and the invasion mechanic (where another player can hunt you down mid-mission) keeps things intense and unpredictable.

Performance-wise, the game runs smoothly and looks great, realistic lighting, crisp environments, and attention to historical details that make each mission feel authentic.

Overall, Sniper Elite 5 is a must-play for anyone who enjoys tactical shooters, stealth gameplay, or the satisfaction of perfectly planned shots. It rewards patience, strategy, and precision, and makes every mission feel like your own handcrafted story.

review_text:
I can see why some might prefer SE4, but it's still a good game.

Gunplay is much improved here, and the maps are designed much more realistically. However, that means that things like convenient vantage points and sniping-focused gameplay are somewhat discounted in favour of a more pedestrian and often loud approach. -It's often quicker and more effective, as the character is surprisingly resilient even in max difficulty settings. 

The inclusion of non-lethal takedown options is entirely pointless, since the guards won't react to blood splatters or missing personnel whatsoever. General alarm is also disappointingly easy to manage, as the enemies will never flank, converge, or make any effort to flush you out. You could camp a spot and snipe them to your convenience, or just leave unseen after an alert was triggered, and things would go back to normal pretty quick. Heck, if you got shot down and managed to revive yourself unseen, the alert state reverts to normal as if nothing happened; Nobody bothers confirming your supposed death, so you can walk away and revert to killing. Moreover, the game lets you quicksave to your liking even at max difficulty settings, so there's no reason to be proactive in stealth, like in some other games.

Speaking of stealth, the game fails to properly convey the state of your visibility, which is problematic when enemy awareness range is as big as it is at max difficulty. Like, it almost feels inconsistent. It used to be that shaded = cloaked, but now only taking cover behind objects makes a difference. This is a degraded experience over SE4 (and SE1 for that matter), as there's no reason to go prone in SE5. Like, mechanically, stealth feels half-baked relatively to older instalments. So much so, that I mostly relied on pistol and melee kills. 

Things I'd like to see in the future include RNG elements in both mission design and map design, as well as enemy placements, in order to increase replayability, challenge and variance. Additionally, I'd like to see deterministic choices that affect the next mission (as in support received, enemy intel etc), and I'd also like to see incentives for engaging enemies at greater ranges, as most occurred in the <50m spectrum and did not offer any significant challenge, largely due to NPC intelligence. And for the love of God, tone down scope flares, or at least make it proportional to the shade they are in or the magnification capabilities.

Infiltrating heavily occupied enemy positions, with a focus on sniping, shouldn't feel like a walk in the park, but it often does in SE5. It's a good sniper game that I very much enjoyed. But it's not a great Sniper Elite game.

I like the expansive maps, but the game seems to favor a Solid Snake stealth play style compared to an "elite" sniper. To clarify, you can spend a majority of the game using only your pistol for stealth compared to your rifle. As expansive as the maps are, I felt there was little to no opportunities to utilize your rifle to take out key enemies that may hinder your progress. I think its partly why you have the option to use nonlethal ammo for both weapons as the maps lack many vehicles and generators that mask your kills or take downs. 

The weapon modification did have potential, but many of the attachments feel unrealistic for the period or don't mesh well with the guns. It would have been interesting to see mastery milestones that accurately reflect variations of the base guns. For example, if you completed long range kills with the Luger, you'd unlock the artillery barrel. If the Lebel was added, completing a series of kills under a specific range would unlock the R35 variant that was reserved for second-line troops. 

There's little to no military vehicles found compared to previous titles like SE: 4. I would have loved to have seen French light tanks repurposed by the German army that roamed the map, particularly for dedicated transportation roles. Or the very least, see remnants of these vehicles from previous engagements before the area shifted occupation. 

What's more disappointing is that a majority of the weapons are mission locked around middle to late game. So, you can't mix and match varying weaponry over the course of the campaign. A prime example would be the RSC 1917 being locked at mission 7. Furthermore, when you find out that SE: Resistance has a wider range of French weaponry with the game costing the same price as SE: 5, you question why it wasn't added as an expansion for the base game or why SE: Resistance exists at all. 

I'm deeply saddened the series is stagnating with the developers seemingly rushing newer titles, while pushing predatory micro-transactions through poor DLC content with a price that goes beyond justification.

[h1] I love this series but this is a step back from Sniper Elite 4[/h1]
[h2] The Bad Changes[/h2]

[olist]
    
[*]The game is way too easy, even on Authentic Plus.

[*]Killcams is a downgrade from SE4 as SE4's killcams are more detailed—i.e. you can see the organs you shot through and also the enter and exit wounds.

[*]Bullet and wind physics barely matter as it’s too simple to line up shots using the range finder and wind gauge in the scope.

[*]Aim assist is useless since you can just trace where the bullet will go using the range finder and wind gauge in the scope.

[*]Map design feels restrictive, removing the freedom and creativity SE4 had.

[*]Long-range vantage points are blocked, which defeats the purpose of being a sniper.

[*]It feels like the devs focused too much on close-quarters combat instead of the sniping that defines the series.
[/olist]
[h2]The Good Stuff[/h2]
[olist]
[*]Secondary weapons actually feel useful now especially the SMGs, spraing is viable now since guns have a tighter spread and reliable performance in CQC and mid-range fights.

[*]Ragdoll physics are more realistic than SE4's floaty ragdolls.

[*]Invasion Mode is a fun way to add challenge after gearing up. When it works, the cat-and-mouse PvP element of Invasion is intense and I find it fun. But it needs to be balanced as the enemies are either more geared up than you or they are cheating.
[/olist]

Enjoyable entry to the Sniper Elite francize. Just some fairly minor improvements over Sniper Elite 4 and some downgrades and otherwise same thing everybody knows at this point. 

[h3] Gameplay [/h3]

Basic combat and level mechanics have been carried over from 4. Main addition is new upgrade system, where player finds workbenches that enable new weapon parts. My feelings on this addition are kinda mixed - aside from resulting creations being vomit inducing ugly ability to slap suppressor onto anything makes mechanics like sabotaging generators next to useless. 

On the other hand as I play on Authentic difficulty setting it makes the sniper rifles somewhat usable. Same couldn't be said for Sniper Elite 4 where I've spend most of my time running around with pistol or stabbing people as using rifle would alter everyone to my position. Especially as without the stupid aimbot hold breath mechanics hitting on first shot often wasn't given. 

What I certainly don't like is how they have ruined the sound detection system. We went from the insanity of SE3 where if you even dared to dash 5 meters enemies would hear you trough 3 meters of walls and 20 meters of open air to SE5 where most Germans are deaf. It's to such a degree that even when I deliberately want to alter enemies to my position I can't - stomping around a stop and whistling does nothing. 

All these changes combined leads to SE being the easiest entry I've played (Of course on par the Resistance cashgrab). Even without any hud, throwing away mags with reload I've never had to abuse enemy AI or save scum my way trough an engagement. 

[h3] Story [/h3]

Story is and always has been dumb and I didn't care for it. It's just an excuse to make interesting level locations and in that it succussed. Just as in other entries you can 9, most of them taking around 1.5 hours to complete if you do all main and optional objectives. 


[h3] Technical side [/h3]

Game is runs well even on subpar hardware, without any stutters or frame drops. Visuals are great, as is the case with most AA and AAA games since 2010s. I think I've noticed slightly less bugs than in 4, but maybe I'm just misremembering. 

[h3] Conclusions [/h3]

In conclusion SE5 is an well polished game definitely worth buying when it's on sale. Given how scummy they do monetization with DLCs I suggest not buying it at full price.

review_text:
It's a good game, to the extent that I bought the DLC on sale.

But it's not very sniper-oriented. SE2,3,4 all had wide, clear, areas with good vantage points that gave this series its' title. SE5 can't have a good sniper experience because of the multiplayer. Good vantage points make the adversarial axis invasion mode too lopsided, and I assume this is why the maps feel so compartmentalised.
I spent hours in this game sneaking around with a pistol, only pulling out the rifle when the game allowed it to be soundmasked (which is infrequently).

The maps feel well designed, if too tight for a sniper game. There tend to be areas to the maps (which feels weird) where you can completely mess up in one part of the map and suffer no penalty in the other parts. Each zone is cordoned off with only a few entryways guarded by a handful of enemies, which feels too repetitive in game, even if established practice in modern titles. Though I do like that the SE franchise has moved away from its' earlier roots of cinematic hallway shooter a la COD.

 I feel that there are too few enemies per map. It's strange to say, but the environments feel empty. This is doubly true when the game says the map is swarming with enemies, and there's only perhaps 50 on the map. Equally, there are too few vehicles. The code and models for tanks are in the game, and only appear...twice? And a third time in DLC? There is a discrepancy between the narrative telling us how important these bases are and the lack of challenge when assaulting them. 

Suppressors ruin the game experience, yet make it tolerable to begin with. The pistol being silent but weak is a SE staple. The enemies rushing to the downed enemy and just leaving them there feels unfinished and a poor choice by the devs. The method of shooting once and escaping just doesn't work in such small spaces crowded with enemies. That takes planning and killing half the map to be possible, at which point you are already immune to the consequences of your actions. So suppressors are a must to avoid the poor vantage points and lack of sound covers. In future, "easy" should have plentiful sound cover (planes, extra generators), with little sound suppression on the guns themselves, whereas "hard" should require more planning to get the job done, even if it means killing fewer enemies and sneaking more often.

The "Axis Invasion" mode is very fun, especially with friends and self-imposed limitations. I feel bad for all the casual and new players who aren't aware that it's turned on by default. It's weighted against the Axis, but this makes it more fun when you get the perfect shot, and incentivises the Axis player to be a counter-sniper by leveraging their knowledge of the map's sightlines.

The DLC feel fine, but only fine. They suffer from being less well designed overall and a little gimmicky. The DLC weapons are utterly broken and dominate in Axis Invasion (annoyingly so). I wanted more content, and it definitely is more content, though pricy for what it is.

The whole game feels like a less well made Hitman game: maps with castle boxes, simplistic, deaf, and forgetful AI, sneaking over being brash. It's missing a vision of its' own identity.
That being said, it's easy to have fun and I've had a really enjoyable experience. It's a bit expensive, so only get it on sale.

Addendum: why is there an option to *not* kill the nazis?

Controls this time are even snappier and more responsive, letting you deliberate your next move easier. You have a more comprehensive attachment system, gorier x-ray shots with a lot more anatomical detail packed in, improved UI elements, art direction during cutscenes, optional kill list targets in every mission, and more collectibles. Locations have also been improved, with better traversal like with ziplines and climbable vines/moss. It's essentially just more of what fans of this series already loved, and I wouldn't have it any other way.

review_text:
Sniper Elite 5 brings together the best of old-school charm and modern aspirations in an enjoyable “so bad it’s good” gaming experience. Developed by Rebellion Developments, this instalment takes players on a thrilling journey back to World War II, where you once again step into the boots of Karl Fairburne, an elite American sniper. Tasked with sabotaging Operation Kraken, a mysterious Nazi project in occupied France, players are immersed in a covert operation packed with suspense and action.

The visuals are a treat, showcasing the dedication of the development team with detailed environments and character models. While the overall design has some shortcomings, the UI/UX stands out as a shining example of excellence. It’s a slick, intuitive interface that feels refreshing compared to the game’s more outdated mechanics and design choices.

Sniper Elite 5 offers sprawling sandbox environments, reminiscent of the recent Hitman series. These expansive levels encourage exploration and allow a multitude of approaches to completing objectives, ensuring high replayability. The freedom to experiment with strategies adds a lot to the appeal. However, it’s not without flaws.

The enemy AI is one such flaw. Despite the impressive sandbox design and engaging sniper gameplay, the AI lacks finesse. Enemies often huddle together, making them easy targets and breaking immersion. Their behaviour feels scripted and unrealistic, which can make the game feel overly “gamey.” Moments of unfairness - like enemies peeking around corners - further detract from the experience. This is the kind of thing you’d expect from other players in multiplayer, not from AI opponents, and it can be quite irritating.

Movement mechanics are inconsistent too. Ledges, ladders, and platforms can be awkward to navigate. Sometimes jumping down or off obstacles works perfectly; other times, you struggle for no apparent reason. It’s obvious that some areas are “designated” for jumping and grabbing. The cover system, while functional, feels basic and clunky, making transitions between cover points less smooth than desired. Maps, although vast and enjoyable, suffer from obvious and restrictive boundaries. Barriers, fences, or blown-up cars are clearly hand-placed by developers, breaking immersion and limiting freedom in otherwise expansive environments. The movement controls feel rigid, almost tank-like, and the animations - for both characters and the environment - lack finesse. Some movements look unnatural, which can disrupt the experience.

On the positive side, Sniper Elite 5 has a comprehensive skill tree, allowing players to progress and customise their play styles. This gives a delightful sense of growth and personalisation. Whether you prefer stealth or all-out action, the game caters to a wide range of approaches. The rank system, medals, and ribbons for achievements further enhance the sense of progression. Completing challenges and earning rewards motivates players to dive deeper, creating a positive and engaging loop.

The voice acting is a whole different adventure - it’s like a bad soap opera! Dramatic, campy, and over-the-top, it’s hard to take seriously. But, in hindsight, it adds to the charm and contributes to the 80s B-movie vibe: so bad it’s good. Another minor gripe is that the game doesn’t acknowledge your loadout choices in cutscenes, which feels like a surprising oversight.

Sniper Elite 5 perfectly captures the highs and lows of gaming over the years. It pays tribute to the stealth action genre while grappling with outdated mechanics and design choices. Despite its flaws, there’s a certain charm in the imperfections, making it a lovable, if occasionally frustrating, experience.

To sum it up, this game is a showcase of brilliance amid missed opportunities. Its vast sandbox environments, skill tree progression, and replayability offer glimpses of greatness. Yet antiquated mechanics, animation issues, AI quirks, and a lack of polish hold it back from full potential. Die-hard fans or those chasing nostalgia may find it satisfying, but anyone seeking a flawless, cutting-edge experience might be disappointed. Here’s hoping a sequel will hit the target dead centre.

review_text:
Most of the missions are repetitive. Go to point X, pick up a certain file, find some object, deliver something, etc. Worst part is that you don't get infinite satchels unlike SE4 to blow up the AA guns for side-missions. Close to half of my gameplay time was me and my friend trying to find a satchel to get full stars / completion for the maps. Too much focus on the killshot cutscenes but instead it just comes out looking worse than the prequel. They last for unnecessarily long too. You can disable them from settings, but I actually enjoyed them in SE4. Just not in this title. The game also feels somewhat like a running simulator. Huge maps but barely any enemies. When they do eventually come (in specific places only, such as buildings or mission areas), they come in hordes and catch you off-guard. SE4 had them much more evenly spread out so you could have action most of the time and not feel like you were just going on some sight-seeing picnic. 

Upgrade system is meh. Most of the changes in this sequel are to prolong the playtime of the game, nothing else. Some weapons and upgrades will only unlock by the time you reach completion, at which point most of the people will likely just move on to a different game. You need to achieve some specific criteria in specific maps to unlock a few of the weapons / upgrades. SE4 did it much better by giving you skill points as you completed the campaign and leveled up. You could choose which weapon you wanted to unlock, and then the upgrades were unlocked by just using that weapon to get kills in various methods. I felt the previous approach to be much more player friendly and easier since you wouldn't have to worry about having to try out a map once again just for the sole reason of unlocking something. Me and my friend completed the campaign, played one survival match (we were on the last wave and the game crashed), and then never touched the game again.

That being said, not everything is terrible. You still do get a similar shooting experience and feel of the Sniper Elite franchise. It is fairly more hardware-intensive than SE4, but like with any modern game, if you keep your setup expectations within reasonable limits, the game will run okay. Worked on Linux using Proton in case there's anyone from the open-source community considering giving the game a go. Gave issues connecting with my friend on Windows for coop one day, but just closing and restarting the game fixed it.

[h3] 5/10 [/h3]
A decent game if you get it on a hefty discount, but certainly not worth full price. Honestly just go buy SE4 instead if you want to have a fun time and not feel like you're doing some chores.

review_text:
## 🎯 Single Player  
The base campaign maps (without DLC) look great – big, detailed, and atmospheric. Some areas are perfect for stealth, but I often wish there were more opportunities for true long-range sniping. The level design is impressive, but replaying missions quickly becomes repetitive.  

For achievement hunters, it can be exhausting. A good example is the “Wolf Mountain” mission with Hitler – killing him in a dozen different ways just to unlock achievements feels like filler content. It adds hours of repetition without much creativity from the developers.  

I’ve logged around 350 hours in the game, and while the campaign is enjoyable, replay fatigue is definitely real.  

---

## ⚔️ Axis Invasion  
Axis Invasion is probably the most exciting addition to Sniper Elite 5. Dropping in as a Jäger sniper to hunt down another player completely changes the atmosphere of the campaign. It’s tense, unpredictable, and often thrilling.  

Unfortunately, this mode suffers from serious balance issues – usually against the invader:  
- You can’t loot fallen soldiers for extra weapons, traps, or grenades. You’re stuck with two grenades, a mine, and a medkit.  
- The invaded player has big advantages: looting gear, using phones to track you, and even seeing hints of where you’re approaching from.  
- Worst of all, “Sniper Focus” feels like an unfair advantage – allowing the invaded player to see your location through walls and prepare an ambush.  

Camping makes it worse. Many players clear the entire map of AI, plant mines everywhere, and then sit in a high spot (like a church tower) with perfect vision. Most of my deaths as an invader were simply from running into yet another mine.  

AI isn’t helpful either. If enemies are shooting at the campaign player, I should get an exact location update. Footstep sounds are also too quiet, making sound-based tracking unreliable.  

---

## 🛡️ Survival  
Survival mode is fun, but it highlights a big flaw across the game: there’s no proper tutorial explaining mechanics, scoring, or what actions give the most points. You have to figure it all out yourself.  

Difficulty scaling is also frustrating. Getting a gold medal feels almost impossible on lower difficulties like *Civilian* or *Very Easy*. Maps are sometimes designed to overwhelm you with enemies from all sides, leaving no chance to respond. The mode is intense, but it lacks balance.  

---

## 🔫 Multiplayer  
I’ve only played a few dozen matches, but the main issue is clear: **everything requires grinding**.  
- You unlock weapon attachments in the campaign, but then you must unlock them again in Axis Invasion.  
- In Survival, you also need unlocks, or you’re stuck with bare-bones gear.  
- In Multiplayer, you have to grind all the way to level 50 to access the full arsenal.  

This system feels unfair – new players are stuck with basic weapons, long aim times, and no attachments, while higher-level players dominate. On top of that, there’s a “Prestige” system where you re-grind levels from scratch for small perks. Honestly, it feels lazy.  

Other issues:  
- **Easy Anti-Cheat** doesn’t seem to stop cheaters, but it does eat resources, cause micro-stutters, and add lag.  
- The **wheel menu** is clunky. In combat, it blocks the screen and wastes time. Hotkeys for ammo and explosives would’ve been better.  
- **Weapon customization** is excellent, but loadouts reset across game modes. And you can’t name custom loadouts, which makes things confusing.  

---

## ✅ Pros  
- Beautiful maps and textures  
- Axis Invasion is exciting and unique  
- Wide choice of sniper rifles and secondary weapons  
- Deep and satisfying weapon customization  

## ❌ Cons  
- Repetitiveness kills replay value  
- Poor balance in Axis Invasion  
- Too much grinding across every mode  
- Easy Anti-Cheat hurts performance  
- Wheel menu slows gameplay  
- Lack of realism in animations, physics, and AI  

---

## 📝 Final Thoughts  
Sniper Elite 5 is a good game – even a very good one in some areas – with beautiful visuals, strong sniping mechanics, and a brilliant idea in Axis Invasion. But it also feels unfinished, with too much grinding, weak AI, and mechanics that often frustrate more than they entertain.  

For me, Sniper Elite 2 / Sniper Elite V2 Remastered still holds the crown for the most satisfying overall experience. Sniper Elite 5 is revolutionary in parts, but disappointing in others.  

My advice? Wait for a good sale, grab the Season Pass bundles, and give it a try. It’s worth playing – just be ready for grind, bugs, and missed opportunities.

Some say this is the best game of the series, others say it’s just a dumbed-down SE4. I’m honestly somewhere in between. Overall, I had a blast with it and in many ways I do think it improves on the previous game.

The usual Sniper Elite formula is still here, but there are some cool additions: silent non-lethal takedowns, non-lethal ammo, and a crafting system. Nothing game-changing, but they give you more ways to play. The maps are also really well designed, especially the night missions.

The main issue is the size of the levels. They’re waay too big. A normal mission can take close to 2 hours, and if you’re like me and want to check every single building while staying fully stealth, it can stretch to 3 hours or more. The DLC missions are even longer, almost like they’re stretched on purpose. My first run ended up at 54 hours, and that was just one playthrough, main game plus the 2 DLCs.

And here comes the biggest problem: the DLCs and season passes. The base game has 9 missions, which I can justify paying $50 for. But then you’ve got 2 season passes with 5 extra missions for $65. I’m not even sure what sort of logic gymnastics I should use to justify that. $115 for 14 missions is just not reasonable, no matter how long they make them.

I can recommend the game for what it is, because it really is a lot of fun. But grab it on sale, since I don’t see how someone could justify $125 for 14 missions. And no, making them 2 hours long is not a justification.

Sniper Elite 5 is fun, but it's nowhere near worth $60. The only reason I bought this game is because it goes on sale for $12 on a semi-regular basis. Still, it's a fun time with friends. The invasion mode is incredibly tense and shows how easily games can be made tense and interesting without needing constant action.

The biggest problem is the map design. The maps are HUGE. They feel a lot bigger than the maps in Sniper Elite 4 and this causes the missions to drag on. The average mission WILL take more than an hour. Easily over 2 hours if you plan on playing stealthy. And because the maps are wide open, a single firefight usually lights up the entire map. This makes playing loud less fun.

This game also features the usual Sniper Elite jank: Enemies can often see through dense foliage and other fully-opaque surfaces, so often times you'll be hiding behind a piece of cover only to discover that it wasn't mapped properly and the enemies can see you as plain as day. Speaking of things not being mapped properly: there are many sections in the game where you can hang from ledges, but the developers seemingly forgot to allow the player to drop down off of them, even when there's clearly ground less than a foot below you and it's obvious that you were supposed to be able to climb up and down that way. Lots of low walls can mantled, but some can't for seemingly no reason.

The new gunsmithing idea seems neat and I like the idea that you can now have different variants of the same gun (like unscoped Kar98s for the average infantry and suppressed SMGs for the snipers), but the system doesn't really feel like it adds much to the game and it feels like the system was added purely because other games at the time were doing weapon customization. Honestly, the development time could have been much better spent adding new enemy types (like adding medics, who would always carry medical supplies and be able to revive incapacitated enemies, but penalize the player's points if killed).

The non-lethal takedown option is cool, but I would love to see it expanded on beyond just a second melee takedown button. I think adding a Metal Gear Solid style holdup system that would let you take prisoners could be pretty cool.

This game is an improvement on Sniper Elite 4 and it's a fun experience, but half of the game feels uncooked. I hope Rebellion will take their time with the next game. I hope they reel back some of the unnecessary parts of the game and focus on the unique blend of stealth infiltration and sniper action that the series is known for. I love Sniper Elite and hope it does well. At least Rebellion's not selling anime laser guns and Nicki Minaj skins like Call of Duty

review_text:
This is a good game with plenty of replayability, so long as you're willing to accept a more dated paradigm that limits where you can go on the map.  There are some large areas that you can explore freely, but a significant portion of each map consists of intersecting paths with walls (hedges, buildings, etc.) on either side.  There are plenty of places to explore, multi-story buildings, ladders, and so on to keep the terrain interesting within those boundaries.  Because the maps are so huge and the paths have so many intersections, the limitations aren't really a problem; but people who are accustomed to open world games may be in for a bit of a shock.

The shooting mechanics are excellent.  You can choose to stay in 3rd person for the non-scoped weapons, but if you go into 1st person view (C on the keyboard), you'll find a pretty realistic experience with sight movement, wind, bullet arc, and so on.  The anatomically-correct impact camera is shockingly accurate, both in its depiction of bullet trajectory and the gory details of what happens to targets based on the location of impact.  I find it refreshing for a shooter franchise to accurately simulate the effects of bullets, explosives, and the environment, rather than treating every character and object as a bag of hit points with two or three hit boxes.  An inch in one direction or another actually matters in this game.  Fair warning: it's quite gory.

For the most part, stealth and enemy AI are well done.  Once you understand the idiosyncracies of the game, it's a lot of fun to sneak around and take out enemies.  However, if you don't understand the range at which enemies can hear each of your weapons (which, again, is pretty realistic), how to use the environment to mask the sound of gunshots, or how to avoid getting surrounded, you may be headed for a rough time.  This game does a good job of rewarding skill and punishes tactical mistakes fairly harshly.  My one criticism is that if you alert some enemies, they'll sometimes call in ALL their buddies and camp out in the area of the disturbance for quite a long time.  On one hand, this is somewhat realistic, since they actively investigate the places where you might be, check corpses, and investigate malfunctioning equipment.  However, if you don't understand that this is going to happen, you could end up being mobbed by 20 enemies from all directions who then proceed to hang out around your hiding place for 5 minutes.  Pro tip: if you or your shots are detected, move immediately.  Don't move into an area until you have cleared an escape route from that area.

The map and objectives are also quite interesting.  As you explore and gather intel, you'll uncover more objectives or details about existing objectives.  You'll learn safe combinations (so you don't have to spend explosives to open them), find hidden weapon stashes, and learn about advantageous sniping perches.  This game heavily rewards exploration, and is better for it.

Overall, this is a good game for fans of stealth-heavy shooters.  Just be aware that it doesn't follow some modern trends that you may be accustomed to.

review_text:
Compared to earlier entries into the franchise, Sniper Elite 5 is a little arcade-y. They've worsened many of the stealth features: there are less noise sources to disguise shots, the level design can be a little close quarters at times, and the AI is generally less predictable in a bad way, as in unrealistic. It seems that stealth isn't always an option anymore, which is a risky design choice seeing as the entire premise of the series is that you're a sniper. 

Although the traversal system aims to turn SE into a more immersive direction, making you more of an action figure who can jump and climb anywhere, the implementation is pretty rough, and there is quite a lot of geometry which breaks the realism, and otherwise frustrates the player. 

I found myself playing SE 5 more naturally, by which I mean the learning curve is quite gentle, but I fear that's because they've simplified things for the masses. Let's face it, most of the player base likes the idea of stealth, but ultimately after one mistake they go guns blazing. It seems Rebellion is leaning into that tendency. This would explain why there seems to be less sniper nests, and generally less emphasis on proper positioning. You can quite easily run away or gun everyone down to get that ALL CLEAR and start again. The same can be said for the weapon customisation. It's simply too easy to get the best guns and even the camo unlocks are ridiculous, as in the contrast and scaling not the historically-accurate design. 

The SE5 graphics seem on par with SE4 but I am getting more screen tearing with the newer release, and there are some lighting issues, particularly with vegetation, which is a big loss for a sniper game. Let's not even get into the story because this is Sniper Elite, and if you're here for fleshed-out dialogues and developed characters, you're playing the wrong game. 

So, who is playing this game, and enjoying it? Well, if you like the idea of walking around in a faux-stealth fashion, whereby you can coincidentally time a sniper shot with a passing plane but most of the time opt for your SMG or pistol, in a historically significant setting that is generally interesting to explore, then this game is a good addition to your casual roster. However, I do fear that the Sniper Elite formula is quickly becoming outdated and there will need to be an entire overhaul, both in terms of graphics and game engine, if the franchise wants to remain relevant for much longer.

In general, I enjoyed the game and did get my money's worth out of it (55.2 hours of gameplay to finish the Campaign, but I'm not going to try for 100% Achievements since there are many I'll never get -- nor will I play the other modes).  But, even though the game was released over 3 years ago, it still has many irritating aspects and bugs.  So, since there are plenty of Recommend reviews, I'm going with a Not Recommended here.  Here are the details of my gripes:
[list]
[*] Every time I start the game, it opens a browser and navigates to https://www.epicgames.com/id/activate?userCode=... trying to get me to link my Steam game to an Epic account.  This has been reported since at least 2022.
[*] Every time I join my wife's game to play the campaign in Co-op, it defaults to the Monika Grep character instead of the Harry Hawker character I always select.
[*] I suppose that there must have been at least one World War II black, female, Scott in Special Ops somewhere.  But, I find it irritating that the developers are emphasizing that character.  If they'd have not made her a Scott (thus widening the pool of possible candidates), I'd have been fine with it.
[*] The secondary missions that appear as we move through the maps seems to be designed to draw out the game (which doesn't need it since each mission takes roughly 6 hours to complete).  Almost invariably, as we move through the maps and discover things that spawn those secondary missions, the actual mission location is somewhere far behind us instead of somewhere in the vicinity or somewhat ahead.
[*] Randomly, the crowbar and bolt cutters disappear from our inventories.  This has been reported since at least 2022.
[*] Once again, the pistols in the game (specifically, the Welrod) are ridiculously underpowered.  I refuse to believe that being shot with any pistol at close range would do less damage than merely throwing the pistol at the enemy instead.  Many a time, the wife and I would pump 4 or 5 pistol shots each into the head of some nearby enemy and have him shrug them off.  It's gotten to the point that I'll just close with the enemy and melee him instead of shooting him with those worthless pistols.
[*] The apparently random ability of our characters to vault over minor obstructions is really annoying.  Sometimes, we can climb walls and jump over small fences.  Other times, we can't.  Pick one.
[*] Destroying tanks is ridiculously hard and persnickety.  What's the point of having flashing red weak areas on tanks, and the existence of panzerfausts, anti-tank guns, mines and armor piercing ammunition if none of them actually kill the tank?
[*] Mission 7's stone eagles (and one in Mission 8) and some other collectibles are crazy hidden.  They're completely un-findable without a walk-through.  Those kinds of collectibles should be discoverable with a standard, thorough exploration of the map.  Not hidden-away and visible from just one spot while looking in a specific direction.
[*] I don't know if this is a function of my wife having played through parts of the game before, but several times, we've run into blue-eyeball sub-objectives on the map that are missing the actual task we're supposed to do.  Specifically, activating alternate starting locations.  In Mission 7, we ran into a safe where we were told we'd found the intel we needed to open it.  But, when we went back to the safe, we still couldn't open it.  When we blew the safe with a satchel charge, there was nothing at all in it.  And, the blue-eyeball icon on the map refused to disappear and kept nagging us about opening the safe and telling us it was a couple of meters away from us no matter which direction we approached it from.
[*] After finishing the campaign, I noticed I had not gotten the Tinkerer Achievement/Medal.  It said I'd interacted with only 23 of 24 workbenches.  Yet, examining the details of each of the 8 missions with workbenches shows that I'd gotten 3 workbenches in each.  Since 8 x 3 = 24 (not 23), and I KNOW that I found and interacted with all 3 workbenches in all 8 missions, that medal appears to be bugged.
[*] After a while, the game seems to stop making Auto Backups.
[*] While playing co-op, the game disconnected us several times.  Also, one time the game crashed my entire computer.  I can't remember the last time I've had a computer crash (it's got to have been multiple decades ago).
[*] And, finally, the game uses Denuvo anti-tamper, kernel level anti-cheat, and Easy Anti-Cheat.
[/list]

review_text:
A Sharpshooter’s Masterclass in Tactical Gameplay

Sniper Elite 5 hits the mark in nearly every category that matters. It’s a masterfully crafted tactical shooter that combines stunning visuals, immersive realism, and finely tuned gameplay to deliver one of the most satisfying sniper experiences to date.

From the moment you load into your first mission, the graphics impress. Environments are richly detailed, from the dense forests and crumbling châteaux of Nazi-occupied France to coastal gun batteries and sprawling industrial complexes. The world feels alive and reactive, with a level of environmental fidelity that enhances immersion at every turn.

The storyline continues the tried-and-true formula of Karl Fairburne’s silent war behind enemy lines, but it does so with a sharp sense of purpose and urgency. Each mission is woven into a greater narrative that feels both personal and impactful — offering players a meaningful sense of progression and purpose.

Realism is one of Sniper Elite 5's most impressive achievements. Ballistics are deeply satisfying, with authentic bullet drop, wind resistance, and scope calibration. The iconic kill cam returns, more brutal and cinematic than ever, but never feels overused or gimmicky. It rewards patience and precision, two things the game constantly encourages.

The weapon variety is excellent, and each can be customized extensively. Whether you prefer a suppressed bolt-action rifle, an SMG for close encounters, or a silenced pistol for quiet kills, the game allows you to tailor your loadout to your playstyle. The gunplay is weighty, deliberate, and deeply rewarding.

What truly elevates Sniper Elite 5 is its replayability. Every campaign mission is set in a sprawling sandbox teeming with opportunities, alternate routes, hidden intel, and dynamic enemy behavior. I’ve replayed missions multiple times and still discover new vantage points, traps to exploit, and stealth paths I missed before. It’s a game that rewards exploration and experimentation — the more you play, the better and more strategic you become.

The difficulty settings are also worth praising. Whether you’re a casual player who just wants to enjoy the story or a hardcore tactician who craves authentic military simulation, Sniper Elite 5 scales beautifully to match your skill and preference.

Cons? I honestly don’t have any. The game delivers exactly what it sets out to do, and it does it with precision and polish.

Final Verdict:
Sniper Elite 5 is a tactical shooter done right — intelligent, engaging, and endlessly replayable. Whether you're a first-time sniper or a veteran of the franchise, this installment stands tall as the definitive Sniper Elite experience. Lock, load, and take the shot — you won’t regret it.

Rating: 10/10

review_text:
Fifth numbered installment of the Nazi ballbusting simulator. The game takes place in Vichy France, 1944, after Germany(SEV2, 1945), Africa(SE3, 1942), Italy(SE4, 1943) finally we got a (likely) final piece of the puzzle on Karl's WWII journey blowing up Wunderwaffes. The game remains all the same, empty lung, xray killcam, all the traps and shootings. The guy is a sniper, so the sniping is what he does. Done talking. And if you ever get tired of blasting German balls... For special guests we got the Japanese nuts to bust this time. Since you still can't commandeer vehicles you'll have to do a fair bit of legwork, but the game always throws a group of Nazis to kill along the way to ease your bore. Maps themselves could've been better though, as they feel often too restrictive, with paths blocked with uncrossable barbed wires and fences forcing players to make detours. Graphics, nothing groundbreaking. But its primitive, outdated antialiasing is problematic. It is almost non existent, tweaking between off and ultra has barely any difference. Nothing like distracting pixelated images to ruin the beauty of Mont Saint Michel and other pleasant landscapes of Francia. The game only offers FSR1 as its sole upscaler, so that also cannot be a help to smooth out the image. The base game has 8 missions which is on par with SE4 and SE3, technically there's a ninth one but that finale level lasts seconds to finish. Having both season passes adds 5 additional levels including the obligatory Hitler one. 

Like the previous games SE5 offers players weapon customization. And in my opinion, this hurts the game because of how extensive it is this time, rather than the lack thereof. Various options are present not only for rifles but also for every secondary and pistol, every major part of the gun tinkerable. With iron sights and scopes now available for weapons of all 3 slots, easy pinpoint precision is now possible with secondaries and sidearms, making rifles completely obsolete in a lot of situations. And once you unlock silencers, the game's difficulty dives faster than a Junkers Stuka divebomber. I know, it gives more freedom to players with their loadouts, and that's always good. But it inadvertently also created overpowered meta combinations that are objectively superior over others. If you value practicality over everything there's no reason for you to use most weapons provided. Reviews for all the DLC weapon packs are in mixed-mostly negative range also because of this I believe. They fail to differ. Why bother with other guns when a silenced, 6x scoped Strumgewehr 44 with damage clocked up to 11 with no scope glints can easily handle most tasks, with your trusty Karabiner 98 for occasional long range kills and armor?

With multiple starting spots, challenges and unlocks it encourages players to replay its levels several times... But the actual replayability? Not much. There's barely any deviation from your usual approach that can be made. The goals of the mission remain the same. All hostile NPCs are enemy personnel, thus viable targets, there is zero reason to sidestep and unnecessarily prolong the mission avoiding them. Just pick them all off, burst their heads, lungs, balls, or whatever. To inject some level of freshness into this routinely loop developers implemented an online mode that allows players to take the role of a Nazi sniper(technically, you can't play as a Nazi, all the crooked crosses in uniforms of playable Germans are censored) in others' games. As an invader you scan German NPCs to create your web of informants to track down the enemy infiltrator, and it's a good mechanic. I had a fair amount of fun in this mode gunning down newbies struggling to learn the ropes... But if both sides are actually competent, the mode quickly turns into a slog that often ends in the favor of the host(allied sniper) because of the focus mechanic, a closerange wallhack(this is disabled in authentic difficulty but hardcore players are rare) which can't be used by the invader.

20 years ago there was an overabundance of WWII games, not anymore. Call of Duty, Battlefield, all have moved on, and today Sniper Elite is the one remaining arcade shooter game still clinging on to its original setting. For people who are interested in the conflict or the time period, or enjoyed the previous games, as long as players are aware of what they'll be getting into $40 for complete edition is a price worth paying to kill Hitler and his gang for the fifth time and learn about human anatomy. But do not expect any more than what you've already experienced.

Absolutely recommended!

It is a solid entry in the series that improves on its predecessor, especially for rifle enthusiasts. While it has some technical issues, the tactical stealth game play remains engaging: it's finally a chapter in which you actually sniper a lot, it's very satisfying. 

I played at "Sniper Elite" difficulty setting, the experience varies significantly with lower settings. I played on a 3060Ti, everything at ultra, 60fps rock solid. 

The Good:
- Significant improvement over the previous chapter with enhanced rifle mechanics
- Distinct weapon personalities - each firearm feels unique and satisfying
- Challenging AI on higher difficulties that actively tries to outflank and ambush you
- Excellent sound design - both immersive audio and realistic sound-based detection system
- Detailed, well-crafted scenarios that reward careful planning

The Bad:
- Animation invincibility frames: enemies become temporarily invulnerable during hit reactions
- Inconsistent damage model: some enemies are unrealistic bullet sponges
- Questionable weapon ballistics: completely wrong bullet drop calculations (e.g., 1911 pistol)
- Artificial level boundaries: visible areas blocked by arbitrary "mission area" restrictions instead of natural barriers

The Ugly:
- Sluggish controls: controls are horribly sluggish and often miss inputs. 

Conclusion:
Despite its flaws, this is a good tactical stealth game that series fans and newcomers alike will enjoy. The core sniping mechanics and improved AI make it worth playing, even if some technical issues can be frustrating sometimes.

Sniper Elite 5 marks a compelling evolution in the long-running stealth-action franchise, delivering a meticulously crafted World War II experience that blends tactical sniping, open-ended level design, and thrilling third-person combat. Building on the solid foundation of its predecessors, this installment refines the core gameplay mechanics with smarter AI, expanded player choice, and a sprawling campaign set primarily in occupied France, where resistance fighters seek to dismantle a secret Nazi superweapon project. The game shines most in its level design—large, detailed maps invite players to approach objectives with unparalleled freedom, whether by long-distance sniper shots, stealthy infiltration, or all-out combat. Each map is layered with verticality, numerous vantage points, and environmental hazards, encouraging creative strategies that reward patience and planning.

The signature bullet-cam mechanic returns, more cinematic than ever, offering satisfying slow-motion shots that track the bullet’s deadly path through bones and organs with graphic precision. This visceral feedback reinforces the game’s identity, delivering a uniquely brutal but oddly poetic form of violence that fans have come to expect. Beyond sniping, players can also employ a wide arsenal of WWII-era weapons and gadgets, with an improved customization system that allows meaningful tweaks to firearms’ performance and aesthetics. The stealth system is deeper too, with enemy patrols exhibiting more varied behavior and awareness, making silence and camouflage vital but never tedious.

Graphically, Sniper Elite 5 impresses with photorealistic environments, lifelike character models, and dynamic weather effects that influence visibility and gameplay tactics. The immersive audio design further elevates the tension—every distant gunshot, rustling leaf, and whispered radio chatter pulls players into the battlefield. The narrative, while not the game’s strongest suit, offers enough intrigue and character moments to keep the pace engaging, with performances that add weight to the resistance fighters’ plight without overshadowing the gameplay.

Multiplayer modes expand the game’s replayability significantly, featuring a range of competitive and cooperative options. The addition of an extensive mission creator and mod support empowers the community to build and share custom content, extending the title’s lifespan well beyond the main campaign. However, some players have noted occasional AI inconsistencies and minor bugs, particularly in stealth detection and pathfinding, though ongoing patches have addressed many issues promptly.

Overall, Sniper Elite 5 successfully balances accessibility and depth, offering a rich, rewarding experience for veterans and newcomers alike. Its combination of tactical freedom, brutal sniper combat, and immersive WWII settings makes it a standout entry in the genre, proving that the series still has plenty of precision and punch left to deliver. Whether stalking targets from hidden perches or engaging in tense close-quarters firefights, players will find in Sniper Elite 5 a nuanced and satisfying simulation of the deadly art of sniping.

Rating: 8/10

review_text:
Sniper Elite 5 is a great game—if you haven’t played any of the previous entries in the series. One feature I really enjoyed was the ability for players to invade each other’s games. It made co-op with my two friends a lot more engaging and added some unique, fun tension to our playthroughs. Beyond that, though, the improvements are pretty modest: slightly better graphics and larger maps.

Unfortunately, those larger maps don’t necessarily make for a better experience. Compared to Sniper Elite 4, the level design in SE5 feels more open—but not in a good way. SE4's maps had tighter pacing and more deliberate route design, which made missions feel more focused and satisfying. SE5’s openness often feels like it dilutes the gameplay, making it less immersive and a bit scattered.

To be clear, I’m comparing SE5 directly to its predecessor, because that’s the most relevant point of reference for me. If you’re new to the series, SE5 might be a great entry point. But for returning players, Sniper Elite 4 still feels like the better game overall.

Another major downside is the AI. It’s noticeably worse in SE5. I’m not sure what changes were made under the hood, but the AI behavior feels clunky and inconsistent—not just here, but also in Sniper Elite: Resistance. It’s a step backward.

Visually, the game is decently polished, but the graphics feel dated despite being a bit sharper than SE4. There’s also something off about the engine—it just doesn’t feel as refined or responsive, which affects the overall gameplay experience.

All things considered, I’d give Sniper Elite 5 a 5.5/10. Technically, I’d recommend it—but only if you’re buying it on sale. It’s not a bad game, but for fans of the series, it might feel more like a downgrade than a true sequel.

Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants a bit of stealth action. The game succeeds at the experience it is trying to sell. 9/10

review_text:
The latest addition to the mainline Sniper Elite series, though at the time of this review it had been out for quite some time. If you know and love the series, you'll get mostly the same deal here as you did with the previous installments. You get to visit interesting locations and shoot nasty people in nasty places from afar to stop the aforementioned nasties from cooking up some kind of super weapon that will surely win them the war. I personally prefer the more challenging previous installment, but this is a good time regardless. Get to it! Oh, and do check out Axis Invasion mode!

If you are unfamiliar with the series, you play as Karl Fairburne an OSS sniper during WW2, and this time you are deployed to France, around the time of the allied invasion, to investigate and stop a Nazi plot: operation Kraken. This all unfolds in the span of 8 missions of the main campaign, where you have to make your way through spacious open levels that have you tackle various primary and secondary objectives before extracting.
The main staple of the series is sniping your enemies - you never would have guessed. Your kill shots trigger a bullet camera and x-ray shots of the victim on impact. Gross, satisfying and it really never gets old. The rifle is supposed to be your weapon of choice, but you also carry a submachine gun and pistol and you can melee kill enemies as well. Unfortunately, in my opinion, sniping takes more of a backseat to stealth killing by way of the latter two options. That is if you go for a stealth approach, which is how this game naturally plays for most people, I would guess. You can definitely go loud all the way as well, but that's not where the gameplay shines and I don't really enjoy that play style myself.
You’ll level up and unlock new skills throughout the campaign, and the same goes for weapons and modifications for those weapons. This time around there are a lot of those modifications. Most of them have clear advantages and drawbacks and it's up to you to assemble a kit that you feel matches your play style best. Being a stealth player myself, I tend to favor modifications like suppressors and stuff that increases aim stability.

In addition to the campaign there are also other modes, like surviving against waves of AI enemies on various maps of the campaign and from the multi-player mode. Speaking of which, yes there is also multi-player, with modes like Team Match and No-Cross. I like team match the best, but fair warning: toxicity ahead.

Though by far the best mode in the game is Axis Invasion. It is simply the single best idea that Rebellion has every included in any of their Sniper Elite games. If enabled, and to be clear it is fully optional, this allows another player to invade your campaign missions as an enemy sniper, adding a lot more challenge to the game. It's fun to play from both perspectives, but I must admit I like playing as the invader the most. 
Theoretically. Mostly. You see there's a huge drawback to the mode, being that the invader is at really big disadvantage in all difficulties except the hardest one: Authentic. Otherwise the campaign player will be able to gauge your approximate direction / location at all times using focus-mode, be able to spot you though walls using focus mode, and be able to shoot you thru most cover (including brick walls) with armor piercing rounds. Naturally, there are unfortunately plenty of players that abuse this just to grief invaders, and it often turns what should be a fun cat-and-mouse game, into boredom and frustration. Also, beware of players the load into missions that have been cleared of AI enemies and that are full of lethal traps for the invader, using stacked mines, TNT and whatnot. So A+ for the idea, but the execution leaves a lot to be desired. In my experience, the best way to engage with this mode is as the campaign player on Authentic difficulty.

Some final words on technical issues I’ve experienced. The Easy Anti-Cheat included in the game can seemingly mess up at anytime and remove you from online play, whether that is a mode like Team Match or Axis Invasion. General stability has also been an issue for me, with regular crashes to desktop, unsure what the problem is there. Finally, the game is by no means free of minor bugs and jank, which will seemingly at this point never be fixed.

review_text:
Set against the backdrop of World War II in France, the game immerses players in a meticulously crafted environment filled with stealth action, tactical gameplay. As a sniper named [i][b]Karl Fairburne[/b][/i], players are tasked with taking down high-profile targets and sabotaging enemy operations, all while navigating through designed maps that encourage exploration and strategy.

[h3]GAMEPLAY MECHANICS[/h3]
[i][b]Sniper Elite 5[/b][/i] builds on the established formula of its predecessors, offering a blend of stealth and sniping mechanics. The game introduces refined mechanics for movement and shooting, allowing for more fluid gameplay. Players can utilise various tools at their disposal, including a wide array of weapon modifications, traps, and distractions to outmaneuver enemies. The addition of new traversal methods, such as climbing and vaulting, enhances verticality in gameplay, enabling players to find optimal sniping spots or stealth routes.

One of the standout features of the game is the emphasis on tactical planning. Maps are expansive and cleverly designed, providing multiple pathways and opportunities for players to approach missions differently. This encourages creativity and experimentation, offering a rewarding experience for those who enjoy calculating their next move with precision. Additionally, the return of the iconic slow-motion X-ray kill cam showcases the visceral impact of long-range shots, enhancing the sense of satisfaction when executing a perfect sniping technique.

[h3]VISUALS[/h3]
Graphically, [i][b]Sniper Elite 5[/b][/i] is a remarkable achievement, showcasing detailed environments that reflect the wartime setting. From lush countryside to ruined cities, each location is intricately designed. Lighting effects, weather variations, and dynamic shadows contribute to an immersive atmosphere, while character models and animations enhance the visual fidelity of the experience. It also includes [i][b]ultra-wide[/b][/i] support, where you can spot those sneaky Nazis lurking in the corners of your vision.

[h3]AUDIO[/h3]
The sound design complements the visuals perfectly; the sounds of gunfire, environment, and even the subtle strategising of the battlefield create a rich auditory experience. Voice acting adds depth to the narrative, bringing life to the characters while conveying the tension and stakes of the missions.

[h3]NARRATIVE[/h3]
While [i][b]Sniper Elite 5[/b][/i] emphasises gameplay mechanics, its story offers enough intrigue to keep players engaged. The narrative revolves around thwarting Nazi plans in France, with [i][b]Karl Fairburne[/b][/i] facing off against formidable foes. The storyline, while not overly complex, is delivered through dynamic cinematics and mission briefings that add context and motivation to the gameplay.

[h3]ATMOSPHERE[/h3]
The atmosphere has been enhanced with inspiration from real historical settings, locations, and weaponry, immersing players in the gritty realities of war. This attention to detail elevates the experience and provides players with a sense of connection to the period.

[h3]MULTIPLAYER[/h3]
[i][b]Sniper Elite 5[/b][/i] expands its offerings with a robust multiplayer component, featuring cooperative and competitive modes. The ability to team up with friends for shared objectives enhances the overall experience, allowing for collaborative strategising. The inclusion of a unique PvPvE mode, where players can compete against one another while dealing with AI enemies, adds an exciting twist that keeps the gameplay fresh and unpredictable.

[h3]REPLAYABILITY[/h3]
The game's structure encourages replayability, with various challenges, collectibles, and unlockable content waiting to be discovered. Different difficulty levels and customisable options allow players to tailor their experience, making it suitable for both sniping newcomers and series veterans alike.

[h3]THE LOWDOWN[/h3]
Overall, [i][b]Sniper Elite 5[/b][/i] is a worthy addition to the franchise, successfully balancing engaging gameplay, good visuals, and an immersive atmosphere. Its combination of tactical shooting and stealth mechanics offers a rewarding experience for players who relish strategic gameplay. While the narrative may not be groundbreaking, it serves its purpose well by providing context for the action. Additionally, the game features robust multiplayer options and high replayability.

Whether you’re a skilled marksman or entirely new to the sniper genre, this game has something for everyone, making it an impressive addition to the world of tactical shooters. If you’re ready to embrace your inner sharpshooter and take down enemies from a distance, grab your gear and prepare to snipe your way through World War II with a smile. Just remember: it’s more than just a game; it’s a fantastic excuse to don your camouflage pyjamas!

3rd person OTS camera is jank, with what you're seeing in your crosshair not aligning with what you can shoot.  There's no cover system to speak of.

And one of the major crimes of SE5 -and of Rebellion now in general- is their horribly expensive DLCs, which are complete and utter garbage.  NONE of them are worth the money.

And finally there's the whole DEI nonsense where half your character choices are POCs and girl bosses.

Don't know how much longer this company plans to milk this title before people finally get fed up.  Kind of regret this purchase.

It is a pretty good game.
The first campaign map is beautifull and give you a good impression of being in france due to the hedge and trenches here and there. The map is large and there are typical 4 main missions on every map and you can aproach the target from many direction you like and in any order you like. I think that is great.
Other maps are huge mansions or even a huge city with a tall building in the middle. Its big, impressive and the city itself require you to find the right way in since you cant go in a direct line.
It is also worth to think about what target you do first, since if you silencet he big guns shooting then you cannot use their explosive sound to hide your sniper rifle shots.
You can also bump into patrols, trucks and hear the germans speaking.
You can do full stealth or full auto if you like, but in my oppinion your are more of a sabortour than you are a sniper so you often sneak and use silenced weapons vs your sniper rifle.
personaly i prefer to be the sniper and do it from a distance but quite often i get notised anyway due to no noice that can mask my gun sound or other guards discoverying the dead enemy and stuff like that.
I think this part should be changed a bit so it become more easy to snipe vs it ending in a gun battle.
You are more or less a one person army / sniper vs everyone els and well you dont want to go in making allot of noice you are the mix of a sniper / sabotour and not being discovered is your biggest advantage once its gone its you vs everyone from all directions. I feel like the game kind of force me away from being a sniper and into being a sabotour and close range combat vs using my sniper rifle most of the time. This is both good and bad.
I like the first campaign map both function as a tutorial but also open up very quick and allow you to desided what to do. THere are sabotage missions, kill the officer mission and he is not just standing still but walking around so you maybe have to go and look for him.
You can also booby trap corpses and machines.
One thing that i did find a bit comfusing was how to pickup weapons on the battlefield.
I found out that you can take a weapon and use it but once it run try you drop it.
You cannot replace your start weapons but only upgrade them. Honestly i think its okay and i got used to it.
I also found it comfusing to figure out how to use the medicit.. It turn out you Hold in Q and then a wheel is shown now select the medikit/bandage and next hold in F key to use it.
The same goes with grenades ect.. I had kind of hoped you just press 1-9 and that was it but no.
Sound is great, visuals great, houses are great and they all look realistic inside.
There are also side missions and hidden stuff such as shoot 3 eagles on the top of buildings or killing x person in a special way give you an award. THere are also small snow men and other stuff that you can shoot and collect in the game world.
The game also keep track of your kills and what you do so you can get ingame awards and XP to get new skills along the way.
The AI is pretty decent, example if they hear you they come looking for you and will search and after a while go back to their original patrol area again.
I will call the game an action game inspired by ww2 germany with a mix of sniping, sabotour, shooting and then a fictive story. Not bad, and i have all the other sniper elite games, but this one is better due to the game having a larger less liniar open world kind of thing.
You can even play co-up in the campaign or jump into other peoples games as a hunter shiper who have to take dodwn the other player.. There are also other game modes.
All in all not bad.  ( lucky there are no timer on the missions, so you can take your time, setup traps and stuff )
You can get new upgrades to your weapons by finding workbenches on every map. It is especially important on map 1 where you can get silencers that will be a big help for the rest of the game. So look for workbenches everywhere.

Quite fun for those who like slower and more methodical game-play, at least when you're playing stealthily that is, but even loud & proud combat has it's downtime. I personally enjoy campaign and invasions the most, whether I'm the one doing the invading or instead being invaded as the host, both are quite enjoyable, that is when you don't invade a game where they're farming invasion kills on the easiest difficulty and have killed everyone on the map. Multiplayer (8v8 PVP) I'm not a huge fan of personally nor do I really care for the survival game-mode but they are good additions for those who like that sort of thing. Funny enough I would've never played this game if I had never played Sniper Elite: Resistance on game-pass, I only bought this game and all of it's DLC (heavily discounted) because of the fact that I had become aware of just how much content was flipped from this game to Sniper Elite: Resistance, so naturally I wanted to see what the origin point was for all of it, and I was pleasantly surprised. Anyway, highly recommend, campaign is fun, co-op campaign is fun, invasions are fun, good fun all-around, find myself continuing to come back to it for a reason I can't quite explain, just very enjoyable game-play in general, scratches the itch as they say.
