review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a bitter sweet game. It's probably one of the best playing games I've ever played but it's mired with some of the most public and controversial fallouts ever between a developer and a publisher which very infamously saw Hideo Kojima leave Konami and Konami effectively stop game development for a long time leading to the cancellation of silent hills, it's an incredibly famous and well know story and not one I want to dive into but it is important to know due to the unfinished state of MGS5 the game lacks a true and proper ending and is sufficiently bloated to compensate for missing chapter 3. 

MGS5 is the first MGS game to put gameplay first. Gone are codec calls, gone are 70 minute cutscenes(sorta) and gone is David Hayter. What we now have is an open world MGS that puts the focus on gameplay, systems and detail. 

I do need to stress that the story is absolutely terrible, it really ruins the mystic nature of the games, introduces absolutely embarrassing female characters that really show the misogynistic nature of Kojima which is surprisingly worse now even compared to the B&B core and also tries to go for a plot twist that worked infinitely better in MGS2. If you care about MGS lore this game is pretty bad and these constant prequel games always have the best gameplay but utterly ruin the already messy plot of MGS, this isn't even factoring in the missing chapter. 

What this game does right is gameplay, everything is incredibly fun to play, from stealth gameplay, combat, the open world, base management. All of it comes together to create a fantastic game that has so many systems that it's no wonder we've never seen anything like this being replicated again. 

I really must praise the level of detail in the stealth system, no game has this level of insane detail, the amount of things that can be used to manipulate guards is staggering and the wide amount of tools you can use is impressive. Whilst I'm annoyed eating and healing has been dropped from MGS3 I do love that they really expanded on the sabotage elements, sneaking into an enemy outpost and disabling communications with C4 and watching them all scramble to call reinforcements is amazing. Guards also adapt to player tactics, if you do too many headshots they wear helmets, too many night ops then they'll use more lights. This can also be sabotaged by sending your teams on missions to destory supply lines and it's just amazing. 

There is also an online mode, PVP MP is pretty dead but I played it extensively when I played this on Xbox and that was a good time. You can also infiltrate player bases which is always a super fun challenge. 

Music and graphics are absolutely insane. The ost of this game is amazing and sins of the father stands next to snake eater as a fantastic bit of original music. The licenced music also adds to the 80's theme and fits surprisingly well. The graphics are so good and the game runs smoothly which isn't surprising considering this is a 10 year old game. The fox engine really was an amazing bit of tech.

Overall this game is riddled with problems but it's also the best playing game I've ever experienced, it's a really hard game to actually recommend but I do think this is one of the greatest stealth games ever made. I also do love venom snake and whilst the story sucks, the retcon with venom is actually pretty great. 

It's a shame this was the final MGS from Kojima, whilst it did get critical acclaim it does feel more like he went out on a whimper rather than a bang. It's been a grim time to be a MGS fan but with Konami's regained interest in games and the recent MGS3 remake there might be life left in this franchise.

review_text:
10 years later it's still unmatched as a 3rd person stealth action game. As a Metal Gear game, there's less story and cutscenes, the bulk of the plot is in the cassette tapes, that also replaced CODEC, same as it was in Peace Walker. In many aspects it's an expanded Peace Walker, and it benefits from having played MPW beforehand. Also Ground Zeroes is the equivalent of the MGS2 tanker chapter and some progress carries over, so it's highly recommended to be played first.

And why do I have 900+ hours on it? The online features of FOB and PF present a long progression system where you get extra items, and S+ and S++ soldiers that allow you to get your unit levels up to 160. There are some broken weapons and items in the 100+ levels but it takes a long time to get there, and the harder FOBs are balanced against this high level gear. It's totally optional, you can be done with the story and put it down, but if you fall in love with the amazing fluid gameplay, this game will give you endless hours of fun.

There's also an online multiplayer mode, right now it's sparsely populated and there are hackers, but it's some fun deathmatch stuff. Also beware there are a lot of people that hacked their game to get max everything (only S++ soldiers, resources, GMP, tanks, etc), so if you - like me - play legit, it's gonna be a though fight in the PF ranks, but still possible! (I am at PF rank AAA+ right now) Also don't be so scared of FOB invasions, you only loose a small fraction of your unprocessed materials and about 10 soldiers, afterwards the invader has a few days cooldown so they can't spam you. Just don't invade others and you will be mostly left alone, with maybe 1 or 2 invaders a week.

review_text:
I originally played TPP on PS4 about 10 years ago, and this is the first time I’ve ever beaten an open-world game twice. I always thought open-world games lost their replayability because of their repetitive nature, but this playthrough proved something to me: if the gameplay is truly captivating, none of that matters. In terms of depth and variety, I honestly think nothing—except maybe Zelda BOTW/TOTK—comes close to what this game achieves.

Gameplay is everything, and this game absolutely nails it. It’s easily in my top 10 of all time purely for its gameplay. Even with the 3-minute helicopter deployments, it still has the best flow in the entire Metal Gear series, in my opinion.

You’ve all heard the usual complaints about this game:
	•	“Main/Side Ops are repetitive.”
Sure, but when the gameplay is this good, even your 20th armored-unit takedown feels fresh.
	•	“The story doesn’t conclude properly.”
I actually think it fills in Venom’s arc really well. Yes, the Liquid/Mantis storyline doesn’t fully wrap up, but honestly, the MG series has always had missing pieces in its timeline—even after Kojima went full lore-dump mode in MGS4.
	•	“Konami’s greed stopped Kojima from making his dream game.”
Maybe, maybe not—but Kojima was already losing passion for Metal Gear, and we’ve all seen how the Sony–Kojima partnership went. Spoiler: Death Stranding is a much more deeply flawed game compared to this masterpiece.

The music is incredible, the graphics still hold up, it runs beautifully on the Steam Deck, and somehow the online servers are still alive after 10 years.

9.5/10

review_text:
[b]Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain[/b] just never clicked for me.  The pacing felt all over the place: some cutscenes dragged on forever, others made it seem like the story was finally gaining momentum, only for the game to swerve into a tangent for several missions.  Any mission involving the supernatural group known as "The Skulls" completely took me out of the experience.  They are frustrating rather than tense or exciting, and they feel out of sync with the grounded stealth gameplay the series is known for.

The deeper I got, the more repetitive it became.  Most of Act 2 is made up of modified rehashes of Act 1 missions, and the side ops all blur together as copy-and-paste scenarios at different outposts.  Even the main missions practically demand multiple playthroughs: your initial run, then replaying to clear side objectives that only unlock after finishing the mission [i](see note below)[/i], and then replaying yet again for an S-rank that usually requires zero kills.  Multiply that by the repeated missions in Act 2 and suddenly you're doing the same tasks up to six times.  And don't even get me started on the opening hospital sequence.  It goes on forever, constantly swapping between cutscene and gameplay so you never know when the skip button will work.  Yes, you may end up sitting through it multiple times too.

I know the game's development was notoriously messy, with Konami and Kojima clashing behind the scenes and parts of the narrative reportedly left unfinished.  That context explains a lot of the unevenness, but it doesn't make it any easier to play through. review_text:
[h3]"Boss, you killed a child? Amazing mission complete! That right there is why you're the best Boss. The one and only!"[/h3]

Metal Gear Solid V is a game that somehow manages to be both a deeply serious war drama and one of the most absurd sandboxes ever designed, where every stupid thing you do becomes a legend. And that contrast is exactly why it works.

I already knew the franchise, and I actually tried MGSV for the first time about eight years ago. And I dropped it, probably too early. Back then, all I really absorbed were the memes and the confusing revelation that more than one Snake exists.

Only after finishing Death Stranding recently did I feel the urge to return to MGSV, and I’m glad I did.

[b]Gameplay[/b]

What makes MGSV exceptional is its sandbox design - a stealth-sandbox hybrid unlike anything I’d played before. Missions can be approached from countless angles. The game just hands you a toolbox and says: "Figure it out". It reminded me of Death Stranding in that sense: the joy of pure autonomy, where every victory feels earned, and every failure becomes your own story.

One of MGSV’s most brilliant achievements is how its anti-war message is expressed not just in dialogue, but directly through gameplay. Enemies adapt to your actions: kill too many, and they start wearing heavy armor and helmets. It’s a subtle, realistic reinforcement of the game’s unspoken rule: "don’t kill unless you must."

Yet the game never forbids combat. In fact, it makes fighting so enjoyable that sometimes it’s hard not to indulge. Especially when it comes to XOF, mercenary executioners with absolutely no humanity. I took enormous satisfaction in hunting them down. I replayed the Skullface mission many times even after I’d stripped the entire base of every resource, probably committing a full-scale mercenary genocide in the process. One-man army delivering justice. And then there’s that infamous ten-minute jeep ride. I didn’t skip it the first three (?) times.

[b]Story and Symbolism[/b]

The story ended up impressing me the most. I absorbed it with genuine delight. I jumped through every bizarre hoop Kojima set up to unlock secret missions and true endings, and I did it willingly.

Even in its hidden content, Kojima’s symbolism shines through. For example, having to defeat Quiet seven times to bring her back. MGSV’s narrative layers reward obsession, and I was happy to indulge.

But what struck me the hardest weren’t the twists or secrets - it was the way the game occasionally drops all irony and reminds you that war isn’t spectacle, but pain you can’t dodge. There are moments when all the absurd freedom of MGSV suddenly collapses into one blunt truth: sometimes you have to do what no one else will. There’s no stealth workaround, no trick, no mercy. Just a decision so heavy it shakes even a legend.

I could talk about the story for hours - but in short, it delivered some of the most memorable emotional beats.

[b]Are there any downsides?[/b]

The game isn’t flawless. Some difficulty spikes - for example, the sudden encounters with the Skulls - felt unfair. The game barely prepares you for them, forcing you to improvise under pressure. Still, these moments rarely overshadow the experience as a whole.

[b]The Vibe[/b]

MGSV has a unique atmosphere - a blend of absurd humor, heavy seriousness, and the exhausted PTSD-soaked aura of a war veteran clinging to whatever humanity he has left.

The game is serious, but it also knows that serious faces are just masks. And sometimes it mocks that seriousness - intentionally and beautifully.

It’s a rare combination: emotional weight and mechanical freedom.
A world where every mistake, every triumph, every random act of stupidity becomes part of Big Boss’s legend - or whoever you choose to be.

Metal Gear Solid V was one of my most anticipated games ever. I loved MGS4 and I was ready for whatever Kojima cooked up next. And honestly, the first act really is a masterpiece. Even with that, I still put over 100 hours into it because I honestly loved it. I just wish we could have seen the complete vision, especially since there are concepts floating around for Act 3. Still, this is absolutely worth playing and it runs great on the Deck.

review_text:
An Absolute Stealth Masterpiece with Lore That Bites Back

Hours Played: 30
Rating: 10/10 (Highly Recommended)

If you're looking for the ultimate evolution of the stealth-action genre, look no further than Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain (MGSV TPP). I’ve sunk countless hours into this game, and it remains one of the most rewarding and purely fun experiences on Steam.

Gameplay: Freedom, Funk, and Fulton

At its core, MGSV is an awesome stealth action 3rd person shooter, but the level of player freedom it offers is unmatched. The open-world environment is a sandbox where every mission is a puzzle with infinite solutions. Do you go in during the day with sniper support? Or infiltrate at night using only CQC and silenced weapons? The choice is yours, and the moment-to-moment gameplay—crawling through the dirt, tagging enemies, and pulling off the perfect extraction—is incredibly polished and satisfying. Plus, who doesn't love attaching a balloon to a sleepy goat and sending it up to space? The base-building and recruitment systems are addictive and give a real sense of growth and consequence to your actions.

Story & Lore: Crazy, Wild, and Essential

For series veterans and newcomers alike, the story here is a triumph. The lore is crazy and wild in the best ways. Hideo Kojima takes classic Metal Gear themes of war, identity, and loyalty and cranks them up to 11. The narrative is often complex, sometimes confusing, and always deeply rewarding. It features some of the most memorable characters and jaw-dropping twists you’ll find in gaming. Don't worry if you haven't played the previous games—you'll still enjoy the ride, but if you do some reading, the sheer scale of the Metal Gear universe is intoxicating.

The Verdict

If you are looking for a game with rock-solid third-person shooting, unparalleled tactical stealth, and a truly unforgettable story, then this is the game to get. It's a technical marvel, a mechanical masterpiece, and a truly essential piece of gaming history.

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a bizarre game to try and talk about because it sits at a particularly awkward crossroads. It is arguably one of the best games of the 2010s, taking the exploding genre of open world games and cracking it open by offering players extreme freedom in the way they tackle tightly-designed missions. This push and pull between developer intention and player choice could have easily been a tension point, but ultimately works because a player’s ability to complete a level is entirely based on their own resourcefulness and creativity. Within a player’s toolkit are nearly infinite ways to complete their mission objective, with the player only being limited by the tools they have on-hand or intrinsic objectives such as high mission rankings or a desired low kill-count. These are all great attributes and are a huge part of why MGSV is hailed today as a masterpiece. 

The issue with that framing is that MGSV doesn’t exist in a vacuum. Kojima’s Metal Gear is perhaps the single most-revered game series in existence, with each one being hailed as a masterpiece of gameplay, storytelling, and technical achievement. As impressive as MGSV is, it is directly competing with its predecessors, and the comparison is not particularly flattering. As fun, slick, and rewarding as its action is, the game’s storytelling and pacing ultimately disrupt that experience in a way the game never really manages to outrun. 

The game is ultimately paced to have two distinct arcs, with one being the effective “main” conflict and the second arc laying the groundwork for how MGSV connects to the rest of the Metal Gear franchise. Of these two arcs, the first is by far the most-interesting, containing 32 episodes with the majority of them containing important story content. While most of these missions are excellent, some really fall short of expectations, leading to a few duds in an otherwise excellent list. And, honestly, if you wanted to check out after Mission 31, I don’t think I would blame you. Most of the story of MGSV is, perhaps intentionally, disjointed, hazy, and dreamlike, intentionally setting up conflicts that connect to the rest of the series. These are largely presented in the form of Mother Base cutscenes, forming a clear and present disconnect between the gameplay and story that the game never manages to shake. 

Perhaps the game’s biggest sin is that it’s simply meandering and filled with padding. Out of the 51 missions (prologue included) present in the main game, 24, by my count, are either challenge missions with specific restrictions in-play, or are completely unrelated to the game’s story and are largely disposable. Most of these missions exist after the conclusion of the first arc; another reason the second arc manages to fall so flat. Of the 19 missions present in the second arc, 15 are of this type, leading to an abysmal 4 main story missions past Mission 31. And, of these 4, one is a partner mission and another is a repeat of a previous mission, just with extra story context added in. This is a huge part of why the back half of the game feels so empty and underwhelming: because nothing you do makes a difference. Much of this is also because the game’s actual conclusion, Mission 51, was never properly finished. There’s a lot of documentation out there online about it, and I would encourage you to check it out if you’re left wanting more after Mission 48. Based on unfinished cutscenes and concept art, it probably would have been the game’s best mission, and I doubt it would have left fans disappointed. 

But even among many of these complaints, I actually have quite a few positive things to say about the game’s story and presentation. I might be alone in thinking this, but I REALLY enjoy MGSV’s codec tapes. The game has a TON of extra context and information contained in tapes players unlock as they progress through missions. Most of these are either designed to further elaborate on cryptic elements of the main game or provide historical context for the larger story, but some of them are also there just as fun side-stories that play out on Mother Base. Of these, my favorite has to be “The Hamburgers of Kazuhira Miller,” which unironically got me to really appreciate fast food burgers. If you can sit through that and not crave a Bic Mac, you are stronger than I am. That said, none of these tapes are necessary for story purposes and you can just as easily ignore them. Perhaps the most-interesting and important tapes are “The Truth” tapes found right at the end of the game. If you’re interested in what happened to the main cast of Snake Eater following MGS Ground Zeroes, they’re worth a listen. 

I also really enjoy how much side content the game has. The game has 157 Side-Ops, most of which are simple side-missions that can be done in the open world. Most of these showcase MGSV at their best, with specific small goals in play that players can attack in any way they want without having to worry about score or rank. There are plenty of duds in this selection, but the vast majority are pretty engaging, with missions like “Eliminate the Armored Vehicle Unit” and “Extract the Highly Skilled Soldier” taking up much of the list. As interesting as side content is in the main world, some of the most-interesting content available takes place on your iDroid. The game has a particularly engaging system of progression, where you work to grow Mother Base and even online content where you can compete to infiltrate each-others bases. I’m not personally that interested in MGSV’s online side, but it can be a huge draw for extending playtime. I know a few people that have put more hours into the game’s online content than the main game, so it’s definitely worth a look.

I want to maintain that MGSV is still one of the best games of its time and absolutely worth a playthrough. But I also want to point out the game’s failures, as I don’t think it is as easy to recommend as many of its series predecessors. If the lack of a solid conclusion to its story and overall emphasis on freedom sound like potential deal-breakers for you, I’m not sure you should bother. Still, even with all its shortcomings, I think MGSV earns its title as a Metal Gear Solid game. It’s not a perfect entry, but it’s a brilliant action game that manages to brilliantly balance an intricately crafted world with deep and rewarding gameplay.

review_text:
An [okay] game. The worst game in the MGS series, not worth playing unless you are really, really interested into MGS. The story itself provides a lot of context that bridges the MGS timeline. However, it takes so much time just to get those pieces feels awful, and storytelling is not like the other MGS games.

The reason behind all the flaws in the game is "Live-Service" and mixing online with Single-player elements. The MB Coins, aka "Time-savers" are especially criminal and a huge red flag for any game. The presence of time-savers means game elements are designed to entice the purchase of the coins, making game elements less interesting, rewarding less to take up more of your time. Personally lost all interest in "collecting" and side activities and did not bother with them after I realized that I could just swipe my credit card instead of playing the game.

[h3] Story [/h3]

Completely disconnected storytelling, drop in from a helicopter, find the target, and extract via helicopter. Over and over, with just a few exceptions. The areas felt similar, and overall, each mission felt more and more repetitive.
The story itself felt fragmented and incoherent. Some of the main missions offered little to no story, felt like a chore.

Disconnected storytelling, fragmented story, 'time spent' to 'story delivered' ratio is awful. Nothing like the previous games.

[h3] Replayable Missions [/h3]

This was especially weird and contributed to the issues with the story and storytelling. Nothing wrong with them being replayable, except each mission had the same loop of drop-in-> infiltrate ->exfiltrate, which caused the lead to the previously mentioned story issues.

On top of that, each mission had optional objectives that, often, especially early, were impossible to complete within a single run. Additionally, those optional objectives were hidden until you complete the mission. FURTHERMORE, each mission had scoring with fat rewards, which required effectively to focus on the main objective and doing it fast (apparently, cutscenes do not stop the "mission timer", leading to a lower score). 

Thus, if you want to complete all objectives, you have to play the second time since you don't even know them until you complete the mission. The later in the game you replay it, the easier it is to complete them. So, maybe you just focus on the main objectives so you complete that S rank, but without the prior knowledge, it's harder to get the S.

This scoring and unknown secondary objectives are awful if you just want to play the game and enjoy the story. If you play on your own pace and explore/discover some of the objectives, you are likely to neither complete all nor get the S. Meaning you'd have to replay the mission twice to get S and objectives. The S giving a fhat reward means you should simply ignore and go for the main objective, but this is just awful.

[h3] Base management [/h3]

Base elements are nice, until you realize, hey, why would I spend these 5 minutes collecting 100 "materials" if I can swipe my card and get 10000? Hey, why do I bother clearing outposts that take so much time and risk so much to extract a few A or A+ soldiers if I can swipe a card and get 45 of them?

Without swiping your card, you are likely to fall behind on the development and which will simply make you spend more time to complete the mission instead of making it more challenging.

The only other downside for the research and progression was that it leaned heavily into offensive rather than stealth, offering little to make stealth easier or something different than using a tranq-pistol.

I still can't believe they cut Kaz and Snake's sex scene, I'll never forgive Konami for releasing this game in such an unfinished state smh 😔

All jokes aside during my playthrough on both PS4 and PC I've had an absolute blast playing! For anyone who's played Ground Zeroes it's especially the same gameplay system but more refined and versatile with each and every mechanic blending in with the next leading to one of the most dynamic stealth games I've played in recent memory, the open world does a great job serving as a somewhat dense play ground for the player to experiment with the mechanics the game provides especially when you slowly begin upgrading Snake to expand upon his arsenal of weapons and gear opening up new opportunities but sadly while the open world is one of it's biggest strength it's also one of it's biggest flaws as overtime the more you play the game it ends up detracting from the game in a way as most of the areas are somewhat empty excluding animals in the wild and enemies in small enemy outposts you can encounter not to mention the lack of indoor areas or even regular civilians you can encounter randomly roaming around doing certain tasks that could potentially save from enemies which could've helped to spice up the gameplay a bit more.

Sadly the biggest offender for me is the story or more accurately what parts of the story wasn't cut from the game leading up to release. Don't get me wrong I love the story and what Kojima and his team were trying to do from the writing (despite how cheesy or poorly written some of it was as per-usual knowing Kojima games) and acting all the way down to the incredible cinematography leading to some of the most beautiful and expertly crafted shots I've seen in a game let alone one that came out in 2015 all thanks to the Fox Engine I especially loved what I thought was supposed to be the final scene after beating Sahelanthropus, note that I said "what I thought was supposed to be the final scene" since apparently there was more that Kojima and his team wanted to do with the story but never got to do due to conflicts with Konami at the time leading to the game getting released in a somewhat unfinished state (which is unfortunately very clear later in the game as you're forced to replay certain missions again along with a few new story related missions) and the cancellation of Silent Hills after Kojima left Konami which still pains me to this day and the worst part being that Konami proceeded to let a potentially great game engine essentially go to waste aside from using it to create a somewhat meh looking survival MGS game and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ MGS3 themed pachinko machine.

While I'm happy to see that Konami has learnt from their mistakes and have started doing the Metal Gear Solid and Silent Hill series justice again while Kojima is off creating his own horror game and whatnot I'm still a bit sad that we never got Kojima and Del Toro's Silent Hills and that the Fox Engine was kind of left to the sidelines, I guess you could say we got something akin to a 'phantom pain'. 

On a more positive note despite my problems with the game I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Metal Gear Solid 5 and highly recommend it to anyone interested in the stealth genre, as someone who grew up with stealth games I had a blast playing this and think you will too! I hope this helps :D

review_text:
Stealth gameplay, perfected.

I was a bit worried at first by the open world nature of the game; I thought it wouldn't lose focus as an experience. However, every area is carefully constructed and, while you have to revisit some areas a few times during the campaign and the side missions, you get an increasing amount of tools to toy with and you can discover several paths to your objective. Some of these tools may feel a bit unserious, but MGS as a series has always had unserious moments.

Some call the main story unfinished, and I'm not sure I entirely agree. It does feel a bit rushed in the second part; either that, or the pacing of the intended storyline is a bit wonky. It's hard not to get invested in the events of the story (especially if you've been along for the ride for the entire MGS saga) and to get attached to the characters, both recurring and new. There are some strong, emotional moments which had a big impact on me.

It runs well on relatively dated hardware. I had no remarkable issues during my entire run. 

Bear in mind that the game tries to strongarm you into an online PvP component, but there are workarounds (some a bit obscure). Some monetization choices are a bit sketchy, especially in a paid game.
I'm glad it's there, as a true endgame once the story is complete to keep playing around with increasingly powerful tools, but it's not for me. You can access a PvE equivalent of the PvP component, but I felt it doesn't scale as well in difficulty compared to player-crafted bases.

All things considered, it's a must play if you are into Metal Gear; for everyone else, the story can get very convoluted to the point of feeling esoteric, but the stealth gameplay is still likely unmatched.

[h2]Short Summary[/h2]
A somber quest for revenge fueled by loss. Build an army and become a legend in a tactical sandbox with unparalleled freedom and a deeply addictive progression loop.

[h2]The Takeaway[/h2]
[list]
[*] [b]What Works:[/b] Unparalleled gameplay freedom, a compelling progression loop, and immaculate cinematic presentation.
[*] [b]What It's About:[/b] A grim quest for revenge that explores themes of loss and the personal cost of becoming a legend.
[*] [b]How It Plays:[/b] A system for player expression and a management loop where field operations fuel the growth of your mercenary army.
[*] [b]Core Tone:[/b] Somber and grim, with a profoundly melancholic mood that permeates the entire experience.
[*] [b]What to Consider:[/b] The story is incomplete and ends abruptly, with its narrative delivered sparsely through optional audio tapes.
[/list]

[h2]Main Review[/h2]
[b]METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN[/b] is a story driven by revenge and defined by loss. You are the commander of a shattered mercenary army, tasked with rebuilding your forces to strike back at those who took everything. But this is also a personal descent; you are a demon, a man consumed by a quest for vengeance. The narrative explores the cost of this retaliation and what it means to become a legend, forcing you to build a myth while grappling with the phantom pain of your past.

The gameplay is a masterclass in tactical freedom. Its strength is a near-perfect loop that serves as both a system for player expression and a compelling management simulation. You will infiltrate enemy outposts using a vast arsenal of tools, extract soldiers and resources to grow your army, and build your offshore headquarters into a global power. Every action in the field directly fuels your growth, creating an addictive cycle of progression that is presented with stunning cinematic flair.

The world is defined by a somber and profoundly melancholic tone. Its vast open landscapes are often lonely, reinforcing the grim nature of your quest. The narrative is delivered at an episodic and fragmented pace, presented like a television series where the full story must be pieced together from brief cutscenes and hundreds of optional audio logs. This structure creates a sense of detachment, perfectly mirroring the protagonist's own phantom pain.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
This game is for the player who finds story in action and values gameplay systems above all else. It is not for those who require a complete, satisfying narrative, as its story ends abruptly and is delivered in a sparse, unconventional manner. If you want one of the most sophisticated and empowering tactical sandboxes ever created, [i]then this is a mission you must accept.[/i]

review_text:
If you’ve ever wanted to crawl through 200 meters of Afghan sand while a cassette player blasts ’80s jams and a horse defecates on cue, Metal Gear Solid V is your destiny. This isn’t just a stealth game — it’s a confusing fever dream where you can Fulton-extract both goats and Soviet soldiers into the sky while somehow keeping a straight face.

The plot? Oh, it’s simple. You play as Big Boss, a man with a horn in his head, missing nine years of his memory, and the moral compass of a guy who can either tranquilize everyone or turn half the map into balloon art. Every mission begins with a dramatic helicopter ride and ends with you asking, “Wait, who are we actually fighting again?”

You’ll recruit an army of soldiers who shout “Boss!” in unison every time you sneeze, run a military base that apparently funds itself through bear kidnapping, and fight an evil organization that communicates entirely in metaphors. The stealth is brilliant but also optional — since you can ride a flaming unicorn, call in an airstrike, or just wear a cardboard box and still somehow fool elite soldiers.

Kojima’s love for cinematic storytelling is here in full force: 20-minute cutscenes explaining why revenge is bad, followed immediately by a mission where you punch fire demons with robot arms. Thematically consistent.

By the time the credits roll (for the fifth time, because every mission has credits), you won’t know what The Phantom Pain actually is — emotional trauma, unfinished plotlines, or the literal pain in your wrist from micromanaging Mother Base menus.

But despite the chaos, it’s addictively fun. Few games let you sneak into a compound, steal a tank, airlift a sheep, and end with A-Ha’s Take On Me blaring through your helicopter speakers. It’s tactical espionage art.

Final Verdict:
10/10 — would extract another goat.

It took me a while to come around to liking this game between the overly-long introductory cut scene interwoven with mere seconds of gameplay followed by a starting mission that throws you into the deep-end face-first; but once I found my footing, it was actually a pretty fun experience. Once you play long enough get the stealth down and unlock the base-building elements and/or, alternatively, long enough to unlock the grenade launcher for when things go sideways, it's pretty exciting. 

Mark all your targets, sneak in, knock out a guy, sneak around some more, throw another guy to the floor to knock him out, sneak around some more, accidentally alert the guards because they catch you mid-animation knocking out another guy while sneaking around, pull out grenade launcher, blow sh*t up, run half a continent away long enough for the enemy guards to forget you ever existed, and then sneak around some more.

There was one mission that kind of annoyed me because you have no choice but to fight some elite enemies to secure the target vehicle and said enemies will destroy the target vehicle if you try to just run away with it, but other than that, there was never a moment where I hit the point of "eff this game" and threw my controller out a window once I actually knew what I was doing--And thank goodness for that, because I only had the one window and it now gets very cold in the winter.

As for the story....Meh. It's a Metal Gear Solid prequel, so on top of the plot being overly convoluted and pushing the suspension of disbelief to its limit, you kind of already know how things will turn out for everyone.

Иронично, что эта игра способна вызвать фантомную боль у игроков, так или иначе опробовавших предыдущие части. Посмотришь с одной стороны: вроде как, картинка приятная. Изумительное ядро геймплея, чего в жанре не появлялось толкового ещё со времён Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, отличная графика, очень воодушевляющее начало, как всегда хорошая озвучка и кадры постановщика. А с другой: абсолютно ненужный открытый мир, тотальная недоработка многих аспектов игры и вездесущий гринд, проигнорировать который -- выстрелить себе же в ногу. Это уже не говоря о достаточно "фантомном" сюжете, убрав который из основного таймлайна Metal Gear Solid мы ничего не потеряем, и даже больше -- сохраним его целостность, не прибавляя лишних вопросов. 
С геймплейной же точки зрения всё, на первый взгляд, замечательно. Ровно до тех пор, пока вас не будут ставить в тупик странные обязательные условия. Предположим, что вы решили пройти игру никого не убив, путём полного стелса -- купили себе снайперку, стелс-броню... и в какой-то момент вам на голову падают генномодифицированные "черепа" с интересными мета-человеческими способностями, которые бесцеремонно ломают ваш стелс и требуют от вас большей огневой мощи или гаджетов, которыми вы не располагаете. И что же делать? Просто сбежать, увы, не вариант. Вот и приходится почти у конца миссии прервать её, поставить на разработку всякие пулемёты да гранатомёты, а пока они разрабатываются (что, конечно же, занимает время) идти гулять по пустому открытому миру. Вот так вот.

Всё бы ничего, но это случилось после Ground Zeroes - игры, которая будучи по факту демо-версией, на голову лучше основной The Phantom Pain. В ней есть этот самый кор стелс-экшен геймплея, вместо пустого открытого мира -- детально проработанная база с огромной долей интерактивности, а гринд заменён на реиграбельность -- словно Hitman, только на основе локального стелс-геймплея.
Считать ли плевком в лицо то, что такой хороший потенциал был заменён недоработанным гта-клоном вперемешку с жрпг -- каждый решит для себя сам. И я даже не обижен тем фактом, что вторая половина игры это повтор всего, что было в первой, нет. Просто я ожидал от Metal Gear Solid немного не этого. Ground Zeroes показала, что серия движется в новом направлении, но The Phantom Pain взяла и сделала резкий поворот на 180 градусов, по сути повторяя MGS: Peace Walker, но уже более масштабно. А стоило ли? То, всё-таки, была игра на PSP, где гринд оправдан в полной мере. А тут?

“Metal Gear Solid V — симулятор шпиона с синдромом белки”

Начал играть, думаю: «Ну всё, я легендарный Солид Снейк, тень войны, мастер стелса!»
Через 3 минуты: случайно выстрелил в козла, охрана подняла тревогу, вертолёт с неба, я лежу в кустах и свистом пытаюсь заманить собаку. 🐐💥

Игра учит терпению и позору одновременно.
Ты 20 минут крадёшься, ползёшь, идеально обдумываешь каждый шаг…
И потом какой-то солдат на вышке замечает твой ботинок — и всё, оркестр, сирена, ты снова в бегах, с криками “QUIET, ВЕРНИСЬ!!!”.

Кстати, о Quiet.
Когда она рядом — всё идёт идеально.
Когда её нет — я попадаю по себе, взрываю грузовик, и теряю коня в болоте.
А потом нахожу его в небе — потому что я, видимо, отправил его домой через FULTON. 🐴🎈

Фултон вообще — лучшее изобретение человечества.
— Поймал солдата? Отправь в космос!
— Танков боишься? Отправь в космос!
— Козу жалко? Отправь в космос!
Я реально устроил космическую ферму из всего, что шевелится. 🚀

Каждая миссия начинается с фразы:

“Будь тихим, будь незаметным.”
И заканчивается криками, взрывами, пожаром, и мной, бегущим по базе в трусах, потому что костюм сгорел. 🔥

Сюжет? Глубокий, философский, драматичный.
Но я ничего не понял, потому что всё время отвлекался на то, как ДДОГ украл у меня гранату и убежал в кусты. 🐶💣

Итог:
11/10.
Симулятор спецагента, который не знает, что делает, но делает это стильно.
Игра, где можно шпионить, падать, гореть, дружить с лошадью и случайно отправить самого себя в орбиту.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain — это не игра. Это образ жизни, запах пота и взрывающаяся база. 💥🕶️

review_text:
Amazing gameplay wrapped in a world that forgot a bit of its soul.

The Phantom Pain is a really fun and technically impressive game. The controls, mechanics, and overall gameplay are some of the best in the series — everything just feels smooth and satisfying. From a technical side, it’s near perfect. They clearly put a ton of work into how this game plays, and it shows.

That said, it’s missing the soul of a Metal Gear game. It doesn’t have those funny voice acting moments, the weird humor, or the wild personality that made the older games stand out. It feels a bit too modern, sometimes even kind of dull.

Another thing that really disappointed me was the change in voice actor for Big Boss. Instead of bringing back the legendary David Hayter, they went with Kiefer Sutherland. It was an odd choice that never quite felt right, and honestly, they could have easily had David back. His absence takes away a bit of that familiar Metal Gear charm and emotion that defined the older titles.

If it didn’t tie into Peace Walker or the larger Metal Gear timeline as well as it does, I’d probably find this game frustratingly hollow. The story connection is what gives it meaning — without that link, it would feel like a beautiful but empty shell.

There are a few goofy voice acting moments sprinkled throughout — little callbacks to the older games — but they’re rare and usually show up in unexpected spots.

One of the game’s biggest flaws is how repetitive the missions can get. It’s cool that the world is semi–open world and lets you approach objectives however you like, but after a while, it starts to feel like you’re doing the same things over and over — extracting people, killing targets, sneaking into bases, or stealing supplies. It’s fun for a time, but it can wear thin when missions lack deeper variety or stakes.

Spoilers ahead:
I really liked the twist that the “Big Boss” you play as isn’t actually him, but a doppelganger — and that he’s the one who ends up being killed in the very first Metal Gear game. It’s a clever retcon, and I think that’s very smart on their end… or, well, Kojima’s end.

Overall, The Phantom Pain is a fantastic game that nails the gameplay but misses some of that classic charm and weirdness. Still, it’s absolutely worth playing if you’re a fan of stealth games or the Metal Gear series in general.

My personal score 8/10

[b]MGS V: The Phantom Pain is likely one of the best games ever made. This is despite the fact it’s unfinished, making it a somewhat diamond [strike]dog[/strike] in the rough.[/b]

The game’s presentation is near immaculate. The visuals are fantastic — still outclassing many modern releases. The cutscenes (of which there are plenty) feel like old cinema, something Kojima clearly wants to make. And the soundtrack is a chef’s kiss to the 80s.

The gameplay is perfect. Perfect AI, perfect gunplay, perfect stealth, perfect systems that just come together in a perfect way. It feels like Kojima’s final love letter (knowing he was tired of making these games and hoped this would be his last) to the fans. Perhaps the only disappointment is its open world: within missions, it’s designed wonderfully, but outside them it’s the size of an ocean with the depth of a puddle. There simply isn’t much to do apart from a seemingly endless amount of repetitive side-ops. Afghanistan suffers less from this than Angola. However, would the game feel worse as a linear experience? Most likely.

The story is both finished and unfinished. We get a conclusive ending to [spoiler]Skull Face and XOF[/spoiler], but all that remains of the ending for [spoiler]Eli and Sahelanthropus[/spoiler] is concept art. For me, this isn’t a deal-breaker — I wasn’t invested in Kojima’s Lord of the Flies subplot and found the [spoiler]child soldiers[/spoiler] more annoying than impactful, both narratively and mechanically. Otherwise, the story is excellent.

When you’re done, your last step is the Last Day in Outer Heaven fan comic.
[i]Thank you, Ahab. And goodbye.[/i]

In a twist that probably everyone but me expected, WE ARE ALL V (Venom Snake). We carry on Big Boss and Kojima's legacy even when they no longer can, we hold them in our hearts and let them breathe again through the stories we create in this wonderful game.
I give Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain a 10 out of 10.

review_text:
V Has Come To

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is both a masterpiece and, in some ways, a disappointment.

On the gameplay side, it is one of the most polished and reactive open-world stealth sandboxes ever made. The core loop is endlessly satisfying. Kojima Productions doles out tools, gadgets, weapons, and upgrades in a way that keeps you hooked. Unlocking new development items to experiment with never gets old. The Fox Engine still looks great even a decade later, with tight controls, smooth animations, and a level of detail that makes every infiltration feel special. Weather, time of day, guard routines, buddy support, vehicles, and Snake’s prosthetic arm all feed into each other to create endless emergent gameplay. Sneaking into an outpost with Quiet covering you or slipping past patrols in a sandstorm with D-Dog never loses its thrill. Ground Zeroes was the proof of concept, and this is that idea fully realized.

The story is where MGSV falters. The prologue is one of the strongest openings in the entire series. For a while it feels like the setup for Kojima’s most ambitious narrative yet. But the pacing doesn’t always hold. Story missions can be captivating, but others feel like filler. Side ops are fun and resource grinding is addictive, yet it is easy to fall into that loop and drain momentum from the plot. There is less of the urgency and high stakes that defined earlier games. Exposition is tucked into cassette tapes, which fits the tone but risks being ignored, leaving some players to miss key context until long after it mattered. Recycled missions and unresolved story threads weigh down the second half, and the absence of cut content like “Mission 51” leaves the whole thing feeling unfinished.

Presentation is still outstanding. The Fox Engine remains impressive, and while Afghanistan and Africa aren’t the most varied open worlds, they stay engaging thanks to their detail and interactivity. The sound design is stellar across the board. The score hits hard, and licensed 80s tracks blasting from your helicopter or through your Walkman during infiltrations give the game a nostalgic edge. It is a game that sounds as good as it plays.

The Phantom Pain is arguably the greatest stealth sandbox ever made, wrapped around a slightly unfinished plot. As pure gameplay, it is unmatched. As a Metal Gear saga entry, it is brilliant and somewhat frustrating. Even with its flaws, my time with it was unforgettable. Warts and all, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain still stands tall as a titan. It is simply one of the best video games ever made.

Recommended.

Incredibly good game. Probably the best open-world stealth game I've ever played. It makes TC: Wildlands or any of the Far Cry games look like a McDonalds playground in comparison.

So many options and different ways to tackle outposts and missions. Even after 100 hours there were still tricks I hadn't learned, like throwing inflatable decoys of yourself (yes the game has those, and the enemy does as well) on enemies to knock them out. The enemies will have conversations, sleep at night, and switch posts at specific times. They also react to weather changes like rain and sandstorms. All of this can be used to your advantage. But be careful, as the enemy's equipment will dynamically change to counter your play-style!

It's been banged to death but the story is definitely lacking. Although a lot of cool story threads are established, none of them are resolved in a satisfying way. Important parts of the story are relayed through cassette tapes that you have to listen to on your own. The game also ends very abruptly in a way that will leave most players feeling confused. But as long as you know this going into the game it's not [i]that[/i] bad.

Despite this there are so many stand-out moments in the game, from the amazingly intriguing intro (watched a streamer play it and bought the game immediately afterwards) to [spoiler]rescuing Miller and bringing him back to the base, the Sahelanthropus, the outbreak in the base quarantine zone, and the big twist at the end[/spoiler]. The cinematography on display in the cutscenes is also great. Beautiful lightning and attention to small details. It really does feel like a movie at times. Also a character in one of the cutscenes acknowledged the camera man which I thought was pretty funny.

The graphics are great as well. Some of the textures are kinda low-res, and the game came out before PBR was really a thing. But it makes up for this with excellent use of lightning, solid character models, and effects like depth of field to hide any imperfections. It's locked to 60fps but can be unlocked by changing one of the config files. Check out tha guides.

I'm planning on exploring the rest of the Metal Gear Solid franchise now that I've play this one to completion. I've never really understood why the series was so beloved and just thought it wasn't for me, but I've changed my mind now.

review_text:
So, MGSV is one of those games where the gameplay and the story feel like two different beasts. On one hand, it’s probably the most fun, polished stealth sandbox ever made. On the other hand… it’s also the weird, messy end of Kojima’s saga, with some heavy twists about Big Boss.
Gameplay – The Sandbox of Dreams. This is where MGSV shines. You’re dropped into huge open maps (Afghanistan, Africa), given a bunch of tools, and told: go wild:
-Wanna sneak in at night with a tranquilizer pistol? Do it.
-Wanna roll in on horseback with C4 and blast the whole base to bits? Also valid.
-Fulton balloons to kidnap soldiers, tanks, even sheep? Hell yeah.
It’s like stealth Legos — the freedom is insane, and the mechanics are so tight you’ll spend hours replaying missions just to try new stuff.

Story – The Phantom Pain (of Missing Pieces)
Here’s where it gets controversial. MGSV is meant to be the “missing link” between Snake Eater/Peace Walker and the original Metal Gear games. But it never quite feels finished. A whole chapter got cut, and you can feel it.
Still, what’s there is dark. You don’t just play as the noble hero anymore. You see Big Boss’s fall — or more accurately, his transformation into the legend/tyrant we knew was coming.

Big Boss’s Dark Turn
Without spoiling every mission detail:
-The game plays a long con on you. You think you’re playing Big Boss, the legendary soldier. But actually? You’re his phantom — a body double molded into believing he is Big Boss.
-The “real” Big Boss uses you as a decoy to protect himself and his vision. Which is brilliant, but also super shady.
-This twist flips the whole saga: the Big Boss we idolized? He was already heading down a manipulative, almost villainous path. The “phantom” just carried part of the burden for him.
-It’s Kojima saying: heroes don’t just fall — they drag others down with them.

Ocelot – The Frenemy or Best Fiend Forever and Ever
And then there’s Ocelot. This dude has been the ultimate double (or triple) agent the entire series, and in MGSV he’s… surprisingly chill.
-He trains you, helps you run Mother Base, and honestly feels like one of the few people you can rely on.
-His loyalty isn’t really to you, the Phantom, but to the idea of Big Boss. He knows the truth and still plays along, because he’s obsessed with the legend.
-Their bond is this strange mix of friendship, manipulation, and respect. You get the sense that Ocelot sees himself as the keeper of Big Boss’s myth, making sure it survives no matter how twisted it gets.

The End of the Saga
MGSV doesn’t end with fireworks. It ends with a gut punch.
-You realize you were never “the real Big Boss.” You were the pawn, the phantom, the guy who takes the fall so the legend can live on.
-The “real” Big Boss walks away in the shadows, already preparing to become the warlord we fight in the first Metal Gear.
-It’s not a clean ending — it’s a haunting one. The saga doesn’t close with triumph, but with betrayal, identity loss, and the sense that the legend of Big Boss was always built on lies and sacrifice.

Final Verdict
Gameplay: 10/10. Best stealth sandbox ever made.
Story: Half-finished, but the parts we got are dark, powerful, and redefine the saga.
Big Boss: Not the hero we thought — his descent into shadow is brutal.
Ocelot: Loyal to the myth, not the man. His bond with Big Boss is weirdly tragic.

If you play it for closure to the saga, it’s more like a gut-wrenching reminder: legends are built on pain, lies, and phantoms. And remember We are Diamond Dogs

review_text:
Giving this game a thumbs down really hurts.  Metal Gear Solid on PS1 is my favorite game of all time, and I have played through it more than a twenty times.  I also grew up playing Metal Gear on the NES, and despite its flaws, still hold it in the highest regard.  I think Hideo Kojima is an absolute genius, but like many people of his caliber, needs someone to bring him back to earth from time to time.  From what I can see, no one was there for this game.  After MGS1, I was never really able to connect with this franchise.  Despite this, I played through all of them until I hit a wall with MGSV.

The stories got more weird and the characters failed to live up to my expectations as time went on.  MGS2 pulled the rug out from under Snake fans, and while MGSIII brought the series back to the bad ass hero, I think the die on Metal Gear was already cast.  The last straw for me was seeing my beloved character Snake as a weak old man in MGSIV, but still, I stuck with the franchise because it’s Metal Gear.  How could you not???

Perhaps it was because of the limitations of the PS1 that I found the first 3D game so enthralling.  It had some oddities, but it always felt grounded in a reality that seemed like a slightly warped mirror of the real world.  While I didn’t like a lot of games in the series, I still count myself as a fan and, like all Metal Gear games, I bought MGSV day one.  I got through about 20% before I gave up and it fell into distant memory.  I recently restarted and had every intention to finish, but I just can’t trudge through the game anymore.

All this said, there is a lot to love here.  What this game gets right is absolute perfection.  There is no denying that Hideo Kojima is a master of storytelling.  Unfortunately, where MGSV lags is an anchor that weighs down the overall experience.

The Good:
	1.  Kiefer Sutherland is a great replacement for David Hayter, who was for me the definitive voice of Snake.  I even appreciated that they went a different route to distance Big Boss from the MGS1 Snake.  He delivers a masterful performance and really shines in every scene.
	2.  The storytelling and direction are top notch, though not without hiccups.  When he is down to earth, Kojima knows how to create an amazing narrative.  While it does go out into space from time to time, the good parts outweigh the bad.  If you can cut through the crazy, there are great themes and truly mind altering experiences.  
	3.  The stealth and general gameplay mechanics are solid (pun intended).  I had some trouble with previous MGS games, but this one clicks, after some work.  It is not easy to master, but once you do, you can kick some serious butt in any fashion that you choose.  Stealth or commando is totally up to how you choose to play.  This type of freedom was attempted in other games, but always fell short in comparison to the limitless options in MGSV.
	4.  The choices for environment, weapons, companions, and overall customization are unmatched. While this can also be a detractor at times, Kojima made such a deep sandbox game, that I have to put this in the win column.  It can be overwhelming, but gives you absolute freedom.  It’s an open world game that lets you explore in a fashion that feels real and organic.  
	5.  The music isn’t a huge focus in this game, but when you do get to hear it, you tap your foot. Kojima is a big fan of David Bowie, as am I, and his taste in music is spectacular, IMO.  He even names the troop “Diamond Dogs” after the famous Bowie album.  While I don’t think this is Bowie’s best album, I can see why Kojima loves it, particularly because of the ties George Orwell’s 1984 novel. Kojima is a deep person, and his love for this resonates with me.  Beyond just the Bowie songs, the music kicks all kinds of ass.  The tapes you collect throughout the game are incredible 80s jams that really leave a mark.
6. This is a Hideo Kojima game!  If you are a fan, you will love it at its core, even if you don’t like some elements.  If you’re not a fan, you can still get a lot from this game.  Nobody spins a yarn quite like Hideo Kojima.  Even if you’re not a story driven person, once you get past the forced narrative, the game will knock your socks off.  There is always something about Metal Gear games that makes you want to go a little further.  As much as I want to trash the departure from what I love, Kojima makes yet another addictive game.

The ???
	1. You will play it and love or hate it regardless of what I say.  Every minute will make you feel something, and this is what makes Kojima an absolute master.


The Bad:
	1.  From the start, you are forced into a tutorial that drags on, and that kind of sets the tone for the whole game.  I get that you need to learn the mechanics, but most games give you a short cutscene and some prompts.  MGSV makes you run through 30 minutes while hobbled, with stopping points every few minutes.  This is one man’s opinion, but I think Kojima is too far up his own ass.  On my replay, I found myself angry with the game because it wouldn’t just let me play. You MUST got through the narrative.
	2.  While often a plus, the side missions of this game eventually become a hot mess and fall into the trap of (insert open world game here).  You can go anywhere and do anything, but it is usually the same thing over and over.  It took me a while to realize that the side missions were repetitive.  What makes it worse is that the game keeps throwing them at you without you knowing… until you do.  I played a ton of them until I kept seeing the same spots over and over. Eventually I realized that it was the same problem I had with Spider-Man on PS4.  I beat up the same enemies to no end, so the game keeps me occupied.  The worst part is that missions and drops in this game cost money, so you can eventually end up upside-down whilst trying to level up.
	3.  Too much choice becomes a massive problem in this game.  Mostly this comes down to base management, but creeps into other areas as well.  I get that the devs wanted to earn your money, but this becomes too much game, IMO.  At times it feels like a mashup of tower defense and 3rd person shooter.  There are moments when the game forces you to engage with mechanics that don’t gel with what some of us want.  If I could ignore this part, I would give it higher marks, but the game always tries to draw you back to base management and keep you connected to a PVP game.  See next point.
	4.  Constant connection is not a thing that should be in single player games.  I get it for games that are all multiplayer, but when the core is single player, there is no reason to be connected.  This game actually punishes you for being disconnected by reducing the amount of money you have.  For me, this is one of the biggest sins in this game.
	5.  Clunky gameplay haunts MGSV.  I did say in the “good #3” row that the gameplay was solid, but that was in comparison to other MGS games.  MGS games have always been a bit off for me, and while this was definitely improvement, the gameplay fails compared to other games in this category.
	6. Kojima is too far up his own ass. I said it more than once here, because I truly mean it.  This man is super talented, and IMO one of the greatest storytellers of all time, but someone needs to knock him off his perch.  Metal Gear Solid was branded on the box as Tactical Espionage Action.  I’m not saying you can’t go deeper, but you created a game where the hero was a cross between Snake Plisken and James Bond.  The character doesn’t have to stay a 2D trope, and can evolve, but moving him to a secondary character or a weak old man does not sit well.  This game fixes much of that over time, but you still suffer in earlier areas due to being a newbie.  Stop making Snake feel like a character that just fell out of the womb.

Metal Gear Solid 5 is my favorite of the entire series. This is the ultimate stealth sandbox game full of countless gadgets and weapons to play around with. Also, there is no reason for a majority of your play to avoid killing anyone, so you will actually make use of your entire arsenal. You only need to constrain yourself when going for the best ranks in each mission. In addition to the totally revamped gameplay, the management simulation aspects return from Peace Walker, but greatly expanded. Even if you find these aspects of the gameplay tedious, I encourage you to engage with them to their maximum and capture tons of soldiers to fill Mother Base and your FOBs. I personally thought it was a lot of fun and makes this game truly feel expansive and ambitious.

Somehow, they managed to tie up almost every other game in the entire series into a nice, neat little bow. Despite taking a step down in terms of great characters, make no mistake that this is still absolutely the Metal Gear you have come to know and love, but with brand new gameplay. There is a sorrowful lack of David Hayter in this game. However, everyone, Kiefier included, puts on a great performance. Kazuhira Miller and Huey in particular are standouts and also series alumni. 

I just want to throw in here a big JUSTICE FOR KOJIMA. It is well known that this game was not actually completely finished to his satisfaction and to most of the fans as well. The ending is kinda sudden and a bit of a letdown. Still, the rest of the game is absolutely incredible, despite the shortcomings I still think it is my favorite. And Kojima is probably my favorite game director of all time. Only Sam Lake an Hidetaka Miyazaki give him any competition. 

The multiplayer mode was pretty fun back in the day, but I don't think it works anymore. The FOB stuff, however, is still functional today. Still, you can do absolutely everything in the single player without worrying about that at all and that's really the best part of this game.

review_text:
A Masterpiece of Gameplay, Haunted by an Unfinished Story

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain represents one of the most significant dichotomies in modern gaming. It is, without a doubt, a masterpiece of open-world stealth and tactical freedom, yet it is equally a victim of its own ambitious, and ultimately incomplete, narrative.

The Good:

 *Unparalleled Gameplay: The core gameplay loop is near-perfect. The sheer number of ways to approach any objective is staggering. Whether you go in guns-blazing, use stealth to Fulton extract every last soldier, or creatively deploy support items like decoys and sleeping gas mines, the game never limits your creativity. It is a sandbox of espionage excellence.

  *  The Mother Base Management: The meta-game of building and expanding your Mother Base is incredibly addictive. Researching new gear, managing your staff, and sending combat units on offline missions adds a deep and rewarding strategic layer that perfectly complements the field operations.

  *  Polished to a Mirror Shine: The Fox Engine is a technical marvel. The game runs flawlessly on a wide range of PCs, with silky-smooth performance, stunning visuals, and incredibly responsive controls. This is a port done right.

The Flaw:

  *  The Phantom Story: For a series known for its complex, cinematic narratives, the story here feels fragmented and incomplete. The second half of the game relies heavily on mission replays, and key plot threads are either resolved abruptly or left entirely unanswered. You can feel the absence of Kojima's final touch, leaving a narrative "phantom limb" that long-time fans will acutely sense.

Verdict:
Despite its narrative shortcomings, the 100+ hours of gameplay are so exceptionally crafted that they are impossible to ignore. This is a must-play for any fan of action or stealth games. It is a five-star game in its mechanics, haunted by the ghost of what could have been a perfect narrative. Highly Recommended.

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is not a game, but a set of crutches, fragments, and unfinished ideas glued together just to sell you something.

Storytelling comes through dragged-out episodes, especially in the beginning (I don’t want to watch Snake flying and landing for half an hour every time - it just wastes my time). And those constant “Directed by Hideo Kojima” credits completely kill the atmosphere.

The plot is delivered in pieces, with no integrity. One whole chapter is just cut out — I didn’t even realize the ending was the ending, ahaha. Storylines are abruptly dropped. The conflict with Eli and Metal Gear just vanishes. Tapes replace cutscenes. Key story details are thrown into audio logs. Zero and Cipher are barely shown, even though the plot was built around their influence — they remain “off-screen.” It feels unfinished. The game ends as if you stopped watching a TV series halfway through the season.

After mission 30 the copy-paste begins: the same missions but on “Extreme,” “Subsistence,” or “Total Stealth.” That’s not new content — just artificial padding. Side ops are nearly all the same (rescue a prisoner / capture a base). The huge maps of Afghanistan and Africa are actually empty. Outside of missions there’s nothing to do no interesting activities, random events, or a living world. The game is dependent on online features, and offline players get a stripped-down experience, left grinding repetitive side ops.

Still, the game does have strong points. There’s huge freedom of choice: you can complete a mission in dozens of different ways. The advanced AI adapts - enemies start wearing helmets, setting up spotlights, reinforcing guards. Everything ties into tactics: environment, weather, time of day, gear, companions. The atmosphere of the “80s war” is enhanced with the music of that era (tapes, radio). And you really feel like you’re building an entire army (which made it heartbreaking to have to shoot your own men during the outbreak mission).

In the end: an engaging start to the game wrapped in a mess of broken story and gameplay.

++ Cinematic cutscene direction and presentation
++ Great visuals
++ Interesting characters 
++ Interesting story with great twists/moments and very interesting themes (war, language, identity)
++ A ton of (optional) additional lore and story (tapes)
++ Very fun and deep gameplay, large freedom/customization
++ Very attentive and "smart" enemies

- Mission 45

This game has been sitting in my library for 10 years now. I finally got around to playing it.
The most noticeable feature are the cutscenes (directed by Hideo Kojima!!), which were almost like a movie, with interesting camera angles, slow motion and crazy stuff happening. The overall visuals are great with a lot of details. While the characters and the story are interesting, and have some great twists, a lot of story/lore is dedicated to hundreds of tapes. This is optional, but I would still recommend listening to them. The story also tackles interesting themes like: war, language and identity. Language especially really made me think and was a big part of the story. Another big selling point is the very large player freedom with a ton of customization, tools, weapons, buddys, vehicles, etc. You CAN play however you want to, but stealth is still the focus. This is reinforced through the very fun, deep, and responsive gameplay and the attentive and "smart" enemies, which you can collect like pokemon and put them into your base.

The bad points concern the big, empty open world. This is especially bad in the first map: Afghanistan, where there are unscalable mountains and guard posts everywhere, making traversal a pain in the ass and a waste of time. What do you do in such big, empty open worlds? You drive for a few minutes, and play very similar and repetitive side missions. Call a helicopter, and extract. Again. And again. And again. Making this game into an open world was a mistake in my opinion: I would have preferred linear missions with less time wasters, while experiencing the great story in a better way. Just like, let me think... EVERY MGS GAME BEFORE THIS!? Another big negative point concerns the infection mechanic. It was a novel idea, I admit. I still had to google, WTF was going on, an then had to check 500 soldiers... The next negative shoutout goes to Mission 45: fighting 5 tanks, which eat 4-6 rockets from my upgraded RPG, while (randomly?) oneshotting me, was more resets combined, than I had in this game UP TO THIS POINT! The last negative points concern the technical side: First there are no advanced sound options for anything. Second: this is just a bad port, there is no mouse support in menus and the hints still use controller inputs, which helped me nothing, being on KBM.

Play for the great gameplay, cutscenes and story, don't waste your time with too many side missions.

I have a few issues with this one. 
1) The game does not support ultra wide resolutions. This is a big turn off for be because I find the massive black bars on the side of my screen very distracting. I consider this a minor issue because most players won't run into this.

2) There is an FPS lock at 60 FPS. I have a PC that can run this most likely at my monitors refresh rate of 144Hz, so let me run the game at 144 FPS. I don't really think this is an issue but wanted to mention it for anyone that would have a problem with it.

3) During the pro-log it would tell me to pause the game to go look up how to take cover. This alone took me out of what should be an intense moment while you are sneaking around trying to escape. This is very minor and most likely not a problem if I would have been playing with a controller.

4) I found all the perspective changes as you are going through the pro-log very jarring. A good example is when you crawl under a bed it would switch into first prison view and then back to third when you crawl out. The one worst one for me what when you are hiding from the guards looking for you it switched from your perspective to the guy leading you out of the hospital. Sure it kind looked cool from the angle the set that scene for those 10-20 seconds, but very unnecessary to switch the view. This is a little more of a major issue for me.

5) There was too much show don't play in the short time I played. What I mean is it didn't really feel like I was playing as much as I was just watching. Let the player be the one to shot the sprinkler to put the fire out. It just felt like every 2 minutes it was some sort of cut scene.

I do know that there is a way to edit the files to unlock the frame rate and make the game run at a ultra wide resolution, but on PC we shouldn't have to do this. I also understand this is going to come off as complaining to complain, but this was enough for me to not be able to enjoy the game. I do know that this is considered one of the best stealth games out there and I'm kind disappointed that the pro-log was such a big turn off for me.

[quote][b] Rating: 9/10 [/b][/quote]
For a long time, I was looking for games similar to Wildlands. I love that one. Now, I regret why I didn't play this before. It's been in my library since years and always ignored, among 100s of other.

For a open world game released in 2015, its graphics still hold up to my standards. Unlike modern slop games, this game runs fantastic even on old 1060. Game is capped @60 FPS, but you can easily overcome with LS Frame Generation or mods. 

[b]They totally nailed the gameplay aspect of this game[/b], reminds me of Wildlands but only more tactical. Like, your suppressors break after a limited use. You can silently interrogate enemies for information. You can blend in your environment with cartoons, camo dress, sandstorm, etc. If you approach in stealth, you can't rely on mindless shootings like we do in other games lol. You have to engage your mind. Now don't get the idea that this game is realistic, cuz it isn't. [b]It's just fun.[/b]

If you fail stealth? You can always resort to violence and it's legit fun. [b]They nailed shooting mechanics too.[/b] In fact, its faster and more efficient lol. But enemies adapt to you. Use too much combat? You'll see more armors. Use too much sniper, you'll face more sniper. So on. It's open world and there are a number of ways you can deal with an enemy. It's up to you. Bombard them with heli, order your pet or buddy, maybe one man army?.. you can. Game is sci-fi. You can imagine the rest.

[b]BUT it's not all roses and sunshine.[/b] While the actual cutscenes and story in general is great, [b]they completely broke the immersion after Mission 31 (Chapter 1). They mindlessly 1:1 copied many story missions with same cutscene[/b] but different difficulty or parameters and it truely hurts. It was like a joke. Like preparing a delicate art after spending several days and then just randomly throwing it in waters. I have never seen any game as badly rushed in other half. There are total 50 missions so you can imagine how many levels they make you play again just for sake of completion. [b]Game is way better off without them, LITERALLY.[/b]

Plus, to understand the part of story and its logic, you need to listen several audio logs. Now, that was a real torture too. I know it's optional, but I don't want to torture myself to understand them lol. Make less of these please. It is very unsatisfying ending. Plus these repetitive missions break the immersion so much that it only amplifies that. No, it did not feel like prep for new entry. It just felt unfinished to me and I guess most players out there too. [b]But the core game is so good that EVERYONE COMMENDS THIS.[/b]

[b]Just make sure to play Ground Zero first as it's a 1 mission banger prologue.[/b]

I'd "heard of Metal Gear Solid" back in the day, but never really got around to playing it. 
Naturally, skipping to the last entry in the series made the story somewhat confusing at times.
However, I was absolutely blown away in terms of the actual game and experience.
Highly recommend.

GRAPHICS:
May be slightly dated now, but it holds up well and the look / feel is beautifully done.
A lot of players can likely max the settings out to ultra and still get buttery smoother performance too.
The visuals and overall design create a vivid and captivating world (day/night, Afghanistan and Africa).
(TIP: turn off the HUD, on-screen markers and crosshairs for a 10x more intense and immersive experience.)

GAMEPLAY:
Incredibly thought out and detailed.
Enough realism to make it fun and immersive, but not so much that it's tedious. 
It blends the stealth and action elements perfectly to suit whatever play style you prefer.
You can make it extremely challenging and intense (max stealth), or you can become a one-man army.
Whichever you choose, the movement and action is fluid, but the combat rewards strategy.
The mechanics are intricate yet smooth and allow you to gradually hone your ability once you get the feel.
(Tip: change the "slow movement" key to Left ALT.)

In all, an extremely enjoyable and impressive game that feels high-quality throughout.

Also, there are several "to be continued" screens in arbitrary places...

This brings us to another point, the gameplay loop. The story is so forgettable, that halfway through, I had to read up on what had happened. This is mostly due to the available Side Ops. Unfortunately, I am a stubborn completionist and did all of them, 150 to be precise. A selected few are necessary to unlock more main missions the rest of it are the same three or four kinds of missions just at various locations. After the third repeat, it gets incredibly boring. The open world areas feel incredibly bland as well.

The game also has an online component which is okay-ish. You are able to infiltrate other people's bases and steal resources. This was a nice break up after the 10th soldier extraction in the row. Still, the options to modify one's defences are fairly limited. By the fifth FOB you invade, you've seen all the layouts and enemy positions.

Now for some more gameplay, and that is the main selling point, why I recommend this game: You have a multitude of options to approach missions and tasks. That is, when they work. The gameplay feels clunky and more often than not, certain mechanics don't work consistently. I'm not talking about change in enemy behaviour, according to your playstyle. That's absolutely fine and continuously ups the difficulty. It's more the way, that weapons aim-correct even if you don't want, that snake is unable to walk over the slightest of ledges, and more often than not, inputs are either ignored or delayed. Still, it works *most* of the time.

Lastly, Quiet: There could have been a dozen other ways to tell Quiet's story without leaving her with a bikini top and torn leggings. The forced camera angles on her cleavage feel cheap and I don't seem to be the only one with that kind of sentiment, as there are mods to put [i] more [/i] clothes on her.

That is, barely, a 6/10 for me. In my eyes it's playable but can easily be a frustrating clunky mess. If you can get this game with a major discount, you should.
