review_text:
As Big Boss stands before the sea, ashes in hand, I sit here having finally 100%'ed one of my favorite games ever. There's a lot of contention in this entry that's steadily eased as time has gone on, as more and more information behind this game's development came out, it's hard to imagine that destiny did not favor this game's creation in spite of every reason it should have failed. In this, I feel Kojima's team realized how bittersweet this game truly was, given Boss's only recent revival in Delta.

I could talk about the infinitely replayable gameplay made better by a dedicated community who have overhauled its limitations into a true sandbox. I could talk about the obviously unfinished story brought about by Konami's (and Kojima's) frequent managerial mishandling. I could mention that half this game's core feature was cut into an online base raiding mode akin to Shadow Of War's. But ultimately, none of that matters in the face of the final product presented which is a complete realization of MGS's gameplay loop in a setting that directly evokes the game's themes of independence and loss.

Metal Gear Solid V is not a happy game. It asks a lot in its somewhat uneasy handling of various topics from child soldiers to nuclear deterrance as well as a lot of patience in listening to the supplementary lore that is provided as you progress. Behind those barriers, an expertly crafted story of revenge and war almost, almost reaches its mark. The elephant that stomps all over this game's cohesion left a sour taste in the community's mouth, almost insultingly so. Though, that was [i]nine years[/i] ago and as we've come to grow into this pain, this loss, it's almost thematically appropriate to believe that Kojima knew what would come from the constant development issues. In that way, it's nothing new to say that the loss of Act 3 is appropriate to the game's themes but that disregards the finality that's present. In many ways, this is Snake's best and most polished showing.

The gameplay, if you're unfamiliar, is "Tactical Espionage Stealth!" This rings true, mostly, in game. Many missions will task you with infiltration, exfiltration or elimination as you build up Mother Base into thousands of soldiers' home. This development, as expected, comes with a complete retinue of gadgets and abilities. You'll be allowed to take a curated set of allies into the field, their uses all varied and adjustable by the gear they carry. The magic of MGSV is the interlock of these two systems. Every soldier, weapon or resource you extract using your patented Fulton Recovery Device reinforces your abilities in the field, grants you intel, or enables new methods to interact with the base building. In spite of how developed it is, I (greedily) wish there was much, much more to get lost into but you can casually play this game and experience a good wealth of this development. 

The aesthetic quality of the game is held up remarkably well by Kojima Production's proprietary "FOX Engine." Everything is picture perfect and the complete package puts many, many modern devs to shame. I would say this is the best looking MGS ever, which is a heavy compliment given the fidelity of Delta's lighting/texture work. Kojima's art team absolutely came prepared for this project and it is a beauty to play.

The short of this long winded rant is that this was my first MGS and I understood nothing. The gameplay alone compelled me forward and now that I've gone back with a greater understanding of the series, I think it is utterly remarkable. Don't play it first, play MGS3, play Peace Walker, then come back and you'll be prepared to see the end of Naked Snake's prime. Truly, unequivocally amazing. I could not say enough about this game.

review_text:
[h2]  Narrative & Game Play [/h2] 
Rare is the 3rd person action shooter that I can wholly respect but not enjoy. My 10 hours spent in this game were enjoyable, but something about the stealth, shooting, and base building mechanics didn't click with me. Nor could the bombastic narrative keep me engaged. I truly believe this is a personal preference as I fully recognize this is a highly polished and well crafted stealth action game.

The story is wild, and if this is your first Metal Gear game like me, it might be worth trying to watch a lore video before hand because this game will explain literally nothing and the first chapter is bonkers. I do think I had a hard time connecting to our protagonist as a lot of people talk at me, but he doesn't say much at all. While this can let you transpose your personality onto him, its hard to understand the reverence he's earned. However, all of the writing in this game has been quite carefully considered and I fully recognize there is a good story to be told here. 

Game play is slow, methodical, and a bit silly. There are many ways to approach your objectives with a huge variety of weapons. My biggest disconnect is likely that I was very bad at this combination of stealth mechanics, didn't get much better in my playtime, and struggled to get back into it. I believe the game could be a lot more enjoyable with the later unlocked weapons and gadgets, but the grind to unlock them is pretty steep.

I do hope that one day this game will click for me, but for now, that's where I have to leave it. 

[h2]  Performance & Technical  [/h2] 
The game runs well and looks great. The options menus are pretty expansive and rebinds are plentiful. It seems this game was quite well optimized.

[h2]  Value & Consumer Practices [/h2] 
If you like the core game play loop, this is a highly tier pro-consumer game. There is a metric ton of content in the base game, even when it was full price at launch. There are a huge variety of weapons & cosmetics to be earned, licensed music, and a highly polished game. 

As stated above, the game is a bit grindy which may push time sensitive people into buying the coin DLC. The rest of the DLCs are inexpensive, but they're low value cosmetics and emotes which. review_text:
Since its release almost a decade ago, MGSV is the only non-multiplayer game I've consistently and regularly come back to.
After over a thousand combined hours on consoles and steam, I can confidently say that it is one of if not the best stealth game ever made. 

There are some elements that are notably weaker than previous MGS games, namely the open world providing too much downtime, the intrusive base management + resources, and surprisingly the lack of a consistently present story (regardless of its quality). The first two can easily be minimized through modding, and the story does still fulfill the minimum requirements to connect Peace Walker and the original Metal Gear, so I'd argue that these elements affect the experience as much as you let them.

While lacking some of the charm of previous games, the gameplay of V takes all of the best elements of the series and blends them together perfectly. Every situation allows for countless different approaches, to the point where you could even forego stealth entirely and play the game as a third person shooter. Unlike previous games where you could really only sneak through or clear from afar, the scale of the areas allow you to do both of those methods and anything in between, not to mention enemies being able to adapt and react to your playstyle. On top of that, the scoring system adds strong replayability that previous titles lacked, though it can be too strict at times. 

The games age hardly shows at all. The only noticeable factor is characters heads being obviously computer generated compared to more modern AAA titles, but other than that, I could believe that it was made in 2030 and sent back to release in 2015.

If you enjoy stealth shooters at all, MGSV is the first and best title I would recommend, and it also functions as a solid starting point for the series. 

9/10

review_text:
Ah, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. A masterpiece wrapped in mystery, stealth, and just a dash of madness. Hideo Kojima's swan song with Konami is, without a doubt, one of the most ambitious and open-ended stealth action games ever crafted.

Gameplay – 9.5/10
First things first — the gameplay is bloody phenomenal. You’re dropped into massive, open-world environments (Afghanistan and Central Africa) with absolute freedom to approach missions however you like. Stealthy takedowns, guns blazing, air strikes, or a tranquiliser dart to the head — it’s your show, boss.

The controls are tighter than ever, and the variety of gadgets you can use (cardboard boxes, decoys, silencers, Fulton balloons) adds so much tactical flavour. It’s one of the rare stealth games that doesn’t punish you for improvising — it encourages it.

And let's not forget your buddies: D-Dog (what a good boy), D-Horse, Quiet (a deadly sniper in a bikini), and D-Walker — each adds a unique playstyle and charm.

Story – 7/10
Now, here’s where things get a bit wonky. The game kicks off with an explosive, surreal hospital escape and a powerful narrative setup. You’re Venom Snake, rising from a coma and building a new army — Diamond Dogs. Sounds like classic MGS stuff, right?

But the plot fizzles out a bit after the first act. Missions start to repeat, and the infamous Chapter 2 feels unfinished. Many reckon Konami pulled the plug on Kojima before he could truly finish the story, and it shows. That said, the twist involving who you really are as Snake? Brilliant. Pure Kojima.

Visuals & Sound – 10/10
Visually, the game is stunning. The Fox Engine brings every grain of sand and blade of grass to life. Animations are silky smooth, and weather effects like sandstorms genuinely affect gameplay.

The soundtrack is also top-tier — from the haunting main theme to ‘80s classics like The Man Who Sold the World and Take On Me on your in-game cassette player. And let’s not forget Kiefer Sutherland as Snake — a controversial casting, but he plays the strong, silent type rather well.

Content & Replayability – 9/10
You can pour hundreds of hours into this game. Building your base, capturing soldiers, developing tech, replaying missions for better ranks — it’s endlessly rewarding. The multiplayer component (Metal Gear Online) is decent too, though it’s not the main draw.

Final Verdict: 9/10
Despite its messy story pacing and an ending that feels more like a to be continued than a proper send-off, The Phantom Pain is a stunning achievement. It’s one of the finest stealth-action games ever made, and a fitting — if bittersweet — farewell to Kojima’s iconic series.

In short: Brilliant gameplay, tactical freedom, and deep mechanics make this a must-play — even if the plot leaves you with more questions than answers.

in other games in the series where the shooting mechanics are HORRIBLE, plus the added mouse and keyboard support, this is a big upgrade
the buddies are really cool, and being able to use them for recon, combat etc etc was really fun, although sometimes overpowered. at the same time, having quiet snipe from the rooftops while i infiltrate while the enemies are distracted was incredibly satisfying

mother base was.. fine. i didn't mind it in peace walker, because peace walker was a bit of an oddball at the time in terms of structuring it into missions and having the mother base gameplay etc, so i was willing to give it a pass. this time, it just felt like more of the same, except the added frustration of staff being moved on their own, and then when i did auto-sort, the added torment of staff being put into roles they were not accustomed for (like it putting an e rank in medical when it has a c in r&d, but someone with a c in both would be in r&d). very much liked being able to actually physically visit it, even if the drive / helicopter rides between platforms were really long.

the missions were also just fine. the majority of them consist of: sneak into area, grab intel/prisoner/kill target/follow target, move to secondary location if there was one, extract via heli. not really much variety. i understand that there probably wasn't too much room to expand due to the game being genre-specific, but in that case, a lot of them could have been side ops; most of them felt very inconsequential and filler-y. the times where it did stray from the formula, they, personally, weren't very fun and instead turned into big action shooter sequences involving blowing up tanks or fighting the skulls, sometimes forcing you to cast stealth to one side like in mission 45.

speaking of the skulls, again, they were okay. they were an intriguing challenge in the beginning, and were honestly kind of scary, but when the time comes to actually fight them, it just felt tedious, especially in the mission where you fight 4 of the armoured ones in the airport. i don't mind a challenge, but it should feel either a. fair, or b. like a puzzle. most of the time it was neither, and they were just a health bar to chip away at. also the sniper ones SUCKKK

the story is the thing i cared about the most going into this, because obviously, it's metal gear. again, it was fine, but had some weak moments. a lot of chapter 1 lacked agency for me, and it was just mostly meandering taking on odd jobs with the slight undertone of building again to eventually take revenge on cipher. then, they would just show up. the moments when questions were answered, or even the prosaic moments with characters simply interacting were really good, but there were some noticeable lulls. the pay off was pretty decent, but it didn't have as big a spectacle as it should have, personally. also sahelanthropus felt a little underwhelming, but it was cool to see how much it looked like rex.

chapter 2. obligatory "mgsv is unfinished" but it's true. chapter 2 has 7 new missions, a few side ops, and not much else going for it. cutscenes will just happen out of nowhere, sometimes they don't, and you have to look up the unlock requirements like it's a dark souls quest, and a lot of the things set up that feel like they have energy just don't really pay off (yes i am aware of mission 51 but it doesn't excuse it not being in the game.)

by the time chapter 2 wraps up, you play an entire mission again, which should have just been a few cutscenes, and the story just kind of ends. this was the game that was supposed to bridge peace walker to metal gear 1, but there still remains a hole for me personally. it's a shame it'll likely never be kojima coming back to fill it. 

overall, very good game, but it could have been much better had it had more time and not had the kojima-konami feud brewing during its development. excited to see its gameplay work in mgs3 (my personal favourite)

review_text:
Gameplay-wise, I found Metal Gear Solid V to be really impressive, although it didn’t necessarily need to be an open-world game. You can approach every mission in multiple ways, and there’s a great variety of tools to help you achieve your objectives.
Story-wise, the game is divided into two chapters. Chapter One is fantastic, really unique and creative in how it delivers the story through various forms of dialogue. The way the narrative gradually unfolds over time is also very well done.
Unfortunately, Chapter Two is a major letdown. It feels clearly unfinished. Some key story elements are left unresolved, and that seriously ruined the overall experience for me. I felt like I had invested a lot of time and effort into progressing through the game, only to be met with a response like: “Well, screw you, player. That’s it.”
It doesn’t feel like an intentional, fragmented storytelling method. It just feels incomplete. And that’s such a shame, because the gameplay and Chapter One were so cool...

So, MGSV is truly an awesome game, but it’s such a shame that Chapter Two wasn’t properly finished. In an ideal world, Konami would go back and fix that; then this game would be absolutely incredible.

review_text:
[i]"Why are we still here? Just to suffer?" [/i]
That line from Kazuhira Miller doesn't just serve as a meme—it's a thesis. Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is less a game and more a controlled fracture. A design marvel wrapped in themes of absence, identity, and the illusion of control. It throws you into vast, living environments—Afghanistan and Africa—that breathe with day-night cycles, dynamic weather, and AI that adapts to your tactics. Start using too many headshots? They'll wear helmets. Prefer night infiltration? They'll bring flashlights. The world watches and adjusts.

Mechanically, it's one of the best stealth-action sandboxes ever created. Movement is fluid, aiming is responsive, and nearly every approach to a mission is valid—stealth, assault, distraction, manipulation. Even something as ridiculous as Fultoning a bear becomes part of the plan. Everything ties back to Mother Base—your expanding home, your personal army. Every soldier you extract, every resource you capture, isn't just flavor—they matter. There’s an odd satisfaction in watching your FOB grow, in listening to recruited enemies now call you “Boss.”

And yet, for all its systems and mechanics, the soul of MGSV is quieter, more fractured. The narrative is disjointed by design. Kojima leans into what’s missing. Scenes unfold in cassette tapes. Conversations happen in shadows. You’re not just Big Boss—you’re a symbol. Or maybe an echo. The game never gives you full answers because it’s about loss, not closure. Chapter 2 is divisive: some call it unfinished; others see it as the point. You become a ghost haunted by the choices of others. You don’t get a real ending—because legends don’t.

Graphically, the Fox Engine still holds up. The lighting, the facial expressions, the terrain—they all feel real. The soundtrack is perfectly curated: "Sins of the Father," "Nuclear," and a sprinkle of 80s classics like "The Final Countdown" and "Take On Me" don’t just fill space—they frame it. And then there’s Quiet’s theme—absolutely devastating once context settles in.

Yes, it has flaws. Mission 51 is cut. Some missions in the second chapter are recycled. Microtransactions for FOBs feel like a publisher’s fingerprint on an otherwise deeply personal project. And Quiet’s design is… well, complicated. But none of it undoes the weight of the experience.

[i] “You’re going to have to choose. Whether to live as a man… or as a legend.” [/i] 
MGSV doesn’t guide you toward that choice—it traps you inside it. You play for 80, 100, 150 hours, building a legend. And in the end, it hands you a mirror.

It’s not perfect. It’s better. It’s honest. And it stays with you long after you uninstall it.

review_text:
(LONG REVIEW UP AHEAD, IF U HAVEN'T PLAYED THE GAME AND NEED SOME CONVINCING. READ!)

For years, Red Dead Redemption 2 was my favorite game of all time. Its graphics, atmosphere, story — unmatched. I used to spend days just fishing and hunting out in the wild without returning to camp, fully role playing in that world. But I think I finally found something better.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a masterpiece. I played it before Ground Zeroes, and to be honest, it was my first Metal Gear Solid game ever — and my first Kojima game too. I didn’t understand ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at first. The game literally starts with you in a hospital, blurry vision for five minutes straight while “The Man Who Sold The World” plays. I was confused as hell.

Then suddenly some psycho chick tries to kill you, a guy saves you, then a floating kid shows up out of nowhere, a dude made of fire tanks a shot from a tank and just shrugs it off. You escape, crash in an ambulance, and then a giant fire whale flies into the sky and slams into you. Then a guy on a horse picks you up and you shoot the fire dude with a shotgun and that somehow weakens him? 😂

It’s insane. It goes from super serious and badass to completely ridiculous, but that’s what makes it so brilliant. Kojima somehow bends tones in a way that shouldn’t work — but it totally does.
The characters have soul, even beyond the plot. The story deals with revenge, loyalty, war — but then you can fulton a sheep into the sky and it’s like, yeah, that’s just normal now. The freedom is unmatched. You can go full stealth or full warlord. I’ve never played a game where you can develop a chopper that blares music while flying over enemies — psychological warfare at its finest 😂.
The base building and army management is just as fun. You can assign people roles, send them on missions, or just beat the crap out of them on the brig and they literally thank you and salute you after. Its wild like are you dead the ♥♥♥♥ ass😂😂.

After every mission the game gives you cassette tapes you can listen to if you want, and they actually explain what was going on — why you did that mission, what happened, etc. I’m guessing it’s Kojima’s way of shortening the amount of cut scenes because people were annoyed by the long ones in the older games. You might play this game and not understand a single thing at first, but by the time you finish it, everything slowly builds up bit by bit. I love that.

And the gameplay… no game ever lets you seduce a Russian soldier in Afghanistan while you’re sitting in a cardboard box with an anime girl on it 😂. It’s simply hilarious.

And the cutscenes… ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. They're long (which I love), and the camera work is unreal. It’s like an actual war cameraman is filming — zooms, pans, close-ups, shaky cam during tense moments — all of it. The lighting, the dust, the smoke, it all feels so alive. Like you’re right there.

And of course, Kojima loves his women. He knew what he was doing with Quiet — she’s definitely sexualized, but her powers and the mystery behind her silence get explored in such a cool, satisfying way. She’s not just fanservice. She's a legit badass.

I know this review’s been long, but this game is just special. To me it’ll always have a place in my heart. I could keep going about how amazing it is, but we’ll never see the end of it, so I’ll just cut it here. I hope you have
as much fun and enjoyment as I did.


Even if you've never touched a Metal Gear game before — like me — it’ll blow your mind.

Story feels unfinished, especially in Chapter 2

review_text:
🎮 Gameplay (Non-Spoiler)
This game features one of the most satisfying and fluid gameplay loops I’ve ever experienced in a third-person shooter. Movement, gunplay, and general control feel incredibly polished. Even just exploring the open world is a joy thanks to how responsive and smooth everything feels.

That said, some key gameplay features are oddly locked behind specific story missions. Unlocking certain mechanics felt arbitrary and disconnected from any natural sense of progression. Still, from a pure gameplay standpoint, this entry is one of the strongest in the series.

🧠 Story (Spoiler-Free Summary)
This is where things get more complicated. The story has flashes of brilliance and strong themes, including political manipulation and the use of child soldiers, but the overall narrative feels disjointed and incomplete. Some plot choices seem designed to patch MGS lore, but in doing so, the emotional weight of your journey gets undercut. I still enjoyed the story all things considered, but only because its tied to Metal Gear.

⚠️ Spoilers Below
Click away if you haven’t finished the story.





The game ultimately reveals that you’re not actually playing as Big Boss, but as a body double who has been conditioned to believe he is. While this twist is interesting on paper, it makes a lot of your actions throughout the game feel hollow. It reframes the experience as a setup rather than a climax.

Huey’s character arc is one of the few narrative standouts. His descent into self-deception and guilt is handled well and adds genuine tension to the story. I've never seen someone lie so much the only one who still believes him in the end is himself, and also the entire world after a few years.

The reveal about Solid Snake killing a body double in the original Metal Gear, may satisfy some lore fans but feels like retroactive damage control. Many players hoped “Chapter 3” would tie things together, especially with the teased plot of Liquid leading a child-soldier uprising. That concept sounded amazing, but it never materialized. In my opinion, adding that content without trimming some of the repetitive late-game missions would’ve hurt the pacing even more.

🧾 Final Thoughts
From a gameplay perspective, this is nearly a masterpiece. If you’re in it for the stealth, action, and mechanics, you’ll love what’s here. But if story is what drives your love for the Metal Gear series, be prepared  have a premature ending patched up by audio logs.

review_text:
As a long time fan of the MGS series I really enjoyed this entry. It's very well optimised, looks beautiful for an older game and plays very well. The controls pretty are well thought out and feel fluid once you get used to a few of the odd mechanics. The story is fun and engaging even if not paced all that well and sometimes not very easy to trigger some story points.

That being said there were a few issues I had with the game which I will detail here (potential mild spoilers):

My biggest issue is with the helicopter rides in to almost every single mission. And just to say that there are about 50 main missions and 150 side ops. So, you're looking at nearly two hundred helicopter drop off and pick up sequences. Many times these rides in can last longer than the quick side op missions themselves. Don't get me wrong, the chopper rides are fun and add to the realism, but they should be optional or just optional for side ops that are not key.

Next is how you trigger a mission. Unless you are close to the side opp or mission, you will need to call in a chopper and activate the mission from the chopper. When at mother base you'll need to call a chopper for every mission apart from target practice. Again, this takes extra time.

Next was the achievements as I'm pretty sure that one or two didn't trigger as I don't have the complete all missions achievement even though I've done them all. I have done the two chapter two final missions, the one with Quiet and the Man Who Sold the World. That reminds me, one of the Quiet achievements is named incorrectly, it actually relates to a later mission.

The mostly optional cassette tape add a lot to the over all story and are worth a listen. However listening to them on mission means you will get intel radios over the top of the tape and miss sections, which is annoying.

Not sure if it's just me but the FOB missions wouldn't work. Also the online side of things seemed confusing and I never got to grips with that side of the game. Not sure if it is still live, I saw other player stats so it could be live.

Chapter two, apart from a hand full of missions, is just a rehash of chapter 1 but harder. Which felt very strange and messed up the feeling of progression.

lastly, development times. I have clocked 59 hours of game play so far and I still have lots of weapons and things to develop as they take days of real time to develop and you can only order so many at a time. Again, it adds to the realism of game but feels over the top, especially the yellow coloured online development items and crew missions.

All in all, a great game with lots of freedom and with plenty of great moments out on missions figuring out
complete them in your own way. But feels bloated and sometimes not very intuitive. There are some fantastic characters and I love how the story ties the other MGS entries together in a really cool way.

I recommend the game but I would say to be mindful that a lot of your time will be spent in the UI and on helicopter rides to and from missions. I believe mods can fix this, but I wanted the true experience, I will perhaps try them and aim to get the last 10 achievements I still have to unlock. Pick up the game on sale if you can and don't forget to get MGS Ground zeros too and play that first for the prologue to this main story.

Replaying it again after several years. Have played MGS 1, 2, 3, 4, Portable Ops and Ground Zeros prior. Brainchild of Hideo Kojima, who is now known for Death Stranding. 

Incredibly complex and moving story leading up to MGS 5. Kojima is a visionary when it comes to weaving historical fact with fiction and integrating his philosophies and perception of the evolution of technology. 

Previous entries had movie length long cutscenes explicating the above. Those worked in the 1900s and 2000s era of console gaming. Come 2015, people want less talk and more action, and this game delivers: 

The cutscenes are now significantly shortened, and exposition is relegated to cassette tapes that are optional to listen to. 

The Fox engine was incredible for its time, offering smooth gameplay on the PS3! It still holds up now and can rival some modern titles. 

The gameplay loop is addictively good, and fans of 3rd person action-stealth will thoroughly enjoy playing it. Incredible open-world game for its time that still holds up well today. Has many elements that encourage replay-ability. 

It may not be the complete experience Kojima wanted to deliver, given what happened between him and Konami. But the core elements of a great game are all present.

review_text: This is one of my Favorite games of all time. This one was controversial, it was loved by critics and fans alike, but the game is unfinished. Unfinished and still one of my favorite games? How? Well let me tell you how, this game has one of the greatest game play loops I have ever experienced. You have your own Mother base that you upgrade throughout the game and when you are ready you suit up for a mission choose your loadout and partner then you roll out at the time of your choice, you pull up on site and you are thrown into an open stealth sandbox where the limits of your company are the only thing stopping you. I like to describe the progression of this game in phases. Phase 1: building your base, kidnap a bunch of goons and convert them to your cause and build up your resources through missions and through on site procurement. Phase 2: collecting specialists to create special gear and build all of the equipment you will ever need. Phase 3: this is my favorite part of the whole game, sit back on your iDroid and scroll through all of your employees, 100s at this point and allocate who would be best where. Look at peoples traits and see how they can excel when placed in the best environment. Someone picking on their team members? Throw them in the brig, or just fire them. R&D not able to produce the quality of equipment you want? Pull some people from another department to produce the equipment you need. low on funds? Sell some of your procured rare resources. Enemies able to see you at night with their thermal goggles? Send your troops to destroy their suppliers warehouses to make it easier to be sneaky. The late game is a massive micromanagement simulator and you are king ♥♥♥♥ with your company at your fingertips and that is why I love it.

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain – The Game That Lets You Fulton a Sheep Into the Sky and Still Cry About Lost Brothers

How do I even begin to describe Metal Gear Solid V? It's not just a game—it's a masterpiece of storytelling, stealth action, open-world design, and tactical absurdity wrapped in a cardboard box. Literally.

✅ Story? Kojima delivers an emotional rollercoaster of revenge, identity, and war, blended with political intrigue and personal loss. It's gripping, dark, and philosophical—but somehow still finds time to let you extract goats via balloon.

✅ Gameplay? Silky smooth. Every encounter is a sandbox of possibilities. Want to go in guns blazing? Do it. Want to sneak past enemies dressed like a bush? Also valid. Want to knock out an entire outpost with tranquilizers, a cassette player blasting 80s pop, and your trusty cardboard box? My friend... welcome to MGSV.

✅ The World? Afghanistan and Africa are beautifully crafted and rich with detail. Dynamic weather, day-night cycles, enemy AI adapting to your tactics (yes, they'll start wearing helmets if you keep going for headshots)... it’s a living, reactive world that respects your playstyle.

✅ Companions? You get a wolf with an eyepatch, a sniper who breathes through her skin, a literal anime mecha, and a horse that can poop on command. What more could you want?

✅ Customization? You can customize your base, your weapons, your loadouts, your helicopter entrance music (shoutout to “Take On Me” and “The Final Countdown”). This is YOUR Big Boss experience.

✅ Hours of content? Hundreds. Side ops, base development, animal rescue (yes, there's a zoo), easter eggs, hidden tapes, full-on conspiracy theories. You can lose days here and not regret a second.

🎵 Soundtrack? 10/10. Kojima didn't have to go that hard with the 80s tracks, but he did, and I salute him.

😢 Downsides? Some story threads feel unfinished due to the game’s famously troubled development. But even then, what's here is still more polished and emotionally impactful than most full games.

Final Verdict: 9.8/10
Would Fulton my own friends just to play it all over again.

Funniest Moment: I once accidentally dropped a supply crate on a guard’s head mid-mission. Instant KO. Tactical brilliance? No. Hilarious? Absolutely.

If you love stealth, deep stories, massive replayability, and tactical gameplay that respects your intelligence—and also enjoy sending bears into the sky via balloon—then Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is the game for you.

Now excuse me while I replay Mission 43 and cry again.

I don’t know where to begin. One minute I was a mild-mannered gamer with a decent grasp on reality, and the next I was galloping across the Afghan desert on a horse that could poop on command, wearing a cardboard box, while a man literally made of fire chased me and a flaming whale exploded in the sky. That was the *first hour*. I have not recovered.

**Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain** isn’t a game. It’s a multi-dimensional psychological field trip hosted by a chain-smoking philosophical warlord named Big Boss who might be you but also isn’t, and your best friend is a sniper who only wears a bikini because she “breathes through her skin.” Science? Art? Madness? I no longer know.

At some point I airlifted a goat, a tank, an entire platoon of Soviet soldiers, and a toilet out of an enemy base using a balloon. I built a floating oil rig army from scratch, had regular Zoom calls with a parasitic linguist named Code Talker, and listened to 1980s pop songs while gunning down helicopters with a rocket arm. I think I’m the villain. I think *you’re* the villain. I think the real villain was the friends we kidnapped along the way.

The stealth? Immaculate. The gunplay? Silky smooth. The plot? Written by an alien who was trying to pass as a human but only watched David Lynch films. I have played 80 hours and I still don’t know who Skull Face is, or why I care, but I do. I CARE.

In conclusion: Metal Gear Solid V is the video game equivalent of waking up from a coma, finding out you’re missing an arm, and being told you now command a private military empire and must fight ghosts. You’ll laugh. You’ll cry. You’ll Fulton a sheep.

10/10 – Kojima is a genius and I need to lie down.

review_text:
MGS V: The Phantom Pain is equal parts brilliance and madness, and somehow, impossibly, it all works. It’s one of those rare games where you’ll be mid-infiltration, perfectly hidden, everything going according to plan… and then you call in your helicopter blasting Ride of the Valkyries while hauling an unconscious war criminal over your shoulder like it’s just another Tuesday. And it feels cool. Because it is cool.

The open-world stealth design isn’t just good, it’s revolutionary. Every encounter is a sandbox. Want to sneak in under cover of darkness with a tranquilizer pistol and your trusty wolf sidekick DD spotting enemies? Perfect. Want to crash through the front gates with a tank, a flamethrower, and a cardboard box covered in anime decals? Also valid. It’s stealth that respects your intelligence while letting you be absolutely stupid. And that freedom is intoxicating.

There’s this incredible tactile joy to everything: mounting a horse, scoping out an outpost, getting spotted and improvising your way out of it. Stealth here is less about perfection and more about flow. Make a mistake? You adapt. Or, you know, call in an airstrike. Same difference.

And then there's the Metal Gear weirdness: defeating Quiet by calling down a supply box on her head. Putting out the Man on Fire with a literal water pistol. Sneaking through the battlefield while your dog rips throats out next to you like it’s his birthday. Every mission has a dozen different stories waiting to happen, and somehow they all feel like canon.

Quiet, by the way, is more than just a gimmick, her boss fight is incredible, her role in the story is quietly (heh) powerful, and she makes for one of the most engaging companions in the game once you’ve earned her trust. Same for DD, who might be the most delightful murder dog in video game history.

It’s not flawless. Chapter 2 kind of collapses under its own weight, repeating missions like it’s run out of gas. But even in its weakest moments, Phantom Pain is still better than most games at their peak.

This is Kojima’s messy, operatic, absurd, unforgettable mic drop. It’s stealth-action sandbox perfected. Play it. Love it. Fulton it into your list of all-time greats, preferably while blaring 'Take on Me' from a cassette tape in the middle of a sandstorm.

And no, 'Invisible' by Duran Duran is not in the game but you can just download the song and put the mp3 file into the CustomSoundtracks folder in TPP's directory. Thank me later.

review_text: The Phantom Pain is a masterclass in open-world stealth gameplay wrapped in the tattered shroud of a story that almost, but not quite, lives up to the Metal Gear legacy. It’s one of the most addicting gameplay loops I’ve ever experienced: infiltrating outposts, perfecting your approach, extracting soldiers with balloons like a tactical Mary Poppins—it’s incredibly satisfying. The Fox Engine delivers fluid movement, dynamic encounters, and a degree of player freedom that feels revolutionary for the genre. Every mission is a sandbox, and the tools at your disposal are absurdly fun. Quiet, D-Dog, Fulton balloons, cardboard boxes; this is Kojima’s playground at its most mechanically refined. But where it excels as a game, it stumbles as a Metal Gear story. The narrative feels unfinished, with key plotlines unresolved and characters who should be pivotal ending up underdeveloped. If you came here expecting the dense, cinematic storytelling of Sons of Liberty or Snake Eater, you’ll get some of that, but not the same usual level. The cutscenes are sparse, the codec is gone, and Kojima’s usual philosophical weirdness is oddly muted until the very end. Still, even with its missing pieces, The Phantom Pain is a flawed masterpiece. It's a bold reinvention that sacrifices some of its soul for the sake of innovation, but what it offers in return is something truly special. It's not the Metal Gear we expected, but it's one we’ll never forget.

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a rare kind of game—bold, ambitious, and hauntingly unfinished, yet still a masterpiece of open-world design and stealth-action gameplay. It’s Hideo Kojima’s swan song with the series, and while it leaves behind as many questions as it answers, the journey is unforgettable.

You play as Venom Snake, a hardened soldier awoken from a coma and plunged into a world of private militaries, shifting alliances, and secret weapons. The story is dense, cryptic, and often told more through tapes and atmosphere than cutscenes—but when it hits, it hits hard. It’s not just a war story—it’s a psychological slow burn about identity, revenge, and manipulation.

Gameplay is where The Phantom Pain shines brightest. The open-world missions set in Afghanistan and Central Africa give players an unprecedented level of freedom for a stealth game. Want to infiltrate silently at night with tranquilizer darts? Go loud with explosives and airstrikes? Drop in on horseback or ride a cardboard box down a hill? All valid strategies. The control you have is exhilarating, and every mission feels like a sandbox puzzle with dozens of possible solutions.

Mother Base acts as your hub of operations, growing as you recruit soldiers, develop new gear, and invest in resources. It's a satisfying layer of progression that ties directly into your performance in the field.

That said, the game’s biggest flaw is its incomplete narrative. The second half feels rushed, and some storylines (including a major one involving a key antagonist) are left unresolved. It’s no secret that development troubles behind the scenes left their mark.

Despite its imperfections, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a triumph of game design—fluid, flexible, and endlessly replayable. It might not give you all the answers, but the depth of its gameplay and the power of its themes ensure it leaves a lasting impression. Phantom pain is a difficult game to review. Like a lot of Kojima's output it's insane, weird, genius and divisive all at the same time. It's the game on steam I've put the most hours into so I know I like it but I recently talked to someone who found it impenetrable so I felt like writing a review to just sum up my own thoughts on it. MGS5 is a 3rd person stealth action game that like the previous entries was always pushing the limits of what could be done with the visuals, story and gameplay.

It's the type of game where you ride on horseback, chasing down armoured vehicles and shooting them with an RPG. It's the kind of game where you spent 40 minutes carefully sneaking through a fortified base, past searchlights, mines, patrolling guards and vehicles only to get spotted right before the objective and proceed to blow someone away and then sprint like a madman with a POW over your shoulders as the entire world converges on you. It's the type of story where one minute you're debating whether to shoot child soldiers for blood diamonds and the next you're fighting a man on fire with a supersoaker.

It blends the serious with the absurd in everything it does in a way matched only by the yakuza series. Your prosthetic arm has a rocket punch. Why? because that's cool. You fight concrete zombies who can sprint 100MPH and air drop your dog because you miss him so much. Metal gear more than anything is a vibe. You can engage with it as a serious political thriller, as a military power fantasy, a philosophical treatise or as the stupidest, most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ up it's own ass musings of an auteur.

I can't promise you'll like this game and there are legitimate problems that even it's die hard fans will admit to such as it's rushed and incomplete ending due to behind the scenes meddling but frankly you shouldn't even start with this one. Play the earlier games like MGS1 or 3 and if you're still interested after finishing one of those then you're locked in. There's no getting off genius kojumbo's wild ride at that point.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain – A Masterpiece That Still Echoes in 2025
Rating: 9.8/10

Ten years after its original release, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain remains one of the finest examples of open-world stealth-action design. It’s a game that not only revolutionized its genre in 2015 but has aged remarkably well, continuing to inspire developers and captivate players in 2025.

Gameplay & Mechanics – 10/10
The freedom of approach The Phantom Pain offers is still nearly unmatched. Whether you prefer sneaking in under the cover of night, orchestrating silent takedowns, or going in guns blazing with heavy support, the game empowers you to play your way. The real-time dynamic systems — day-night cycles, weather, enemy morale — all blend together to create immersive, reactive battlefields. Fulton extractions and base-building remain surprisingly addictive even a decade later.

Narrative & Atmosphere – 9.5/10
While the storytelling can feel fragmented due to cut content and Kojima’s turbulent departure from Konami, the underlying themes of loss, identity, and revenge are still deeply impactful. Venom Snake's transformation into a legend is haunting, especially when paired with the melancholic undertones of "The Man Who Sold the World." The voice work, particularly from Kiefer Sutherland, is understated but effective.

Visuals & Sound – 9.7/10
Thanks to the FOX Engine, The Phantom Pain holds up astonishingly well graphically. From the sun-drenched deserts of Afghanistan to the rain-soaked jungles of Africa, every locale is richly detailed and atmospheric. The soundtrack — a brilliant blend of '80s classics and original score — amplifies tension and emotion with expert timing.

Legacy – 10/10
In 2025, MGSV is widely recognized not just as a great Metal Gear game, but as one of the most influential games of its generation. It paved the way for modern stealth design and open-world innovation. Its DNA is visible in games from Hitman to Death Stranding to Ghost of Tsushima.

Verdict:
Despite its imperfections and behind-the-scenes drama, The Phantom Pain endures as a landmark in video game design. It offers an unparalleled sandbox of tactical freedom, rich with nuance and atmosphere. If you've never played it — or if you're returning for a replay — there's no better time to appreciate this modern classic.

Score: 9.8/10

This may be one of my favorite games that I've ever played.

Typically (at least for me), open world games can feel too empty or too overwhelming. I find the stealth mechanics forgiving enough for someone like myself (a new Metal Gear player), yet the AI does not feel dumb enough that I get the impression I'm being pitied by the game. On some missions, it definitely does not pull its punches (those who played Traitor's Caravan early game, dealt with those dumb children in Blood Runs Deep, and tried to S-rank A Quiet Exit know what I'm talking about.)

All flaws aside, I find this game incredibly addicting and keep coming back to it. I love grinding all the side missions and side objectives, and have definitely gotten more than my money's worth.

review_text:
In terms of being a stealth action game, you will not find better game play anywhere else as far as i'm concerned. The moment to moment sneaking is tense, the world feels lived in due to excellent enemy AI and interactions between them. This is my 4th (5th if you count mgr revengeance) Metal Gear, and I think that this one easily takes the cake for the gameplay. I'm the biggest stealth fan in my friend group and they were subjected to me gushing about how much fun it was to sneak around, 

Going past the sneakiness, I do have to deduct points for the very disjointed story, as It was easily the weakest out of the ones i've played. not sure if this was directly due to the mission based design, but it probably didn't help.  I'm also aware that people say the game was rushed, and Konami didn't give Kojima and his team enough time to create a product that we could've seen. That being said though, This game did manage to get me to cry on *that one mission* and it definitely gets brownie points from me, because Its been a good while since a game has made me cry. 

Loving the gameplay so much, and also loving the idea of 100%ing games, I did go through the soul crushing process. Like I said the gameplay carries, but the sheer repetition of the side missions was unbelievable. They would've been okay had they not made you replay the same 15 or so side missions, UP TO 13 TIMES. My god i know they wanted to pad out the content, but that was the most tedious thing i've done in a good while. 

I also do think the forced "loud" sections were also not the greatest, as while i think the gunplay is pretty good, but the combat suffers greatly due to the movement. Snake would repeatedly get stuck on rocks that are like a 30 degree incline and just wouldn't go up. This definitely cause some frustration in both stealth and gunfights, and was just another obstacle I had to deal with while playing.

All that being said, I would consider this to be one of the best games I've played in a good while, despite my self inflicted suffering in going for the 100%. If you are a fan of the stealth action genre, this game is probably the best and most evolved you can get, at least for now. I'd give it a 9/10 with that last point being taken for a weaker story, and movement mechanics that did mess me up more times than I can count.

Listen, I only have 2 hours on PC but hundreds on Xbox circa 2016 and let me tell you something. This game is living proof that game developers have gone to utter ♥♥♥♥ since around 2020. This game looks better and runs so much better than games being put out for the last five years and is so in depth with content. With that being said, let me say a few things.

This was the last game I bonded with my brother over before he joined the military and I started college, it was hands down some of the best times in gaming we shared and brings back so many memories of how satisfied we were building up our separate bases and giving each other pointers to different things. It's so amazing that almost 10 years later, this game literally looks and feels as if it should have been released around today's time and puts so many games to shame.

The only MGS game I ever played before this was the first on PS1 when I was around 4 years old, so I have no idea what the lore was and jumping into it with no idea, made it that much more intruiging.

how could a very on par mil-sim structured game revolve around extremely fictional lore with some humorous, yet emotional elements added. It really makes for such a fun game especially if you're thinking about picking this up before the new one releases.

Also, UE5 is the death of games imo, the whole time I have revisted this game, I have been extremely mad at how developers post 2020 have taken gaming with micro-transactions, skins, same game but reskinned and different developers, same concepts. Although what sets this apart, is all of this is found in game. The best part, is collecting different tapes of music from the 80s and listening to it while being an utter badass mowing down enemies or running through the different biomes. 

Seriously, this is a huge refreshment and has reminded me why around 2015-2019 was peak in gaming.

If you like mil-sim, don't want pvp or multiplayer, a good and intriguing story that's very strange, yet makes up for in combat and traversing, please do yourself a favor and pick this up.

I remember being a big ARMA player since ARMA 2 and with ARMA 3 being 2 years fresh, this game felt like the better alternative for me that gave that scratched the specific gaming itch I always craved. Coming back to it, I feel the same. 

I hope this helps or was interesting to whoever sees this in 2025!

review_text:
Resumindo minha experiência, diria que Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain é um jogo de extremos — com momentos de pura genialidade, mas também com lacunas difíceis de ignorar. É um título ambicioso, com um sistema de jogabilidade refinado e um mundo aberto surpreendentemente bem construído, mas que sofre com cortes narrativos e uma sensação de incompletude, fruto de bastidores conturbados no desenvolvimento.

No lançamento, o jogo impressionou pelo seu polimento técnico e jogabilidade sólida. Diferente de muitos títulos da época, The Phantom Pain era estável, fluido e surpreendentemente responsivo. A Kojima Productions criou uma das mecânicas stealth mais refinadas já vistas, dando ao jogador uma liberdade estratégica incomparável. A IA dos inimigos, os sistemas de clima dinâmico e ciclo dia/noite, além das diversas possibilidades de abordagem, tornam cada missão única.

A narrativa, no entanto, é um ponto polêmico. Metal Gear sempre foi conhecido por suas histórias densas e cinematográficas, mas aqui, a estrutura episódica e a ausência de um terceiro ato consolidado prejudicam a experiência. A trama de Venom Snake, que gira em torno de vingança, identidade e manipulação, tem momentos de peso — especialmente nas fitas cassete e nas cenas entre personagens chave como Ocelot, Kaz e Skull Face. No entanto, o ritmo irregular e a sensação de que o jogo foi “interrompido” antes de sua conclusão deixam um gosto amargo, ainda mais para fãs da franquia.

O Afeganistão e a África, os dois principais mapas do jogo, são ambientes vastos, com um design repetitivo em certos pontos, mas com grande riqueza tática. A gestão da Mother Base é outro destaque: construir, expandir e recrutar soldados para sua própria fortaleza militar cria uma sensação de progressão constante, que se encaixa perfeitamente no tema da reconstrução após a queda do Big Boss.

O sistema de customização é profundo, com dezenas de armas, equipamentos e companheiros (como D-Dog, Quiet e D-Horse), cada um oferecendo formas diferentes de encarar os desafios. É possível ser letal ou pacifista, explosivo ou furtivo — e o jogo recompensa todos os estilos com criatividade e consequência.

Apesar disso, há tropeços: a repetição de missões com pequenos ajustes para esticar o conteúdo, a ausência de capítulos prometidos (como o famoso “Capítulo 51” cortado do jogo), e o uso recorrente de assets podem cansar. Além disso, para quem busca uma conclusão épica e coesa, The Phantom Pain pode parecer inconcluso — uma obra-prima pela metade.

Mesmo com esses problemas, Metal Gear Solid V é uma experiência única, com uma jogabilidade que permanece insuperável até hoje. Para quem valoriza liberdade tática, sistemas interligados e uma imersão militar densa, vale (muito) a pena. Se você é fã da franquia e ficou dividido no passado, talvez seja hora de revisitar esse capítulo com um novo olhar — não como o final que esperávamos, mas como uma das maiores ousadias do gênero stealth.

Currently have over 200 hours total. Truly a great game, and the most complete Metal Gear experience, in terms of gameplay and mechanics. AI as a whole is also good, especially given the game's age. Enemies adapt to your playstyle, which adds to the immersion. If you don't find it challenging enough though, you can always tweak it with mods. 
Optimization is top notch, as it was also released on PS3 and Xbox 360. However, the fps is capped at 60 and can only be uncapped by modifying the game files or with mods.
The opinions on the level of freedom you're given here compared to the previous, more linear entries in the series vary. I personally find that the open-world approach works well and I like that you can complete the game in any way you see fit, as long as you get the job done. Hell, you don't even have to use Snake to complete missions, but I do so purely by principle.
The game's weak point is definitely its story, which Konami never finished. Some missions, especially the side ops, can also be quite repetitive, but other than that, 0 complaints. If you're a Metal Gear fan, you should already own this game, but if you don't, definitely get it.

"Now do you remember? Who you are? What you were meant to do? I cheated death, thanks to you. And thanks to you I've left my mark. You have too – you've written your own history. You're your own man... From here on out, you're Big Boss."

Those words sum up Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain — a haunting farewell, a masterful conclusion, and a reflection on identity, loyalty, and legacy. This isn’t just another game in the series; it’s a mirror held up to the player, asking what it means to be Big Boss.

The gameplay is near perfection — fluid, open-ended, and endlessly creative. Every mission feels like your own story unfolding. The stealth mechanics are refined to an art form; each encounter feels dynamic, unpredictable, and alive.

But beneath the gameplay lies something deeper — an emotional current that runs through every moment. The themes of revenge, loss, and the cycle of violence are beautifully, painfully told. Kojima’s storytelling blurs the line between player and character, between Venom Snake and Big Boss, until you realize you were part of the legend all along. It’s not just a twist — it’s a revelation that redefines the entire saga.

The world itself is lonely, vast, and strangely beautiful. The isolation of the Afghan desert, the wind sweeping through the fields of Africa — every location reinforces the story’s quiet tragedy. The soundtrack, too, is unforgettable: 80s hits that somehow fit perfectly into a war-torn, morally gray world.

Sure, it’s not flawless — the ending feels incomplete, the pain of unfinished chapters lingers — but maybe that’s fitting. Big Boss’s story was never meant to be clean or perfect. It’s about the scars we carry, the choices we make, and the legacy we leave behind.

When the credits roll and you hear those final words… it hits you. You’ve walked in Big Boss’s boots, carried his sins, and finally understood his truth. The legend comes full circle — and it’s yours now.

Arguably the best metal gear solid experience you can have beyond the main two classics, MGS2 and MGS3 -- My favorite being MGS3 with how quintessential the camouflaging experience was where you could literally pick the right choice of garments to bring your visibility down to 99% invisible and crawl right under guards feet.

That feature, unfortunately, doesnt exist much in MGSV The Phantom Pain. Camouflage is a thing kind of but there's no UI to tell you how good your choice was and the choices are extremely slim, eventually you either put on a defensive suit or a sneaking suit and all the camouflage choices remain untouched. That's my one let down of this entire experience.

Now everything else is the best. I mean it touches on the same stealth gameplay from every modern MGS game but improves it tenfold except now there's equipment diversity and metaprogression. Rememer Big Shell, the oil tanker facility you invade as raiden in metal gear solid 2? Well you literally HAVE ONE that you build from the ground up. You build facilities that unlock features, hire staff to power those features, you develop more platforms that make your base bigger allowing for more staff-- its so fricken cool to watch how it all expands and its because of your recruitment in the field, your resource capturing, and your choice of expansion.

Another big part of the game is equipment developing, theres a metric butt-load of different guns to play with, each having their own multi-step upgrade tree that will need certain prerequisites to develop-- some requiring special skills you have to find on a soldier in the field. BTW to get those guys you knock them out and duct tape a rocket balloon to their butts and they get shot up into the atmosphere where a quantum entangled Revolver Ocelet is waiting to take him home to your Outer Heaven fortress.

The gameplay I described in itself is enough to warrant you to play, its fun, easy to get into yet can be very difficult at times, and allows hundreds of different approaches to solve each problem-- yet the best part is none of that, its the deep story accompanying every metal gear game. What will drive you to keep going is what happens next, and it only gets more interesting as you progress. 

38 hours in and i only just now started listening to the little tapes you unlock as you complete certain missions, they tell you background lore from the world through conversations with the main story characters, or it could be simple banter about distrusting someone you met. It's intentional worldbuilding that you discover right when you start to hunger for more information. This game tells you a story but you cannot guess it like other stories, you have to wait and find out, through struggle and success you're rewarded with little bits of story just to keep you hooked until the next mission.

review_text: Excellent game. Both the stealth and the action combat are fun, and the game offers a wide variety of unlockable weapons and unique equipment to use. The game is very much a sandbox, and the playthrough feels unique and personal to you since there are so many possibilities. Do you want to distract the enemies and sneak past them, or go in guns blazing? Can you kill them all before they call for backup, or did you already destroy their communication equipment? Do you want to kidnap your downed enemies, or hide the bodies? Maybe you should interrogate them first to see if they can tell you where some important items or people are, but have you gotten a translator on your team to figure out what they are saying? You get the picture. On top of all that, there is plenty to collect and customize, as well as a lot to manage if you really want to get meticulous about the personnel you recruit to your base and some of the peripheral activities. The dynamic weather system also provides interesting effects, such as being harder to see at night, the sound of rain hiding your footsteps, or employing IR vision to see enemies in sandstorms. The story is interesting enough, the environments are cool (and occasionally pretty spooky,) and you gain some helpful buddies to deploy with you on missions throughout the game, each of which has their own unique functions and equipment to unlock. I am genuinely impressed at the amount of detail in this game. It is definitely worth full price, and if you get it on sale you are getting a bargain.

The controls are bit clunky, but okay. You have a gun and the silencer only lasts 5 bullets. You can't jump, and you have to press a button to climb over anything. The graphics are nice enough. You spot enemies and they show up on your map. At one point there were some enemies chasing me and then there was gas everywhere and they turned into skull monsters. You can make cardboard boxes to hide in? And them air dropped to you out in the field? I assume it's part of MGS lore.

review_text:
That was my first dive into the Metal Gear universe (not counting the MGS V: Ground Zeroes cause it's basically the same game that acts as a prologue to this one). I was a big fan of Splinter Cell series as a kid, (thanks Ubi for killing it off 🤬) so I gave this game a chance without any expectations.

When I dived in into it I thought that I signed up for some single player game that will take me 15 - 20 hours at most and boy oh boy, I was SO wrong.
I clocked 160 hours into it, but there is so much stuff to do that after completing all the story missions and a significant amount of side ones, i'm only sitting at about 50% overall game progression. 
I didn't expect this game to have two open world maps and a very complex base building and online component, that was probably the thing I was most surprised about, but of course in a very good way.
Also crazy amount of weapons and items to develop.

I really liked the story and the conclusion of it, really didn't see that one coming, although (to not spoil too much) there was a hint about it, but I only realized it after I completed the game, really cool stuff.
I was surprised about the amount of licensed tracks from the era. My song of choosing for when my helicopter arrives to pick me up was Rebel Yell by Billy Idol.

I wasn't a big fan of a few boss fights with big opponents, but that one isn't necesarily bad, I just my personal preference.
I could also write more about fantastic graphics - hell - insane even considering the game is 10 years old, fantastic audio and soundtrack and other stuff, but I'll just say that If you like spy/stealth type of a game then it's a must play. Even if you want to play loud, I still really recommend it. I'll most likely come back to it in a few years or something. 

Two thumbs up 👍👍

review_text:
I think my fixation with this game started when I was helping my ex girlfriend catsit for a couple that was her friend. They had an PS4 with this game and when I saw it, 10 years ago, it had just launched, so I was definitely interested in playing a couple of hours. I spent 3 days on it... then they arrived.

Fast forward some years, 2021 or around that, I started my journey on MGS. Decided that I wanted to play it again, bought MGS V, but no way I was going to play it without knowing what I was playing, so I when I had the opportunity, grabbed my cousin PS3 and bought all those earlier MGS games and spent some years on it. Brushed past easily I, II and my pace started slowing down on III, months went by and finally completed it, but still an amazing game. Another year went by while trying to pick up IV and finish it, but at first it was a chore as the pace of the game is pretty different, with that many cutscenes and story, but oh, it was worth it. 

Then, at last, it came the time to grab that copy of MGS V and play it. And I know I deserved to play it, as I fought all those PS1 and PS2 controls on those earlier games, and endured the 4 hours of amazing but tiring MGS IV cutscenes. Booted up the game after finishing Ground Zeroes and started. It was everything I remembered, setting off alarms, showing my lack of stealth skills and having to rambo my way past all of those enemies as soon as they notice me sitting there like I'm supposed to be invisible (something that happens frequently).

Until now, my experience has been nothing short of magnificent. The system is well built, the emphasis the game have on stealth shows that those enemies aren't dumb, and as soon you are detected, they don't forget you that easily as most games are. They remember you for a while and it definitely makes the mission harder. The conversations they have are also interesting, between useful informations of that mission to just pure gossip (and you like gossip, don't you?). Also, how the games handles introducing each new thing to you is very well done, showing you one thing at a time without making you feel bored, for example, the mission that you extract an armourer only on the second map, only then you can mess up your weapons, when you already have unlocked a bunch of options to mess with it. Or when you unlock base defense, and then you have another element to take care, the games seems to pace itself quite good on it, never letting it get boring and always having something new to get used to.

The storyline is pretty confusing, as the chronologically starts after III, and I, II and IV have other protagonist being set years later. So I think it's worth playing the earlier games or at least watching videos to understand what's going on, the implications of the things you are doing in the game and how they will affect the future. It's interesting looking at it that way, because the game it all about that. Watching the past unfolds in the future, involving themes as cold war, USA and Soviet Union, private militias... sometimes things look like as it's supposed to happen in our own timelines, such as the microchip thing on MGS IV, almost like a Black Mirror thing. It kinda makes you reflect on it.

After completing the game, here's the part 2 of the review.

So... Yea, here's some lil spoilers ahead.

I think I expected more to the endgame, I mean, it kinda explains a lot of things but it does not feel like a true ending, and maybe that's kind of it as the story progresses much more on the other games. It kinda introduces and explains a lot of things and that's it. But I also feel that this game has a lot of replayability, with those earlier missions in a harder challenge, such as go full stealth or other ways of making it harder. And in 2025, there's not much interaction on the online mode, I mean, you can try, but it won't be the same as when the game was newer. I heard stories about the game and it looked like it was quite something. Well, give it a try, it will be a couple of hours of fun time, but nothing more than that. And well... I gotta say, MGS series was quite an experience and I truly recommend you trying all the games. The lore, the way systems improved and were introduced, the advancements the game went thru from 2000 to 2015, and also the way Kojima handles everything, just perfect. With all of that said, I kinda expected more of this game, I mean, it really was worth it, but I had such high expectations that well, it kinda left me with a bittersweet taste, nonetheless, this game is a 9 out of 10 game (maybe 8 as the online isnt that viable in 2025). Go play it.

review_text:
Things I like:
- Both the world & story are immersive.
- The stealth mechanics are very well executed, feeling natural & logical all throughout.
- The game presents an acceptable amount of challenge. Not too easy to the point of boredom, but not too hard to be unforgiving.
- The graphics are great for the time it was made in, and still hold up today.
- D-Dog. Enough said. :3
- The game is non-woke, meaning that the devs are not afraid to add in attractive women and have camera angles randomly focus on their chests & asses.
- Emblem customization can (and does) get hilarious. I managed to get mine to resemble the Dairy Queen logo.
- Decent sound engineering.
- The music is great and perfectly fits the atmosphere & art style.
- The UI is simple, uncomplicated, and likewise fits the atmosphere & art style. It also does not get in the way of your LOS the same way Armored Core 6 does.
- It wasn't intentional by the devs, but the rain is soothing.

Things I don't like:
- Without mods, the game caps itself to 60FPS.
- This game is not meant for keyboard & mouse controls--you NEED to play with a controller for full functionality and a good experience.
- As someone who prefers Sony DualShock controllers, the inability to change the button icons to anything besides those of the Xbox 360 controller is very disappointing.
- There are too few missions for my preferences, even post-game.
- D-Dog cannot ride in trucks nor tanks, making him extremely easy to accidentally run over.
- Placing a Claymore mine at a certain slope grade will cause it to immediately blow up in your face.
- I understand this was done for balance reasons, but suppressors wear out at an unrealistically fast rate. Where are these made? China?
- Excluding enemy FOBs, which are just copies of Mother Base, there are only two enemy regions to explore: Afghanistan & Central Africa. Is that really the best you guys could do? Adding as little as a third region would make the game a lot more interesting.
- This was the last Metal Gear game developed by Hideo Kojima.
- There is little reason to use D-Horse or D-Walker once D-Dog and Quiet are unlocked.
- Quiet cannot equip armor to make herself more resilient, [spoiler]but she CAN equip cosmetics that, according in-game lore, should suffocate her. How the ♥♥♥♥ does that make sense and armor doesn't?[/spoiler]
- Quiet's boobs are not big enough for my tastes.
- Quiet's boobs jiggle too excessively for my tastes.
- If there in an option to manually transfer GMP from your online account to your offline account, I have not found it. If it doesn't exist, it should exist.
[b]- Metal Gear Online apparently doesn't work. Every time I launch it, the game crashes, and I'm not the only one who has this issue.[/b]
- MB coins are a ♥♥♥♥♥ to grind for, requiring microtransactions if you want to get them faster. Even worse, the coins required for building new FOBs drastically increases the more FOBs you create.
- Staff are too easy to acquire, take too much time to level up, and you run out of space for them very quickly. There is also no way to turn off staff hiring following a mission, forcing you to constantly accept new staff and fire existing staff to make room for them.
[b]- If you experience a network error at any point during an FOB mission, it counts as a loss, which is not fair in any sense of the word. I'm no computer scientist, but there is no reason you need a constant connection to the servers anyway. You should be able to just download the FOB data, do the mission locally/offline, then upload the results to the server once connection is reestablished. [/b]
[spoiler]- Metal Gear Sahelanthropus cannot be controlled. I know the Metal Gear franchise is focused primarily on destroying mobile suits (known in-universe as "Metal Gear"), but as a mobile suit enthusiast, I want to destroy Soviets via Sahelanthropus the same way I would destroy the IMC via the Titans from Titanfall.[/spoiler]

Overall:

Good game with that uniquely Japanese level of care. There are however some noticeable flaws, especially regarding the online system. Great for people looking for both a good story and a good adventure. You will find a way to sink your time into this.

review_text:
As a long time MGS fan, MGSV ranks quite highly among the best in the series and was certainly way ahead of its time when it was originally released back in 2015 and arguably (game-play wise) is still leagues ahead of most modern open world games today. 

Unfortunately it’s biggest pitfall, is the story. I have played every single MGS game to date and the expectations and hype for MGS V were huge, as it turned many of the exciting and ambitious fan theories regarding the games story turned out not to be true. 

Instead we were given a game with an unfinished story and in turn most of the background to the story is given via hidden cassette tapes. 

The decision to not have the legendary David Hayter return to voice ‘Big Boss’/‘Snake’ and to instead bring Kiefer Sutherland was a strange choice but without delving into spoilers does make sense from a story point of view but his lines are very few and far between and do not have the same impact as one might imagine. 

It’s a very frustrating game in those aspects, particularly for an MGS fan, gameplay-wise for me; the open world, content, base building, combat, recruiting soldiers and above all the stealth mechanics’s makes this game an immediate recommendation for anyone, newcomers and fans alike…

…However long time MGS fans like myself are still struggling to understand how a game could be so disappointing in regards to its story telling, particularly when we were fooled so hard by the trailer’s for the game before it’s release.

We all got played like a damned fiddle and we will all carry our own “Phantom Pain” until the end of our days

review_text:
I still remember the first time I played Metal Gear Solid on the original PlayStation—not the old SNES Metal Gear, but the 1998 classic that revolutionized stealth-action games. As a kid, I was hooked, playing it over 50 times just to beat the infamous torture machine and save Meryl. Unlocking the stealth camo and infinite bandana felt like monumental achievements back then, and those moments cemented my love for the series. The game introduced me to the genius of Hideo Kojima and the deep, layered storytelling that would become a hallmark of the franchise.

Fast forward to Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain, and I can confidently say that it has earned a spot in my top 10 best games of all time. The gameplay in The Phantom Pain is nothing short of phenomenal, with stealth and movement mechanics that are simply fantastic. The freedom to approach each mission in your own way—whether by sneaking through enemy territory undetected or launching an all-out assault—is deeply satisfying. The fluid controls and the vast arsenal of tools at your disposal make every encounter feel like a personalized experience.

That said, one aspect I found frustrating is how the game seems to penalize aggression while rewarding a more passive, non-lethal playstyle. While I understand this aligns with the series' stealth roots, it can feel limiting for players who prefer to take a more direct and lethal approach. It would have been nice to see a better balance where both aggressive and stealthy strategies felt equally rewarded.

Visually, the game is breathtaking, with its sprawling landscapes and meticulous attention to detail immersing you in its war-torn world. The FOX Engine truly shines, delivering smooth animations, dynamic weather systems, and environments that feel alive and reactive. The sound design is equally stellar, with a haunting score and top-tier voice acting—Keifer Sutherland’s performance as Big Boss adds a grounded intensity to the character.

As much as I admire the gameplay, the story feels like a bittersweet note. While it explores compelling themes of revenge, loss, and identity, it falls short of the narrative depth and emotional weight of earlier titles. The absence of Kojima's signature cinematic flair in key moments, possibly due to the well-documented production struggles, leaves certain aspects of the story feeling incomplete. That said, the plot still has its share of gripping twists and memorable moments, making it a worthwhile journey.

What truly sets The Phantom Pain apart is its ability to immerse you in its systems. From building and managing Mother Base to experimenting with gear and companions like D-Dog and Quiet, the game constantly invites you to engage and explore. It's a game that challenges your creativity, rewarding you with moments that feel uniquely your own—a rarity in gaming.

For all its strengths, The Phantom Pain is a culmination of everything the series stands for: stealth, strategy, and storytelling wrapped in Kojima’s inimitable style. It may not hit every narrative note, but it’s still a masterclass in game design and an unforgettable experience for fans and newcomers alike. A true masterpiece that has more than earned its place among the greatest games of all time. (Snake Eater is super close too)

review_text:
I've been a MGS fan for decades, but the time came to actually get back into the fight and play some of the games linking the Cold War era MGS3 with the classic titles from the PS1 era.

The immersive game play and story were unexpectedly addictive. I've been a fan of JRPGs all my life, but the Action Stealth genre had never been something I thought would appeal to me-- boy was I wrong.

I expected to play through what was effectively an interactive movie. What I got was an open world, incremental experience that made me really feel like I was "Big Boss". 

The hidden gems and nuance of the writing were refreshingly open-ended and the ability to play 'your own style' (with consequences) make this an incredibly intelligent and adaptive title. Not even its age (nearly 10 years) has slowed this game down or made it seem like it was dated.

This is the exact standard of product I'd expect out of Kojima.
