review_text:
MGS V is a big bath of Kojima's home brew that you can only really get from him which makes it both the easiest recommend and also the toughest sell I could make.  Ten years from release and there's still nothing like it on the market and the combination of ideas means it's still to this day so utterly unique.  It's bursting with creativity and ingenuity and there's just no end to it.  Everything feels so crammed together that it fitting forms it's very own diamond.  It's still flawed and there are a couple of things I felt could have changed but this is well in hindsight and nothing to deter anyone.  This is the only MGS game that I've ever played and even so the game has strong enough legs to stand on its own and I never felt lost for long in it's train of thought even if by the end it runs out of steam and is laying down the track as you barrel towards the end.  The game swings from being one of the most inspired thought-provoking written things I've ever played to then the most sloppy and sometimes embarrassing material ever to see on screen.  You WILL get your money's worth and you WILL be confused but once you're strapped in it's hard not to stay on for the ride just to see what's around the corner.  I was sad to see it end after so long and I only wish there was more of it.  

I completed 78% of the content in 83 hours and I'd recommend this game to stealth fans looking for value for money.  This is one of the best optimised games I've ever played.  It's stunning and runs amazingly well.  It worked with my X1X controller.  The only problem I had with it technically was it sometimes didn't close and I had to manually close it from the task manager but I never lost a save in doing this.

### **Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain – A Review Written in Cipher**

> “V has come to.”  
> But has he really?

In *MGSV*, you’re not just playing as Big Boss.  
You’re playing as *a ghost*.  
A **phantom**.  
A **reflection** of the man.  
A **construct** born of grief, revenge, and manipulation.

This isn’t just a game. It’s a **meta-commentary**. It’s **Kojima’s requiem** for a series he *knew* he’d never finish the way he wanted. It’s the **greatest unfinished masterpiece** in gaming history — a legend not because of its completeness, but because of how loudly its **silences scream**.

---

### **"Kept you waiting, huh?" — The Illusion of Control**

Let’s talk about Snake.  
*Punished "Venom" Snake.*  
He’s the main character. Right?

Wrong.

You’re a **stand-in**. An empty vessel molded into Big Boss’s likeness. The game opens with you in **first-person**, your face literally **carved into another man’s identity**, your memories rewritten, your voice silenced.

You’re not the legend. You’re the **myth that sustains him**.

You’re not Snake. You’re the **player**. You’re the one being manipulated — by Zero, by Ocelot, by Kojima himself.

And when the final twist comes? You realize it was never *your* story to begin with.

---

### **Open World, Closed Heart**

The world is massive. Endless outposts. Dynamic weather. Day-night cycles. Fulton everything. Cows that explode. D-horse takes a dump on command.

But something's… missing.

There’s **no real boss fights** in the classic Kojima sense. No convoluted Codec lore dumps. No lengthy philosophical monologues about war or memes or genes.

Because **this isn’t Metal Gear Solid.**  
It’s the **shell** of Metal Gear Solid.  
A **phantom**.

You, the player, are chasing the ghost of a game that doesn't fully exist. Just like Snake is chasing a legacy that isn’t his. It’s *thematic brilliance disguised as an unfinished sandbox*.

You’re punished. He’s punished. We’re all **Punished Snake.**

---

### **Quiet – The Silent Scream**

She breathes through her skin. She doesn’t speak. She’s been made *deliberately sexualized* in a way Kojima claims is “explained by the story” — but the real reason? She’s a commentary on player gaze. She dances in the rain. She hums. She **kills entire platoons**.

And when she finally *does* speak, it's a **code** — to save your life.

Then she leaves, without a word.

Quiet is both **fanservice** and **subversion**. A character that **shouldn’t exist**, but does — haunting the game like a memory you can’t quite recall, beautiful and terrible and lost.

---

### **Skulls, Parasites, and PTSD**

- Skull Face? A villain whose motives are buried under layers of burned flesh and broken ideology.
- Code Talker? Speaks in riddles while his tongue fights against the horror of bioweapons.
- Huey? A sniveling traitor gaslighting everyone, the ultimate *"I didn’t do anything wrong!"* energy.

Everyone is broken.  
Everyone is compromised.  
Even your home — **Mother Base** — is a ticking time bomb of betrayal and disease.

You build it. You staff it. You visit your men. You shower the blood off your body.  
And then **Chapter 2 hits**.

> ***Shining Lights, Even in Death.***

You walk through your own base, silenced pistol in hand, mercy-killing your infected comrades as they *salute you*. They thank you as they die.  
You don’t get a choice.

The game *forces you* to carry out a massacre in silence, surrounded by mournful strings and whispering ghosts.

You feel the **phantom pain** of loss — not because it’s taken, but because **you gave it willingly**.

---

### **Mission 51 – The Missing Truth**

There is no ending.  
There is no closure.  
Just **a cut mission**, an unfinished arc, and a tape titled *"Truth."*

Mission 51 was supposed to wrap it all up. But instead, we get a message:

> *“From here on, you’re Big Boss.”*

The **player becomes the legend**.  
Not because you earned it, but because someone *needed you to believe it.*

That’s Kojima’s final trick.  
That’s the true Metal Gear.  
You’re not finishing a story.  
You’re being *weaponized* to carry the myth forward.

---

### **The Final Tape – "The Man Who Sold the World"**

The opening song is no accident.

> *“We passed upon the stair… spoke of was and when…”*

It’s about identity. Ego. The **lie of self**.

You were never Snake.  
You were the **mirror**.  
And Kojima stares into that mirror, too — realizing this would be the last time he'd *be allowed* to tell this story, before Konami pulled the plug.

This isn’t just a game.  
It’s an **autopsy of legacy**.  
It’s Kojima looking at his life’s work, and asking,  
> *“What if it was all a lie?”*

---

### **Final Thoughts – No One Will Ever Do It Like This Again**

**Metal Gear Solid V** is a masterpiece **because** it’s broken.  
It’s beautiful **because** it’s unfinished.  
It’s powerful **because** it makes *you*, the player, complicit in the illusion.

It’s the only game where **the twist is that you were never the protagonist**.  
It’s the only game that makes you feel the loss of something that never truly existed.  
It’s the only game that dares to whisper:

> “You’re not the hero. You’re the ghost.”

This game doesn’t end.  
It fades.  
Like a memory of a war that never happened.

And yet, I keep hearing the voice in my head:

> “V has come to.”

But maybe he never left.

review_text:
I've never played any of the other games in the series, so I'm very intrigued about why there are flaming whales and intangible, teleporting bikini girls intermixed with what is otherwise a stealthy military game.  I'm about 10% of the way through, and I'm enjoying the "power creep" of the enemies, Kiefer's acting, and the overall "vibe".

Capturing people with tranq darts as a staffing method is weird, (especially when you consider how many of their friends I've murdered) but fun so long as you suspend disbelief a little.

The base management aspect is a little less interesting, but not so cumbersome as to be annoying.  Just have to remember to deploy people and build things from time to time.

I'm guessing there's a way to fulton out the huge crates, but I haven't figured out how, yet, so resources are a little slow to build up, but aside from the sniper rifle and the bazooka, I haven't felt the need to buy much anyway.

The cardboard box is silly, but you have to use it to capture former "diamond dogs".  

The (ahem) camera work on "Quiet" is... okay, I'm not complaining, but it's a little "obvious" when it lingers or zooms during the cut scenes.

I miss my horse for travelling from one base to another, but that dog is OP.  Gotta love a clairvoyant, one-eyed puppy.

I really hope silencer durability is something you can upgrade, or you can carry additional ones to equip, as I don't like the "supply drops".  It's also silly that you can't set a weapon down if you drop in a weapon eg if I switch out my sniper rifle for a rocket launcher, I should be able to go pick my rifle back up, not have it disappear.  (but that's a minor complaint as it doesn't come up much)

All 'n all, enjoyable, and a story and gameplay I'm looking forward to exploring.

I might edit this review later if the flaming whales are never explained ;-)

This is far and away the "best" game in the Metal Gear franchise when you go by certain metrics. Mostly combat, and moment to moment gameplay. Everything I have to say has been said more articulately by others over the last 11 years, and we all know the story by now. Kojima's firing leading to this game being completely and nakedly unfinished. It has no third act. The knife twist is the reveal that we were likely to get a remade/retold Metal Gear only to have all those plans ruined by corporate leadership so out of touch they thought pachinko machines were a better investment for this IP (right before Japan cracked down on pachinko with gambling laws LOL). 

I love this game. More than I can express here. But I can not in good conscience recommend anyone else who isn't a series completionist play it. 
The disappointment that it leaves, and the HATRED that you will feel for Konami isn't worth it to bring into your life. I played this game on launch on PS4, and going back to it just brought all of those emotions back. They have not dulled, and the knowledge that Death Stranding 2 is right around the corner isn't making me any less furious for the possible future we were denied.

If you must, then I URGE you to please stop after the first act. Once you clear the mission SAHELANTHOPUS, feel free to stop as soon as you feel bored. There is no more meaningful story left in the game, and only really filler missions and dangling plot threads that lead to nothing. The FOB missions were a neat idea, but not fleshed out enough to keep anyone hooked. IDK if anyone is still playing MGO or if it's still even on. I didn't try it. 

Long live Kojima!

[quote][url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/33401179/]Follow my curator page for more recommendations![/url][/quote]

Still the king of open world stealth action. 
Playing this again a decade after release and it has barely aged a day. The story is a mess (though has some cool bits), pacing can be whack, and some other issues but none of that matters because the gameplay and AI is just that good. I recently played some Wildlands and Breakpoint, which share some surface level similarities, and while Breakpoint wins over in gunplay and sounds the enemy AI and general options available to you leave so much to be desired. 

Sneaking up to a base, spotting targets and marking high value soldiers to capture. Planting some C4 on anti-air radar, comms equipment, and heavy weapon emplacements. Interrogating an enemy to reveal the hostage location, making your way there someone you didn't account for spots you. Dive behind a wall to blow the C4 and call in a support chopper. Making a mad dash to the hostage location, rockets popping off from your air support while your chosen song (for me; "Old" by Machine Head) blasts through the speakers. Running to the LZ with the hostage over your shoulder, bullets whizzing by. 
Mission cleared, funds received, new weapon developments unlocked. 

No other game captures this feeling. And thats just one of many mission types and experiences to have in MGSV. The only one that comes somewhat close is Mercenaries. 

And the AI, nearly perfect as far as enjoyable enemies go. Their sight is nearly perfectly tuned, difficult but fair. Hiding in grass and using camo works how you would expect most of the time. They are very dynamic and have wide patrols and even change guard/ sleep when night hits. If you do get fully spotted by an enemy and they start shooting or begin to shout out the whole base will know where you are which is a little cheap feeling but you can break sight line and lose them.  Far too many games the enemies are clairvoyant, or have eagle vision, or once aggro'd just stupidly conga-line to your position but not here. Diversions actually work, setting an explosive off on the far end of base may prove beneficial to shake up the guard positions. Hit and run tactics even with loud weapons work as the enemies wont just magically know where you are without visual contact.

Progression is solid with unlocking new weapons and gear, all sorts of cool gadgets and equipment to use. With many options for both stealth and going loud. 

The soldier capture with fulton device is brilliant and creates a whole extra layer of gameplay as every enemy you come across may be a piece of loot to gather and change how you approach a mission. Going up to a guard outpost and see 3 guys talking to each other, yeah you could throw a grenade and make short work of it but one of them is S rank in R&D which you need for some new weapons so now you gotta figure out how you wanna extract him. 

That combined with enemies getting new equipment to counter whatever you do often (helmets added if you headshot often, gas masks if you use smoke grenades etc) really shakes up the formula. Too many stealth games fall into just headshotting enemies, melee takedowns, and occasionally hiding a body.

Some minor downsides: Some menu controls like moving the cursor in map screen feels like its emulating a stick and sucks. Cover system doesn't want to work 70% of the time, there is no hard button for it, only rubbing against a wall to activate it. 
Gunshot sounds are weak, even the mod that's supposed to improve doesn't help much. 
No FOV options, though I've somewhat accepted the limited fov as a gameplay concession. 

All in all just a great fun time, especially if you want to get creative with how you approach missions. There is just no other game like it even after all these years. Even if other games have improved or included individual elements of this, as a total package it really is unique.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain Is a Masterclass in Open-World Stealth and Storytelling

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is one of the most ambitious and rewarding games of its generation. From the first moment, it pulls you into a tense, morally complex world where every decision feels meaningful. The story of Venom Snake, revenge, and the consequences of war is gripping and layered. Some plot threads may feel unresolved for long-time fans, but the brilliance of the narrative lies in its subtlety and the way it lets players feel the weight of their actions.

Gameplay in The Phantom Pain is extraordinary. The open-world environments of Afghanistan and Africa are alive, detailed, and dynamic. Each mission can be approached in countless ways, from careful stealth to all-out action. The freedom to tackle objectives your own way makes every playthrough feel unique. Stealth mechanics are among the best in gaming, with intelligent, reactive AI that keeps you constantly engaged. Mistakes are opportunities to adapt rather than punishments, and every successful mission feels hard-earned and satisfying.

The Mother Base system adds an incredible layer of depth. Recruiting soldiers, managing resources, and developing new weapons and technology creates a living world that evolves with the player. Watching Mother Base grow over time provides a tangible sense of progress and achievement that complements the main missions perfectly.

Visually, the game is stunning. Lighting, weather, and environmental detail create immersive worlds that are both beautiful and strategically challenging. The day-night cycle and dynamic weather influence gameplay in meaningful ways, requiring you to adapt your tactics. Sound design is equally impressive, from subtle environmental cues to the haunting musical score that amplifies tension during stealth operations.

While the game is near perfect, it is not without minor flaws. Some story elements feel fragmented, and a few side missions can feel repetitive. The pacing, due to the open-ended structure, occasionally slows. However, these issues are small compared to the overall polish, creativity, and depth of the core experience.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a triumph of design, storytelling, and gameplay. It combines freedom of choice, emergent gameplay, and emotional narrative in a way few games have ever managed. It challenges you, rewards creativity, and leaves a lasting impression. Every hunt, every mission, and every strategic choice feels meaningful.

If you are looking for an unforgettable open-world experience that blends stealth, strategy, and storytelling at the highest level, The Phantom Pain is essential. It is not just a game, it is a masterclass in what interactive experiences can achieve, and it sets a standard that few others will ever reach.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain – A Masterpiece That Got Kojima’d

Let’s be real—MGSV is the best stealth game ever made... and also the most painfully unfinished. Hideo Kojima built an espionage sandbox so absurdly good that you’ll forgive the fact that Konami took a hacksaw to the ending and buried the remains in an unmarked grave. It’s like being served the greatest steak of your life—only for the waiter to snatch your plate away mid-bite and whisper, "That’s all you get."


---

The Story: Kojima’s Wild Ride (Until It Derails at Full Speed)

You’re Big Boss. Or are you? (Cue dramatic zoom.) The plot is classic Kojima—military conspiracies, betrayal, and enough cassette tapes to make a 90s kid weep with nostalgia. By the time you’re done, you’ll either:

A) Have a PhD in Metal Gear lore.

B) Be convinced Kojima was making it up as he went.

C) Both.


And then there’s Skull Face. This guy makes Bond villains look like amateurs. His grand plan? Not nukes, not world domination—just straight-up linguistic genocide. That’s right, he wants to erase the English language. And his death scene? A monologue so long, I swear I started growing a beard halfway through it.


---

Gameplay: Stealth So Good, It’ll Ruin Other Games for You

This is where Phantom Pain flexes so hard it tears its own shirt. The stealth is perfect. Want to:

Ghost through an enemy base like a shadow? Done.

Go full John Wick and turn the place into a war zone? Also done.

Fulton extract a goat for absolutely no reason? You bet.


The AI is scary smart. Headshot too many soldiers? They start wearing helmets. Sneak at night? Get ready for an army of guards with night-vision goggles. It’s one of the only games where being too good actually makes it harder.


---

Mother Base: The World’s Deadliest Daycare

Managing your private army is weirdly addictive. You kidnap soldiers, send them on missions, research new weapons—it’s The Sims, but with more war crimes.

And then there’s D-Dog—the best boy in gaming. He sniffs out enemies, tears out throats, and somehow makes war adorable. If you’re not taking him on missions, I don’t know what you’re doing with your life.

Oh, and Quiet. Kojima’s excuse for her outfit? "She breathes through her skin." Science called BS, but let’s be honest—we’re here because she’s a god-tier sniper who hums Take On Me while popping skulls at 500 meters.


---

The Phantom Pain (AKA: Where the Hell is the Ending?)

Just when the story should reach its peak, the game goes "Nah, we’re done here." Missing missions, cut content, and an ending so abrupt it feels like Konami physically dragged Kojima out of the studio mid-sentence. It’s like watching The Godfather only for the film reel to catch fire before the final act.


---

Final Verdict: 10/10 Gameplay, 6/10 Story Delivery

MGSV is a flawed masterpiece. The gameplay? Unmatched. The freedom? Unparalleled. The fact that it’s clearly half-finished? Painful. But even in its incomplete state, it’s still one of the best stealth games ever made.

Pros:
✔ Stealth gameplay so good, it ruins other games.
✔ Fulton extraction never stops being funny.
✔ D-Dog. That’s it. Just D-Dog.
✔ Quiet’s humming. (Don’t judge me.)

Cons:
❌ The missing ending will haunt you.
❌ Skull Face’s monologues could put insomniacs to sleep.
❌ Konami happened.

Score: 9.5/10 (Would be 11/10 if Kojima got to finish it.)

Should You Play It?
If you love stealth, absolutely. If you need closure… maybe replay MGS3 and pretend it’s the real ending.

Simply the most original take on a franchise that only mildly re-invented itself upon each release.

Then MGS5 is released and it massively reinvents itself for the better in every aspect. Its open world. Both maps are huge. It can be played full stealth, full out third person shooter mayhem or a combination of both.
A brilliant game engine, an insane attention to detail, infinite replayability, a sense of humour, coupled with an eccentric and fun story just lead me to conclude that this is the open world game design other open world games need to emulate. Theses a Base building section, you recruit members for your covert army from enemies you defeat. Do you like that tank the baddie is using?  Airlift that sucker out and now its YOUR tank! Raid outposts and bases for materials, save the wildlife in the war zones if you want, brutalise the enemy, or take want you want and vanish like a leaf on the wind. It's truly an open game. 

With 50 story missions which can sometimes take hours ( if you want them to), and around 175 side missions ( all but a few are optional), this game is worth its asking price. 

If you like open world games, this is for you. I simply cannot give this game enough credit for its brilliance.

But it now, and be prepared for a wonderful all encompassing experience, that, at this time, I can not ever see being equalled

review_text:
MGSV is among my most played games. Other stealth games I've enjoyed include Splinter Cell, Dishonored, and Hitman. MGSV absolutely hits the spot as a giant open-world stealth sandbox. Even 10 years after its release, it still holds up—both the gameplay and the graphics.

The freedom to complete missions however you like is unmatched. You can go full stealth or guns blazing if you want. You unlock a lot of weapons, gadgets, and tools which make replaying missions lots of fun just trying out new approaches. Different companions support different playstyles too, whether you want to zip across the map or have combat support. After playing for a bit, I'd encourage you to look up how others play because you'll have these "aha" moments all the time learning how to make full use of the kit the game provides.

At times, it's a wonderfully silly game too, and one that doesn't take itself too seriously. The cardboard box, for example, being a totally valid stealth tool. You can also put posters of women on the outside of the box to lure guards to you, then knock them out. Or you can request supplies via parachute and drop them directly on an enemy's head. Just look up videos on YouTube of people doing funny things in MGSV and you'll get what I mean.

I didn't play any previous MGS games and just jumped right into this. As a result, the story was confusing at times. I'm not sure how much of the confusion is just it being a Kojima game though. In any case, some major story beats probably didn't hit as hard because I didn't play the previous games, but it's still an enjoyable and interesting. Cutscenes are very cinematic. There's a lot of underlying messages and themes in the story.

I've gotten 2 long playthroughs of ~80 hours each, once at launch and another more recently. And I still haven't unlocked everything or replayed every mission the way I wanted, so there's a lot of game left for me still. So if stealth games are your thing, you'll probably get a lot of mileage out of this game.

review_text:
[h2] ... It has been nine years [/h2]

Nowadays, AAA games are often frowned upon for their substandard quality, self-inserts, and meaningless political ideas that add no value to the game and interest no one. However, Metal Gear Solid V is a proper, high-quality blockbuster that truly deserves the AAA label.

Even though the game is over nine years old, it not only holds up against today’s competitors but also surpasses them in multiple ways.

The gameplay is immaculate and refined to the highest standards. It is quite simple, easy to understand, and accessible even for those who have no experience with or do not enjoy stealth games. There are no rough edges or any form of technical sluggishness (with the exception of the horse). Though it is a stealth game, nothing stops you from choosing your own approach, whether going in guns blazing, calling your chopper for assistance, or launching airstrikes to decimate your enemies.

The graphics, art style, and FOX Engine are amazing. I have seen and played many new games that are supposed to have great graphics, but most of them suffer from extremely poor optimization and start looking outdated after a few years due to uninspired art direction. The FOX Engine, however, handles graphics exceptionally well and delivers one of the most optimized gaming experiences. This game even ran on the old Xbox 360, and it doesn’t look terrible on it. Unfortunately, Kojima Productions had to abandon their own engine after parting ways with Konami.

The story is a controversial topic within the Metal Gear community...some love it, while others hate it. Personally, I quite like it, along with the game's tone and themes, especially considering what happened before the Phantom Pain incident. Visual storytelling takes a more prominent role here compared to previous Metal Gear games, where the narrative was more direct. Many small details can easily be missed on a first playthrough, making a second run more interesting.
Some players suggest that MGSV should not be played as a first Metal Gear game due to its unconventional story, but I disagree. As someone who had never played a Metal Gear game before MGSV, this title sparked my interest in the franchise and turned me into a Metal Gear fan.

The cutscenes, unfortunately, are fewer than I would have liked. However, the ones that are present are top-notch and masterfully directed. Every detail (voice acting, animations, camera work, lighting, and background music) has been carefully considered and executed perfectly. Thanks to the fluid single-camera perspective, the cinematography feels unique and immersive.

After completing the game multiple times, I can definitely sense that something is missing. It is not something technical that is missing. The story of Venom Snake and Diamond Dogs ends abruptly, and while the game fully justifies its price tag, there’s an undeniable feeling that something is missing... something that should have been there but was removed... leaving you with a lingering phantom pain...

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a sensational stealth sandbox superbly straddling serious and silly. While the graphics & PC control scheme are definitely starting to show their age, the infiltration & extraction gameplay absolutely holds up to this day. The biggest letdown for me was how it implemented story progression in the later stages of the game, being both intentionally obtuse and requiring the player to replay missions in order to unlock more of the story.

Without a doubt, Metal Gear Solid V is the highest quality open world stealth game I have played to date. Where a lot of games will simplify enemy alertness levels to three basic states: unaware, suspicious, and alert; MGSV keeps more nuance in a way that is extremely immersive without impeding the player’s understanding of what’s happening. This is done using intercepted radio communication, which is an absolutely genius move on the game designers’ part. It’s both diegetic and very literal: guards can say “I’ve found a knocked out guy in the dumpster” and HQ will radio everyone at the base to stay alert, and now you know exactly what’s going on, even without a yellow marker above everyone’s head. Further adding to the immersion, comms are in the correct foreign language, and you’re only provided subtitles if you have a translator on staff. You can also play around the enemy force’s reliance on their radios: the entire base won’t become alert unless the person that finds the corpse calls it in, so if you can stop them before they make the call, no one will be any the wiser. This is in stark contrast to a lot of games where all enemies are connected to a hivemind and instantly know where you are or that a body has been spotted, et. cetera. The alertness states are simultaneously complex, nuanced, and intuitive: this is a masterclass in stealth sandbox design.

I never had thought that I would find this game a masterpiece which went under my radar for 9 years.. Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is damn solid and wholesome gaming experience and the way that how it succeeds to invent itself over and over again chaining me to my chair for hours and hours, made me realize how addicting and destructing the gaming can be to busy adult life. ^^

Jokes aside, the thing which makes it even more amazing is that its almost a decade old game and technically nothing becomes even close to the features that let's you to be an ultimate commando going guns and cannons blazing like Rambo or wiping an entire village of enemies in silence like a Predator. Stealth is one of or even the hardest genre to create properly for it needs so strict and delicate work to provide an outcome that gameplay won't feel too frustrating or too easy. The experience should be hard to master, but yet again so easy to learn and rewarding. This is the thing where the game shines like a diamond thanks to features like Reflex Mode and eternal freedom to choose your tactical approach on big wide open areas that gives you just the right amount of freedom and mercy to fix a mistake, but yet again won't forgive you much more than that. Although even if you should mess up bad you are usually gonna be okay for Snake can take a bullet or two, especially if you have handled most of the enemies at breaking point. In my whole playthrough I cursed unfairness only few times while messing my well proceeding stealth and all the rest of hundreds of times I knew that blowing was on me and only my own mistake. While stealth gets a bit more complicated when the game proceeds this is compensated by achieved technology making the game even more entertaining! By unlocking even better assets and weaponry with money achieved throughout main missions, side missions and sold resources you'll find yourself taking the enemies quicker and badassier and just when you might feel satisfied the game provides you with something even better. All this huge variety of tactical approach is set into big open world of two large areas welcoming you always with something fresh. 

In addition of doing missions and earning money you also manage your base that is pretty straightforward, but adds a nice features to fill it by volunteers and enemies you extract from battlefields. Each recruited has different skills and especially in the beginning it is always exciting to be able to extract some very talented enemy to your ranks, especially after you have risked the whole operation to neutralize that one guy non lethally. The safest and most stable way is to kill enemies of course, but getting some specialist to your team can be that crucial it'll be wothy to take the chance. The better your staff is the better your stuff is - shortly describing this is about your gear, support, intel gathering tools, and medical assets. After certain point getting enemies extracted and volunteers become so easy that this is no longer so huge deal, but especially in the early missions the talented specialist or elite among normal soldiers is like a rare Pokemon waiting to be tamed.

After spending over 90 hours with it and beating the main storyline, only thing which bugs me could be described as phantom pain for the feeling that something is missing and was cut out - a flaw in the game which despite of this ranks so high in my book. The storyline is odd and unfinished and while it delivers some epic cutscenes with twists and turns somehow the execution dryes out a little bit, but just enough that it is obvious that devs and Hideo Kojima might have ran out of time to transcribe the plot and rearrange/recompose some scenes. review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain
Overall Rating: 4.6/5
"I won't scatter your sorrow to the heartless sea. I will always be with you. Plant your roots in me. I won't see you end as ashes. You're all diamonds."
This is the last Metal Gear Solid in the franchise. It’s also Hideo Kojima’s final creation under Konami. This game is amazing, both in story and gameplay. You can explore an open-world map, raid outposts for resources, and recruit soldiers to upgrade your base.

Story
The story in this game is near perfection, with an incredible plot twist. At first, you might think you can predict where it’s going, but by the end, everything you expected will be turned upside down. Hideo Kojima masterfully manipulates the player—just like in The Man Who Sold the World.
Story: 5/5

Gameplay
The gameplay in The Phantom Pain is more casual compared to previous games in the franchise. Unlike older Metal Gear Solid games that had a health bar, in this one, Punished "Venom" Snake has regenerating health. When you're spotted during stealth, you enter slow-motion mode, giving you a chance to react and correct your mistake. However, in challenge missions, slow-motion mode, checkpoints, and health regeneration are disabled.
The enemy AI is highly intelligent—if you knock someone out or kill them without hiding the body, enemies will enter caution mode and conduct thorough searches. Nearby outposts will also go on high alert. There are tons of small details in the gameplay that make it feel immersive. You should definitely try it.
Gameplay: 4/5

Voice Acting & Soundtrack
The Metal Gear Solid franchise has always had incredible soundtracks, and this game is no exception. Who let Donna Burke cook? The music in this game is absolutely fantastic. Sins of the Father is iconic, but other tracks like Nuclear and The Man Who Sold the World are equally perfect.
The soundtrack is well-integrated with the cutscenes, making them even more impactful. The voice actors also did an amazing job—Ocelot, Snake, and Miller all sound incredibly realistic, with voices that match the tone and emotion of the scenes.
Voice Acting & Soundtrack: 5/5

Graphics & Performance
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain was released in September 2015—almost a decade ago, huh? Yet, its graphics still hold up and can even be compared to modern games. Thanks to the Fox Engine, the visuals were cutting-edge for their time and still look stunning today.
Performance-wise, it’s also impressive. I played on an MX330 (which is worse than a GTX 960), set the graphics to medium, and still managed to get around 60 FPS. The Fox Engine is seriously well-optimized.
Graphics & Performance: 4.5/5

Overall Thoughts
This game excels in almost every aspect—story, gameplay, soundtrack, and graphics. However, some of the side missions feel repetitive, and the more casual gameplay might not appeal to longtime fans of the series. Still, overall, this game is a masterpiece.

Hideo Kojima is a god. Konami, on the other hand... not so much.

Kazuhira Miller: "Cypher sent us to hell, but we’re going even deeper. Take back everything that we have lost."
Punished Snake: "Kaz, I'm already a demon."

review_text:
MGSV: The Phantom Pain is one of the best open world games out there. With two open environments (three if you count Mother Base) and hundreds of main and side missions, MGSV will keep you busy for a long time. I've sunk hundreds of hours in this title on several platforms, and always come back for more.

Highlights:
-Large open world settings with a range of environments and enemy bases/outposts
-Missions can be replayed from day one to try new tactics and complete side objectives
-Incredible arsenal of weapons that can be customized to your preferences. Same goes for vehicles
-Great selection of companions that adhere to any playstyle
-Adaptive enemy AI that will adjust behavioral patterns to better counter your most common playstyles
-Helicopter support and evac/insertion makes for a realistic feeling of entering and exiting a combat zone
-Air strikes, weapon drops, supply drops, and vehicle drops make it easy to change your tactics on the fly
-Basebuilding is pretty fun and adds a new layer to the game. If you don't like it, it's also not hard to ignore it

Overall thoughts:
Story: 8/10 - it never really gets a solid ending and not everything is tied up
Gameplay: 10/10 - absolutely peak
Missions: 9/10 - some repeat/challenge missions can get annoying, but the ability to replay any mission is a great bonus here
Weapons/Gear: 10/10 - a range of customization and upgrade trees. Plus you can get Ocelot's revolver and hit trickshots to one-hit most enemies in the mid to late game
Visuals: 9/10 - a few small issues, but nothing to really be concerned over
Soundtrack: 10/10 - you can listen to music and narrative tapes at any time

I give Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain ten overpowered sniper rifles out of ten. Highly recommend even if you aren't a fan of previous entries.

review_text:
Oh boy… where do I even begin? As a longtime Metal Gear Solid fan, I’ve always loved the series—its deep lore, unique gameplay, and the special magic that makes every entry stand out in its own way. Metal Gear Solid V is no exception.

Let’s start with the good: the gameplay is, without a doubt, the best in the series. It’s smooth, addicting, and incredibly fun, with a gameplay loop that keeps you coming back for more. Every stealth encounter, every tactical approach, and every moment spent in the field just feels right. However, while the gameplay is nearly flawless, the story is where things get complicated.

The potential for an incredible narrative was there, but due to the infamous Konami vs. Kojima fallout, the game was left unfinished—and you can feel it. There are so many plot threads that start but never conclude, leaving you either confused or disappointed. The main missions are hit or miss—some are epic, classic MGS moments, while others make you wonder, Was that really a main mission? The side content is plentiful but often feels like filler, existing more to extend playtime rather than to enhance the experience. But because the gameplay itself is so good, you don’t mind most of the time.

Despite the missing pieces and the hollow feeling some story beats leave behind, MGS V still works. When you finally reach the end, you walk away feeling both satisfied and bittersweet—fulfilled yet aware that it could have been so much more. And yet, even with its flaws, it’s an easy 9/10.

Would I recommend it? Absolutely. Just be prepared for an amazing, but slightly unfinished, Metal Gear experience.

The ending of MGSV:TPP is one of the best ever, if only Kojima could have finished the final act, this might have been one of the best games ever made.

review_text: MGSV is a good Metal Gear game, but the integration of online features and lack of female characters besides Quiet made this game difficult to play through. I got the game on sale and it took me three plays of the prologue and putting the game down for the run to stick. Online features can mostly be disabled, but this is not accounted for in game progression so I experienced high difficulty by part 2. The whole Mother Base thing also turns out to be a vehicle for online stuff and Ocelot later on tells you to do what you want and build a [spoiler] nuke [/spoiler] if you feel like it. Or not. But it's part of the online thing, so it never gets mentioned again even though Emmerich would have a lot to say. Quiet is the best character in the very convoluted and confusing story which otherwise seems to be about Men with Problems. She's a strong character that has to deal with harassment from ally and enemy soldiers, and the need to be mostly naked is acceptably explained by the whole [spoiler] parasite [/spoiler] thing. Although I could have done without the gratuitous cinematography. Other female characters include nurse that gets killed by Quiet, scientist that gets killed by Snake, or [spoiler] Strangelove who gets killed by Emmerich after having his child [/spoiler]. One standout problem with the story ended up being integration of the online character creator (in which you can only create a man with the same face options as the Diamond Dogs NPC men) with the story in the true ending, which I couldn't follow and mostly skipped. The metal gears don't feature very prominently, but the fight with [spoiler] Sahelanthropus [/spoiler] is memorable. The gimmick fights, i.e. [spoiler] The Skulls and The Man on Fire [/spoiler] provided a lot of frustration. The devs did a good job on the cinematics, but I found myself skipping some of the [spoiler] parasite and child soldier [/spoiler] sections. Overall, the basic structure of the missions between story segments was enjoyable and the game actually isn't that long, so it's worth a playthrough, even if you might end up shaking your head at the writers and director.

review_text:
Hideo Kojima’s Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is an ambitious, genre-defining stealth-action experience that pushes the boundaries of open-world gameplay. Released in 2015, this installment in the long-running Metal Gear series refines the franchise’s signature mechanics while introducing new ones that elevate the player’s sense of freedom. Set in the 1980s, the game follows Big Boss—now known as Venom Snake—as he rebuilds his private military organization, Diamond Dogs, and seeks revenge on those who destroyed his former group, MSF.

One of MGSV’s greatest achievements is its open-world structure. Unlike previous entries that relied on linear levels, Phantom Pain drops players into vast, dynamic environments in Afghanistan and Central Africa. These settings are meticulously crafted, filled with enemy bases, wildlife, and varying terrain that influence tactical approaches. The ability to freely plan missions, scout locations, and decide how to engage enemies makes for an incredibly immersive experience.

The core gameplay is some of the best stealth-action ever created. The responsive controls, fluid movement, and detailed enemy AI work together seamlessly to create a rewarding experience. Players can use a wide range of gadgets, weapons, and support options—like calling in airstrikes or using the iconic Fulton extraction system to recruit soldiers and resources. Every mission feels like a sandbox of possibilities, encouraging creative problem-solving.

Despite its strong mechanics, the game’s story is one of its most divisive elements. Unlike the heavily cinematic narratives of previous Metal Gear games, MGSV opts for a more fragmented storytelling approach. Key plot developments are often delivered through cassette tapes rather than cutscenes, which can leave some players feeling disconnected from the story. While the themes of revenge, identity, and the cost of war are present, they don’t reach the same narrative depth as previous titles.

Kiefer Sutherland’s portrayal of Snake is another controversial aspect of the game. While his performance is solid, Snake has significantly less dialogue than expected, making him feel more like an observer than an active participant in the story. This is especially noticeable compared to David Hayter’s more expressive portrayal in past entries. The game’s antagonist, Skull Face, has an intriguing presence but ultimately lacks the depth and complexity of past Metal Gear villains.

The game’s online component, Metal Gear Online, offers an additional layer of replayability. With tactical multiplayer battles and base infiltration missions, it extends the gameplay beyond the single-player campaign. However, the online mode suffered from balancing issues and microtransactions that frustrated some players at launch. Over time, patches improved the experience, but it never reached the same level of acclaim as the main game.

Visually, MGSV is stunning, even years after its release. The FOX Engine delivers highly detailed environments, smooth animations, and realistic lighting effects that bring the world to life. The attention to detail, from the way characters react to the weather to the animations of different weapons, showcases the game’s technical excellence. Sound design is equally impressive, with realistic weapon sounds, immersive ambient noise, and a memorable 80s-inspired soundtrack.

One of the biggest disappointments of MGSV is its unfinished feel. The abrupt ending and the infamous missing Mission 51 strongly suggest that Kojima’s departure from Konami led to a rushed conclusion. While the existing content is substantial, the lack of closure to key storylines leaves lingering questions. Fans have speculated on what the full vision for the game might have been, but unfortunately, it remains incomplete.

Despite these flaws, MGSV remains one of the best stealth-action games ever made. Its innovative gameplay, deep mechanics, and open-ended mission design set a new standard for the genre. Even with its storytelling shortcomings, the sheer amount of player freedom and emergent gameplay ensures that no two playthroughs are ever the same.

In the end, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is both a masterpiece and a missed opportunity. It delivers an incredible gameplay experience that is unmatched in its field, but its incomplete narrative and lack of closure prevent it from reaching the heights of Metal Gear Solid 3 or Metal Gear Solid 4. Still, as Kojima’s final contribution to the series, it stands as a testament to his visionary approach to game design.

review_text:
What a disappointment when you realize that this game is maybe only 50% of what it was originally planned to be. The second half of the story was never integrated, possibly due to the fallout between Kojima and Konami at the time.

What you get is a stealth action game set in a visually impressive but completely lifeless open world where you meet nobody besides enemies, prisoners and a few animals, padded with grind-heavy content, dull NPCs you never get to know well enough to form any kind of connection with, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ microtransactions, and a ton of unnecessary features that bloat the experience like an Excel sheet. The base-building and personnel management, the unnecessarily large research tree, the endless helicopter rides that become a chore, the constant name-dropping at the beginning and end of every single (side) mission, the combat dispatch missions which are not missions but simply excel ♥♥♥♥- none of these things deliver on what was always the heart of the series, alongside its stealth gameplay: the story.

The story just never takes off. The whole thing gets cut off just when it starts getting interesting. Many key plot points that could have made for great cutscenes are instead relegated to long-winded audio recordings- some stretching up to ten minutes. And the big reveal at the end? It’s not satisfying at all. The final twist simply isn’t that great, so it doesn't serve as a true ending, and as already mentioned, only half of the story is told anyway. The rest is left as nothing more than an incomplete cutscene (you can find it on youtube), barely 30% finished. In the end, the only truly memorable part of the game for me was the prologue (Ground Zeroes and the first mission of The Phantom Pain). The rest? Well, meh.

So, what was enjoyable? The core gameplay is solid, as it already was in Ground Zeroes. Stealth action is fun, and the game gives you plenty of room for creativity in how you approach missions. But it's not perfect. The overwhelming number of features and bloated equipment system seem to be compensating for elements that aren’t well-integrated. Just the fact that I never needed to use night vision (except for a single story-driven moment), coupled with the oddly bright night lighting- no truly dark nights in this game- shows that, although it is fun, fundamental aspects of the stealth gameplay aren't polished. And then there are the outright bizarre features. I didn't feel like I was Venom Snake- but Snake, the Enslaver.

If you want the full Metal Gear experience, of course, you still need to play MGS V. But considering that both Ground Zeroes (an overpriced demo) and The Phantom Pain (unfinished) were, and still are, blatant rip-offs, I can't say I'm happy. I expected more. And I must also admit that these two games have made me question my perception of Konami.

review_text:
Aside from Ground Zeroes (which is very short and basically the same game) MGSV was the first full Metal Gear Solid game I’ve ever played so I approached it with no expectations many long-term fans of the series might have had when the game came out. In 2015 many of them expressed disappointment with the game, mainly because it was quite different from earlier installments and felt unfinished. While there’s some truth to both of those points, they shouldn’t be a reason to skip this title.

Let’s start with this - if you’re new to Metal Gear games, feel free to start with MGSV as far as I’m concerned. When it comes to the chronology of the series, the events of MGSV take place a bit earlier in the timeline. Of course, if you played MGSV: Ground Zeroes, the experience will feel a bit more complete. Some of the revelations won’t have as much impact if you are not familiar with the Metal Gear saga but it won’t ruin the enjoyment. Overall, the focus of MGSV is more on the open-world stealth gameplay and micromanagement, rather than exploration of lore.

All story-related context aside, this game is essentially a power-fantasy wish fulfillment if you ever wanted to have your personal, technologically advanced mercenary army (Private Military Corporation) which answers to no country and no ideology, only to itself. To put it simply, 9 years ago a black ops organization known as XOF tried to bring you down but you got back from the brink and set out on the quest for revenge. The theme of revenge is often explored in the story and the way characters struggle with revenge, loss and betrayal. Story will feel relatable if you ever struggled with similar feelings.

Between missions you’ll spend a lot of time building your offshore Mother Base, organizing staff, developing new weapons and equipment, customizing vehicles, exploring hidden features and discovering funny surprises - a signature trait of Hideo Kojima’s works. Abundance of features make the game feel very large in scale and also “contemporary” even after a decade. It’s obvious a lot of thought went into the game’s design when you play it.

As your base, army and arsenal expands, you’ll feel a rewarding sense of progress which also carries over to the multiplayer mode. There are two kinds of MGSV multiplayer: Metal Gear Online which is the typical team-based multiplayer and then there’s FOB infiltrations where players infiltrate each others multiplayer mode bases and try to steal resources that can be used in singleplayer campaign as well.

When it comes to singleplayer campaign, the setting feels unique. The game takes place in 1984 but the technology characters use is sometimes more advanced than what we have today. The whole setting of the game feels like an interesting blend between real-life history, tactical espionage and these random over the top sci-fi elements which at moments feel almost supernatural. Some things feel like they were intentionally made to be ridiculous but this is what gives MGSV its charm.

Campaign has a lot of replay value - you can go back to previous missions to earn higher ranks, complete unfinished side objectives, look for additional specialized staff or resources, earn emblems and achievements. You can complete previous missions not only as the main character Venom Snake but also as some of the soldiers you recruited to your army. For example, you can play as a female character too.

High replay value redeems the game from the fact that around 60% through the campaign, the missions begin to repeat themselves. Many missions late in the game are just recycled missions from previous chapters tweaked with new conditions. Whether this was done by design or a consequence of rushed development due to Kojima’s issues with Konami is debated to this day. For some, this ruins the entire game but for me MGSV turned out to be one of the most engaging gaming experiences in years by the time I tried it out. If you like open world sci-fi action stealth games with memorable characters, deep techno-thriller lore about espionage and secret organizations more powerful than governments, original ideas and addicting sense of progress, I think there’s a high chance you’ll end up feeling about this game the way I do.

review_text:
This game is magic
It is either the most complex stealth simulation on the market you can get or at least is in the top 3 for sure.

Yet as a metal gear game it feels empty. With Previous games in the series being completely stuffed to the limit with cutscenes, with talking through the radio with over the top enemies and peculiar situations, genius commentary etc.

This game is mechanically the best Metal Gear ever, but story wise is the worst. Plot is unfinished or feels unfinished, it is a lot of reading in between. Everything is very vague and yet complex. 
I'm struggling to describe it myself. That "Phantom pain" thing, something which affects you yet is kind of not there? You feel it, you feel it's presence but it's just you hurting, you lacking something which were here but now is gone... Knowing Hideo Kojima, the game or idea for the game was meant to be just like that. This guy never seems to shy away from some extravagant ideas. Plot is for sure something unalike in comparison to general AAA games.

This was my first metal gear game, which took me upon a 200h+ ride of gameplay (different account). Introduced to me this absolutely magnificent series which is now my favourite game series ever.
I was mostly Splinter Cell, Thief, Dishonored, Hitman, Deus Ex fan, so this game mechanically clicked perfectly. Other metal gear games never were really that deep with stealth mechanics; Sure MGS games are stealth games, but they are pretty basic with the theme and not really intuitive in terms of controls. There were some gimmicks that enriched gameplay but generally there were not realistic yet they were really deeply intertwined with cause and effect systems.

E.g. In mgs3 you could destroy a supply shack, which then caused enemies to be hungry all the time. So making poisonous traps, or baiting them on foul food was viable gameplay option. But no one told you you could affect the rest of the game and game mechanics like that, that is completely optional. All of the game takes place story wise in a couple of days in the same place, so that is for sure realistic (defending realism in mgs games). But crawling around, staying still, hiding inside a cardboard box are basic and gimmicky.

So MGS 1-4 are plot gems comparable to Jojo's bizarre adventure comedy wise with cartoonish sneaking mechanics and over the top action scenes from 90s action movies.

MGS 5, Phantom Pain is mechanically stealth simulator, on par with Splinter Cell chaos theory in the movement departament. But this game supports failures brilliantly, unlike most stealth games. In this genre you are generally bound to quick save/quick load all the time until you memorise a whole level. In here you are given tools to fend for yourself in different scenarios and situations. Quiet ones and loud ones.

But story is not given to you, it is flashed at the beginning, but the rest is hidden in cassette tapes, which you have to look for by yourself without the game suggestions AND if you are not the fan of the series (don't know previous games and their plot), you most likely won't understand very much of it.

So this game should be recommended to fans of the military, stealth, recon, resoluteness, stealth, guns blazingness, helicopters, searching for big mechs, stealth, just to suffer memes, mercenary life, sacrifice, philosophy of war.
But if you want to sitback and enjoy a coherent story, soak in great cutscenes, wait for big plottwists then look at the previous entries in the series.

review_text:
One of Kojima's finest, and misunderstood masterpieces.

The FOX engine provides one of the smoothest and crisp gameplays you'll ever receive out of the Tactical Stealth Espionage genre, with satisfying movement, gunplay, and graphics that still hold up in 2025.

The Story:

The story is one of the most misunderstood parts of the game, and this is largely due to people either not being well-versed in Metal Gear lore, or simply lack story comprehension, which in this game, is told a lot more differently compared to previous titles.

Instead of CODEC calls, most of the conversations that are important to the story are contained in cassettes, which you have the option of listening to. I believe this to be something that Kojima implemented, as a means to not cause people to complain or be bored if these were done as CODEC calls, because there is a LOT of conversations, way too many to fit into CODEC's. 

The story is crushing, it is a representation of veiling evil as "good", with pursuit against "evil" being an act of revenge, veiled as "justice". 

[SPOILER] 

The biggest part of this "good" veiling as "evil" is the way the real Big Boss turns his most trusted lieutenant to be a phantom of himself, to uphold Diamond Dogs while he works in secrecy to develop his own plans. He uses his phantom the same way the US government used Big Boss in the end of Metal Gear 3, a pawn for a bigger picture in the war economy.

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain
Released: September 1, 2015
Developer: Kojima Productions
Publisher: Konami

The End of an Era:

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain was more than just a game, it was a defining moment in gaming history and a turning point for the Metal Gear franchise. Directed by Hideo Kojima, the game carried the weight of the series’ legendary legacy while also serving as Kojima’s swan song before his controversial departure from Konami. With this final installment, Kojima delivered a technical and gameplay masterpiece, but one with an incomplete narrative that left fans with, fittingly, their own “Phantom Pain.”

Revolutionizing Stealth Gameplay:

At its core, The Phantom Pain was a groundbreaking evolution of the stealth action genre. Taking place in an expansive open world set in Afghanistan and the Angola-Zaire border region, the game gave players an unprecedented level of freedom. This was a drastic shift from the linear level design of its predecessors, emphasizing player creativity and adaptability.
The stealth sandbox allowed players to approach missions with a variety of tactics, whether through silent infiltration, full frontal assault, or clever distractions. The depth of options was staggering, thanks to the diverse arsenal of weapons, tools, and companions. From tranquilizer pistols to sniper rifles, cardboard boxes to decoy balloons, the game encouraged experimentation. The Fulton Recovery System, allowing players to extract soldiers, vehicles, animals, etc, added a strategic layer to every encounter, tying directly into the game’s base management system and lore by obtaining tapes or mission ending information cutscenes. 
The AI, responsive and adaptable, made every mission a challenge. Enemies would wear helmets if you relied on headshots or deploy mines in routes you frequently traveled. Or both. Combined with dynamic weather and day/night cycles, the emergent gameplay kept even repetitive missions fresh.

A Brilliant But Fragmented Narrative:

The Metal Gear series is known for its dense, cinematic storytelling, but The Phantom Pain took a more restrained approach, favoring player driven narratives over lengthy cutscenes. While this design choice worked well with the open world structure, it came at the cost of the intricate storytelling fans had come to expect. 
The game begins with one of the most memorable prologues in gaming history. Players wake up in a hospital as Venom Snake (Big Boss), barely escaping a harrowing attack. This sequence sets the tone for a story steeped in themes of revenge, identity, existential crisis, and the cyclical nature of violence. As Venom Snake rebuilds Diamond Dogs and seeks revenge on Cipher, the narrative gradually reveals shocking twists, including the revelation that Venom Snake is not the “real” Big Boss but his body double, another key deception within the Metal Gear timeline.
Main Missions are shown as “episodes” in a tv show. Leading one to believe that there was a whole lot more in store for the story. Especially at a time where Konami wanted and successful Live service title.
Quiet, a true antithesis to “sexy-just-because” female characters. Fan service doesn’t erase the fact that Quiet is a strong, well written character that doesn't need a man to save her. That puts her on a level comparable to The Boss, who is one of the most impressive female characters to ever grace a video game.
Miller, Ocelot, Eli, all shine when shown on screen. Ocelot with countless nods to past events, making this feel all the more nostalgic, especially for veterans of the series. 
Despite its ambitious themes, story, characters, the story suffers from a fragmented structure. Chapter 2 is especially criticized for its reliance on recycled missions and an abrupt ending. The exclusion of Mission 51, including Eli’s rebellion and the fate of Sahelanthropus, left the narrative feeling incomplete. This incompleteness is widely attributed to the troubled relationship between Kojima and Konami during development.
For fans who had invested decades into the Metal Gear saga, the unresolved storylines felt like a betrayal, leaving them with lingering questions and a sense of loss.

“The Phantom Pain”:

The title “The Phantom Pain” is both literal and metaphorical. It references Snake’s physical condition, missing an arm and leg, and the psychological scars he and other characters endure. The game’s core themes revolve around loss, identity, and the creation of legends, how the truth is viewed. These ideas resonate deeply, not just within the story but with the players themselves.
As the final chapter of Kojima’s involvement with Metal Gear, the game left fans with their own Phantom Pain. The missing narrative pieces, the knowledge of Kojima’s departure, and the uncertain future of the franchise created a void that felt almost intentional, as if mirroring the game’s themes of absence and longing.

Technical Mastery, The Fox Engine:

The Phantom Pain was a technical marvel. Built on the Fox Engine, the game showcased stunning visuals, lifelike animations, and incredible attention to detail. From the vast deserts of Afghanistan to the lush jungles of Africa, the environments were richly detailed and immersive.
The audio design also deserves praise, with a haunting score by Ludvig Forssell and standout performances from Ocelot (Troy Baker) and Robin Atkin Downes (Kazuhira Miller). The licensed 1980s soundtrack, featuring hits like David Bowie’s “The Man Who Sold the World,” added an atmospheric layer to the game, evoking both nostalgia and melancholy. Also adding to the plot massively. 

Impact on Gaming:

The Phantom Pain set a new standard for open world games. Its blend of player freedom, reactive AI, and emergent gameplay influenced countless titles in the years that followed. Few games have managed to offer such a seamless combination of narrative depth and mechanical complexity.
For the stealth genre, it was a revolution. It showed that stealth could thrive in a non linear, player driven environment.

The Controversy, Kojima VS. Konami:

The behind-the-scenes drama between Hideo Kojima and Konami is an inseparable part of The Phantom Pain’s legacy. Kojima’s departure from the company was one of the most publicized conflicts in gaming history, with rumors of budget cuts, rushed production, and corporate interference overshadowing the game’s release. The incomplete narrative and the exclusion of Mission 51 are widely seen as casualties of this fallout.
Fans rallied behind Kojima, viewing him as a visionary artist constrained by corporate interests. The resulting game feels like a monument to what could have been, further solidifying its bittersweet reputation.

A Masterpiece and a Missed Opportunity:

Despite its flaws, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is undeniably a masterpiece. It revolutionized gameplay mechanics, redefined the stealth genre, and delivered some of the most memorable moments in gaming. Yet, it also left fans with an aching void, a sense that something vital was missing.
This duality is what makes The Phantom Pain so unforgettable. It is a game about loss, longing, nostalgia, melancholy and the impossibility of closure, both for its characters and its players. Fans of the series still discuss its mysteries and unfulfilled potential, a testament to its lasting impact. 10 years later. 

Press F:

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a game that simultaneously fulfilled and betrayed expectations. It gave us unparalleled gameplay freedom and a haunting narrative, but it also left us yearning for the completeness that never came. For fans, it was the end of an era, a brilliant yet flawed farewell to one of gaming’s most iconic franchises.
It’s this mix of brilliance and imperfection that ensures The Phantom Pain will be remembered not just as a game, but as an experience, one that, like its name, lingers long after the credits roll.

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is an ambitious and innovative game that delivers some of the best stealth mechanics and open-world design ever seen, but it’s not without its flaws. While it’s a technical masterpiece with unparalleled gameplay systems, it also feels incomplete and emotionally hollow in places, leaving a bittersweet impression.

The gameplay is where The Phantom Pain truly shines. The stealth mechanics are incredibly polished, giving you complete freedom to approach missions however you like—whether through careful infiltration, tactical sniping, or full-on chaos. The open-world design complements this perfectly, with dynamic environments that encourage experimentation and adaptability. Every mission feels like a sandbox of possibilities, and the game consistently rewards creativity and skill. It’s a level of player agency that’s rarely matched in the stealth-action genre.

However, the open-world structure can sometimes work against the pacing. While the maps are large and detailed, they often feel empty and repetitive, with filler objectives and recycled mission designs padding out the game’s length. The endless grind for resources and staff for Mother Base, while satisfying at first, eventually feels more like busywork than meaningful progression.

The story, a hallmark of the Metal Gear series, is where The Phantom Pain falters. While there are moments of brilliance and Kojima’s trademark cinematic flair, the narrative is noticeably incomplete, with key plot points unresolved and the second half feeling rushed. Big Boss’s journey lacks the emotional weight of earlier games, and long-time fans may find the story’s disconnect disappointing. That said, the characters are memorable, and the game’s themes of revenge and betrayal are compelling, even if they don’t fully land.

Technically, the game is stunning. The Fox Engine delivers incredible visuals, fluid animations, and lifelike AI, making the experience immersive from start to finish. The soundtrack and sound design are equally phenomenal, adding tension and atmosphere to every mission.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a groundbreaking stealth-action game that sets a new standard for gameplay freedom, but its pacing issues and unfinished story keep it from being the definitive Metal Gear experience. It’s still an essential play for fans of the series and anyone who loves stealth games—just be prepared for a mix of brilliance and frustration.

METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN is the kind of game that will make you question your life choices while simultaneously making you feel like the coolest person in the room. One minute you’re sneaking through a jungle, silently taking down enemies, and the next you’re riding a horse while firing rockets at tanks like it’s a normal Tuesday. Seriously, you spend hours stalking through enemy camps, hiding in boxes, and giving cardboard cutouts a new meaning. It’s a game where stealth is key, but let’s be real, sometimes you’ll just throw caution to the wind, cause chaos, and try to outrun helicopters in your underwear. It’s absurd, it’s brilliant, and the moments of pure insanity make it unforgettable. Just remember, if you don’t get spotted, you’ll feel like a ninja—but if you do, you’ll have an army of enemies chasing you like it’s an action movie. And hey, there’s no better feeling than dropping from a helicopter with style.

METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN is an open-world action-adventure game that gives you total freedom in how you approach missions. You play as Venom Snake, a legendary mercenary leader who’s out for vengeance after a brutal attack on his army. The game offers a huge world to explore, ranging from war-torn deserts to lush jungles, all while giving you the freedom to tackle missions however you want. You can go in all guns blazing, silently infiltrate enemy camps, or even use animals (yes, animals) to help you out. It’s a blend of tactical combat, stealth, and vehicle hijacking, all wrapped up in a storyline that will keep you hooked. The mechanics are smooth, the open world is rich with detail, and the bond between you and your team feels real as you build Mother Base—a central hub for your operations. The side missions are varied, offering everything from rescuing hostages to collecting resources and upgrading your gear. And don’t forget the famous buddy system—whether you’re using a wolf or a helicopter as backup, there’s always someone (or something) at your side. It’s a game that lets you do whatever feels right to you, with a story that’s equally thrilling and full of emotional depth.

What truly makes METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN stand out is its combination of storytelling, open-world gameplay, and insane attention to detail. From the way the environment reacts to your actions to the intricacies of managing your own army, everything feels alive. The stealth mechanics are top-notch, and if you’re sneaky enough, you can complete missions without ever being seen, which feels absolutely incredible. But when things go south, the chaos is equally satisfying. Plus, the story is deep, with twists and turns that will leave you questioning everything you thought you knew about the series. The game is visually stunning, with fantastic animation and attention to detail in the world-building. The pacing of the story is perfect, balancing intense action sequences with slower, more reflective moments. If you love stealth-based games with a gripping narrative, open-world exploration, and plenty of freedom in how you approach things, METAL GEAR SOLID V is a must-play. It’s a masterpiece that combines fun, strategy, and storytelling in a way that few games can. Definitely recommended for anyone who loves a mix of stealth and action with a side of utter chaos.

MIXED REVIEW if I could so:

Never seen a harder case of "monochrome/Black-white" game.

Every overwhelmingly possitive aspect of this game has a equally gaping flaw counterweight, making the game inconsistent and feel like a chore to play, sacrificing itself for a longer playthrough and forcefully fitted mechanics that will make you wonder if the whole Kojima/Konami drama surrounding this game's release was due to the inconsistencies and unfineshed characteristic of the game.

Even if the story is kind of a fragmented mess its still a Kojima story, set after the greedy release of Ground Zeroes, Snake awakes from a 9 year coma in a Cyprus Hospital where he was hidden from the Cipher organisation who 9 years earlier destroyed his base. Snakes missions from now on will have a dual purpose, discover Ciphers plans and build back the Diamond Dogs Organisation and its funds.  

This enticing story is brought down by a fragmented and unfinished walkthrough where every couple missions you are requiered to take the Helicopter and go to mother base so Ocelot or Miller can explain a worthless online mechanic that Konami wants you to play, honestly i think you can expect to spend hours on dead time traversing a fake open world or in the loading screens of a Helicopter, specially brutal when the game was so much filler and feels overstreched, even if we do not take into account a second unfinished chapter that requieres you to do 3 repeat missions to advance 1 main mission and therefore streching 8 missions into 32; beats me why they decided it was better to leave this on and hide the lore and mainstory behind cassete tapes optional to listen to.

Music choice is masterfull and in-game mechanics are a peak for the time it was released , but the way this mechanics are implemented on repetitive missions where you can exploit 1 or 2 main mechanics like bullet time or sleeper guns forces the player to set arbitrary restrictions on itself to maintain the game fresh till the end.
