review_text:
Spoilers.

I have a love/hate relationship with V. While it has the most refined gameplay of all the Metal Gear games, it doesn't have the most cohesive and finished story out of all of them. 

Gameplay wise it's fantastic, you can do so many moves like crouch walk fast/slow, crawl or "belly walk" as i love to call it, roll while crawling left to right, kick people off their feet with your hand/leg while crawling and so many more. The gunplay is clunky at first but it works really well and I love how you cannot be 100% accurate unless you aim down the sights like in real life. Sadly the gameplay falls short since most of the maps are really empty and open areas are very abundant, you have like 4 places? That are really suited for espionage gameplay and sneaking around. Afghanistan has two bases and Africa the same where you can truly utilize your abilities to the maximum and that's a shame. Shooting the radios and throwing food to enemies are all gone, same with changing your camouflage on the whim depending on the situation which i guess it's realistic? But not quite fun, the multiple outfits Big Boss had were the bread and butter of his gameplay in my opinion, couple that with his CQC that V does very well

The customization, base building and staff recruitment are all fun, from the gun customization which is honestly insane to the base building and base defending modes all have their flair. Base building can become really annoying, the resources are very hard to get offline which makes the online part of it a big deal which is just bad game design imo. 

The story and mission structure is when the game truly falls apart. The characters are interesting but most are just characterized in the tapes, same with their dialogue. There are 6 and a half hours of cassette tape dialogue completely relevant to the story, dialogue that should have been said in the actual cutscenes. I get that MGS4 had horribly long cutscenes but we could cut at least 2 hours of the tapes and introduce them in the cutscenes. With this setup you keep the tape player that wasn't a bad idea but to completely rely on it was just a horrible decision. At this rate i'd go to MS4 again to see the cutscenes rather than sit in the map idle or in the chopper to just listen to 6 hours of dialogue on a blue backround, we went from bad to worse in an attempt to fix? the problem that MGS4 had. 

Ocelot is...there in the story, that's everything i have to say for him, my favorite character in the entire series in just in the backround most of the time and talks down to Kazuhira whenever he has an idea. At least Kaz got more moments and truly shined here, his complete 180 in his personality was interesting, i'm not a big fan but i understand where he comes from and why he's like that. Quiet is by far the worst in the cast, you don't need dialogue to characterize a person but Quiet was always a blank slate for me, she didn't do much for the plot really, just gave some signs about plot related stuff and was apparently in love with Venom which was cute but then again, i don't even know what kind of person she's supposed to be, i cannot characterize someone who isn't involved in the plot that much and her horrible portrayal. Sure, making a character sexy isn't the end of the world but someone who spends 95% of the game in a black bikini in the heat of Afghanistan, has no lines and is pretty much used as a plot device when the story calls for it is truly disgusting.

Whenever there was talk of the parasites, she walked in, when the parasites started affecting people, they used her to show that we must kill them, when there was talk of a spy in Motherbase, they jumped to strap her to a chair and electrocute her despite helping Big Boss all this time? And tortured the one person in the entire base that never said a word? By Ocelot?? The guy who fought tooth and nail with Kaz to let her on missions with Big Boss, you know, where they will be alone and very easily to kill considering she's pretty much the best sniper in the entire series?? I get that she needed sunlight to breathe and i get why she couldn't talk but all of this is weirdly places when she has animations showing you her bare cheeks every time you got in the chopper, yeah, she has an animation for that and considering the iDroid (menu) is transparent you'll see it regardless if you want to or not.

Quiet's whole act at the finale of her arc was dumb, sure she couldn't talk to tell her the feelings she harbored for Venom but at the same time made no attempt to show him that, they just have one scene playing in the rain that was cute but that's it. She could have written him letters or used sign language, imagine how cool it must have been for you to have to actually learn phrases in sign language to use Quiet's abilities in the gameplay, her signaling you enemies, asking you to throw grenades for her to shoot for redirection or ask you what to do, that would have been so cool but alas, we need to dumb her down to fit the "language" narrative the whole game has, she could have been the shinning light in the whole plot, making all of Skull face's arguments make sense but also invalidate them all, we can communicate without words just fine. 

Skull face was very cool as a villain, his whole speech about how language is weaponized against people in real life was eye opening in some moments, how much culture, expressions and personality are lost and another argument on why colonization was so damaging to people all around the world. Shame that most of his dialogue is found in the tapes which weren't bad to exposition him before meeting him and his dialogue with Major Zero was super cool, probably my favorite tape in the whole game but it truly hurt his character to have so much dialogue out of the cutscenes. Also he's the second villain that never got a boss fight in the series, I get why Hot Coldman didn't get one but Skull face was perfect for a new kind of boss fight in the series since he's an assassin above all else, how amazing it would have been to fight him in an arena that forced you to use every sneaking tactic your learned and make the most of it while he did the same with the same arsenal. Come on this is the guy that is heavily implied to have killed Joseph Stalin, for the people who don't know he died in his own bathroom, the building surrounded by guards and staff and he was never seen and this guy is deformed from head to toe, just to give the idea. 

Tretij Rebenok and the Man of Fire were by far the coolest characters in cutscenes but you can never convince me (like Ocelot tried to in the tapes) to make his powers a "normal" occurence, like come on this is the same series where we have actual ghosts.

Many people didn't get why Sahelanthropus was dangerous and call him a "paper tiger". They aren't completely wrong but the whole idea/existence of Sally was that if people found out he truly exists, it would spark WW3. This is a bipedal Metal Gear with guns from head to toe, from rockets to his electrical laser to his sword whip to his famous peanits flamethrower. Until MGSV the biggest Metal Gear we had was Peace Walker that is pretty much the most impenetrable Metal Gear ever to exist. Sally didn't need to be powerful, didn't need to be impenetrable, he just needed to exist to be dangerous. He was still a formidable foe to fight, being fast since he's walking like a human, can jump thanks to Tretij and switch between his weapons without effort and the whole body being made of depleted uranium was super dangerous given that he had metallic Archaea built in it or at least was thought of being added which potentially made Sally the biggest nuclear bomb known to mankind.

The missions were also super repeated and the whole act 3 that was supposed to finish Liquids arc was cut. For all we know Liquid has a fully functional metal gear with him that just...disappears? That doesn't break the continuity at all (obligatory sarcasm)

review_text:
It's really good, but . . . if you know, you know
games amazing but not finished, lots of questions left unanswered, some stuff rushed some stuff dragged out too long. Overall though while the story is left behind in some aspects, it's still up there in it's odd state. It's all lifted up by the music that's also, pretty good. What is definitely lacking though is just the environment. If you've played ground zeroes then you should know that ground zeroes is probably the best map in metal gear solid v and outside of that it's going through empty african fields with a few huts and a lot of soldiers. Mgsv does try to alleviate this with a couple more areas and bases that are rather unique and interesting to approach, but honestly as uninteresting as the environments are, the gameplay never suffers.

Gameplay is in fact mgsv's strongest aspect. There is roughly no game that has done what this game does for stealth combat. Trust me when I say I have looked. Tom clancy's wildlands and breakpoint, while trying a lot of the same stuff, loses just as much that is special in order to simplify it into a 7/10 third person shooter first and a stealth game second. Tools or dynamic methods of approach all are kept to a minimum. I would give the sniper elite franchise a close second for having a rather close formula that is comparable to mgsv, however sniper elite is still focused around shooting first, enemies, the environment and dynamic methods of approach second. 

What metal gear brings to the table that's so special that isn't done by really any game is everything around the shooting if you couldn't tell. Enemies have unique behaviors that are necessary for having a good stealth game, but also not the focus, just serviceable enough to pass and not bad enough to be a detriment. However the methods of interaction you can have with them can be shooting a sleep dart while they're looking over the edge of a lookout post to make them fall over, which if anyone's underneath can knock them out too. You can distract them with boxes that trick them into thinking it's their commander or a lovely person on initial glance to get by or maybe even capture them, just a few fun things like that without mentioning that there's an interrogation system that is both simple but adds a lot to making the game what it is. 
Outside of the npc's you have plenty of ways to go through areas, you can climb up walls, or shimmy up crevices, you can ride a horse through the middle of their base and just lay against the horse's side to hide. Maybe if you want you can send that same horse out to a blocked pathway and distract them all by making the horse defecate on command. You can airdrop in any vehicle you've captured or call in a bomb strike. 

It can be difficult to say exactly why this is all special added together, but a good example of a situation is how you can throw a smoke grenade into the back of a jeep before driving it out into the middle of an area and diving out the side and rolling into some tall grass as the smoke spreads throughout the area. Then while everyone's blinded you can call your dog to jump up and slit the throats of everyone there without being seen. It's the open endedness that while ordinarily would make an open sandbox game that would demand for you to make up the fun as you go such as in breath of the wild, kenshi or minecraft, this is instead offering enough direction to not ever make you question what you're doing, something I'd later appreciate about helldivers 2, or why certain tools are available as it's all part of the mission and everything has a situation where it would be the most optimal thing to use making this guided, but also an open sandbox except the need or want to experiment is instead offered up as more of a demand unlike most sandbox games which all of this is to say the game is something special.

I think the only missed aspect about this game would unfortunately be 2 things, the missions and mother base.

my problem with the missions are the same with the story, after roughly 15 missions or so the game stops telling a story and roughly just keeps offering challenges, nothing interesting or unique just another thing to go try. This isn't bad and I really did enjoy them, but when it gets bad is when it picks back up in the story only to have 12 final missions before you get to see the ending and the final missions are all quite literally, the same missions done earlier in the game just with modifiers. I love the modifier idea for missions, I just wish that instead they were settings you could enable or disable for each mission instead of the game saying it's a whole new mission especially since it gatekeeps the ending.

Now about mother base...
This game has a whole system around capturing soldiers to "recruit them" which builds up stats in your base to unlock crafting recipes. This is how it paces out the tools given to you so you're not too overwhelmed by your options but still making you excited for what you can use next. Unfortunately it's not done very well. You'll often need tons and tons of resources to go with these recruits or even resources to pick up more recruits which is done by doing the jankiest collectathon system of all time in game. You look for sparkly spots on the ground that show diamonds and give you the in game currency. Or you can pick up small boxes for fuel or something. If it was just capturing enemies it would be one thing, but the whole system is bottlenecked by resources and later they try to get really ambitious with the system for certain story sequences that require you to know a lot about your members. Don't get me wrong it's all still cool, but it's clear that there was a lot more that wanted to be done here and this is all they could do. 

All of this being said though, having an extra encouragement to spot enemies is appreciated and really cool. Just beyond that main point it's pretty rough.

Please try this game, it get's pretty cheap and even though they don't drop the price as much since the mgs collection came out, the game is well worth 30$ and it also pretty much runs on anything while still looking amazing. It's all absolutely worth your time.

review_text:
A gold standard of gaming that is largely unmatched today. Moving around and playing as Snake just *feels* good. All the movement options with detailed animations (rolling, dolphin diving, even crawling on your back) give you a ton of control over how you move through space while always feeling responsive and precise. It gives you so many fun toys to play with, too—decoys, C4, sleep grenades, remote strikes, companions. You can throw a grenade and have Quiet shoot it midair to blow up a helicopter hovering overhead. This is a game that *wants* you to explore and exploit its mechanics, and Kojima has thought of everything.

So much of this game is done to benefit immersion, and it’s something very few other games even attempt. Every menu in-game is actually Snake himself looking at a menu — it’s minor, but jarring when you go to play a different game and the menu is just a bunch of graphics that takes you out of the gameplay. Call in supplies or weapons and watch them descend on a parachute from the sky like they were just airdropped in. This game world feels *real* in a way other games don’t. 

Multiplayer is interesting and a bit of a mixed bag. FOB missions are a creative take on Dark Souls invasions that allows for both synchronous PVP and asynchronous PVE multiplayer, though these days it’s rare you’ll actually have an invasion/defense occur. I find FOB missions fun but repetitive, with a skill floor that goes up very quickly once you start getting to higher tier FOBs. Seriously, go check out high level FOB gameplay on YouTube, you need some *serious* skill to even think about infiltrating a 4/4 FOB with S+ staff and security devices. If you like skill-based grindfests you might dig it. I find it captivating for a bit every now and then, but eventually it grows stale.

Everyone complains about the story and, yeah, compared to the other Metal Gear games this one is weaker and more subtle with its storytelling. However, it still has a better story than 99% of games. It’s a different style of storytelling than other MGS games as Kojima was experimenting with narrative for an open world game. How well it succeeds is up for debate, but in any case what’s here is much more complex and interesting than most AAA games.

And the graphics still look phenomenal. That this game was able to run at all on PS3/360 is incredible. Running through the jungle blasting Maneater is an unmatched gaming vibe.

Simply the best stealth action military shooter out there. One of the most sophisticated enemy AI designs that makes for an excellent sandbox design. They adapt to the playstyle the player employs. Use guns and they wear body armor, only do headshots and they wear helmets, play most missions during the night and they come equipped with night vision goggles and flashlights, sneak a base through unconventional paths the enemies will set up mine fields there, etc. The gun play is also extremely satisfying, each and every weapon have a good punch to them. Guns also have bullet drop distance like in MilSims. Game also offers first person shooting for better accuracy. Both maps are faithful recreations of the countries they are based on, though of course every locale in the game is fictional.

I like the vast array of options available to the player for both pacifist style and lethal style gameplay. Very few games do this.

Base building is a cool feature. You create your own army and they help you develop better weapons and gear. It is a missed opportunity though that you can't call on your army in the open world. it'll just be you, your companion (D-Dog, D-Horse, or Quiet) and Pequod.

The game has a good selection of soundtracks ranging from MGS originals to licensed songs from the 80s. Oh and Invisible by Duran Duran is most definitely part of the OST collection, always was and always will be.

The story is great but it is clearly incomplete. Though this is the first Metal Gear game I've played, I could still see the apparent lack of story content like how the ending just sort of happens. Though the audio cassette tapes reveal a lot of details its not enough. The lack of story is more obvious when I got to know more about MGS lore. This game answers plenty but again not everything. Though I'll admit I'm satisfied with how the game is because of how brilliant the gameplay is despite the lack in story. I wish Venom Snake talked more though, Kiefer Sutherland did a terrific job voicing him.

Graphically the game holds up well even by today's standards. The character models are highly detailed. The FOX engine is probably the most efficient and resource light game engine I've ever seen. The game can run well on weak hardware too. Its a shame that it only got used in a few titles and abandoned. Could've developed into something even more.

REVIEW EDIT (previously I said the MGO3 aspect was dead but I am proven wrong, its still thriving but with a small playerbase). Played MGO3 and it's quite fun and chaotic. Friendly community but be prepared to be out skilled and out matched. Though don't be discouraged and give it a shot. Seen videos of FoB base raids (where you infiltrate other player's military bases) and that seemed really fun but I haven't done that myself in the game yet (don't want no infiltrators on my base lol).

I'd recommend this game to anyone, its a masterpiece even with the flaws in storytelling. One of the few games that I can keep playing again and again. 10/10 in every-way.

I finished the story mode after 386 hours and so the world feels empty when I return to FOB.

Unfortunately we all reach this point but its bittersweet.

After 3 restarts and 7 years since the start on my old laptop, I could never finish the game properly (may that be due to switching places or switching devices constantly). When I first got the game I did it due to excitement on discovering my second Metal Gear game (first one was MGR) and I can say confidently as a guy who absolutely LOVES STEALTH this is the best stealth shooter you will ever find. Period.

Constant discoveries and switching of hardware and fanaticism about stealth kept bringing me back to this game. A final Big Boss game and discovery of an ending that loops the Metal Gear back. I strongly incline to play this game even if you don't want to spoil the series, due to how fun and really forward it is in gameplay (compared to even modern games!).

The graphics are insane. The sound design is crisp. The dialogue is intriguing. The environment is impactful. The relationship with the world is....unforgettable. The character building of Snake and how you play him really shows your connection of how you see the Big Boss of this series.

Multiplayer FOB raids which was not included before in MGS series is an amazing idea, showing another "end-game" way of going way and beyond the simple stealth game. Building your own army, raiding others, growing stronger and FEELING the progression is truly shows that Hideo and his subordinates are masters at work.

If I go into how detailed this game is then this review would be unreadable to be honest, but you can trust me. The more you play this game the more you will realise how everything just works. Everything is catered so that you can utilise everything at your disposal. Everything has impact, depending on your usage of gadgets and it's not like RPG of course but you really can feel the environment adopting to you.

Switching Codecs to Audio Logs was a really smart idea I believe. Yes it removes some suspense but I think it still holds up. Being able to play them anywhere, whatever and whenever is a really good idea. The audio logs really give you an idea on the world and with how good the voice acting is (also the transcript) makes you want to continue to listen to them again and again.

Cut-scenes really make my day. It's rare compared to other MGS but damn do they feel good. I can't believe I discovered more of random ones when somebody for first time attacked my FOB (I tried FOB invasion only this year due to being a coward lol) and I can say I am always impressed by an insane "camera work" (which really ups the immersion and storytelling). Completing the game makes me realise I won't be able to discover some new ones and maybe that's why I am thinking of slowly giving up on doing 100% knowing that there's really nothing special about it (for me at least).

Would I recommend this game?
Absolutely, Metal Gear Solid is a must play series for anyone who plays games. The game introduces amazing characters with plenty of personality. An introduction of amazing story which is not always go-happy, but very thought provoking. And, of course, amazing gameplay (which might of course be confusing in other MGS, but in here it feels natural and even intriguing).

Please do not pass this game, even-through its owned by KONAMI. You would be really making it a disservice. Regardless of how "unfinished" it is I would say it's more then enough to feel like a completed story.

What else I can say. 386 hours and hopefully more. I can't wait for a day where I will play other Metal Gear Solid titles (playing Portable Ops on PSP now). I watched all of playthroughs but I am sure I will experience it fresh and I will enjoy my brain tingling from how dope this over-analysed (and in good sense) game plays.

review_text:
MGSV:TPP is a top-notch stealth experience. While the prologue takes its sweet time introducing you to basic mechanics, afterward the game quickly leans into its strong suit - field operations. Each mission assigned to you can be approached from many sides and in many ways. It is certainly possible to go in guns blazing, but if you choose the stealthy approach and succeed, you will be rewarded with both in-game prizes and greater real-life satisfaction. 

The stealth mechanic itself is very well-polished. Enemies react reasonably. Sight ranges and sound dispersal mechanics feel intuitive and fair. The tools in your arsenal are many and varied, so if you get bored of doing chokeholds, you can absolutely switch things up.  As a keyboard+mouse player, I’d appreciate more buttons for various actions, but the game is far from unplayable, even if some controls are a bit janky. 

Fans of the MGS franchise probably also care about the game’s plot. However, as a newcomer into this universe, I found the story rather opaque in part due to the, frankly, perplexing method of delivery (cassette tapes to reveal important information and the weirdly unnatural dialogue). Not to mention that the lore as a whole is a bit… unconventional. Add to this that MGSV’s high degree of “gamification” is not very conducive to storytelling, and you have a recipe for a story that is a brick wall for those without prior knowledge. It is a really good thing, then, that MGS:V makes it easy to focus on its gameplay elements. Or a bad thing, I guess, if you are a lore-buff. 

MGS:V shines brightest in its early and middle stages. Story-wise because the game’s 2nd chapter is unfinished, which is not just my opinion, but a well-known fact among the community. And gameplay-wise, because the initial relatively-low-tech environment forces you into a game of patience where timing is everything. Since late-game upgrades give you access to abilities which are pretty much superhuman, the emotional payoff for any successful takedown is proportionally smaller. Eventually, you can become a one-man army, and rising enemy difficulty levels and counts cannot quite keep up. 

Thankfully, MGSV features a truly silly amount of challenges, many of which give you the incentive to take the minimalist route. Clearing missions isn’t particularly hard. Clearing missions while leaving no traces of your existence is very much so. The game leaves it up to you to choose wherein your goals lie, a design decision that other titles shouldn’t be afraid of adopting. 

Freedom of tactical approach and the freedom to define your own goals combine with near-impeccable stealth mechanics and a spectacular variety of possible operations to make MGSV truly a titan in its genre. 

The best I-was-never-here simulator out there. 8/10.

OKAY, i've spent 94.3 hours playing this game and here's is my review...

This game is something else. It’s totally different from any third-person shooter I’ve played before. The gameplay is so unique and fresh, with features you just don’t see in other games. What’s cool is that you can play it however you want—you’re not stuck following the story or the mission structure like in other rigid third-person shooter.

You can go full stealth mode like a ninja or go in guns blazing like Rambo—it’s your call. Features like the Fulton Recovery System (where you can "abduct" enemies), the Buddy System with partners like D-Dog or Quiet, and managing your Mother Base all make the game feel so rich and full of possibilities.

BUT... The story feels unfinished. Honestly, if Konami had given Kojima Sensei another year or two to finish the game, it could’ve been perfect. Even so, the story is still engaging enough, especially if you’re a die-hard Metal Gear fan.

even so, as someone who has played MGS 4 and Snake Eater, the shift to an open-world setting threw me off a bit at first. But once I got used to it, I realized it’s actually a great change. It gives you so much more freedom to explore and experiment, and for the Metal Gear series, it feels like a breath of fresh air.

What makes this game extra special is that it’s the last Metal Gear game created by Kojima Sensei. Maybe that’s why he went all out and poured every crazy, brilliant idea he had into it.

So, would I recommend it?
Absolutely!
If you’re into open-world games that give you a ton of freedom (without being overwhelming), or if you just love creative and unique gameplay, this game is a must-play. For a Metal Gear Solid game, this one’s up there with the best—even with its flaws.

[quote=-Gray Fox, Metal Gear Solid]"We're not tools of the government or anyone else. Fighting was the only thing... the only thing I was good at, but... At least I always fought for what I believed in."[/quote]

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain stands as Hideo Kojima's final opus in the legendary franchise, and what a farewell it turned out to be. Like a perfectly orchestrated military operation, every element of this game comes together to create something truly remarkable, even if it leaves us with more questions than answers

[h3]The gameplay is nothing short of revolutionary for the series[/h3] 
Gone are the linear corridors of Shadow Moses, replaced by vast, open landscapes that serve as your tactical space. Every mission becomes a playground with many solutions - whether you're calling in D-Dog for backup, asking Quiet to provide sniper support, or riding into an enemy base on D-Horse while blasting "Take On Me" from iDroid. Yes, the grind for GMP to develop advanced gear can feel tedious, but each new gear in your arsenal opens up fresh approaches to infiltration

[h3]The soundtrack deserves special mention[/h3] 
Beyond the licensed '80s hits like "The Man Who Sold The World" [i](which carries deeper meaning than initially apparent)[/i] and "Friday I'm In Love," the original score perfectly captures both the loneliness of the Afghan desert and the tension of a nighttime infiltration, but in order to find all these bangers you ought to explore the world for these precious cassettes!

[h3]Now, about that story...[/h3]
 The narrative is where things get [i]complicated[/i], in true Metal Gear fashion. The plot itself might seem straightforward compared to previous entries, but there's a fascinating theory worth exploring: What if the 'V' isn't just for "5" or "Venom"?(Is it Peace or Victory)
[b]Possible Spoilers Ahead[/b]: [spoiler]What if we're experiencing another VR simulation, similar to Raiden's training in MGS2? Consider the evidence: The hallucinations, the peace symbol callbacks to Peace Walker, the fragmented nature of the missions, and most importantly, the themes of phantom pain and manufactured reality. Just as MGS2 questioned the [b]nature of digital information and manipulation[/b], MGSV might be questioning the very nature of identity and memory. This would explain some of the game's the surreal whale scene (MobyDick reference?), the frequent hallucinations, and how certain missions repeat with increased difficulty (very VR-like). The way characters appear and disappear, the inconsistencies with established Metal Gear lore, even the game's obsession with "phantom pain" itself - it all points to a deeper layer of reality manipulation that Kojima never explicitly confirms or denies...[/spoiler] This ambiguity seems intentional, leaving players to grapple with questions of reality versus simulation - a theme that's been present since Metal Gear Solid 2. Unfortunately, with Kojima's departure from Konami and Metal Gear Survive's different direction, we may never get concrete answers

[quote=-Big Boss, MGS: Peace Walker]"The truth is what you make of it."[/quote]

The game's technical achievements can't be overlooked. The Fox Engine delivers stunning visuals while maintaining smooth performance across platforms. The attention to detail is staggering - from the way sand sticks to wet clothing to the dynamic weather system affecting stealth gameplay, soldiers adapting to tactics and the Cardboard box! The online Forward Operating Base (FOB) missions add another layer of depth, creating a persistent world of espionage and base defense, though they might not be everyone's cup of tea

[i]Is it a perfect game? No. But its [b]imperfections[/b][/i], much like the shrapnel in Big Boss's head, serve as a reminder of what was and what could have been. MGSV represents both the pinnacle of stealth-action gameplay and a bittersweet farewell to one of gaming's most influential series. 
And with the MGS3 remake on the horizon and somewhat recent release of the Master Collection, there's never been a better time to dive into the series. The Phantom Pain might not tie up every loose end in the Metal Gear saga, but it's an incredible stealth-action sandbox that pushes the boundaries of what games can be

review_text:
I beat the main and all mandatory side missions in 46 hours, and have never beaten a Metal Gear game before. After I got the achievement for beating the final mission, it mentioned that only 17.5% of players had it, meaning only about 1 in 6 people got to the end of the game. I think this proves that, despite the reviews, most people don't actually like the game enough to even complete it's main story. These are the reasons as to why I think this is the case.

The game is very easy, no matter how you choose to play it. Playing stealthily is a breeze due to factors like the enemies' terrible vision. Once, I accidentally started a mission during the day while wearing night camo. I went prone in a mostly flat open area, yet the first enemy to spot me only did so after staring directly at me from about seven meters away. The enemies are also highly predictable. Once you learn their movement patterns, you realise you have plenty of time to make your moves before they even start turning around.

Going in guns blazing is just as simple. You can easily take down dozens of enemies without coming close to death. Even if you get hurt, all you need to do is hide in cover until your health regenerates. Bringing a companion/buddy along makes the game even more trivial. The only thing that might make someone consider it difficult is the reliance on checkpoints instead of manual saves, making it so that a single mistake will see you playing part of the mission all over again, but even this can be cheesed by selling a single material to force a checkpoint.

The gameplay quickly becomes repetitive, not only because of how easy it is but also due to the open-world design. Half of your playtime will literally just involve travelling from one place to another, which is made even more tedious by how barren the world feels. 95% of the map is just wasteland with a few easily avoidable guard posts scattered around, serving only as a way to connect the separate main bases.

The game is also far too long. It took me about 40 hours to beat all of the main and mandatory side missions, though it honestly started to overstay its welcome about 20 hours in.

The last dozen missions are especially tedious. Each one only takes about 5–10 minutes to complete, meaning you can spend just as long travelling there and back as you do playing it. It's a minute in a helicopter to reach a landing zone, then once it drops you off you have to travel for a couple of minutes in order to reach your objective. Once the mission is done, you’ll have to walk all the way back to the landing zone, wait for the helicopter to arrive, and then sit through the ride back out of the map. It’s easily the worst part of the game.

There are also a few annoying quirks. For instance, you can’t climb up or down certain objects while prone, even though it should be possible. Additionally, your character can get stuck on objects like barrels. Despite being cylindrical, they’ll cause you to walk in place until you step backward.

As someone who doesn’t particularly care about the story in most games, I’ll share some quick thoughts without spoiling anything. The story has its ups and downs. The sci-fi elements and technology are among the most interesting and creative concepts I’ve ever seen, and I always enjoyed seeing the robotics the developers came up with. The story also has some genuinely funny moments and has a good moral to it. However, I'd say the moral is near impossible to discern from the story alone, so you’ll likely have to look it up in order to fully understand it.
	
On the downside, the characters are hit or miss. A few of them are well-written, with clear motives and distinct personalities, but the majority have little to no development. Some characters leave you unsure of their goals or reasoning, and a couple could be cut from the story entirely without any meaningful impact, as shown by the fact that you can kill one before recruiting them, and all you lose are a few cutscenes and one mission that doesn't effect anything else.

The story is also rather eccentric and bizarre, which may or may not bother you, depending on your personal taste.

If the game were half as long, I’d recommend it. However, considering how long it takes to beat, I can’t. The map is too empty, the game is too easy, and the missions are too repetitive for me to say otherwise.

Since most of the reviews on this game are about the main story, I would instead like to write this review on the online portion of the game, specifically Metal Gear Online 3 (MGO 3). MGO 3 is essentially the only multiplayer game that I play, and it keeps bringing me back. There is something so satisfying and fun about it, and its uniqueness repeatedly draws me in. 

One of the striking unique points of MGO 3 is the inclusion of non-lethal options as well as lethal. Taking out foes with non-lethal is (typically) more difficult that simply going for kills with lethal, but it comes with benefits such as being able to rack up points and fulton enemies (which is very important in the Bounty Hunter game mode). Non-lethal requires more skill than lethal, however that makes it all the more satisfying when you are able to pull it off. Furthermore, the option of CQC is something I adore, it is such a rush whenever you are able to perform CQC and do 'true combos' to guarantee a stun on your enemy. It can take a bit of time to learn, but once you master it I find it to be incredibly fun. Some examples include a guaranteed headshot from grab release and placing an explosive mine under a target being fultoned. Other small quirks such as interrogating the opposing team to expose enemy locations and quirky playstyles (like a smoke + NVG non-lethal stealth loadout I have or magazine stun loadouts) allow for player experimentation and increased enjoyment.

Onto the game modes, only one is consistently played today and that is Bounty Hunter. The great thing about this game mode is that it is a simple death-match but it rewards going non-lethal. Other game modes may be played from time to time, but if you go into any lobby chances are it is going to be Bounty Hunter. The other game modes are Cloak and Dagger (stealth incentivised gameplay), Sabotage (defend or destroy a target), and Comm Control (basic defend/capture territory).

That said, MGO 3 can be quite hard to get into especially nowadays. Its quirks can be unfamiliar to new players and the dwindling playerbase means that although there is usually one lobby in most parts of the day, you will most likely be playing against dedicated and skilled fans with 500-1000 hours (I even saw someone with around 7000 hours), so expect to struggle a bit as you learn the ins and outs of the game. The lag in this game can be pretty bad depending on your internet and who is hosting, often leading you to die through walls among other things. It also is not the most balanced game with some weapons being quite hard to deal with (like the grenade launchers). The game is also notorious for cheaters. From personal experience, I seldom encounter very obvious cheaters (such as speedhacks and aimbot) so it is not so much of an issue that the game is unplayable. But allegedly there are an amount of players who use more subtle cheats such as lagswitching. However, this has not been a big enough of an issue for me to not be able to derive any fun from the game.

I often see MGO 3 get compared with its predecessor MGO 2, with individuals claiming that MGO 3 is a downgrade from MGO 2. I have not played MGO 2 myself but from some of the videos I have seen MGO 2 has better game modes and potentially a better loadout system as well as a greater focus on stealth, but MGO 3 shines when it comes to the fast paced gunplay and the combos which I mentioned earlier. I think rather than being a 'downgrade', MGO 3 is simply very different to MGO 2 so fans of MGO 2 were likely disappointed because of this. Since I never played MGO 2 this was not an issue for me.

In short, the uniqueness of the game and satisfying gameplay keeps drawing me back to hop on for yet another match. It can be hard to jump into at first, but if you already have finished the base game, I would suggest giving it a try.

Update after 1000 hours: Since originally writing this review, I have gone on to get invested in the other online component of the game, FOBs. Whilst I enjoy it a lot just like MGO 3, it suffers from more issues than MGO in my opinion.

For starters, it is much harder to get into FOB PVP compared to MGO, in large part due to the resource grind. You can develop most of the 'meta' loadout with two FOBs and not too many resources needed, but the amount of materials you need once you start going beyond grade 8 equipment as well as the third and fourth FOB platforms is simply ridiculous. It takes a couple of hours to accumulate enough resources to develop what you want, and then you have to wait up to around two weeks (real life time) for some to finish developing. On top of needing a decent supply for when you deploy for PVP it is no wonder that people resort to resource cheats.

Unlike MGO, you have a much larger arsenal at your disposal so one would think this would allow for more varied play styles and loadouts; however this is not true. The meta has developed around grenade launchers (specifically stun grenade launchers) and it is difficult to go with anything else against skilled players using such equipment. On top of this, there is a worse balancing issue than MGO, with equipment such as energy walls and auto-wormholes going so far as to be frowned upon amongst many dedicated players. I still find PVP fun even with the meta loadout, but a part of me feels a bit sad that I cannot as easily mess around with different playstyles like I can in MGO.

Overall, I cannot easily recommend getting into FOB PVP for most players and if you chose to do so it is a time investment. However, there is simply nothing else like it and it is no wonder why there is still a dedicated community of players still playing 10 years on from the game's initial release.

Approach missions your way : silent and ghost-like, or guns-blazing chaos with a rocket-arm high-five.

Tactical espionage. Existential dread. One incredibly expressive cardboard box.

[h1]If there is a textbook example for game design, Metal Gear Solid V would be it.[/h1]
The gameplay loop is fun and engaging. The individual missions are fun on their own, but things get even better when you replay the missions with upgraded equipment and improved skills (from you playing the game). The mission and upgrade loop is so addictive! The game encourages you to think outside of the box. Some missions require you to do a recon section before finding a target's location, but if you play the mission again and remember where the target is, you can just skip the recon part and finish the mission quickly (rewarding you with a higher score and extra resource for the upgrades). While stealth is usually not compulsory in the mission, the game rewards you when you go for a stealthy and non-lethal approach. You get to capture enemy soldiers and convince them to join you when you go non-lethal (and it's much easier to go non-lethal with stealth). Soldiers in your base unlock more upgrade options and field support, which further feeds into the core gameplay loop.

The narrative of this game is also superbly crafted. MGS is heavily inspired by action and spy movies of the 80s and 90s, with over the top action, conspiracy theories (the good kind in spy movies, not the disinformation spread on social media) and some sci-fi elements thrown in. There is also a heavy anti-war subtext to the story, which I love. The narrative also comments on how the dominant cultures in the world destroy other ethnicity through warfare and mass media. With that said, a lot of people would probably just enjoy the fun action parts without paying attention to the more important messages of the story.

I can't believe I have waited 9 years to play this game. Some of the newer games I played in the past few years don't even come close to the excellence of MGSV.

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain es mucho más que un videojuego; es una experiencia inolvidable que combina una jugabilidad impecable, una historia cautivadora y una presentación audiovisual impresionante.

La jugabilidad brilla por su libertad: puedes abordar cada misión como desees, desde un sigilo perfecto hasta un caos explosivo. El mundo abierto es inmersivo y detallado, ofreciéndote infinidad de maneras para explorar, planificar y experimentar. Cada decisión importa y cada herramienta que desbloqueas amplía tus posibilidades estratégicas.

El sistema de gestión de la Mother Base agrega una capa de profundidad que te hace sentir que realmente estás liderando un ejército de élite. Además, la mecánica del Fulton para extraer recursos y soldados es divertida y adictiva.

En cuanto a la narrativa, es una historia emocionante que se mantiene fiel al tono de la saga Metal Gear. Los giros en la trama, los personajes memorables como Big Boss y Ocelot, y las temáticas profundas sobre la guerra, la venganza y la humanidad son fascinantes.

Visualmente, es una joya. Incluso años después de su lanzamiento, el nivel de detalle en los escenarios, las animaciones y los efectos de iluminación sigue siendo de primer nivel. La banda sonora complementa perfectamente la acción, y el doblaje es excelente, especialmente la actuación de Kiefer Sutherland como Snake.

¿Es perfecto? Quizás no, pero lo que logra entregar es tan impresionante que los pequeños detalles quedan eclipsados por la grandeza de todo lo demás. Es un juego que te hará pensar, sentir y disfrutar durante horas.

Si eres fan del sigilo, de las historias bien contadas o simplemente de los juegos que te permiten total libertad, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain es imprescindible en tu biblioteca.

¡Gracias, Hideo Kojima, por esta obra maestra!

I finished the story mode after 386 hours and so the world feels empty when I return to FOB.

Unfortunately we all reach this point but its bittersweet.

After 3 restarts and 7 years since the start on my old laptop, I could never finish the game properly (may that be due to switching places or switching devices constantly). When I first got the game I did it due to excitement on discovering my second Metal Gear game (first one was MGR) and I can say confidently as a guy who absolutely LOVES STEALTH this is the best stealth shooter you will ever find. Period.

Constant discoveries and switching of hardware and fanaticism about stealth kept bringing me back to this game. A final Big Boss game and discovery of an ending that loops the Metal Gear back. I strongly incline to play this game even if you don't want to spoil the series, due to how fun and really forward it is in gameplay (compared to even modern games!).

The graphics are insane. The sound design is crisp. The dialogue is intriguing. The environment is impactful. The relationship with the world is....unforgettable. The character building of Snake and how you play him really shows your connection of how you see the Big Boss of this series.

Multiplayer FOB raids which was not included before in MGS series is an amazing idea, showing another "end-game" way of going way and beyond the simple stealth game. Building your own army, raiding others, growing stronger and FEELING the progression is truly shows that Hideo and his subordinates are masters at work.

If I go into how detailed this game is then this review would be unreadable to be honest, but you can trust me. The more you play this game the more you will realise how everything just works. Everything is catered so that you can utilise everything at your disposal. Everything has impact, depending on your usage of gadgets and it's not like RPG of course but you really can feel the environment adopting to you.

Switching Codecs to Audio Logs was a really smart idea I believe. Yes it removes some suspense but I think it still holds up. Being able to play them anywhere, whatever and whenever is a really good idea. The audio logs really give you an idea on the world and with how good the voice acting is (also the transcript) makes you want to continue to listen to them again and again.

Cut-scenes really make my day. It's rare compared to other MGS but damn do they feel good. I can't believe I discovered more of random ones when somebody for first time attacked my FOB (I tried FOB invasion only this year due to being a coward lol) and I can say I am always impressed by an insane "camera work" (which really ups the immersion and storytelling). Completing the game makes me realise I won't be able to discover some new ones and maybe that's why I am thinking of slowly giving up on doing 100% knowing that there's really nothing special about it (for me at least).

Would I recommend this game? 
Absolutely, Metal Gear Solid is a must play series for anyone who plays games. The game introduces amazing characters with plenty of personality. An introduction of amazing story which is not always go-happy, but very thought provoking. And, of course, amazing gameplay (which might of course be confusing in other MGS, but in here it feels natural and even intriguing).

Please do not pass this game, even-through its owned by KONAMI. You would be really making it a disservice. Regardless of how "unfinished" it is I would say it's more then enough to feel like a completed story.

What else I can say. 386 hours and hopefully more. I can't wait for a day where I will play other Metal Gear Solid titles (playing Portable Ops on PSP now). I watched all of playthroughs but I am sure I will experience it fresh and I will enjoy my brain tingling from how dope this over-analysed (and in good sense) game plays.

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is, without a doubt, a masterwork of modern gaming, combining unparalleled open-world gameplay with an emotionally gripping narrative. As the final chapter in Hideo Kojima's legendary Metal Gear series, it’s a game that leaves a profound impact, both for its gameplay mechanics and the deeper, more subtle themes it explores.

First, let’s talk about the world. The vast, beautiful, yet haunting landscapes of Afghanistan and Africa are meticulously crafted, and the open-world design allows players to approach missions in countless ways. Whether you’re sneaking through the wilderness on horseback or calling in airstrikes to disrupt enemy convoys, the freedom to experiment is a constant thrill. The AI is intelligent, with enemies reacting realistically to the environment, forcing you to adapt your strategies. You can go stealthy or go loud, but either way, the level of control you’re given over your approach is unmatched.

The gameplay itself is a true testament to Kojima’s vision of melding action with strategy. The game offers an intuitive and deeply satisfying combat system. Stealth is just as rewarding as direct confrontation, and each playthrough can be drastically different based on the player's preferred tactics. The level of detail in the game world is astounding—things like the day-night cycle and weather conditions impact how missions unfold, making each encounter feel dynamic and alive. The introduction of the “Mother Base,” a home base you manage and expand, adds yet another layer of depth, as you recruit soldiers and develop new technologies to aid in your war efforts.

The story, however, is where The Phantom Pain takes a more somber turn. It’s a narrative filled with pain, loss, and the consequences of war. Big Boss, the central figure, is a deeply conflicted character, and the game delves into the personal and philosophical struggles of those involved in global conflict. The game explores themes of revenge, identity, and the toll of military operations, all wrapped up in the tragic fall of the protagonist. The narrative is complex and sometimes cryptic, with moments of brilliance and emotional weight that hit hard long after you’ve finished the game.

But perhaps the most notable aspect of The Phantom Pain is its unfinished feeling. There are story threads left unresolved, especially considering the game was released in a somewhat rushed state due to Kojima's departure from Konami. This left some players with a sense of ambiguity and longing, as key plot points are left unanswered. Despite this, the game still offers an incredibly satisfying experience—its gameplay, world-building, and character depth more than make up for any missing narrative closure.

The soundtrack is another highlight. With a mix of melancholic original compositions and classic rock tunes from the '80s, the music mirrors the tone of the game perfectly. Tracks like “Sins of the Father” and “Quiet’s Theme” bring an emotional resonance to the quiet moments and action sequences alike.

Ultimately, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a game that stands as one of the greatest achievements in modern gaming. It’s a game that encourages exploration, rewards creativity, and, more than anything, offers a meditation on the complexities of war and the human condition. Kojima’s penchant for storytelling, combined with the innovative gameplay mechanics, creates an experience that will stay with you long after the credits roll. While its unfinished nature may leave some feeling unsatisfied with certain story aspects, the journey through its world, its gameplay, and the character of Big Boss himself is unforgettable.

One of the best games I have ever played because I find the overall story, aesthetic and (most importantly) the gameplay to be deeply entertaining. I put in 300 hours into this a few years ago, and every once in a while I think about picking it up again. If you enjoy previous MGS games and open world games, I think you will find this one very satisfying. 

The progression of increasingly powerful tools for the missions feels fantastic because it routinely rewards you with more fun ways to handle tasks. You gain the ability to approach the goals in different ways without it feeling too repetitive, which is imperative to open world games. Sneaking, if that's your style, feels more impactful here. You get more options to sneak around and pull off moves with or without the need of weapons. If you choose to be more noisy with your approach, you can do so with the knowledge you will be challenged, but you won't feel like the enemies are impossible to combat. The game feels fair.

The story is decent, just not as iconic as previous MGS games. There are plenty of great moments, but I can see why some people feel a bit disappointed with some plot points. I will admit I am always up for whatever is happening with this series, so It's hard for me to shake the feeling that some people 'just don't get it'. But some parts of the story felt either uninteresting or half finished. This is also the first MGS game I have played where the bosses and main antagonist haven't made enough of a lasting impact. The boss fights have been good. Though not as legendary as MGS1 or MGS3, but at least still fun. Their stories just did very little for me. Perhaps I am unfairly comparing fundamentally different games, but we buy these games with a certain level of expectations established by the developers and (more so imo) previous games in the series.

Anyways, fantastic title that compels me to post a review where I usually don't care to do.

review_text:
You may know me as Big Boss, but even legends like me have a thing or two to say about MGSV. After all, this game is my story—or at least, one version of it. Let me walk you through what makes it worthy of the Diamond Dogs' seal of approval... and where it leaves me with a bitter taste, like the sandstorms of Afghanistan.

The game is ambitious, sprawling, and tactical. From Afghanistan deserts to African jungles, it captures the brutal beauty of the world I had to traverse. The open-world design gave me the freedom to approach missions however I see fit—stealth, guns blazing, or even calling in an airstrike. All while I was listening to the Duran Duran's Invisible tape. Oh gosh, how much I love that track. It’s a far cry from the tight corridors of Outer Heaven. This freedom is where The Phantom Pain shines. I felt like a commander, a strategist, shaping the battlefield as I go. You might even say it’s the ultimate battlefield sandbox.

Mother Base is a fine addition... hell, it feels like home. Building it up, recruiting soldiers, and managing operations gave me the sense that I was creating something bigger than myself. It reminded me why I fight, why I lead. The bond I developed with your troops, especially a few standouts like Quiet and D-Dog, brings a certain humanity to the game. They became part of my family, my war machine. But at times, it felt like I was doing more managing than leading. Too much paperwork, not enough boots on the ground.

The storytelling? That’s where things get... complicated. Kojima weaves a tale filled with intrigue, betrayal, and pain. Always pain. But as Big Boss, I couldn’t shake the feeling that some parts of my story were missing. Entire chapters seemed... absent. The focus on an unfinished legacy, on phantom pains both literal and figurative, left me questioning if the story was about me or something else entirely. It's clever, but it also stings.

And then there’s the twist. Let’s just say it left me feeling like a pawn, not a king. It’s hard to lead an army when you’re not sure who’s wearing the eyepatch. Still, the raw emotion and grit make it impossible to turn away. The mission becomes your life. Your obsession. Just as it was mine.

So, would I recommend it? If you want to understand what drives a legend, if you want to feel the weight of command, and if you want to build something from the ashes of war, then yes. Play it. But don’t expect all your questions to be answered. Like the phantom pain of a lost limb, some wounds never heal.

Snake out.

review_text:
A big, juicy eulogy to Kojima's magnus opus, written, directed and also partially interpreted by Kojima himself. Our heroes live in a terrible, unlikely, weird post-cold-war-meets-sci-fi world where colours are a luxury but steel and lead dominate hearts and thoughts. Most missions are set in desolate monochromatic parts of Afghanistan and central Africa, where even wild animals must be "rescued" from being home and be sent on a steel monstrosity in the ocean. The sense of doom and circularity of evil is tempered by a lovely wolf-dog and from a hyper-sexualized, mute sniper woman kept in captivity and fueling the fantasy of this men-only facility called Motherbase. All this is shot in a deeply cinematic way, with a clearly recognisable Kojima take. The camera [i]even shakes[/i] in a very Kojima way. 
Nobody ever looks for redemption, peace or even just to ease the pain. On the contrary, pain for phantom that it may be is seen as the anchor to fuel those deeps desires of vengeance. And then, on top of this, my horse gets "fultoned" (transported home with a overall-type harness and a self-inflating balloon which carries an attached lift line) and makes a weird sound every time.
How can this chaos work? No idea, but it does. Big Boss' sole moment of peace are when he's in a solitary mission silenty taking out enemies, with no thoughts, just concentration and action. And despite the bonkers storyline and the soldiers who thank me every time i slap them, you keep playing it mission after mission, knowing that something majestically designed can be around the corner. Or not.

This game to me is love and hate. When i started it took me several hours to decide if I actually liked it. It was good enough to continue but bad enough to keep asking myself if it was for me or not.
In the end it was worth it and i'm glad for having given it a chance.

This game truly leaves you with a strange feeling, close to phantom pain. In terms of plot, it starts like a common spy thriller, with an abviously evil antagonist and a bunch of guys, who are not saint either, but who certainly look better. The first chapter's plot is pretty much predictable and does not offer anything surprising. The second chapter though... At the first look, it appears to be half-baked and unfinished. But the general mood and the messages differ drastically from what we could see at the beginning of the game. When I finished the story, I truly felt deprived of something. Like there was something I really wanted to maintain, but lost it forever. I'd say that, in terms of the main story, what starts as a plain and simple revenge tale, ends up as a manifest of grief, pointlessness of war, and dark shades of loneliness of those who see the world through the scope of the rifle. I still don't really know, how to perceive the ending of this game. It feels unfinished, it looks unfinished. But in the end, this emptiness and understanding of what comes after this in the general MGS storyline, truly creates an odd feeling of loss.

When it comes to gameplay, it really delivers. The amount of various stealth and combat mechanics really allow you to approach your missions differently. I truly loved the concept of being forced to adapt to fast-changing circumstances. At first, I was savescamming, trying to be the sneakiest guy ever. But the more I played, the better I understood, that this game wants you to improvise, because due to the open world model, every plan can go downhill in a fracture of a second. The sheer amount of gadgets and various weapons you can choose from make me feel like I can really experiment with my playstyle. When I got tired of sneaking around and just wanted to do some optional missions and blend some action in, I just changed my equipment to machine guns, missile launchers, ordered tanks from above, and the game never punished me for playing shooter.

At the same time, sooner or later, I reached the point of understanding the main flaw of this game. Progression. The local system of base building and staff extraction takes a long time to reach a considerable progress. If you want the best guns, the better suits, and generally if you want to make your gameplay smoother and perhaps adjust it to your personal style, you will inevitably reach the point, when you'll have to grind the optional missions for money and resources. I personally did not find the local open world annoying. It's empty, and there's literally nothing to do except for clearing the outposts in search of high-grade staff and resources for expanding the Mother Base. However, those missions are truly a sandbox and can be completed in numerous ways. Nevertheless, at some point, your base reaches the limit of personnel, so you will be forced to expand it. In order to reach high levels of all units you need for unlocking the top-tier gear, you will have to spend a lot of resources. But it's not the problem itself. The problem is that they need to be "recycled" first, and this recycling, as well as the actual platform building, is done live, when you play the game. And it takes hours. So I ended up in a loop: I needed to wait, say 2 hours, until my platform gets built; in the meantime, I completed side missions to kill time; The enemies get stronger with each mission, but your gear remains the same, so you need more staff to raise your HQ level; so you need recources and money; so you wait and grind, wait and grind.... And I really was stuck like this until, at some point of the plot, a secondary base is unlocked, and the process of farming speeds up dramatically. But the thing is, when you really make your build and get the gear you always wanted, the game will probably be nearing its end. Not like it's a bad thing, but the grindwalls they put a lot of good stuff behind can get really annoying sometimes.

As for the main missions, I really enjoyed most of them, except for a few of those that made me fight in the open, which truly makes this game a third-person shooter, whether you wanted it or not. However, making you replay the same main missions during the second chapter seemed weird. It seemed weird because those were literally the same missions with slight difficulty alterations. It looks like they needed to fill your playthrough with something, but they either lacked time, or budget to make it more unique. 

In general, I really liked this title. It's also important to say, that I never really played any other MGS games, and only played Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance before this, so this is my first Metal Gear Solid experience, aside from watching some lore videos. And it was really a fun to play through. I think this game introduced me to this great franchise, and for that I'll always be grateful.

review_text:
One of the best games I've ever played! No doubt what so ever. Shooter or otherwise.

TLDR version: I'm skipping the story here as it's very subjective and depends on if you are invested in the whole MetalGear world. The game play is a complete masterclass in combat and AI. You start with some basic weapons and tools. After building up your base and army. You unlock some truly game changing gear and tools. However the enemy is also evolving and continuously bringing new challenges forcing you to adapt and keep on changing your load-out and arsenal to counter them. The game-play loop is simple however gives you so much variety that it never feels the same. Even doing the same mission multiple times (very essential to the game play here) feels very different for a verity of reasons. This game is better then most modern shooters. With better AI.


Let me start by saying, that I played most of this game on the Steam Deck and it runs as smooth as butter! easy 60fps with mid or even high settings. Just amazing to be able to run a game that looks this good on the steam deck.

The game starts with a story portion, a very dark one at that (not my personal preference however I've played most MetalGear games so I was already used to it)
After the start of the game that also is a tutorial to get you started with missions and objectives etc. You are set free to work through the main missions and do any side missions available to you as well however you see fit.

I do want to highlight the structure of this game and something that I've seen in many negative reviews.
The entire game is played on 2 open world maps. You only have access to one at the start. While going through the main story missions you will unlock the second map at some point, then you will have missions on both. One map is in a desert area (many reviews are like: it's all sand and mountains what is that all about. Well that is where it is supposed to be!!). The other map is green. The maps are based out of different countries and therefore the map design is based on these locations.

The open world with missions is just brilliant as a world design:
So you start a mission: you get choppered in and ride your horse to the mission location. Do the mission and then? If you are not doing a story mission. You basically are free to roam the open world freely after completing the mission!
Why you might ask? Well you can simply drive to the other missions location and do some resource gathering on the way. Or even scout for new soldiers to "Recruit" for your personal army. You can even effect the next missions you start by getting rind of something in the area that might put you at a disadvantage. 
The whole sandbox nature of this open world is just crazy, and you appreciate it more and more as you continue playing and start to see how the enemy responds to your growing power. Yes the same locations that you visited before will start having new types of soldiers, equipment, air support, and tons more variety. That makes playing any missions like a new experience even if it's at a location you already did other missions in. The objective will be different, the enemy locations and patrols, other military units in the area of that come visit can create a very different game play loop. 

Getting stronger and the story gets better:
When you start you are weak and have limited weapons and tools, as you grow in power you unlock so many new weapons, weapon customization and attachments, and entire army base with facilities that you upgrade with resources you acquire while out on missions, that will allow you to research even more crazy weapons and tools.
You can take pretty much anything of value while out in the open world, to build and expand your base! you see enemy base weapons, take them, you see containers with resources! Yes take them. You see high skilled soldiers! you guessed it! just take them for your own army. See a tank, car, something that moves! take it!
This part of the game is also just so cool, because as you progress and do harder missions you will find more resources, and more highly skilled soldiers, these are the key to progress further as you need them to increase your ability to get specific support while out on the open world, and find people who can increase your ability to research items in the various labs you will have. This makes any soldier a person of interest for you as they can be of great value to you.

You cat get pretty much anything delivered to you while out and about:
One other simply amazing mechanic of this game is that while you are out and you just did a mission, you want to free roam and want a different load-out, companion or anything you have in your arsenal? Your army will deliver it to you by helicopter in a few seconds. You can do this as much as you want (it costs some cash, but nothing to actually worry about too much).
You can pick a place for your airdrop to land to make sure it's convenient for you, even if it means that is on the head of an enemy who is in a tough spot and you can't easily get by them. So the airdrop will land on their head and know them out! This really never gets old!
Also you have limited ammo capacity and your weapon attachments like silencers wear out, so you will be calling in supply drops every now and then during long missions to make sure you are stocked up on ammo and attachments etc.

After playing for a while you will really see your base grow from a small rig to a massive network of rigs in the ocean, see all of the soldiers you "recruited" walking around your base, it's really a great thing to see when you fly back after the missions.

The weapons and your entire arsenal is also just great all round, this is something that has always been the case in MetalGear games and here it's even more varied and gives you the freedom om taking whatever you want on missions, Even this is it's own game mechanic as everything you take has a cost, and if you want to build up cash. You could run a mission that can help you steal some expensive equipment while barely taking anything with you on a mission and then selling your expensive goods to gain cash. You also have to kind of manage your money as research and such also cost money and you should avoid going bankrupt as your soldiers will start to leave if you can't pay them. This is easy to manage generally, however it also adds a layer of depth to the game and makes you really want to take everything you can while out on missions.

I really can't believe how good this game is to be honest, especially for a game make quite some year back. It's better then most modern shooters and should be played by anyone interested in FPS games, and especially stealth games.
It offers so much content, infinite replay-ability. A story that is something you really can't get in modern games anymore and all of this runs super well on any mid spec PC and steam deck. And on sale regularly making it an absolute bargain.

This game is one of if not the best stealth action game ever from a strictly gameplay perspective. There's so much stuff to do and guns to use, upgrades to build, missions to complete, mods to install, fobs, pf league, I mean there's almost too much content which is why it was so hard for it to stick my first couple times playing. It feels like everything in the game world interacts with the player in one way or another and there's so much open ended-ness in how each area is built, leading to tons of variety on how to play. Traceless runs are some of the most rewarding mini challenges I've done in a game, where you can't use anything but your wits, trial and error, and so much Noctocyanin that snake should've overdosed 100 times over.

Sadly one would expect a ground breaking story from a Metal Gear Solid game and I think they struggled here. This game really got bungled by the Konami/Kojima drama. It's story has a good starting point but near the middle it becomes an absolute slog of repeat missions with pointless modifiers to pad out game time and then it just ends. I think some of the problems fizzle away because they finally get explained but it's all for nothing. The story is painfully unfinished, no matter how much die hard copers want you to think otherwise. The entire Lord of the Flies unit's ending was cut leaving a GIANT loose plot thread and in turn didn't sufficiently show how much of a monster Big Boss had become, Skullface as a whole completely undermines the original story of Snake Eater with him "helping snake" making Big Boss seem incompetent, and there's a few too many retcons and fumbles here like the whole parasite thing being what gave the Cobra Unit their "powers". I think if you pick and choose what you want your canon to be here you won't be missing much at all. Still, the final mission (The one that's not a repeat) has such an amazing reveal and a twist that stared you in the face the entire game, although in the long run it just muddies the waters even futher.

 The biggest misses were the removal of the mullet in favor of a pony tail, and making the bandana wayyyyy to short and crease-less. Modded that ♥♥♥♥ out before I even started and never looked back.

Another game where I put in a stupid number of hours on a Playstation console only to buy it again, because "yes Konami, this is in fact, what I want."  The story, while not awful, is the weakest part of this experience, but even if you don't enjoy it you'll get hooked on just how good the game feels once you're used to it.

Using the terrain, the environment, special equipment, and just some good old patience to sneak your way in to the heart of an enemy base has never been this fun.  Or you can crash the gates like a maniac, and kill everything in sight.  Can't be spotted if there's nobody left alive to spot you.

The pure choice in how to tackle your objective is the biggest draw here, and it does it almost perfectly.  Beyond that, there are an insane number of lore dumps (hidden tapes which you can just collect, or take the time to listen to all the way through, literally hours of spoken content there alone), a massive list of items to develop so you can fight however you like, and optional challenges both in standard difficulty and EXTREME versions of many missions.

If you've ever liked Metal Gear Solid, this is without a doubt the definitive experience.  I genuinely can't imagine any stealth game ever coming close to how [b]solid[/b] this is.
