This game is awesome, even if you've never played Metal Gear Solid games before, this gameplay is unique to all of the games before it because it has free roam outdoors - the story is not actually that important and you should just focus on the gameplay, because that is the strongest part of the experience (you can skip most of the story, which is accessible via tape recordings). Also consider that this may be the last 'true' entry in the MGS series now that Hideo Kojima has left Konami, since they still own the IP.

[[Note: You can find out about modding the PC version by looking up the Snakebite mod manager. There are lots of helpful mods that adjust various aspects of the game. I am able to use my helicopter to travel in the open world now, when previously it could only be used for extraction or air support - Check out mods like Infinite Heaven, IHHook, and Zeta to get started]]

MGSV is a great free roaming action-espionage game where you get to build a base of operations and manage your personal army. To unlock new resources and actions you need to complete the story missions, so even if you spend lots of hours doing free roam, you won't actually make any progress towards improving your army - keep this in mind if you feel like the game is getting boring. The game starts in Afghanistan and after doing about 20 story missions there you can also visit South Africa.

You need to use the research and development unit to unlock new items, even if you aren't going to use them. Sometimes an item you DO want is hidden behind an item that doesn't look very interesting (e.g I unlocked a non-lethal shotgun behind a lethal one, which was good for knocking out enemies quickly in close range fights). There is one specialist you will rescue in a mission who allows you to customise guns, and then you can do things like add silencers to your rifles, new scopes, laser sights, different loading mechanisms, and also underbarrel grenade launchers and shotguns - one of my favourite guns I put together is a tranquiliser sniper rifle with shotgun attachment, to put distant enemies asleep for capture or quickly take out anyone who catches me by surprise up close.

Enemies respond to your tactics and the gameplay forces you to mix things up, e.g if you  are always getting headshots, enemies will start to wear helmets to force you to be very accurate (aim for the face) or try a different kind of weapon, if you are using smoke or gas grenades all the time they start to wear gas masks, constantly attack bases at night and they will wear night vision goggles (you can blind them by shining a flashlight in their face) - it feels like you are fighting a responsive enemy who care about their assets.

The base management aspect can be as complex as you like, with a single button to auto-sort staff into their best departments, or you can personally place everyone into their best spot to maximise efficiency. Auto-placement doesn't consider negative traits, so sometimes a staff member might start fights with other people and they all end up in sick bay which actually reduces your base level.

As well as being able to capture enemy infantry to grow your army, you can also find some specialists to give access to unique weapons and skills, and also discover some special allies with totally unique abilities which change the way you play the game - each one has a 'bond level' which goes up as you use them, and a higher bond level unlocks new moves for them.

The game does award full stealth (zero enemy detection or alarms) and non-lethal approaches the most, but you shouldn't feel bad for deciding to kill enemies, because you can easily make up the lost money by replaying those missions with a different loadout at any time.

The game can probably be completed in about 40 hours, but if you spend time experimenting with different items, and trying different approaches to complete all of the bonus objectives in every mission, you can easily get a few hundred hours or more in the single player mode.

As this is the second MGS in chronological order (after MGS3), many of the events of later games haven’t happen yet, but are often foreshadowed in a nice way. One advantage of that is that the game’s plot isn’t as convoluted yet. This game has Hideo Kojima at his worst and best in regards of story, writing, dialogue, camerawork and animation. Unlike previous MGS, V is not a story-dense movie-like experience and the story gets cut in rather small pieces due to the nature of the gameplay. I personally prefer that over IV which was just a movie with some gameplay between episodes. 

 Atypical for a MGS, this game features your own little kingdom to govern. Base building, management and abducting personnel are fun and make it feel like a strategy game. It might feel out of place and tacked on at first, but the fact there is an actual army behind you is well interwoven into the story and specific plot points. Aside of this MGSV is also still a great stealth game and conquering whole bases without a fight is rewarding - but not the only way to play this. You can go in guns-blazing if you want. But since it’s a stealth-focused game, a lot of the game’s options will probably remain under-utilized for many players, like most of the heavy weaponry, vehicles or support strikes. And given how much higher-tier equipment costs in deployment AND development, you often just run around with the bare minimum you think you need instead of just using your tools for fun. This is somewhat bad, ALTHOUGH managing the loadout is a fun aspect in itself – a double-edged sword. Also, either deeply burrowed in the tech tree or found by trial-and-error are dozens of ways to cause mischief and do other shenanigans. Punching a bear in the butt with a rocket fist or enraging it to send it at unsuspecting soldiers? Stunning enemies with a decoy soldier? Playing ‘Take on Me’ every time your helicopter drops you off or picks you up? No problem! This game has much more depth than it needs, but I appreciate it a lot. 

The plot feels a bit too much cut into pieces for the biggest part of the game, due to its mission-based progression. So, while you are kind of trying to find out what happened in the Ground Zeroes prologue, you might not be that invested at first. Some way in, when the main theme of the game becomes clearer [SPOILER: mainly Language and secondarily revenge], the game gains quite some significance in many of the aspects it utilized so far. [Oh, and Chapter 2 is a thing. Wow. I was quite in awe that they basically took everything away that Venom was working for after getting the ‘Happy End’. And then, some major things happen at the very end and make you go ‘oh, that makes sense!’ I’m not an expert in writing, but I felt very satisfied but the plot twists at the end.] 

Aside of MGS Online (which I haven’t played), there are also additional forward operating bases you can build that will be able to be infiltrated by other players (and vice versa); also, friendly competitions and leagues between your and their FOBs can be partaken in. It’s a great way to increase your playtime if you have already finished everything in the game, although the FOB maps can become stale as they naturally do not have much variety. 

This game features an amazing Soundtrack, both in original score and many of the 80’s songs that can be found everywhere in the open world. I kind of became low-key obsessed with that era’s music ever since and gave me a burst of new appreciation for it. Graphically I must stress that this game still looks amazing for a 2015 release, it has fluent & natural animations and it runs unbelievably good on even lower-tier PCs. The FOX engine is incredibly optimized and a marvel in game design. It was also prohibitively expensive to develop. As I said, the best and worst of Kojima. 

9,5/10

Out of the 100s of video games that I've played, MGSV from 2015 remains at the top for me.

The Phantom Pain has the best gameplay in any video game far outclassing games like Zelda BOTW, Skyrim, Apex Legends, Batman Arkham etc. It's because it encompasses numerous gameplay elements, making a very organic playing structure - players can be open, or sneaky or make use of both to manage situations against a very intelligent and adaptable enemy AI. 
The Phantom Pain offers a massive library of weapons and gadgets to use, which are progressively unlocked with the story, making previous missions much easier to complete (most missions are replayable), but also giving players the ability to engage the more difficult challenges every mission offers. In addition, players also have battlefield allies, such as a military dog or a female sniper, who can aid the player in different ways, said allies are also heavily customizable.
The game also comes with 2 entirely different multiplayer modes, one as a story related PVP mode and the other as a general multiplayer mode.

While TPP's story and overall narrative is not as top tier as the 5 great games that came before in the series (which are known for revolutionizing video game storytelling), it still delivers a good plot in vivid imagery, with great characters & dialogue, and some of the best ingame cinematics in video gaming. Audio and music are top notch, voice work is superb and the game is very well optimized for both PC and consoles - nary a bug to be seen throughout an entire playthrough.


Even though the game lacks in some departments, it is jam packed with content and the overall experience is one of a masterpiece, deserving of a rating of 10/10.

The story is over-the-top as always, has its twists and turns and there is of course the Kojima-typical WTF moment at the very end. MGS V continues the narrative of MGS Peace Walker and Ground Zeroes - i.e. you are again playing as Snake aka Big Boss (or do you?). Character design and story are both pretty good, but not outstanding and have been done better in previous MGS installments. To get the true ending you also have to replay several missions at higher difficulty which seems a bit uninspired and may be caused by Kojima’s premature split from Konami. Among the best aspects of the game is the open world which has been introduced with Ground Zeroes in a much smaller scale and which has been heavily expanded in MGS V. Although the world is a bit empty with no NPC’s it gives you nearly unlimited freedom in how you manage your operations. In combination with various gadgets and companions you can approach missions in many different ways - from sneaky to guns-blazing. The gameplay is nearly flawless and picks up the best concepts of Peace Walker and refines them - especially base building and stealing/extracting stuff with Fulton balloons. What makes MGS V truly stand out is the nearly perfect combination of all its various mechanics and its attention to details. It is incredibly fun to try out all the hilarious things the game has to offer - from hiding in the good old cardboard box to distracting enemies with your horse’s poop.

[h1]Dear friends... this is why you keep seeing that "Vanta G. is playing..." notification constantly.[/h1]
My previous review sucked, so I would like to make a new one...
[h2]Is this truly a review, or a story of misery for strangers?[/h2]
First off, I'm not gonna talk about the Campaign or whatever Konami calls it. We all know it. It's awesome, surprising, emotional and so forth. What I'm gonna be talking instead is what keeps everyone on this game hooked: [i]The FOB Infiltration mode.[/i]

Here, you will be managing your own SEPARATE Mother Base in an ocean. [i]This also means more levels and money to you![/i] Sounds great, right? Like all things in life, it comes with a SINGLE drawback: other players can infiltrate your FOB and take all of your stuff. You can of course infiltrate them back, but then they have the chance to re-infiltrate you which then you can-

All I just talked about earlier does not matter. Nobody even dares infiltrate your FOB. You're gonna be stealing resources and staff from corpses or players that haven't touched this game in a decade.

Okay, so, nobody plays the FOB mode... you can just infiltrate anybody without consequences. But when you infiltrate someone's base, that's when the game becomes a [b]Psychological Horror game.[/b]

You will either be met with the easiest FOB ever by mankind or the Dark Souls of something you thought would never materialize. You're not allowed to kill a single person anymore, as that decreases your heroism and overall Infiltration score. Either CQC (99% risk of getting spotted), wound soldiers and extract them before they die, or pull out your rifle with bullets that make enemies sleep or stun and hope to god no one wakes up.

Sure, you've got your sneaking suit to counter with crouching and crawling making noises and NVG-wearing staff. Get to CQC a few guys, but then again, that does not blend with any terrain and it's preferred you use it at night. If you want that [i]day-time infiltration bonus[/i]... well... I don't even dare. Go find out yourself.

Got all of that? Use camouflage that blend into metal and concrete, go full STN and ZZZ for your primaries except for the secondary. You WILL need your lethal secondary to deal with cameras, UAV, and the likes.

This mode, along with going for high-ranking PFs which you think you can take on, will make you instantly ALT + F4 at even the mere sight of that red exclamation mark. That white detection line will make you fear for your life. Are you gonna get spotted when you make a single move, or get away without trouble? The UAVs... they're gonna haunt my dreams. Shoot down one, it goes down just fine. Shoot down the other, it explodes and alerts the entire population of China to your location.

This is what makes this game truly Gear Solid. I love this game.

Played this game on launch for PS4. Got it on sale the other day on Xbox and beat it. Now I got it for PC. Incredible game! The gameplay is immaculate. No other stealth game comes close. Period.

Also, currently I'm limited to a fairly potato-ish gaming laptop (Lenovo. Still good but I wanna say it's over a decade old). And while I did have to turn down the settings, the game still runs impressively well maintaining 60fps with very few frame dips.

Admittedly, the story is not as dense as other Metal Gear titles, but I would argue that's a pro for the average player jumping into the franchise. Metal Gear can be quite intimidating. Ground Zeroes was my first and I'm not convinced I'd be as big of a fan if I had started with 1-4. All this to say, V's story is a little overhated imo. It's a simple revenge plot with enough Kojima weirdness to decide whether or not his games are for you. And while cheesy at times, it does its job well enough to keep you engaged. I actually really enjoy its darker elements. Especially when it teeters into horror territory.

That said, without giving any spoilers, the ending of this game is more profound if you've experienced the rest of the series. At least the Big Boss era games MGS3 & Peacewalker. (Portable Ops too if you want). If you're a newcomer it's fine, it still makes enough sense. Just be aware.

Warts and all, I LOVE this game. Potentially in my top V (pun intended). I know it's dorky to say, but it really makes you feel like the legendary Big Boss! Highly recommend.

review_text:
It's an excellent game overall. Well known for its mainly stealth based story, Metal Gear Solid V is an amazing value for your money when you get it on sale. There is a ton of content packed into this game and it's crazy to think that it's unfinished (if you like to focus on the story). Game play is superb, with tons of ways to tackle a mission. Go the traditional stealth way, guns a blazing, stunning/tranquillise every enemy in sight, bombing the sight with grenades or bombard it from above. If you end up making a mistake and get detected, you can go into reflex mode which slows the game down allowing you to take the shot if desired. Choose to capture soldiers to fight for your cause or animals to save them. have a buddy tag along with you from the trusty horse steed that can ♥♥♥♥ on command, a trusty puppy that grows into a big wolf dog equipped with a knife or stun bat, carry out your own mech walker with either guns, tranquillise pistols or a full on Fulton ballista and finally the sexy sniper quiet to either leave your enemies in fear as she snipes each one down or to tranquillise enemies to help further grow your army.

Speaking of Army, each personal within your army will have a specialised role to progress what you can build all on your Mother Base. Some may be more combat experienced while others are better at gathering Intel or more suited to developing weapons. there are 6 roles total to look out for and each coincide with a certain weapon or tool upgrade. As well as developing more tools for you to use on the field, you can send off your own men who are combat trained to fight around the globe to recruit more people, defend key areas or simply gather resources. There is a lot packed into expanding your Mother Base but there is one problem I personally find with the system. Timers, lots of timers, for developing tier 3 and above weapons to combat deployments (which I see no issue with). My main concern goes into developing higher tier weapons and progressing the mother base. Why? this isn't a mobile game and thankfully you cant pay real money to speed up the process but regardless, its a jarring decision to have this implemented, it makes sense for combat deployments but not for developing items and these can go for up to 3 hours of real game play time for even costumes. 

Story is a bit of a hit and miss. At times its very good but other times, it feels like you are not progressing and simply doing busy work, which is expected from an open world type of game but some of the main missions do just feel like that, not a bad thing but not much to progress story, as you are mainly trying to rebuild the Diamond Dogs and track down the villain skull face and stop his plans. In total there are 38 actual original missions with the other 12 being more challenging replays of older missions but with either the mode Subsistence (which strips you of your gear and has you completing it via scavenging for enemy gear), Total Stealth (a very challenging mode where if you are detected, you will fail the mission) and Extreme which is just a much harder difficulty where deadly attacks will one shot you and all 3 challenges take away reflex mode. Unfortunately, there was a key cutscene that left a massive plot hole in the game, which ended up being a cut mission 51 which addresses that plot hole.

In addition to simply free roaming either Afghanistan or Central Africa, you can complete key side ops which either involve extracting targets or eliminating them, securing blueprints or containers, clearing mines, rescuing legendary animals and more. 

Overall, Metal Gear Solid V is an amazing sandbox hybrid stealth game with many ways to tackle missions and gives you a simulation of building up your army. Filled with tons of content, decent story bits and interesting character, it is a must buy.

review_text:
Kojima's final entry in the Metal Gear saga, The Phantom Pain delivers mixed results, but ultimately stays an enjoyable game in spite of its flaws.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain (2015), is the continuation to the short prologue Ground Zeroes, and direct sequel to Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker (2010). After a coordinated attack on Mother Base by Cipher and XOF left his mercenary company MSF fragmented and a shrapnel explosion sent him into a nine year coma, military legend Big Boss awakens in a hospital in Cyprus. Missing an arm, and barely escaping with his life with help from a mysterious ally, he departs on a quest for revenge against the man who'd taken everything from him, and rebuilding what he'd lost. 

MGSV:TPP for the most part uses the same mechanics as Ground Zeroes, with the new innovations in gameplay introduced there, but with several tweaks. The core structure of the game takes on something more similar to Peace Walker, dividing missions into an episodic format, as well as reintroducing the base building system. Unlike every other Metal Gear game that came before it, TPP brings an open world for the first time to the series. From Afghanistan to a region in Africa, you'll travel through canyons and flatlands and sneak through many different enemy outposts and military bases. You slowly build base facilities, develop powerful new weapons and tools, and extract and sort new mercenaries from the battlefield into your growing private military company. On your travels you'll contend with many new kinds of threats, from armored patrol cars, to tanks, gunships, and heavily armed strike squads. You can use the same spyglass/set of binoculars from GZ to analyze a soldier's facility proficiency (intel, R&D, combat, medical, etc.) and extract them using the Fulton surface-to-air extraction baloons from PW. You can also fulton pretty much anything that isn't nailed down, such as vehicles, emplacements, storage containers, and even animals to give away to wildlife conservation NGO's. Soldiers can speak many different languages, have proficiency in certain subtrades (gunsmithing, medicine, diplomacy, etc.) that provide additional benefits to your PMC. Each soldier, and their ranking, will gradually level up each of your facilities, unlocking new weapons and items you can develop using GMP, your reward currency here, but most items are on a development timer that must run out before you can use whatever you paid for. The iDroid is back, letting you set waypoints, listen to music and audio log tapes, as well as call in missile strikes, buddies, vehicles, weapons, equipment and ammo resupply drops, cover fire from your personal chopper (the Blackfoot piloted by pilots with the callsign Pequod, whose music you can change as usual), or just to pick you up and exfiltrate hot zones. Most missions will be relatively simple, tasking you with rescuing prisoners or eliminating key targets on the map, though some will be more story-heavy and fiercely guarded military bases, and you are free to customize your loadout before each deployment, changing your primary and secondary weapons, equipment, throwables, vehicles you can call in to drive, and even support buddies who will follow and assist you in various ways on your trips. Buddies include the silent sniper Quiet, adopted wolf cub D-Dog, steed D-Horse, and a mobile bipedal armament, the D-Walker. Enemy AI here is very interesting, although not as punishing as the one in Ground Zeroes. They have an adaptive difficulty, changing their strategy depending on how you choose to encounter them. Repeatedly tranquilizing them will cause soldiers to start wearing thicker padding to block penetration, attacking exclusively at night will make them start using flashlights, searchlights and night vision goggles. Usually mixing up your approach a little will prevent this from happening too often, and you should, given the game's sandbox nature. There are many ways you can tackle your stealth, using objects to distract guards, sleeping gas, destroying nearby outpost comms equipment to prevent reinforcements or anti-air radars to stop your chopper from getting shot down, weapons that have tranquilizer rounds or can stun enemies non-lethally, or just kill them outright. Weapon variety is excellent, with SMGs, shotguns, LMGs, revolvers, pistols, snipers (from regular rifles to anti-materiel), grenade launchers, rocket launchers of every variety (regular, homing, burst), and a bevy of heavy vehicles you can call in such as humvees, APCs and tanks. There are also many easteregg and secret items, blueprints and rewards to find stashed away in certain missions and corners of the map. The game is teeming with sandbox elements to explore, to the point I can't contain them in a single review. 

The story is a bit of a mess, as the game is in some ways unfinished, but even the content that is here is handled questionably, as you will mostly get snippets of it through dialogue and sometimes cutscenes. The brunt of the lore is stashed away in audio tapes you'll receive at the end of most missions, which contain vital information that could be easy to miss if you're not scrounging around every nook and cranny of the game. 
The game takes place in 1984, nine years after the events of Ground Zeroes, as Big Boss awakens in a hospital in Cyprus, missing an arm and having shrapnel and human remains embedded deep in his body. The hospital comes under fire as XOF arrives to finish the job they started and snuff out the living legend, but he is escorted by a bandaged ally out of the hotzone and to recuperate at a new Mother Base situated in the Seychelles waters. Big Boss must regroup his scattered allies, rebuild his fallen empire (now renamed to Diamond Dogs) and gather intel and resources before settling the score with the man who took it all from him, XOF leader Skull Face, who has his own ambitions of enacting revenge against the world. He ventures through Northern Kabul, Afghanistan, to the Angola-Zaire border region in Africa to find the answers he seeks, though many of them might not be what he'd anticipated. The game's themes this time are Revenge and Race, illustrating the futility of chasing after your very own white whale, as well as discrimination based on circumstances out of your control such as language and region.

I'd slogged through this game for three years, precisely due to the following flaws I'll list. From the tedious grinding to unlock tools and weapons, the bland and mostly empty open world, the main story missions after chapter 1 mostly being non-story and locking the unlock criteria behind doing side content, and finally it just not fitting the regular tone of the series and feeling alien compared to everything else, MGSV has a lot of issues I can't overlook. After the first 70-hour slog I spent just grinding three years ago, I've come to revisit it and spent another 40 hours finishing up the main story and some side quests. The game suffered development hell and caused Kojima and Konami to split, likely due to Konami feeling too greedy, but as well as Kojima's scope for the game becoming unrealistic to accomplish and burning money, and so the game came out unfinished.

While flawed, I still had a good time with the game, but I'm not sure if I'll ever do a second run for the reasons mentioned above. I suppose I can forgive the game, as it provides you with a pure stealth sandbox unlike most other stealth games out there, something Metal Gear fans might've wanted for a long time. Nowadays it goes on sale every now and then, but make sure to grab the Definitive Experience edition which includes Ground Zeroes.

review_text:
[h1]Disclaimer[/h1]
I 100% completed the game before reviewing. Took around 120h.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
It's good. It's really f. good. There are few games which I feel so strongly about recommending, even fewer that I feel hold up for near entirety of the 100% completion process.

If what you've learned about this game over the years peaks your interest in any way - get it. I will say that without first 100% completing MGS Ground Zeroes you may have a hard time understanding the story, but that's the only caveat here (and Ground Zeroes is a good game in it's own right now, when it costs a normal price).

[h1]Description[/h1]
MGS5 is a stealth-action game where you play a commando/soldier/special-operative and complete different missions while managing your entire support backend including mission support, companions, transportation and even research and development of new weapons and tech.

Game is set in a sci-fi version of 1984. There are superpowers and tech not available at that time. MG series is not trying to be authentic/realistic like Splinter Cell for example.

The story continues from Ground Zeroes and I will not spoil it here. Suffice to say that you play a guy who gets involved with a multi-national conspiracy that threatens the stability of entire world. You will probably not get much invested within the story unless you are deep into MGS series already, at which point you are not reading this dumb review to make sure you want to buy the game, because you've already completed it, have you?

There are 2 large, open-world style maps with many enemy bases on them, and most missions will take place on some preset area of those maps. You can still explore and attack bases without an active mission if you want.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[b]+ Engaging gameplay[/b]
This is a stealth game where if you get noticed - alarm goes off, but most missions don't immediately fail. You can still bruteforce your way through most objectives, shooting enemies and blowing sht up.

Stealth is pretty basic at first, but gets deeper with equipment unlocks. You start with a pistol with sleeping darts that can put enemies out of commision for a while. You can also sneak behind and grab enemies for a kill or a knockout. You may even interrogate captives to gain info about mission objectives or enemy forces.

Later you can unlock things from sleep grenades to long range, silenced sniper-rifles as well as support actions like artillery strikes and equipment like echolocation device or night-vision goggles.

[b]+ Deep and wide systems[/b]
You have a base of operations and while you are on a mission - you can capture and kidnap enemy soldiers for your own army. You can then send them on missions and put them in different jobs at the base, from intelligence and base development to research and development or off-map support teams.

Most improvements require money and resources. You earn money mostly by completing missions, which you can repeat. Resources are procured during missions or in online events/invasions. You can ignore invasions if you don't like the mechanic, but there are NPC bases to invade during events for some easy resources (once you learn to play well).

You can research different items and most of them lead to more research. For example after completing a research of a new grenade launcher, you may unlock ability to research a new version of it that fires smoke, stun or sleeping-gas grenades. The list of different upgrades is amazing and it's easy to find loudouts that you like to play with.

You also have several "buddies" - companions that you can take with you on missions. They also have research associated with them and their equipment, and are a great help on most missions.

Really there's just so much stuff to do here, that it's impressive how well all of those things work together to create an easily understandable and engaging gameplay loop.

[b]+ Attention to detail[/b]
There are many neat things in this game. For example - after every mission you must evacuate the area, usually by chopper. But you can also kidnap enemy resource container and stand on it while it's being picked up by your forces - that way will also extract you from the mission.

[b]+ Holds up for a long time[/b]
It does not get boring, that's it's greatest strength. Sure - there are some better and some worse missions, especially some side objectives and side-ops may get annoying or repetitive, but even then - game itself is still fun, just some situations are less so. I don't remember loving 100% completion for that amount of time (over 100h!).

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[b]- Sometimes iffy controls[/b]
Sometimes you will automatically get up from prone at inappropriate times when you want to remain hidden. Sometimes moving while prone you get stuck on every little piece of clutter or have a hard time to reorient yourself.

[b]- Some side objective descriptions/scripts failing[/b]
Descriptions are unclear or lie to you. Use guides for completionist runs, but even then - many guides are wrong about different things. There will be some frustrasion while completing the game.

[b]- UI[/b]
Too many problems to list. Starting from bad keyboard/mouse support, to some stupid quirks like unresponsive scroll-zooming. Game still plays better with KB+M than the controller (easier aiming), but it's annoying nontheless.

[b]- Assorted, minor annoyances[/b]
Like side-ops spawning when you don't want them, or boring animal completion.

[h1]Lowdown[/h1]
This is possibly one of the best games in recent memory. It has it's issues, but not enough to cut into your general enjoyment of the game. It sets a bar for stealth-action open-world games wich will not be passed soon.

I'd give MGS5 a well deserved
[h1]9/10[/h1]
PLAY. IT.

I'm doing a redux review of this game after a few years as many things have happened. I've not only beaten every Metal Gear Solid game finally (I will have some things to say about this later), but I've also gone and replayed this game on PS5 (precisely, the PS4 The Definitive Experience which bundles Ground Zeroes and all of its DLCs, The Phantom Pain and all of its DLCs, and Metal Gear Online 3, also with all of its DLCs on a single disc, making it the best way to experience this game) in preparation for Death Stranding 2: On the Beach.

Over the last half a decade, Metal Gear Solid became my favorite video game franchise, and with that, Kojima Productions became my favorite studio that frankly, never missed out on a title. MGSV will probably go down as the most ambitious stealth open world game to ever exist. The gameplay is point perfect for a stealth game, and maybe even for a third person shooter, with the only two games who have gameplay as tight and deep as this one which are Rockstar's Max Payne 3, and Naughty Dog's The Last of Us Part 2, although the reason I think MGSV just slightly edges out these two for me is solely because it's a perfect tactical action espionage. This is one of the very few video games which I can play for extremely long sessions without ever getting bored or tired of it, as there are so many different ways to tackle each objective, and the mission design being very open ended just adds on to the enjoyment for me personally. I wouldn't go out of my way to call this a perfect video game, as I do think the design choice for development (be it equipment, guns, your base) or the dispatch missions taking real life time to develop/finish was an extremely lame idea. Another, albeit much smaller issue I have with the game is story related, and it's not because I don't like the story and how it's presented, it's the fact that this story doesn't hit the emotional highs as Metal Gear Solid 1 through 4 do, not to mention the Chapter 2 feeling incredibly unfinished given the extremely rough development hell Kojima Productions went through. These two issues aside, Metal Gear Solid V is without a doubt one of my personal favorite games ever and that'll probably never change, and I'm very thankful that this franchise exists because it means so much to me. It's a game that took me about 150+ hours to 100% on PC, and I'm more than hyped to do it all over again on PS5 too eventually. If you're unsure on what platform to buy this game on, wether you get it on console or PC, you're in for a very, very, very fun time and some of the best, if not the best stealth experience you'll have in a video game, but I would not recommend this being your first Metal Gear Solid game, DO NOT play this unless you've played the previous ones. Thankfully, although while it did take Konami AGES to do it, they made modern ports of Metal Gear 1 and 2, and Metal Gear Solid 1 through 3, bundled up as Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Volume 1, which on sale is one of the best deals in video gaming, and just like MGSV, it doesn't matter where you get it, as it's pretty much a perfect collection and ports on all of the platforms it's on. These games are a must play for MGSV, but, unfortunately so is at least another MGS, which isn't quite accessible, nor is it advised to play it solo as it was designed around co op. Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker, which nowadays you can only buy on Xbox or.... PlayStation 3, is a game set exactly right before MGSV and is a must play before MGSV, as you wouldn't understand most of this story without Peace Walker. Emulating it thankfully is not an issue (RPCS3, Xenia, although I wouldn't recommend emulating the original PSP version as it plays worse), but I do hope that Konami will very soon port it to PC/PS5, and also another VERY crucial game that isn't all that necessary for MGSV (thankfully), but nonetheless, that game is Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots, which to this day is a PlayStation 3 exclusive, and one of the hardest games to emulate unfortunately (for this one I thankfully borrowed one of my friends PS3, bought the disc just to play this game, and while I won't go into details about the game itself, I will say that the performance is quite rough, and that the game is DESPERATE for a modern port). But to wrap this up, MGSV is a must play for any fan of stealth games, but do yourself a favor and first play the first three Metal Gear Solid games, and Peace Walker. It's a masterful series.

review_text:
After playing all of the Metal Gears in release order, this is probably the best one.

The sandbox style open-world allows for so much experimentation, whether it be with the staggering amount of weapons and gadgets you can unlock, or the responsive environments and AI. Once it all clicks, each mission feels calculable and the "tactical espionage" aspect shines. Metal Gear gameplay to me has always been about situational awareness and quick-thinking, two things this game rewards pretty well. It feels especially satisfying to gear up, do recon, and infiltrate a huge base, taking it slow and remaining undetected or having to maneuver your way out of potentially being discovered. Even getting caught can be fun when having to adapt to the AI's alert/search phases, although I do think fighting back can be a little clunky sometimes. The way that the enemy force as a whole reacts to how you play the game is also really cool and adds some variety to playing/replaying missions. Do a lot of missions at night, and the enemies gain flashlights and night vision goggles. If you typically aim for the head, the soldiers get helmets. It's a neat way to make my presence in the game world be felt, and its something I wish more open-world games would do. I'm also a fan of the game's bigger set pieces, especially the areas with multiple paths and levels to traverse (Mfinda Oilfield is a particular favorite). There's also a staggering amount of content in the game, with over 150 side ops, like a million different mission objectives (some of which can only be completed if you replay the mission once you've unlocked some late game gadgets), a whole ZOO to populate with animals, and plenty of unlockable items to get. However, the side ops can get repetitive though, with a lot of the later ones boiling down to extracting/exploding tanks and getting rid of soldiers in full armor. Replayability is really encouraged with this game which is a huge plus for me. In fact, at the time of writing I'm [i] still [/i] trying to squeeze as much time as I can out of this game. Watching the completion percentage the game displays in your helicopter base go up is really addicting.

I think the story gets a lot of flack, understandably so considering that the story itself is light, somewhat confusing and the cutscenes can be so few and far between. I saw someone say that it feels like the narrative is in a state of always feeling like its about to get good and it just never really hits, which I would kind of agree with. But I think whats here works well enough to act as the middle link between the Big Boss/Solid Snake eras (and to be honest I'm a little biased because after playing MGS4, a Metal Gear game thats more focused on gameplay is welcome). Despite all that, I wouldn't say the story is [i] bad, [/i] just not finished and not the main focus. There's some neat fan service moments and the good old Metal Gear memetics are all there. The cutscenes that are in the game are well-directed and stylish with some really memorable moments, and it certainly helps that the game is drop-dead gorgeous.

The original soundtrack is full of John Carpenter-esque, cinematic synth tracks that dynamically change as you sneak around. The licensed soundtrack is filled to the brim with time-appropriate bangers too (even though theres that one song by the Cure that came out like ten years after the game is supposed to take place lol). I do wish there were some more songs from the Metal Gear series as more little collectible tapes, which I think are really fun especially when you zoom with your binoculars and hear a split-second of Hall and Oates in the distance and picking it up becomes a little side note in your mission.

Everyones already said it but yeah it really sucks that the second half of this game is so blatantly unfinished. There's only a handful of original missions after the first half of the game is over, with a lot of reused missions with some sort of modifier on it, and most of the modifiers just kind of boil down to don't get caught or don't get shot. The story kind of just doesn't fully resolve either, although I'd consider the game to have a few endings to certain plotlines, it never feels like it gives as strong of a final send-off like MGS4 does. With some more time, who knows what a full second chapter or even a third would have been like. 

Overall, this game really makes me appreciate what I love about playing the Metal Gear games and it reminds me just how much I miss these games. Everything feels like its designed around the idea of letting you be cool and cinematic, and the non-linear sandbox gameplay makes for some really organic, exciting situations. There's a part where Big Boss says [i] "Anyone here can use a knife or a gun. What you're going to learn is how to use your head"[/i], and I think it kinda summarizes what its like to really get into this game.

200 Hour Edit: This is still the best of the series and probably in my top 3 games. I'm now throwing this game on when I'm talking to friends or just hanging out, and it's a fantastic timekiller. Now that I understand the AI through and through, there are so many interesting situations that you can fix yourself into, and yet it doesn't feel like I'm smarter than the game, but rather that I'm smarter than the enemy, which fits thematically.

It honestly sickens me that I'm recommending anything that Konami has even touched, but I'm only doing so to show that a game that was cut short by them still managed to be one of the better games in the series.

Now, let me preface that I am not a big fan of Kojima. I personally think he is one of the most overrated directors in gaming, and is probably one of the worst to actually work with. Also his cultish following creeps me out immensely. That being said, what he represents in the industry is something I wish we had alot more of. Creativity. And the freedom to pursue such creativity.

This game manages to modernize the entirety of MGS, from the controls, to the gameplay loop, to the story so effortlessly that it blows my mind that the game that came before it was Peacewalker. There really isn't any way to describe this game any better than to say it's simply a "modernized Metal Gear Solid game".

Unfortunately, however, all the modernization and clean game design in the world can't save a rushed, incomplete product, and Phantom Pain clearly suffers with that in some areas. Many areas, actually.

Despite this, though, what remains of what was to be the final chapter in the MGS saga still manages to work well enough to maintain a positive experience in the end, so I won't complain too harshly.

Whats most important however, is that in the end, SNATCHER IS STILL THE BEST KOJIMA GAME FIGHT ME!

Equip your chopper with weapons so that it can fend off any pursuers when you're making a close escape. 

So yes, if you're into military-style stealth infiltration gameplay, pick this up.

The start of the game is probably the most fun, really got me excited for the rest of it, but I was gravely disappointed. The gist of the gameplay is meandering around a desert map, doing what feels like repetitive side-quests disguised as story missions, on top of a bunch of base management crap. 10 or so hours in, each mission feels pretty much the same: go into soviet stronghold and capture so-and-so, or blow up something nearby. Rinse and repeat. No variation.

To make matters worse, the game info-dumps a HUGE amount of gameplay information on you from the start, but gives you no clear way to review it should you need a recap. It tries to cram all the game's mechanics into a short 10 minute tutorial session, which just doesn't work. You'll probably forget most of it by the time the next mission starts because some of it doesn't become relevant until later(such as interrogation.)

There seems to be more emphasis on micromanaging a base to unlock new gear than there is actually playing the game. It's not something you can just ignore, either; starting as early as mission 7 or 8, you pretty much NEED to have a rocket launcher of some sort, requiring R&D at least level 12. The problem is that the game, at least at this stage, only gives you hot trash E or F rated personnel, with a token C or D here and there, making level increases on it absurdly annoying - so, you have to go out in the world and essentially play pokemon with unconscious enemy soldiers to try and get the right stats. 

Navigating the world itself is also annoying. It seems open world in concept, except the travel is railroaded into taking absurdly windy and long routes, with your only means of transport being a horse that's annoying to control, and jeeps which drive about as fast as the horse. You cannot, for some reason, use your helicopter to simply pick you up and drop you off someplace else without failing the mission(or, if you can, the game did a horrible job at making it clear how to do so...as it did many things.)

The stealth mechanics in the game are there with a lot of thought, but honestly feel like a waste of time. You'll try your very best to not be detected, spending upwards of half an hour just to get halfway through a mission, but after getting spotted you quickly realize it's better to just go Rambo and murder everyone; the stealth is too difficult without much reward other than more GMP which the game already floods you with anyways.

Maybe the game does get better, maybe it does change, but if it hasn't done so after 10 hours of repetitive and frustrating menial droll nonsense excuse for "story missions", then how can I be expected to want to continue? It's like a book suffering from saggy-middle-syndrome.

review_text:
This game is fun until 'Legendary Game Creator' Hideo Kojima comes in and mucks everything up. This iteration of Metal Gear Solid is more open than its predecessors, to the point where there's even an open world that exists outside of the missions that you can freely explore. The gameplay is fun, and I adore running around Afghanistan and Africa with D-Horse and D-Dog, but it struggles to balance this new-found freedom with the stealth action and now carries it like a weight. If happen to be discovered (or just decide to play fast and loose), the controls become very clunky - trying to run around a corner and Boss decides to crouch next to the wall, trying to crawl through a bush on not-perfectly-even terrain and he stands straight up in front of a base full of enemies, having to wait a second between getting into position or selecting a different weapon for the button prompt to come up or Snake to actually pull it out. Getting shot doesn't feel as weighty as it did in previous iterations either - gone are rations, in favor of everyone's favorite CoD-style 'breathe heavy with a red screen for a couple seconds and then continue on your merry way' - which is a shame because the open-world aspect would play wonderfully into this. Give me an actual use for all of the medicinal herbs I'm running past - let me make rations and drugs on-the-fly or load them into my e-cigar to enjoy those benefits without needing to call in a resupply.

The skulls are frightening and again confuse the Tactical Espionage Action.. until you realize you can kill them with a couple explosives or a round of regular ammo, allowing you to throw any sort of stealth-style gameplay to the wayside in favor of, once again, brute-forcing your way through encounters. All forced-loud sections of the game boil down into poorly-planned "how quickly can you navigate the menu and call in the helicopter" as opposed to actually feeling like you've beaten, out-thought, or out-maneuvered your adversary.

I actually enjoyed playing the game quite a lot, but every single cutscene killed that joy. The characters are bland and boring and outright unlikable, half of the information and backstory is very quickly contradicted by new information that is neither compelling nor logical. They got a new VA for Snake because they wanted something different, but he's written and delivered exactly as David Hayter always did, except with less energy and more old-man-grumbling rather than comical disbelief. Kaz is blind to everything other than getting revenge on Cipher, to the point that he's constantly yelling at and second-guessing Ocelot and Big Boss; The only time Snake is actually interesting is in tapes, which is incredibly lazy; Ocelot always has this weird masculine bromance energy with Snake, and it's just... weird. Like, if that's the way you want to go, do it, but like... every character is either as interesting as wet paper, or completely insufferable - the story itself makes about as much sense as someone six beers deep trying to explain Kingdom Hearts.

And that's not even mentioning the constant bottlenecks and ways to slow down your progress, to grind materials, or wait multiple hours to develop things, and how a lot of these mechanics that get in the way of you having fun can be bypassed by paying REAL WORLD MONEY. I legitimately think this game would've been better had the devs just phoned it in. As it stands, it feels like every time the devs had to make a decision, they picked the way that made the least sense and crippled any fun the player may have been having.

Short version: Get this game ON MASSIVE SALE (around the $5 mark) if you are willing to mod in a bunch of Extra Ops, visual mods, the "Take Me Off The Grid v2" mod (and probably the timer remover edition of said mod), and a camera mod. Go to the Nexus and start browsing. This isn't something I'm simply recommending to you, I am outright telling you that you [b]WILL[/b] have to do this to make this game a good one worth spending real money on. Otherwise, forget it. Also skip every cutscene imo. 

I've played this game to 96% completion on PS4 back when it came out (didn't feel like doing the very small remedial final things to get the 100%) and I can strongly say that was solely because at the time there was nothing to play on my new shiny PS4 paperweight back at its launch. The moment better games started coming out, this game was quickly uninstalled and has NOT been touched on my PS4 since. I have had this game in my Steam library for years, and just recently I finally decided to mod this game to be able to play it again without wanting to down acetone. [b]Do I think this game is terrible? Not really.[/b] I however think it is easily one of the worst Metal Gear games and is easily [b]THE WORST mainline entry in the franchise[/b] due to how insanely repetitive the content gets for even a MGS game, and how nothing the story is. I will not be getting into whether or not Kojima is a hack, or if Konami's meddling ruined the game or not, I'm not going to go over the WHY this game is the way it is, I will solely leave it to talking about the game itself because the reasons for it are not going to make the game itself become better or worse. The mission types get repetitive within a few hours in, the crafting system making you wait REAL LIFE time, and sometimes a REALLY long time was a scummy way to push micro-transactions to speed things up. The story boils down to a really, really bad science fiction novel on-par with some L. Ron Hubbard literature, and your main protagonist was made to "be easy for the player to assume the role of in their mind" which means Snake here will be the most socially awkward introvert as he just stares at things with his mouth open while sometimes breathing hard enough for the microphone to pick up. No this isn't due to Sutherland being expensive, the Japanese dub of this game and all other languages are just as boring. Anyways, this game is basically a really great engine being used to make one hell of a demo. This game is worth 5 bucks imo. If it's not on sale for anything around that price or lower, don't buy. However, this game's biggest strength being its potential means the community can thankfully (and did) step up and finish this game for them. Various extra-ops gives this game the much needed mission types MGSV needed from the start, and being able to change your FoV to not zoom in all the way up your ass or up to your shoulder just for crouching or going prone makes this game more than playable (by default this nonsense will drive you up the wall). The mods for this game, albeit a tiny bit tricky to install and make sure everything is working right, will make this game if purchased on a sale much, much better. 5 bucks. No more than that. Keep that in mind. Otherwise, stay the hell away from this game. It is NOT worth it unless you get it cheap AND are willing to mod it with at LEAST 18 or so mods, give or take. Non-negligible. Skip every cutscene if you already know this insanely barebones plot stuffed with lingering camera angles that don't need to be there. If you don't know the story I guess it'd be nice to at least have some context as to what you are doing, but I won't hold anything against you if you start skipping everything once you get sick and tired of bad cinematic shots (no, cinematic shots aren't bad. this game just has BAD ones).

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is the latest main entry in the MGS series. It is an open-world stealth game, military-themed but with sci-fi elements. Kinda like Splinter Cell, but more wacky, with hiding using boxes, superpowered individuals, and most importantly the mechas. Sadly, TPP and its prologue Ground Zeroes are the only MGS games that are widely available on Steam. Because of that, it is recommended to play get and play GZ first, as the ending of that game connects directly to the opening of TPP. Both games are also pretty early in the MGS timeline, and if you have access to other titles, only Peace Walker is heavily tied to it.

Other than the stealth gameplay, there is also a base-building feature, where you can develop your Mother Base, recruit people, save animals, etc by collecting the necessary resources. However these don't really impact much of the gameplay, since recruited soldiers are usually automatically assigned. You can still choose to do so manually, though. You can also walk around the Mother Base, seeing your soldiers or doing some of the tasks. You can also play as some of the recruited soldiers if you put them as Combat Unit. This adds a bit more variation and immersion, especially when finishing the 157 (!) side ops.

The best thing about MGSV is the story, but sadly it isn't told very well in the gameplay. While the cutscenes are really cool, the gameplay feels... repetitive and aimless. Most of the quests are just "go here, do this thing" kinda missions. And they can take place in the same location over and over. While its in a way good since it makes you familiar with the place, going to an area 5 or more times with slightly differing objectives and enemy positions makes the game feel monotonous. The most unique area of the game is the first mission, which is very cinematic, but its linear and no other areas feel as modern like that one. Most of the time you will be sneaking in simple military outposts and abandoned villages. And the worst part is that while there are 50 missions, around 1/4 of them are repeat missions but difficult. Like where the enemy deals more damage, some require you to not be detected at all, and some you start without any equipment. 

As for the Side Ops, there is really a lot of them, but most of them are very short and can be completed within minutes. Most of them are generic, but there are several important ones highlighted in yellow. You must finish these ones to progress the story, although I recommend playing the normal ones as well, even simply just to gain resources. I really wish there was more unique side ops though, as aside from the important ones these missions are just rinse and repeat.

One time I stumbled upon someone who said MGSV is better to be played in short bursts rather than all at once, and I agree, that's how I played it as well. It took long for me to finish this game as I switch to other, more gripping games at times. If you play MGSV too much, it will probably get very boring and tiring. One other thing, I'm not a fan of how they handle saving as it uses a checkpoint system. And most times, when infiltrating enemy bases, there are no autosaves other than before you enter the area.

A game is not a mere display of the latest technology, of how good the hair on some character looks, or how detailed and open the environment can be.

Metal Gear, the series, are not mere games. They created a genre. They paved the way for future generations. Everytime you hear the words "stealth" and "cinematic" in a game, it really means "Metal Gear inspired". 
Kojima and his team created what many thought impossible. They paved the way for games to be considered far more than just a "child's entertainment".

So here I am 120+ hours in and still only 41% in.

The ULTIMATE stealth sandbox game with what appears to be near endless ways to entertain yourself and get lost in.

Want to be a master of stealth?  A ghost that NPCs only whisper about?  You can play that way

Want to be John Rambo and come in guns blazing?  NPCs dead in a whirlwind of gunfire and explosions?  You can play that way.

Or how about eliminating foes one by one john wick/pistol fu style?  You can play that way.

Do you covet high scores/high grades after each mission?  Or maybe you are one of those 100%'ers who must collect everything imaginable.  Their truly is something for everyone here.

Now to be perfectly honest, the only real flaw here is the relatively sparse story telling.  As a person who is on the edge of Kojima fan-boyism, IMO the story is kind of incoherent/scatter shot mess.  Its there, but you have to kind of work a little harder to place it in the cannon.  This could also be a function of sheer amount of time you spend doing non-story things.  

Much of the background and story is also buried in the cassette tapes you receive, and if you are like me, are worth listening to if you can.

This review is on the edge of 5 years too late I realize.  But my goodness what a game

TLDR:  Kojima's Metal Gear Solid Opus.  A game that isn't perfect by any means, but is one that I think you can find something to entertain you for YEARS.

review_text:
This is Schrodinger's MGS game, it exists as both the best and worst entry in the series at the same time

Kojima made a masterpiece but wasn't done with it

Konami took the unfinished masterpiece and turned it in to a repetitive, boring grind fest

Half of the story is very good, there are a lot of great mechanics and the story is really interesting and the gameplay is very smooth and solid. Then the second half of the story was unfinished so Konami just deleted it and then make you play the same missions you already did, a second time, with slight variations. This is still the 'main' game

Then it makes you make a fob, then it forces you to participate in PvP, then it lets people steal your money, your materials, and your soldiers, even if you're offline and the game's uninstalled, and the only way to prevent it is to pay for coins that you get 15/day for or real money. All your other resources are constantly draining. You have money, materials, and medine, and everything you do from research to deploying to missions to extracting things consumes all of these. Upgrading a weapon takes resources and deploying to a mission with said weapon costs resources every single time. These are the same resources people can take from you in PvP and the same resources you're going for in end game.

Once you raid one fob you've pretty much experienced everything the game has to offer. Now do that over and over and over again for literally years, spending hundreds of millions of in-game currency and thousands of hours waiting for research completes to squeeze out slightly higher damage values on the same weapons with the same attachments

Worse yet, even a lot of the game mechanics and AI were partially unfinished. Mechanics that have existed as a main-stay in the game series are gone- Where in MGS2 AI had to utilize radios, MGS5 relies on a reflex mechanic, alerting everyone instantly to your location if someone sees you, without them needing to report it. They use the radio but it's sort of more of an illusion over more basic AI mechanics. They also have extremely weird reactions to anything such as too many people being taken out (even if they weren't spotted) leading to all of the AI wandering to a single location somewhere else. The AI can even actively shoot at you without spotting you due to the way their programming was left partially unfinished and Konami tied up the loose ends real quick.

They're very easily manipulable because of their gullible yet psychic behaviors. You can pretty much make them go places in a map without having to give yourself away, or if you're sniping a guard in the face with a sniper rifle and they have a helmet, you can make them turn towards you so you can shoot their face. You can sit there and shoot at the ocean with the bean bag shotgun then move to make all of their AI turn their backs to you so you can walk freely in to the fob core. You can take someone out on the edge so one-by-one all of the AI walk over to him and then stand there staring, waiting to get shot by you. You can use C4 and Grenades to herd literally the entirety of the base away from your very position, but all of that doesn't matter because you can just play as quiet and dash to the end completely unseen within just a couple of minutes and ignore all of the above and the entirety of all of the game mechanics anyways.

Doesn't matter, end-game is literally just mobile game mechanics with a really boring and repetitive FOB infiltration section that will have people invading each other endlessly just out of spite alone

But the first half of the story is the best MGS experience I've ever had

review_text: Nothing really plays like a Hideo Kojima game, and its sad to see this being his last game, with so much untapped potential left on the table due to office politics in Konami. The game, for this reason, is left incomplete. Besides that legacy, that will always tarnish this game, its stellar, but shows its age in design. repetitive mission structure, cutscene directing that screams overindulgence (a kojima trope), and a story that goes in literally every direction. Things like this make the barrier of entry for a game like this very high for those who've not experienced his games, or JRPG's. That being said, the gameplay is unmatched, nothing touches it. the feedback, sounds for various activities, the freedom of approach to the very tactical and often unforgiving bases in the open world. You're left wanting to play it perfectly, and the online FOB component is a welcome addition. However, if you get far enough in this game, you're going to start seeing the cracks well into the second portion of the game (there was supposed to be a third before Kojima was fired from his own game). I don't often feel it necessary to add a drawn out comment, there's plenty of other comments or videos out there, but I hope that this at least provides some insight for those on the fence who've never tried a game of this sort to give this one a chance. This game is worth your time, and doesn't disrespect it, which is much more than can be said for others in this current environment. Give it a go, get through the first slog of an intro, and see for yourself what this game has to offer for yourself.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain looks and runs pretty good even in 2022. Sure some mods might be needed to get it running on 60+ fps, but nowhere near the ammount of hustle you'd have to go through in for example MGR on pc. For me however this game is incredibly polarizing.

On one hand this game has propably one of the best stealth gameplays ever with the possibility to customize everything to your liking, a companion system that works, quite intelligent and competent AI opponents, a base you have to take care of and also a very long and complex story with some of the most iconic scenes in video game history accompanied by a great soundtrack. On the other hand it is so repetetive, slow and sleep inducing that I actually finished Better Call Saul while playing. Perhaps I might have enjoyed the series more than the game itself but it's hard to judge.

More than anything this game makes you feel like an upincomming warlord/military contractor. It does so by introducing many mechanics that are tied to the base. This is personal opinion, but this fact alone ruined the game for me. It just wasn't fun. None of it. It was tedious, boring and you cannot ignore it. Another thing tied to this is the open world. It's big, split into two maps and looks and feels pretty good. It's not completely empty and some outposts are very well designed. But not all of them. A lot of them are 2-5 minutes of driving away from eachother and are just copypasted Ubisoft-style dogsh*t. It's fun for awhile but it gets stale incredibly quickly.

I've played or seen basicly all of the previous MGS installments and must say that this is the most convoluted, retconned and confusing franchise in history. Ever since Kojima started explaining stuff from the games with new games, everything started to fall appart. Funnily enough this game's story isn't the hardest one to follow, even tho it's the longest, but you can still finish the game without knowing what the f*ck happened. I have to say that I honestly feel sorry for people that are heavily invested in the lore, because it must be an absolute headache.

I have to admit that I have only an average cringe tolerance at best, but this series made me cringe constantly. I don't know if it's Kojimas writing or just the translation but truck load of the dialogue is an absolute miss. In TPP it's a toss of a coin. Either you get one of the most iconic scenes in gaming that is used in memes and edits or you get complete diarrhoa comming out of someones mouth. The worst part of this game however is the pacing of the story. It's so damm long and stretched to near its breaking point that it takes about 60 hrs to finish the main story and it still lacks a propper conclussion because Kojima got fired by konami before he could finish it.

I might have been a little harsh in this review but don't get me wrong - this still is an amazing game. It just wasn't for me as much. If you are looking forward to all those new mechanics and want a slow but very immersive, tactical and methodic gameplay it's honestly hard to find anything like MGS V: TPP. Grab it on a sale with GZ and you'll have a great time.

Performance was good, except some initial cutscenes dropping down to 0 fps and freezing the game on the steam deck, forcing you to skip them. For a steam verified game that relies on story, that's already a deal breaker on itself for me.     
   
The open world feels pretty great, allows for a variety of approaches and the new emphasis on scouting out locations is pretty fun and makes it feel even more tactical. Sadly, a lot of the world consists of the same three types of outposts with 4 guards. Don't get me wrong, there is plenty of other variety and approaches, but parts of it do feel stale. Overall, it's still a welcome addition to the franchise. Companions and vehicles add even more tactical depth to the infiltrations.   
  
Another addition is mother base. You expand this base by collecting resources and troops, somewhat similar to mgs peace walker.  However, the huge and bloated system adds very little. Sure, there are research requirements, but it mainly acts as motivation to engage with all the side missions of " extract solider at point x" " drive across the map and steal blueprints from y" and that sort of thing to bolster play time.  There is a lot of unnecessary complexity, when in the end you auto-assign everyone, send your troops on missions without consequence except the occasional pop-up.  Sure, it's optional, but a lot of cool gear is locked behind it, which feels even more sour once you realize you can spend actual money on it to speed up missions.    
    
My second criticism is the story. It's basically the same as ever: deep running conspiracies of the Patriots, cipher, governments, nukes and secret war. Zero innovations on that end, with a villain that's even more uninteresting, uninspired and cartoonish than any in the franchise before. I mean, he's literally called skull face, ffs.  
And then there is quiet. 
Pretty much the only female representation in the story exclusively wears bikini (which she regularly removes) with the camera constantly on her cleveage or ass.  
Did I mention she can't even speak?!?  One (barely) main non-male charecter in the game and she can't speak, because otherwise the world ends???  
And unlike with nier automata, where the creator said it's because he likes maid outfits, they come up with these intricate reasons to justify it, that are on the level of a Loli fan explaining his waifu isn't actually 13 but 3000 because she is a dragon.   
   
The story also had it's moments and I did enjoy parts of the game, but overall I don't think I can recommend it. Additionally, you are forced to connect to servers and agree to shady contracts to access parts of the game. I don't think you can do a lot wrong getting it for 5-10 bucks, especially on deck, but for a fan of the franchise it was a letdown

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid 5 is defiantly worth the money, but is it worth your time? I would say it is. MGSV has some of the best game mechanics of any game I have ever played, on the ground combat is done perfectly. Not to mention the plethora of customization options for your character, weapons, buddy, and HQ. Onto the story, if you have never played a metal gear fame before (like me) this game handles and throws you into the story pretty well. The actual story of the game is very confusing, even up to near the end of the game. If your looking to have a simple story to get through one playthrough or not researching the rest of the story, you might want to skip this one; however, the quiet ending and the true ending to the game (I feel) wrap up the story of MGSV. Many complain that konami ruined the game and made it unfinished, but I feel that the game is good enough as it is. If you're wondering what endgame content there is, you can replay missions to achieve "S rank" and it gives the play a huge satisfaction. Overall the gameplay makes up for the downsides of plot, and outside development, and is a good starter to the series and a standalone game.

While Metal Gear Solid 5 is goofy, inconsistent, and hell of a lot of fun to play, I can say this is one of my new favorite games.

+9/10

I spent the first half hour or so stumbling around a hospital looking up a dude's (who I did not know) hospital gown, terrified that at any moment I was going to see his starfish/balloon knot but also unable to look away - as we crawled through a hospital and I could not help but wonder why he did not have scrub pants like I was wearing.  It was incredibly distracting. (Insert homophobic insults or jokes here - I don't care.)

EVEN MORE distracting was that I was helpless through most of this (understandably I suppose, since I had been in a coma for 9 years, but on the other hand (spoiler? - can there even be any spoilers in the prologue?) I end up riding a HORSE within the hour, which could be the most strenuous things that someone in a decade-long coma could end up doing.

ALSO, I know NOTHING about Konami/the dude who directed this game and their conflict/issues when this was being made.  ALL I knew was that this was a fairly ambitious AAA title as one of the more well regarded franchises in gaming. I was expecting pretty solid story and gameplay. I go from bullet sponge in the hospital, wearing only scrubs and no shirt, to an easily killed grunt in the desert at the beginning of the actual game.

I have NO IDEA what is going on with the Silver Surfer/Human Torch dude and the flaming Nun or whatever she is and why they are following me and saving me/trying to kill me? It seems a bit unrealistic. Even for a video game.

MY BIGGEST COMPLAINT is that I feel WOEFULLY under trained for any of this. I feel like I was thrown into the deep end of the gaming pool with no help and no lifeguard and I'm kind of frustrated.

I think that I am going to un-install and come back later. I got this on a Humble Bundle at a significant discount so I am not upset, but I am disappointed. I was hoping to have found my next Wolfenstein or other aging gem that I could enjoy as I wade through the last decade of gaming that I spent in my own version of a coma (raising young kids),

If I was to recommend this game, it would come with a huge caveat. I think it is good, maybe even great - but I haven't seen that greatness YET. For the current price of less than $20 it is probably worth it, but I wanted to post a DO NOT RECOMMEND post because one thing people keep saying to me is, "It has a 9/10 rating, of course it is good!"  Well, I'm doing my part to try and bring that down a notch. I'm not saying it is a bad game, but for me, at least - it isn't a 9/10 yet.

I'm aware the Phantom Pain is not quite like any other game in the franchise but it’s a fantastic edition to the series. 

The story is good but through no fault of the team that made it, this game is unfinished and it feels it. Once you hit Chapter 2 you’ll find the majority of missions are simply harder versions of previous missions you’ve played, with challenges like “Extreme”, “Subsistence” and “Total Stealth”. There’s nothing inherently wrong with this and they’re all fun in their own right but it does rub the salt in the wound that this game never got to finish what it started. A phantom pain of its own. 

Still I’ve really enjoyed this game! I’ve decided to take a break from trying to 100% it for now as I have been playing it for over 140 hours this past month or so. Currently as of this review, I’ve completed 91% of the game so far. It’s a big time investment if you decide to tackle all of the side content the game has to offer. 

I suppose one minor criticism I have would be about the main female character of this game; one of your three companions, Quiet is practically naked on the battlefield because she “breathes through her skin”. Doesn’t explain why this hardened sniper rolls around boobily in the rain and all of the gratuitous angles of her chest and butt, but alright. It’s pretty cringe to pretend this is for anything but eye candy but you can unlock clothing for her near the end of the game. 

You can manage and upgrade your base for better gear and for online invasions, but more importantly you can tackle and beat up your soldiers at any time to boost morale. It’s great, they love it. 

This game feels great to play and you’ll get as much out of it as you put into it. Like I said before, the AI reacts to your strategies (if you sneak in from the sides, they’ll set up mines. If you use sleeping gas, they’ll wear gas masks. If you get a lot of headshots, they’ll start to wear helmets. Etc) which encourages you to switch it up! Go in sneaky, go in loud, let Quiet handle it all- it’s up to you! 

Also you can pet the dog and he is a very good boy. 

One of the best stealth games out there, I’d love to see the older Metal Gear games ported to Steam in the future.

I love this game, but it is also one of the most disappointing games I've ever played. I never actually beat this game until recently, and it was the first MGS game I played until recently. I didn't understand a thing about the plot when i first played it, and after playing the rest of the series, what I do understand is sullied by the fact it was never finished (or at least feels very unfinished). 

Even aside from that, the fan service in this game is really awful. Quiet is literally just a silent sex appeal tool, the girls in the parasite unite are almost just as bad. Normally I don't mind fan service in games but this game pushes it down your throat so hard that it genuinely ruins parts of game if you're trying to take it seriously. 

Half the story is told to you through 10 minute long audio tapes which you're basically forced to sit through or you risk missing vital information, and might I add that you get several of these tapes every single time you finish a mission. It's exhausting.

Once you finish the first half of the game, they decide to pad out the already long runtime by forcing you to replay several missions from the first half before you can progress the plot. There's no new plot during these missions, the only difference is they have added challenge to them. Would be great as an optional game mode, but it's absolutely infuriating to force it into the main story. 

So, with all these complaints why do i still have nearly 200 hours in this game and a positive review rating?
I don't know how they managed it, but in spite of all the unfinished crap and awful choices made, when they do something good in this game, they do it REALLY GOOD. 

While most of the plot feels like a big run on sentence, the parts of this game's story that stand out are going to be implanted into my memory for the rest of my life. Some of the cutscenes and gameplay sequences in this game are truly amazing.

But the biggest thing is the gameplay, oh my god. The Batman Arkham games had my favourite stealth mechanics until this game came out. I cannot begin to describe the sheer level of variety and options you have in this game. You can literally choose an approach every single degree between bombing an outpost with missiles, rolling in with a tank, stealing the guy you want and flying out of there on a helicopter. OR making sure you're wearing the right camo gear, all silenced weapons, smoking the place out and going in undetected. The game does reward you overall for being more stealthy, but there's nothing stopping you from playing this game any way you want. I will never get tired of it.
