review_text:
For fans of the Metal Gear series, this is a great game to play.  A lot of people are apprehensive about playing it because of the way Kojima and Konami split during its development, but it's a game that I think is well worth playing.

The visuals are impressive.  For a game like this, realism is important to help the player lose themselves in the experience, and it delivers in this department.  On my hardware the game looked and ran well enough that I had no problems at all suspending disbelief and enjoying the events on screen.  What's even more impressive is that  I've played the game on Steam Deck and on my desktop PC, and it looks reasonably great on both platforms running at high to max settings on both platforms and staying well above 60fps the entire time.  I even played it once or twice on my laptop with a Ryzen 5 2500U and integrated graphics, and even there I was able to achieve a playable, decent looking experience at 720p and low to medium settings.  My desktop gaming PC, which is where I play it the most, had the following specs:

CPU: AMD FX 8370 (stock clock speeds)
RAM: 16 GB DDR3 @ 1866 Mhz
GPU: AMD Radeon RX 480 (8GB, MSI "Gaming" variant)

As far as the gameplay goes, the gameplay loop is quite enjoyable because things are a lot less linear.  You start out on a helicopter or at your "mother base", a large facility out in the ocean that is reminiscent of "Big Shell" from MGS2.  From there you will set out on missions, some of them essential, more story driven missions, and many of them optional "Side ops" that do nothing for the story, but allow you to basically accomplish quick little side quests to acquire more money, capture personnel and resources, capture animals, etc.  Once you're in the world however, whether it's a story mission or an optional side op, the world is a lot more open ended than in previous games where you were more or less guided along expected paths towards a desired goal.  It's very "open world", which affords you a lot more freedom in exactly how you accomplish your goals.  The goal might be to extract somebody who is being held prisoner in a village, and you might land a few hundred or even a thousand or more meters out, but from there, you can do what you want.  You can approach from any direction you want, in any way you want.  You can sneak around and interrogate enemy soldiers to extract information, you can turn off their generators or destroy their radios so they can't call in reinforcements, you can have your dog bark to distract enemies, you can hide in a box at a pickup location and let a delivery truck deliver you right into the middle of the enemy camp, you can hide in the latrine and play an audio recording of somebody with diarrhea if somebody gets too close, or you can charge in, guns blazing and call in mortar strikes, call in helicopter gunship support while your helicopter blasts something like "Kids in America" or "Rebel Yell" from the loudspeaker, etc.  How you play and how you accomplish your goals is entirely up to you, and I think it's amazing.  I've spent untold hours just replaying side ops because I enjoy roaming around and playing the game so much.

There's another element to the gameplay and that's the FOB missions.  You can use your resources and personnel to build optional FOBs that other players can then attempt to infiltrate.  Any personnel or resources on your FOB are fair game for skilled infiltrators, so it's a good idea that once you have a FOB, you spend time and energy building up its defenses, researching better gear for your soldiers, etc.  You can also customize where your soldiers patrol so you can focus their efforts on entry and exit points, blind spots, etc.  Likewise, you can also attempt to infiltrate the bases of other players, where you can capture personnel, weapons, resources, etc.  However, if you infiltrate another player's FOB, whether you're successful or not, they will get notified and have the option of retaliating against you, which is useful information since as far as I'm aware you can't otherwise just look for specific players to go after.

The storyline and acting is, I think, great.  Is it the best Metal Gear game?  Probably not.  But I thoroughly enjoyed it.  There are plenty of interesting characters, plot twists, action, deception, throwbacks to previous games, etc.  Even though he's not David Hayter, Kiefer Sutherland did an excellent job voicing the protagonist.  Overall, the story is what a Metal Gear game is about.  Sure, the gameplay is fun, but you don't play a Hideo Kojima game just for the sneaking, you play it for 20+ minute cutscenes and the story, the characters, the places, the optional conversations, etc.  Overall, I enjoyed the story in this game, and it was neat to get to meet some of the classic characters at a different stage of their life.

Overall, as a fan of previous Metal Gear games, I thoroughly enjoyed MGSV, and I still hop on pretty regularly to go infiltrate somebody's FOB, do a couple of side missions, research some new weapon, etc.  If you're a fan of Metal Gear or HIdeo Kojima's work, I would recommend picking this up.  It looks great, runs great and is a lot of fun.

review_text:
Firstly a warning that I'm pretty sure I should have played METAL GEAR SOLID V: GROUND ZEROES first! I only realised it even existed after finishing this one, and so I feel like I missed out a fair chunk on the plot.

This being said, this was my first Metal Gear game and I get the impression that the plot would be outrageously convoluted regardless of how many previous games one has played, so maybe it doesn't matter! But I do wish I'd played GROUND ZEROES first just for the complete experience (even if the fact the prologue is a separate game and far from cheap is pretty annoying!).

As for my other warning. DON'T GIVE UP ON THE GAME BEFORE YOU'VE DONE A MISSION OR TWO AFTER RECEIVING YOUR BASE. When a buddy first recommended the game, I burnt out after the relatively long and slow tutorial/intro and first mission, now with the context of the rest of the game I love this segment, but the first time it prevented the game getting its hooks in me. Took me ages to come back, and I can't believe how much I was missing out (Rich you were totally right!). So if you're feeling like quitting, I'd really recommend giving it a little more time! 

Another thing causing my early burnout was that, in general, I've never got on with more consoley games (or control schemes), and however much I love Japanese stuff, and the vibe of a lot of games coming from Japan, I always find some of gameplay/control conventions that seem to be common a off putting. (No criticism of either, more habit than anything). After I got over that initial segment on my second attempt, I found the style and controls much more compatible with my more western PC gamer sensibilities, and I'm very happy that I don't have to miss out on another wacky Japanese creation as a result!

As for my review though; ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ brilliant game! Loved it! 

Gameplay was fantastic, and for a Metal Gear virgin, I found it to have pretty unique stealth mechanics that I found far more enjoyable than the average. All the fantastic little details, tricks, systems and insanity give even the smallest encounter so much potential depth. 

I particularly enjoyed that the game didn't hold my hand either. Most games feel the need to patronisingly explain every little mechanic and hint at every possible way to solve a problem. MGSV doesn't do this, it gives you the basics, chucks you in the sandbox and the rest you discover for yourself, which I found incredibly satisfying. It's the first game in a long while where I've seen any point in online strategy guides; one might think this is a criticism but I think it's just a reflection of the depth available and the diversity in the "solutions" between guides just goes to show how much fun it can be to solve these different missions. Plus for me, having to occasionally give into weakness and read a guide evoked nostalgic memories of when games used to be a little less self-explanatory and as a result more of a journey of discovery.

As for the story and setting, again fantastic! Just my cup of tea! Over the top, insane, super hammy and just a riot. Not to sell it short either, I think there's some really interesting themes and ideas to be found, and it was definitely capable of evoking some genuine feeling in me too. I only wish I'd been playing metal gear games in the beginning so I could get the full context, but even as a standalone experience I had a blast.

I even got a kick out of the multiplayer elements. It would be a entirely fair criticism to say that the multiplayer FOB stuff has definitely been built to encourage microtransactions and to some might even feel like those frustrating mobile games with there pay-to-not-wait mechanics. Despite this though, I actually enjoyed almost everything about the online mechanics. I never paid any cash into the game beyond the purchase price, so I didn't have the funbucks to skip any of the build times, but for me I enjoyed the effect on pacing, giving me an excuse to spread out my play time a little and I liked logging in to find another part of my little empire had been constructed. Kinda gave it a sense of being a MMO. 

Also, being fundamentally misanthropic and socially anxious, I often can't bring myself to play with randoms in multiplayer, but the asynchronous style of multiplayer interactions in MGSV made me more than usually adventurous. The multiplayer definitely enhanced the singleplayer experience too, really adding to the sense of big and living world. 

I mean I could go on all day about all little things I love about this game. There's really so much to discuss and praise here. It's not the perfect game, but I found even it's imperfections lovable and worthy of discussion.

edit: I've subsequently watched Super Bunnyhop's youtube videos on the Metal Gear franchise, and as someone who missed out on those older releases but enjoyed this as a standalone, it was a fantastic overview. review_text:
This is a review I feel I needed time to think about, and really had see if I wanted to do said review. So here it goes.....

Been a Metal Gear fan since the PS1 and was one of my first games, was a great experience and loved the story, the combat, how attached you feel to each character since it was just deep. That feel kept going into 2, then 3, and somewhat 4, and that feeling was back with PW (and to a lesser degree Portable Ops). I remember seeing the trailer for Ground Zero and felt something was different despite being Big Boss. It felt more detached, but overall interesting. So if you want a good version of TPP play GZ, you will enjoy it more since the Fox Engine kinda works better since it's not trying to be open world, but a Sandbox within a good level design.

Anyways, onto The Phantom Pain.....just how it starts, it feels very disconnected, playing as Big Medic....you lose any sense that you are the moving force in this story. Before the game begins, you lose 10 years of time between Ground Zero and The Phantom Pain, despite a lot happening with Cypher, Kaz, and Ocelot coming into the picture. Even in the hospital, everything is driven by Big Boss telling you what to do and how to move, but that being said, things are actually happening to you while in the mission and plot progression (despite lacking) is moving forward. Once done, and wondering why the hell the Man on Fire is a thing (despite the tapes trying to explain why Volgin is there, it's just fan service), and why the hell or how the hell Kaz got caught from the initial cut scene. 

Then starts the first mission of the game, explaining the open world of this game. This one being partly scripted and written by Kojima it has some plot to it and some movement of it with you being a driving force. During this whole opening scene into it, not once does Big Medic talk.....and that's a huge factor, Keifer has no voice lines in this whole game, I think it is recorded that he has around a WHOLE 5 minutes and 40 some seconds of talking in the whole game. I can tell you that in any other MGS game, Snake talks that amount in the first scene, let alone the whole game. As you are going through the first mission, everything between out posts is just dead land, just nothing happening outside the random truck driving from outpost to outpost.

When you finally get to where Kaz is at, you have some of the biggest issues with this game, and that is the cross development of the title, and it needing to play on the original Xbox 360 and PS3......this game can only render around 10 people at a time. So in that whole outpost that Kaz is held, you can consistently have people popping up behind you and causing an alert since that just popped in since the PC and PS4 versions of this game are just up scaled version of the PS3 and Xbox 360 versions. As the mission is ending and you are saving Kaz from being captured, you run into the Skulls.....now this is an enemy boss-ish NPC that shows up in written missions. Outside Code Talker saying he studied parasites and used them on himself and Quiet....there is no real reason why Skull Face is using them or how they came to be or controlled despite acting Zombie like. But to kill them easy, just throw 2 grenades, and they die... simple enough.

Then Mother Base.....as you are flying into Mother Base, the whole time Big Medic is questioning what he should do, how can Kaz guide him, not questioning anything, like what the hell happened over the years, how did he get caught....nothing Big Boss would do, take charge and lead with Kaz. Anyways, on the base, there is no life, no major NPC you can interact with despite the trailers saying it and showing it. You have random fultoned soldiers walking around not doing anything like what you thought would happen in Mother Base from your pretense that Peace Walker gave since those tapes actually told stories of Mother Base. This Mother Base is just a place were insignificant events happen just to make you come back to make it seem like Mother Base has a living culture, when it does not. Even here rendering more than 10 or so people becomes and issue, to solve that the team made it so that the distance between each platform on MB was insanely long so that they can despawn everyone and bring up the new set of people since the game can only render 10 or so people....so traveling on MB is useless and pointless since it does nothing to make you feel it is worth while or fun, just as soulless as the open world map.

From here, you have your Main Missions and Side Ops. Main Missions for the most part outside the few Kojima wrote, are as simple as this, land, fulton/kill target, leave mission area, get S rank, Mission Complete and How! Nothing dynamic in any regards since most of these missions were made maybe in 10 minutes each (look at this video to see how fast they made missions https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qCs0xxUS5as&ab_channel=RajmanGamingHD ) Due to how trash they were made, there is constant mission breaking bugs were NPCs will lose where they are meant to be, or triggers won't load, and it's not just one mission, literally every mission is this way, and it's not like you need to try to make these occur, just simple playing the game you would as in any other MGS game would break missions here.

For the missions being in an open world, not one thing you do in the missions affect the world you are playing in. Each mission is like its own little instance, so each mission happens in its universe and when you leave, everything you did is undone. 

For Side Ops, you have ones that are marked as Important Side Ops, as to why they are not just main missions, I will never know. Some of them have more interesting aspects to them than regular missions. Most of them though are just stupid little tasks, like Mine clearing 1-10, dynamic, important, worth time, clearly Big Medic needs to do this, not some DD person, but gotta fly 8-10 hours to disarm 6 mines, realism......

As for plot, it was kinda touched, but everything happens begin the scenes, everything is done on a tape where Kaz or Ocelot tells you 'Hey while you were out fultoning people, we got this tape, or got this intel, or stole info from an enemy base about this plan and figuring out who Skull Face is'. Nothing you do in game really drives the plot forward, Only tapes, where it's Kaz, Ocelot, or Code Talker monologing to themselves, rarely if at all Big Medic saying a word. Granted MGS4 had not the greatest writing, but at least Snake talked and questioned Ocelot's actions and his plans with GW making Snake the driving force of the plot.

Outside Kaz, Ocelot, and Code Talker, there is no other NPCs or characters that mean anything to you, I mean who can forget the original and plot important General's Number 2!

As for boss fights, all are forgettable and pointless, Quiet you can beat with a supply drop, sahelanthropus can be cheesed with tanks and armored cars, nothing challenging the player. This game could of done well to introduce Sniper Wolf, and how she met Big Boss (they kinda do it with Liquid, but never completed that plot, thanks hidden mission 51!), or how Grey Fox met Big Boss, or any of the boss in the original MSX games.

For ending the game, when chapter 2 starts, you are doing just random missions, with no given path since Skull Face is dead, no parasites, you are just kinda waiting for things to end, and well they kinda do when you do enough Side Ops, one that happens, you replay the hospital over again.....with the tutorial still in place.....really showing they had no idea what to do with missions or how to keep the plot of this game moving (what little there is). 

As a whole, this game is less of a MGS game, and more of a shooter that EA made. How this is considers amazing 10/10 is beyond me. So thank you and sorry for the rant.

review_text:
Unbelievably disappointing. Worst Metal Gear Solid game, at least from the main ones.

+ Huge amount of content. Tons of missions and even more side missions.
+ Stealth is the best thing here, it works rather well for the most part.
+ Tons of gadgets and pretty nice weaponry to play around with. You can get through using many different strategies.
+ Buddies are really useful.
+ Some scenes in cutscenes are so cool. I really love the cinematography of action and the scenes where they talk about honor.

- Terrible level design. Maps are way too huge. Even at the main base, you need to drive long distances, why? It's so impractical and stupid, also doesn't a bigger base mean easier to spot for enemies? Sure, fast travel exists but it's so poorly implemented and takes so much time with all the loading screens. The two main maps are garbage, tons of rocks in a way, need to go around all the time, insane lack of shortcuts, and driving is too rough since you crash into every tiny rock on the way. Enemy bases are impractical and flawed.
- Awful usage of licensed songs. Sure the songs are great but you can only hear them playing on the radio and once you pick them up they never play again, you can listen to them on the menu, but it kills the dynamic usage...
- Cutscenes are way too stretched out. Most are slow-paced, in many of them, characters speak useless information which could be cut. It's also hilarious how the protagonist is voiced by a famous actor which was part of the marketing, yet he barely ever speaks in the game...
- Some characters like Ocelot and Miller don't have enough importance and runtime in the game.
- Some garbage mechanics like dispatch missions, are so poorly made, and overcomplex.
- Abysmal checkpoint system. It doesn't save before reaching the missions area the first time, but after you die then it starts to save... WTF is that logic? Why do I have to replay the whole getting to the location sections one more time? Why can't it just save the first time? The same happens in every mission. It only gives checkpoints after you die once.
- Fan service. Immature and disrespectful.
- Story isn't even finished.
- Sound mixing is very poor. Dialogues and music are too silent meanwhile the rest of sounds are too loud in comparison. No way to adjust it.
- You can't kill children. This is war, not some family friendly game, yet they still force this sentimentality that murderous kids can be reeducated.
- You can't use all the buddies at the same time. Feels so dated. In many games that are decades older you could use everything. But here you're limited to one buddy at a time.
- Majority of chapter 2 missions are direct copy-paste from chapter one, not only do you have to do the same objectives in the same areas over again, but they were even too lazy to remove the same cutscenes from them... It's beyond lazy to reuse the same content over again, sure they made it harder this time, with limitations, but putting them straight as main missions that are all needed to be completed in order to beat the game is just unacceptable, they're taking us for fools. This is the worst I have ever seen of developer laziness. The game was already very long, why reuse content? They clearly chose quantity over quality here.
- The extraction from areas and flaying to missions are tediously too long. I can understand waiting for a helicopter to get into the mission areas to pick you up, but why do we have to wait so long once you get in? Also, why do we even need to wait for all this crap on the base, why can't the helicopter already be on the base ready to fly? I swear, 1/3 of the game is spent waiting for the helicopter and flying until it gives us a loading screen. It's an obnoxious design.
- Microtransactions. Mainly needed to reduce the upgrade timers which sucks. Speaking of them, some are 24h long. And you can't just leave the game, no they are in-game time, so you have to play for 24h for the upgrade to finish... Yikes.


4/10

[b]Hoofit disclaimer[/b]
This review is primarily for people that haven’t played the earlier games in the series, from what I read if you’ve liked the earlier games whilst you may have some quibbles you will likely like this game.


[h1]Hoofit gets lost in Metal Gear Solid V[/h1]

Hello dear steam-ers, steam-ites? steam users and welcome to a tale of Hoofit playing a truly bonkers game. Now having not played earlier games in the metal gear series I thought I’d jump right into V, well-reviewed and relatively modern it shouldn’t be too much of a problem if I haven’t played previous games I thought. After all most series will have some sort of catch up if you’ve missed earlier games and in other games think Resident Evil its totally unnecessary to have played earlier games.

Well, that was the first issue I had. It starts off with cut scenes which really, really predispose you have some knowledge of earlier games/the Metal gear universe. I had no idea why my character was in hospital, nor why what turns from a ruthless organisation trying to wipe out me and any witnesses plot suddenly has outrageous supernatural beings. I have no idea who the cast of improbably named people were/meant to my char.

That brings me into my second issue. There are a lot of cut scenes in the first hour to the extent where I was watching not playing the game. It really did dampen my enthusiasm for the game. Eventually you get out into the open world but you’re not safe from cut scenes entirely as you get lost in samey missions in Soviet Afghanistan, a bold setting for an Open World game. I didn’t find the gameplay particularly compelling and for a stealth game I could get away with a lot of random blasting as I tried to luck into finding rare items.

review_text:
Pros: 
 - The gameplay. Some elements, like Reflex Mode, might be hit or miss with stealth purists, but for casuals, it's a godsend. Enemies come up with counter-tactics for your bad habits i.e. helmets to protect against headshots. The level is sprawling and the graphics are great IMO. 

- Stealth. It feels refined, on par with Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory. Everything, from your selected camo to day or night, sandstorm or rain, running or crawling, affects your presence and enemies' perception in palpable ways. The controls are tight, and you feel like Big Boss. :-)

The Mid
- (Some) mission designs. It's not that they feel unfun, just that the way the mission plays out is not to my liking. Episode 16: Traitor's Caravan and Episode 18: Blood Runs Deep come to mind. 

Base Management
- Part of rebuilding Diamond Dogs is to create and expand your military offshore oil rig Mother Base, where your spoils of war will be dedicated to. While I don't mind the idea, making Mother Base so large and your subdivisions be spread far apart makes visiting everyone (which does help in morale upkeep) increasingly impractical, since you need to drive or sit in a heli for minutes to get anywhere. 

The bad
- The story. Look, this is a Hideo Kojima story, which means you'll something resembling an interesting talking point, interrupted by toilet humor, scantily clad if not naked women (who in this case needs to be naked to photosynthesize, and yes, this isn't the weirdest thing in MGS), retcons, some combination of parasites, nanomachines, ESP or straight up magic, stuff which throws logic by the wayside as a writing obstacle. 

However, even as a fan of MGS, the vocal parasites aren't the problem. I was interested in Skull Face's ideas. The tapes were fine. I just feel there's more stuff Kojima included 'just cuz' like Man on Fire, Psycho Mantis and Eli, even as someone who's spoiled on the twists, these feel like very fanservicey inclusions. I feel the story comes together less easily than I'd like, repetition of side op missions, the constant dreariness, lack of humor and load of lore-sensitive context makes this a little difficult for newcomers to enjoy. 

Verdict
- Good, but not great like it could've been.

A towering triumph of a video game. If Guns of the Patriots was Metal Gear's death game - the conclusion to its saga, explosive, affecting and final - then MGSV is the series' immortality game. It is the final piece of the puzzle, the missing shard in the grand mosaic that cements the series as one of the finest, most dramatic, cohesive, challenging, innovative and intelligent examples the medium could ever hope to offer. 

People complain about this and that as they always do: that it has no story (it does), that what it has is told poorly (it isn't), and yet even to the wiki-skimming redditors (who will face judgement), the game endures. I disagree that the game succeeds despite its story, but the gameplay Kojima's team crafted goes beyond inspiration, it is utterly unreplicable.

And yes, it is unfinished, I will never stop thinking about how much more we could have had, but that mindset does no one any good. It's strangely fitting that the most salient criticism leveled against a game sub-titled 'The Phantom Pain' concerns the pain of what is missing. 

It is remarkable that Kojima et al. gave us this despite the challenges they were facing at Konami. Anyone else would have buckled, but these people are simply magnanimous; they gave us Metal Gear, not because we deserved it, but because we needed it. Kojima will never die, Metal Gear will never die.

Metal Gear Solid 5: The Phantom Pain is a strange package that offers unparalleled stealth gameplay but only half the deep narrative the MGS games are known for. Narrative-wise, what's on offer here is engaging, and the more muted Snake becomes charismatic in his own less fun, more stoic way.

MGSV is a great time rewarding patient players who focus on building up their base with even more toys to take into the field, offering rewarding ways to expand the gameplay. If you like sneaking, shooting, and story MGSV is for you as it rolls all three in an amazingly tight package, but be warned, the game tends to pitter out towards the 45-hour mark with no real ending and only two open-world maps that feel pretty barren unless you are on a mission. I feel like the game could have benefitted from a city or urban environment as its final location because sneaking around two types of desert gets pretty boring unless you are slipping out of a huge barracks. 

You won't regret your purchase of the last Kojima-directed Metal Gear; despite the bumps in the road, The Phantom Pain is still a masterpiece.

review_text:
This is a great game, though it comes with some caveats.

Pros:
- a staggering amount of content, both in world terms (number of outposts, size of maps) and gameplay terms (number of weapons, tools, quests etc.).
- I haven't played any previous Metal Gear games except Ground Zeroes, but the story seems to be serviceable enough. 
- Quiet booba, if you're into that kind of fanservice
- Both stealth and gunplay are great fun
- Watching soldiers you abduct from the battlefield with Fultons flying up into the air never gets old.

Cons:
- the grind for money and resources is insane. I kind of get needing a lot of resources to build another huge platform to your floating military base, but researching new weapons/tools/equipment very quickly gets very expensive. I also don't get the point of deployment cost. Why do I have to play each mission as if they're constructing each weapon and tool for me from scratch, especially when I put so much into researching the damn thing? It kinda pisses me off how going into the field prepared is punished - it'd be nice if you got a refund on tools you didn't use, weapons you brought back etc.
- a lot of story is delivered to you via audio cassettes you get at the end of missions - you'll need to listen to these while idling, as enemy conversation plays right over it and interrupts subtitles. Quite annoying.
- so much time wasting. Examples:
1) Missions are in real time, but only progress while you're playing. Same for weapon development, automatic resource collection/refining, soldier recruitment etc. As a result it's often to your benefit to just leave your game running overnight and let all this progress, which is really annoying.
2) If you deploy from the helicopter, there will be this 30 second or so cutscene of Snake flying towards the dropoff point, with some mission intro. This would be fine, except it's unskippable, and if you restart the mission for whatever reason, you have to go through the whole thing again! [i]Let me get on with it![/i]
3) The helicopter mechanics in general feel like a massive waste of time. Call in a chopper? Have to wait a minute or so for it to get there. Call in supplies? Wait. Call for a vehicle drop? Wait. Finally get in the chopper? Mandatory unskippable cutscene of chopper taking off, wasting even more of your time.
4) Maps are way too big. There is tons of empty space, leading to a lot of tedious running. You could use a horse buddy, but that takes away your other, way more useful buddies. You could also drop in a vehicle, but the driving physics are awful and you'll have to wait a good bit for it to get dropped from the helicopter. You could fast travel, but only from very infrequently placed points at major outposts. Finally and most obviously, you can use your helicopter to get around (in free-roam) - except you'll have to pay the deployment cost every time you get picked up, because there's no way to simply ride the helicopter from point to point.
5) Credits after every single mission. Yes, I know Kojima made this game, thanks.
- the game gets rather repetitive. If you want to S-rank every mission, do every optional objective, and complete every single side op ([i]157 of them![/i]), you'll be playing for a LONG time, and the aforementioned time-wasting mechanics make it a real chore.
- the game also literally starts repeating its main missions as harder versions of themselves, which is kind of offputting.
- microtransactions. Enough said.

Despite these cons, which are nothing really gamebreaking, there is still a [i]ton[/i] of game to enjoy here, and it regularly goes on sale with the prequel Ground Zeroes for a very reasonable price - right now it's only $7.50. Even if you hate grind and intentional timewasting like I do, you'll still get a great bang for your buck.

review_text:
This game is an exercise in frustration. It wants you to be a "stealth-no-kill" player, but it a) does not give you the tools to do it (you have to research it etc to do it well) and b) it keeps throwing you into "action" set pieces where violence and destruction is the only way out... stealth will be defeated through obvious "cheats" or won't work at all. It might not be so bad if the controls were responsive. They aren't. For example, pressing the sprint button often makes you stop, and then you have to wait a beat to press sprint again in order to make you sprint. This makes dodging in the "action" set pieces to be a chore. Even the simple act of skipping repetitive (and often useless) cut-scenes (for example, the cut scene to pick up an intel document... like... why?) is delayed. 

There is a lot of good points, but it is marred with so much of these annoyances, often not a result of thoughtful design choices but of... well, if it were logical, the choices wouldn't have been made.

Also, there are a lot of weird camera choices for the cutscenes. It would linger almost gratuitously on something that is so painfully obvious, that you wouldn't have missed it anyways. For example, a big honking tank in the background, or ... (trying not to spoil too much)... a "dinosaur" with a ridiculous name. It was painful when it was nonsensical, along with the weird "to be continued" freeze-frame endings (used inconsistently, btw), but it was worse when it was used on a female character that looked like she was put into the game purely to appeal to...well... you know... and maybe "those" types of female cosplayers. It is if the player was a, as the Japanese say, [i]chikan[/i]. And somehow, they shoe-horned lore that makes her choice of running around the battlefield in a bikini and fishnet stockings alright. I wish they had given her more depth in character, but considering how shallow the other characters are, maybe she was on par. She could have been a great character, but there was more time spent making her something for the juveniles (and developers) to lewd at than actually fleshing out (sorry) her story and character. 

And what is with all these soap-opera movie-maker-wannabe styled camera shot choices? Some of it would be better found in a JRPG tinged with teenage angst, but the others were.... like... Well, let's just say that even the student work in the filmmaking-related course that I took in school would be leagues better than this (did not major in filmmaking, but my major required quite a few related classes). I'm guessing the inspiration for the choices came from B-Grade action flicks? Maybe whatever is below B-Grade...  Which would be fine in another setting, but not this type of setting -- unless this series is supposed to be nonsensical, and everyone knew it already since they played previous entries in the series (this was my first foray). It would also explain the stupidness behind the cardboard box. The camera angles and other choices makes it even more difficult to enjoy it. I would just skip everything, but I do like to know the story... even if I have to sit through the ridiculous bits.

With all that being said (typed up while redoing a stupid Action Set Scene for the umpteenth time -- so, forgive me), it does have some decent parts. You can see how many hours I put in, especially considering the rant above. But it is peppered with so many annoyances and inconsistencies that what would be a great game has been downgraded significantly imo. Playing the "Demo" (aka Ground Zeroes) made me say aloud, "Man, I've been missing out on this Kojima thing"... then I played the intro to the main game. Such an annoying waste of time. If I had played that first before the Demo, I would've just returned the game. Probably it was built like that to make you feel frustrated, but I don't think it needed to be taken to that extent. Maybe Kojima had a lot of goodwill to burn due to his previous games, but for a first-time player, his name was just something I saw in gaming news that may have been on par with Molyneux and Sean Murray. 

Thankfully, I had played the Demo so I struggled on with level. So I suggest you play the Demo first before playing the actual game. 

I'm sure the diehard fans would be quick to disagree with my assessment and shout non-logical retorts. But I encourage you to really, really think through -- taking multiple viewpoints into account -- and make your own decision on if you want to really subject yourself to this frustration.

It's too late for me to stop playing... but hopefully this review will save some of you from this frustrating wannabe-movie with poor controls and psuedo-deep characters. 

And now I must make another attempt at finishing this action scene with these stupid, unresponsive controls. Sigh.

(EDIT: I Find the Fulton system both hilarious and fun. Might be the real reason I keep playing.)

review_text:
This is definitely one of the best games ever made. Layered on top of a complex, but not quite convoluted, plot is quite a bit lore, backstory, political intrigue, and thoughtful philosophical discussions that are not only the hallmark of every Metal Gear Solid game but ones that stand head and shoulders above the other entries in this series.

The action is amazing. The staged setpieces make for great interactive cinema. The weapon customization system is complex and rewarding. The system of rewarding good, solid playing and appropriate playstyles is fair and balanced. Level design is great. Every aspect of the user interface is perfect, although the PC version suffers slightly from its difficulty in specifying a specific direction of movement that is inaccessible *unless you're using a gamepad on the pc*. The only other thing I could think of to complain about is that the interior spaces on Mother Base are inaccessible and thus unexplorable. It would have been great to see where Snake sleeps or does business, or even get to see Ocelor's or Miller's quarters, maybe a security room showing different parts of the base via surveillance cameras. These are features that don't detract from the game much, but would have been a nice inclusion. For all of the care that went into all of the level design of this game it mystifies me that not making the interior parts of mother base more explorable was a feature that should have made it in. Think of the space station in Doom Eternal, where you have everything stored in a specific place. All of your trophies and soundtracks. Granted, the airborne command center (ACC, the helicopter) fulfills this role in part, but it's just a tiny, cramped office in the sky. It's not the literal castle of the aforementioned game.

That's it. Two minor complaints, things that could have and should have been, but alas are not. If you find these complains to be insignificant, it's because they are, because literally everything else about this game is perfect. It even RUNS well, online or offline.

This is the perfect game, and like every proper game in a subsequent series it outdoes its predecessors every step of the way. It's no wonder this game earned Game of the Year, and it continues to draw in players even seven years after its release.

My score: 99 out of 100.

review_text:
This was the first Metal Gear game I played when it became free with Xbox Live a few years ago. While I had heard of and even saw gameplay footage of various games in the series beforehand, I never bothered to try and play any of them due to their lack of availability on modern gaming storefronts and my own laziness in regards to other means. Despite not having any prior firsthand experience with the franchise, Metal Gear Solid V turned out to be one of the best stealth and open-world games I've played.

Metal Gear Solid V is not a finished game in terms of its story, with the game abruptly ending in the middle of Chapter 2 with a replay of the prologue that includes previously left out details to try and stitch the story together somewhat. But the majority of main story missions in the game are fun and can be tackled in a multitude of ways. Some missions also have more challenging versions denoted by prefixes such as Total Stealth where being spotted once causes the mission to restart, and Extreme which ups the enemies' intelligence and damage. The side ops are more dubious however, acting as copy-pasted objectives scattered across the map like in many other open-world games. These are usually only worth doing if they are on the way to a more important activity or if you are after that illustrious 100% completion rating. The missions are split across 2 main zones, Afghanistan and the Angola-Zaire border region. The maps are about equal in size and are highly populated with the aforementioned activities and enemy outposts.

Throughout the game you gain upgrades, equipment, and support via Mother Base, which you are always improving through means such as kidnapping high ranking enemy soldiers, stealing vehicles, and purchasing new platforms for your various departments to fit more staff. This of course then cycles back to you getting more upgrades and equipment to use, back to improving Mother Base, so on and so forth. But this process occurs naturally over the course of gameplay and does not feel obtuse or unintuitive. A more infrequent addition you gain are your various partners or "buddies". There are 4 in total, a horse that acts as a vehicle you can call at any time and even hide on, a dog that marks enemies and points of interest, and can stun or kill enemies, a sniper that can mark and dispatch enemies automatically or at your command, and a miniature mech that can be equipped with multiple loadouts to serve various purposes.

While the game suffers minorly from fundamental flaws of modern open-world game design and is unfinished storywise, the content it does have is expansive and engaging and is worth a playthrough even today. Even if you aren't familiar with the Metal Gear franchise, this game works well as an entry point into the series and is just a good game overall.

Открытый экшон и стрельба, ну по правде говоря такое себе, да что там говорить, лучше уж фаркрай наверное насиловать или брейкпоинт. 

Стелс, он тут прекрасен, творческий и может быть очень смешной если пожелаете, ну или наоборот очень серьезный, смотреть как  раскручивается джип подскользнувшись на лошадиных какахах, это конечно что то, причем заметьте, задолго до ваших этих рдров. Погодные условия, маскировка, уровень освещения и шума будут влиять на противника и на ваше обнаружение им. 

Сложная экосистема выстроена вокруг этого. Переговоры противников между собой, например если нейтрализовать противника во время переговоров, то, другая сторона что-то заподозрить и отправит юниты для проверки. 
Будете убивать постовых или патрульных из снайперки, им отправят каски и бронежилеты, уничтожите запасы этих средств защиты, и они опять будут в обычной одежде. Отстрелите ногу или руку, у вас будет возможность наблюдать целый квест с переговорами по рации, и как его сослуживцы будут пытаться окозать ему помощь и обнаружить угрозу. Можно взять в заложники, и понаблюдать как например сослуживец, будет пытаться крутить вокруг вас хороводы, что бы занять более выгодное положение для стрельбы. 

Как-то ночью начал скрытно обстреливать минометную позицию, так я офигел когда минометчики вместо обстрела обычными боеприпасами запустили !осветительные, что бы выявить мою позицию, а другие подразделения начали обстреливать уже со своих позиций. В этом плане это игра до сих пор в золотом пантеоне из когда-либо созданных игр. Что нельзя сказать про открытый мир, он тут малость мертвенький и довольно безжизненный, хотя можно если захотеть упороться собирательством и отстрелом из дротиков редких видов. 

P.S. Имеет смысл пройти Ground Zero и там собрать все нашивки, тогда в основной игре откроется целый список очень полезных доп. заданий, которые будут полезны на начальном этапе прохождения.

Don't let the countless narratives of people telling you the game is unfinished and how the story is supposed to be bad stop you from buying this game. In my personal opinion as a prequel of sorts, this game fulfills what it set out to achieve in every aspect. 

The single player experience is absolutely phenomenal. The game play and the story telling is amazing. I've put over 200 hours in on Playstation before I played on Steam and I can say it's replayablity is insanely high. I can't say much for the PvP multiplayer as I've really only put time into single player and invading FOB's (semi multiplayer but not really due to the amount of abandoned bases). However for a single player experience, whether you're looking for a casual easy play through or looking to really challenge yourself there's something there for everyone.

If you're looking to do a completionist run of this game, I'd say that's where most of the cons come in. A lot of the extra mission objectives can be down right tedious and sometimes require quite a few retries even with knowledge and experience. Unlocking all the weapons takes a lot of time but, there's so much to and see that it doesn't impede on the experience too much.

Highly recommend getting on sale as it goes on sale very often, you're able to get ALL the content for an extremely low price. Out of the entire MGS series this one is undoubtedly my favorite.

review_text:
As the latest entry in Hideo Kojima’s iconic series, the game delivers a vast, immersive, and challenging experience that has captured the attention of fans and critics alike.

Highlights

One of the most remarkable aspects of “The Phantom Pain” is the freedom given to the player in approaching missions. Whether you choose to infiltrate silently, employ aggressive tactics, or explore the environment, the game allows you to choose how you want to play. The open map of Afghanistan and Africa is vast and varied, offering a wealth of opportunities for experimentation. This free-form approach to gameplay is supported by excellent control mechanics that blend stealth with action in a fluid manner.

The graphics and art design are outstanding, bringing an impressive level of detail to every aspect of the game, from the natural landscapes to the character models. The ambient sound is also excellent, with a soundtrack that complements the atmosphere of the game and background sounds that contribute to the immersion.

The game's narrative, although fragmented, offers deep and complex themes, addressing topics such as war, trauma, and identity. The characters are well-developed, and the interactions between them add depth to the story. The game also includes numerous cinematic sequences that are made with remarkable cinematic quality.

Another strong point is the progression system, which allows players to develop their base of operations, recruit soldiers, and upgrade equipment. This aspect adds a layer of strategy to the gameplay, providing a sense of achievement throughout the game.

Weaknesses

However, "The Phantom Pain" is not without its critics. One of the most common complaints is that the narrative, while complex, is often confusing and difficult to follow. Missions are presented episodically, and certain key story elements are hidden in side missions or collectibles, which can lead to a frustrating experience for players who want to understand the main story.

Some missions can also seem repetitive and feel too similar, which can lead to a feeling of monotony throughout the game. This is exacerbated by some design decisions that limit the variety of objectives. Even though the game encourages exploration, certain aspects of the missions can become predictable, which can diminish the overall experience.

Another criticism is the lack of finality to the story. "The Phantom Pain" was released at a time when Kojima Productions was under pressure from the publisher, which led to a conclusion that feels abrupt and unfinished. This lack of closure left many fans disappointed, as there were high expectations for a story that would conclude the Metal Gear saga.

Although the game has imperfections, such as confusing narrative and repetitive missions, it remains a brilliant example of Hideo Kojima's ability to create a complex and immersive universe.

review_text:
As a long standing Metal Gear (Solid) fan, MGSV by far feels like the most "polished" experience to me, mechanically speaking. Sure, the story may be lacking, and it certainly does feel rushed or unfinished in a few places, but the -potential- that this game represents sometimes carries it over the border from "good" to "excellent". 

Everything just feels satisfying and as though it "just works". Similarly, the graphics and smoothness of the experience put it above predecessors in the series, even if many of them had better stories. While I'm not certain I would go so far as to call it my "favourite" Metal Gear game, it certainly makes the decision of choosing a favourite all the more difficult.

Unlike previous games in the Metal Gear franchise, the semi- Open World nature of MGSV gives a far greater feeling of freedom. And while the side missions can feel repetitive, the cumulative experience of the main missions, side content, base management, and distributed lore bring the whole thing together, to such an extent that it made me all the more enthusiastic to seek out the achievements.

This is one of those games where I have to hold back from reinstalling it, because I know I'll play those 295 hours all over again, just to see the full content once more. And if a game can make me nostalgic for it even the moment I've just put down the controller? Well, then it certainly deserves a thumbs up in my book.

review_text:
It feels like every game nowadays has to be "open world". Pokemon, Sonic, Mario, all of these are linear games that are bringing in big 3D environments for the player to explore. Pokemon made an empty and bland world with Legends: Arceus. Sonic is looking to do the same with Sonic Frontiers. And Mario is the only one of these that actually made a world worth exploring in the Bowsers Fury side game they released last year. But the problem is that all 3 of these beloved and renowned series all made worlds that felt artificial, that had no reason to exist other than "it's a video game". That's not to say Pokemon or Mario were bad, or that Sonic is destined to fail, but why open world? Why spend so much time and effort to fix a formula that isn't broken?  Or at the very least, why go open world and leave so little options for the player to solve their problems? Bowsers Fury was the epitome of this, so many shines but they all need to be collected by solving a linear puzzle. And that's not bad, but it makes the open world just a means to reach a new location, a level, a new puzzle.

Why bring this up? Because Metal Gear is a series that has not been open world before this. And I would've argued there's no reason to become open world, because you would just walk or drive to wherever you need to go, do the thing they want you to do, rinse and repeat and you're done. Here's a side base you can infiltrate. Here's some robot you blow up. Same stuff over and over again. But something magical happened with this game.

This game is the first to get it right. Very few games have actually embraced what it means to have an "open world", I would say it is not just being able to explore a world without boundaries, but being able to approach a problem with your own solution. Having the options to overcome an objective, and being offered the creative tools to do so. The only noteable games to do this right, in my opinion, are Zelda BOTW and Elden Ring. But in most aspects, this game is even more than those games.

Long winded speech just to say MGSV allows you to tackle the problems it throws at you in ANY way you want. There is order in the way you get the quests and the order you complete them. The story does not deviate from choices you make. But how you tackle an enemy base is so open ended that just running around and capturing forts could be the entire game with no objective and it would still be a masterpiece. You can do literally anything. The depth is so immense, I cannot cover it in this review. Want to play it classic Snake style with a cardboard box? Sure! Interrogate the guards so you can tell where the others may leave any openings. Or, point the gun right at his head and he'll beg for his life. Set up a decoy in front of a guard, and draw all the attention to one side of the base. Hell, you can even airdrop a gun from the sky onto a guard, knocking him out in the process. I can't go over everything you can do in this game because it is endless. And that is the true open world style. The world is a canvas for you to experiment on.

The world is truly open ended. It's not jam packed with collectibles in every square inch of the map, it feels like it's a real part of the middle east, or Africa. There are trucks with gear that transport to other locations, you can interrupt them for loot or hitch a ride to the center of a base. This is no BOTW, where you explore and find a very diverse world with locations and structures worth seeing around every corner. It is a world you take as your own, a freedom not given to you by any other game.

review_text:
[b]MGSV: TPP[/b] is an absolute juggernaut of a video game. Sadly it is the final Metal Gear Solid as of now, but what an end. Some people dislike the implications of the story and there are a few stupid things that don't make any sense, but overall this game epitomizes the cinematic experience that Kojima sought to create. You do need to know MGS lore to understand the plot, that was my mistake the first time I played. However, it didn't stop me from enjoying the gameplay back then, and now I can appreciate the whole thing these days. I'll leave the analysis to better people than myself, check out Futurasound Productions on YouTube for some truly deep philosophical insight into MGS and KojiPro.

The gameplay of MGSV is the cream of the crop, the bee's knees of third person stealth action. It's amazing just how tight the controls are; your character reacts immediately to your inputs and it just feels so damned good. The shooting is super solid, nothing special I suppose, point and shoot and gun goes bang. Long gun, short gun, silent gun, sleepy gun, missile gun, lots of options and they're all customizable but [b]spoiler alert[/b] you will be using nonlethal 95% of the time to capture literally everyone and everything. 

Oh yeah, forget what you think you know about "tactical stealth espionage" because this game is actually "strategic tranquilizer ballooning." The metagame here is to build up your own personal Mother Base by capturing soliders and equipment throughout your missions and travels. The missions themselves are replayable and rather simple but with many objectives and an arcade-style scoring system, adding a whole extra layer of depth. There are also side-ops to do, also replayable. Now, there is a main story here to follow and I think it's one of the greatest, but its disjointed as hell and hard to piece together. You finish the story about halfway through the completion of the game but its not the end, honestly its the beginning of what I would call MGSV's endgame: FOB missions and nuke disarming. 

A big draw to this game for me is the asynchronous multiplayer component. As you are building your own personal Mother Base throughout your playthrough, so is everyone else who's played the game. Everyone's PF is then rated against each other for offense and defense, but the coolest thing is the ability to invade others. Then you can "capture staff from them" as Ocelot says, but be careful....if you are caught then the other player can join the defense and then its you alone vs a hornet's nest of guards and the enemy player. Its quite harrowing to be on either side of the battle, very exhilarating. Let me give you a hint, grenade launcher sleep rounds are OP. 

There is soooo much to MGSV, its got so many little tricks and nuances and special little moments and such. I really just wanted to get my opinion down on the the gameplay, its one of the best titles I've ever played in my life. I am a huge MGS fan so I just love the entire plot but I'll admit, if you aren't a fan of the previous games then you will not understand the events of this game. However, the gameplay itself is so [b]SOLID[/b] that I can't say only [b]METAL GEAR[/b] fans will like it. The [b]PHANTOM PAIN[/b] can fill a hole in everyone's heart. [b]V[/b] for Victory AND Peace!

Having played Splinter Cell: Blacklist in the past and enjoying the stealth genre, I thought I'd pick up a similar, well-known game of its genre; Metal Gear Solid V, my first step into the Metal Gear franchise.

I was instantly hooked by the fluid gameplay and mechanics, in a unique setting blending realism and supernatural elements. It gives off this serious yet playful vibe that really resonates with me; the story has its somber tones, but sprinkles in some moments of humour and joy in just the right places. The soundtrack is also fantastic, smoothly transitioning between different phases of gameplay and story missions in a way that immerses you in the scenes.

Great gameplay, story, and music is the basis of any good game. However, MGSV is not without its flaws. 

While the helicopter infiltration/exfiltration flow was cool the first few times, by the end of the game it quickly becomes very tedious, especially when trying to complete several side-ops in the same area; you cannot use the helicopter for intra-area travel.

In addition, one of the more controversial topics in the game is the character Quiet; I personally found her character to be well-written, but it is unfortunately offset by her outlandishly revealing design.

Rules and Guidelines For Steam: Discussions, Reviews, and User Generated Content
These guidelines apply to all places in the Steam Store and Community where users can post content. This includes, but is not limited to, discussions, comments, guides, product reviews, screenshots, artwork, videos, tags, and Steam Workshop.

When providing feedback, posting information, or discussing a product in Steam, whether it’s negative or positive, please make sure you are being relevant, constructive and polite. Developers take feedback from all kinds of sources into account, even though they may not have the time to respond to every post or question.

Please note that Administrators/Moderators reserve the right to change/edit/delete/move/merge any content at any time if they feel it is inappropriate, abusive, or incorrectly categorized.

All users are subject to the Steam Subscriber Agreement and Steam Online Conduct.

General Rules
Do not do any of the following:

    Flame or insult other members
    Bypass any filters
    Abuse or encourage abuse of the Post Reporting System
    Post personally identifiable information (i.e. name, address, email, phone number, etc.)
    Bump threads
    Derail a thread's topic
    Post links to phishing sites
    Post spam (i.e. +1, 10char, rickrolls) or Re-post Closed, Modified, Deleted Content
    Repetitively post in the incorrect forum (example: trade requests belong in trading forum)
    Openly argue with a moderator
    Manipulation of the User Review system or voting/rating systems

Content Rules
Do not post any content on Steam containing the following:

    Porn, inappropriate or offensive content, warez or leaked content or anything else not safe for work
    Discussion of piracy including, but not limited to:
        Cracks
        Key generators
        Console emulators
    Cheating, hacking, game exploits
    Threats of violence or harassment, even as a joke
    Posted copyright material such as magazine scans
    Soliciting, begging, auctioning, raffling, selling, advertising, referrals
    Racism, discrimination
    Abusive language, including swearing
    Drugs and alcohol
    Religious, political, and other "prone to huge arguments" threads

No Backseat Moderating
Let the moderators do the moderating. Backseat moderating is when people who are not moderators try to enforce the forum rules. If you see a person breaking the rules, take advantage of the Report () button or simply ignore
the offensive post(s), thread, or review.

Report Posts to Moderators
Should you observe a fellow Community member breaking these rules please report the post or item by clicking the Report () button located on every item, post, and review.

Repeated Offenders
Repeated offenders of the above rules and guidelines will be banned from the Steam Community. Any moderator has the ability to ban a user for violating the rules at their discretion.

review_text:
MGSV: Amazing gameplay, but a subpar story that is all over the place. Let's get a bit into it.

The gameplay. It is absolutely phenomenal. The game plays so well - its engine is optimized perfectly and I stay at 60 FPS. The actual gameplay is fantastic - there are many nonlethal and lethal tools at your disposal to dispatch enemies, and even the more useless items(like the water gun) still has a use; for example, the water gun can disable comms equipment and radars without you needing to waste a shot of your primary weapons or wearing down suppressor durability because of it. The game also has a relatively diverse array of attire for all environments - desert camo, woodlands, and such.

The story is messy and filled with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of filler missions that make the game feel longer than what it actually is, and the story itself does not have a satisfying conclusion... at all. No spoiling because I don't do that, but... it's disappointing.

The game isn't bad. It may not be like other previous MGS titles in story, but its amazing gameplay really carries this game. It also has a small, but dedicated modding community which is worth looking into.

If I had to give it a rating... 7.5/10 or 8/10. It's also 20 bucks which... isn't actually bad of a price. Sales are coming soon though so wait for that.

review_text:
I've been a fan of the Metal Gear Solid since the first game came out on PlayStation 1 when I was a kid. So when Metal Gear Solid V was announced I was excited. I watched every titbit of information released during the game's development, and analysed every trailer on YouTube for minute details. But when the game finally came out I was skint, and couldn't put together a decent PC to play it on. Instead I had settle for the PlayStation 3 version, which I still had a blast with, albeit a low resolution, blurry one.

Now I have a decent PC I've been revisiting the game maxxed out at 1440p and stuffed to the gills with mods, and I can finally appreciate how great it is. The gameplay is some of the best in the series, and there are endless possibilities for tackling missions. You can bring an AI buddy or go in solo, go in guns blazing with air support in broad daylight or sneak in at nighttime, you can swap your tranquilliser gun for a water pistol, you can throw inflatable Snake decoys as distractions, or you can use your robotic stun arm to zap enemies. It's a sandbox to muck around and get creative in.

I played through one of the community side ops and it was like my own mini action movie. I stealthy made my way into a base under the cover of night with my trusty pet wolf, using my nightvision goggles and tranquilliser gun to pick off enemies and balloon them back to base. I ducked into buildings to avoid a helicopter making passes overhead with its searchlight. Finally I was able to reach my objective - planting C4 blocks on two tanks on an open airstrip. A safe distance away I pulled out my binoculars to watch the fireworks and flipped the switch... but only one tank blew up. Now the guards were on full alert, and the helicopter was scanning furiously for me. I made a mad dash for the surviving tank, dodging angry guards now hunting me. I plastered it with the last of my C4, dove behind a concrete roadblock and flipped the switch... but it survived again! At this point I'd been rumbled and guards were firing at me and converging on my position, and the helicopter was starting to circle my way. I fired back and hit a few guards, then sprinted into a nearby air hanger for cover. I called in air support to drop a missile strike on the remaining tank and to provide me with covering fire. The missile strike was spectacular and enormous, and wiped out the tank and most of the guards who were still looking for me. My helicopter started duelling with theirs, but I had no time to watch. I snuck my way out of the base, dodging more guards on high alert. Finally I got out into the open desert and called the helicopter to come pick me and my wolf up to return to base. Mission accomplished.

My essential mods to get the most out of this game are:

[list]
[*] [b]SnakeBite[/b]: Makes it a breeze to install mods.
[*] [b]Infinite Heaven and IHHook[/b]: Allows you to customise so many things it would be impossible to list them all.
[*] [b]I Can't Believe It's Not Reshade (High Contrast)[/b]: Improves the colouring of the game so it looks more like the E3 trailers.
[*] [b]Beyond Ultra[/b]: Increases the level of detail viewing distance.
[*] [b]Infinite Suppressors[/b]: If you want to muck about and have fun then this is a must.
[*] [b]OSP[/b]: Allows you to take no weapons into the field, for that classic MGS feel.
[*] [b]Side Ops Expansion Pack[/b]: Adds 50 new side op missions that are more challenging and varied than the game's default ones (see above).
[*] [b]The End[/b]: Unlock everything in the game. Handy if you don't want to unlock it all again if you've come from another platform.
[/list]

Never in my life have I felt more empty after completing a game.

Metal Gear has been a part of my life since I was 8 years old, when I first got MGS3, and since then I fell in love with the Metal Gear franchise and storyline.

Its characters, its design, its deep backstory and subtle connections to the rest of the series all work so well.

It was beautiful to see all the plot holes be filled in and the secrets revealed in this installment of the franchise, and it set my mind to rest... but now i have no more to look at, no more story to see, only to imagine what happens next... even if it never comes.

But this game is an amazing installment in the series, with its wonderful backtrack to Peace Walker's gameplay with new features and a plentiful amount of missions to endure that will test your problem solving as well as your tactical mind.

Wish we could see more from the Fox Engine in the Metal Gear franchise, bur it doesnt look like we will get anywhere past rising. 

Kojima, you have won my heart again with your storytelling.

Paced obtusely at seemingly random intervals, especially towards those last few story missions and a narrative almost completely severed of significance from its gameplay, Phantom Pain really wants to be treated like the epic closer of a decades long saga, but behaves like a toy, more eager for you play in its sandbox than appreciate what its actually saying. That, and MGS 4 was already that closer, so I'm just at a loss.

Phantom Pain is okay. I enjoyed it well enough, but nowhere near any previous entry. Still, if pure gameplay is more your speed, I'd give it shot. That, and the score is killer as per usual.

Storyline is gripping and brings you in immediately. Top tier cinematography sets the perfect mood, and the voice acting, camera work, and perfect musical score blend in harmoniously to release a masterpiece experience. Likely the most amazing camerawork and cinematics that I have seen in any game. The game is raw, dark, and intense. 

After the initial masterpiece, it turns into an open world game. Here, some of the clunky gameplay becomes an issue, but other interesting elements are added, as you work towards upgrading your base, etc. This concept of a "home" is something I like, and I am sure many others do as well. It gives a sense of ownership over the game and its progression. Cutscenes become less common, and main missions and side missions take over the main game.
30 hours in, and I am still enjoying it. Lots to upgrade and level up, and the progression allows stealth or heavy handed approached.
At around 40 hours, I begin to lose interest, and find it more difficult to continue with this game, likely due to a lack of cutscenes and story that made the first couple of hours exciting. Lots of grinding and clunky movements become apparent. Progression is moving slowly, and I am forcing myself to continue along, hoping that something sparks my attention again. 

Lots of playtime here. It kept my attention for the most part, but if you dont like it in the first 8 hours, give it up. Hours 20-40 will be more of the same. That being said, still a quality game here.

This game should not have been open-world, there is so much empty space you spend a significant portion of the game running through and it serves as a consistent frustration that takes away from the strengths this game does have.

Why should you make use of the in depth martial-arts system, numerous ways to distract guards and sneak around, or interrogate guards, when the game keeps giving you advantages so significant that these systems become irrelevant?

If you play the game in the most optimal way it becomes an extremely dull and repetitive third-person gun game, which is a real shame.

review_text:
Your mileage when it comes to MGSV:TPP is going to depend entirely on why you play these games. If literally all you care about is the game play itself then you will potentially enjoy this one as well. However, if you are one of the folk who enjoy these games primarily for the insane ramblings of Hideo Kojima and his wacky nonsensical writing then this will easily be the worst game in the entire series.

Gone are the days of a elaborate story line and lengthy cut scenes spliced in with old footage. You don't even really have codec conversations this time around either. Instead the game primarily consists of doing out to do missions which range from various activities but generally "go here and capture or kill this guy". On paper this isn't so bad, but when you have like 10 hours of that between anything remotely story-esq it does tend to get boring very quickly.

You will spend the majority of your time with this game attempting to find the point of it. The story beats are exceptionally few and far between. The side missions are often the same thing over and over again but in a slightly different location you would have already been during a previous mission. You get tacked on mobile-esq deployment quests where you can send out random literally who soldiers you capture during the game to get resources after 30+ minutes have passed. You can build a base to increase the rate in which you get stuff, also with timed mobile-esq waiting per each upgrade. It results in the game often feeling like it's going out of it's way to delay you actually playing it.

The worst offender in the game comes from a point late in the game where an event will require you to section soliders with a certain trait in quarantine. There doesn't seem to be a way to search specifically for this trait so you manually have to go through each individual soldier in your base looking for this trait to manually assign them one by one into quarantine. Now obviously this will vary somewhat on RNG, but in my case I ended up having to manually move over 300 soldiers. It was tedium in it's purest form.

Now, some of this is obviously stuff that Kojima wanted to do - but considering he got deep sixed midway through development, I'm going to assume Konami had more to do with what this game ended up being: unfinished, and boring.

As a MGS fan if you enjoy the gameplay aspect of these games you may want to consider trying it - but only if it's largely on sale. If you mostly play for the story? Avoid like the plague.

review_text:
7.8/10 , nearly perfect, amazing story if you bother following it and reading up in-game to really piece the missing info together. The only things that stop this from being a 10 are the lack of extra regions or content, most of the game is played in one major area, with another one being added after that isn't terrible but leaves you wanting a final third section that perhaps follows the Venom Snake story 
( no spoilers but if you know the story you know what kind of section I mean. ) 

The game only falls short in its scale, and while you have lots of things you can do, funny ways to handle situations, interesting missions to undertake and useful allies, you really leave the experience feeling like, 
" man, if only... " for multiple things. I think that generally sums up the experience, and if you have the DLC full version with all the extra equipment + Ground Zeroes, you really get more of a larger picture of Venom's story, but it doesn't continue to the ultimate level of what happens to Venom Snake and who Solid really is.

They call them " cliffhangers " and I agree, this game is one big revolving cliff hanger that makes you wonder where MGSVI is, you really end up invested in the story at a certain point ( if you enjoy the game and MGS as a series of course ) but you never fully get a satisfying conclusion to the plot. 
Without spoiling anything I can say the game DOES explain itself fairly well, you will understand everything in time, especially if you never knew the story behind Venom.

Love it and its always a joy to play, but wishing Kojima and Konami could come to a fair understanding and agreement about the IP and give us a true continuation or expansion, even if not MGSVI.

Highly recommended for fans of the story, and this game teaches you a lot about how confusing it is having so many different Snakes, haha.

review_text: Nine years ago, this was the most exciting game that had ever been released for me. Nine years ago I was disappointed with the story. Nine years ago I was mad that this game was unfinished, and missing crucial plot elements. However, it's been nine years. Metal Gear Solid V is still one of the best games I've ever played all these years later. The mechanics, unique ideas like raiding other players bases, the sheer variety of ways you can complete any mission, this is Hideo Kojima's game design at it's best. Metal Gear Solid V awards creative thinking and innovative gameplay like nothing else I've ever played. This game is and it's cultural impact can never be replicated, a must play for all fans of not only MGS but stealth games in general. Between my almost 400 hours on Steam and close to that on the PS3 version I had on release, MGSV has been one of the most satisfying and memorable gaming experiences of my life. A wonderful ending to the Metal Gear series, closing the loop on the prequel and "modern" series.

review_text:
I can't recommend MGSV strongly enough.  A game that spawned a million memes and years of fan discourse, a game about a Big Boss and all his little pets and friends.  Easily the best open-world game I've played in my life, with a story cut tragically short because of cutthroat corporate cruelty.  Even though it is clear that Director Hideo Kojima and his team's vision could not be completed in this game with the hostile environment, it is without a doubt still one of my favorite games, and well worth every hour sunk into it.  There are no shortcuts taken with the gameplay.  Missions are fun and maps are deviously designed to challenge you to think in 3D and use all the tools at your disposal.  

The gameplay is unmatched.  Free-form military fantasy and high-stealth infiltrations.  Just golden.  Countless unlocks that really change the way you play and feel great.  Tons of vehicles, outfits, upgrades, side quests, and ways to solve missions.

Really it is only the story which can be reviewed unfavorably.  The First Chapter is brilliant and enjoyable, but concludes quite suddenly.  The Second Chapter is...incomplete.  It's very clear that the story is incomplete.  Missions are replayed and maps are reused and scenes are out of order.  The scenes that do exist are largely incredibly good, and the "true ending" is actually quite satisfying in my opinion...but there is just a lot of structure missing to the story and the re-used missions in the Second Chapter do not do the story any favors.  

 Regardless of all story-related flaws, this game is going in my list of favorite games of all time.  I was a bit of a completionist with this game, doing a full S-rank mission goal and achieving it.  I am satisfied with all 187 hours I poured into this game and will probably add many more hours over the years to come, revisiting and playing around on Mother Base and beyond.

I get that the game is sandwiched between Peacewalker and MG1 but it feels like Kojima really dropped the ball. review_text:
This game is really fun, but quite different than any other metal gear game. Being open world the possible ways of approaching a task are huge, however the more you play it the more you may find yourself using the same tactics over and over.

My biggest complaint would be how many similar missions and areas there are. There are almost no interior sections to the game, interiors are typically a safe space where you know you're not going to run into any enemies. This makes the gameplay feel monotonous after a while.

I think this is a good game to come back to on a regular basis, play a few missions and then do something else. If you grind at it you may find yourself feeling exhausted by how repetetive it gets. For example 90% of the missions either involve assassinating someone or saving someone. You end up interrogating enemies to find your target and then go get them, over and over.

Also fulton extraction is both a blessing and a curse. It's a really great concept that changes the game quite a bit from past metal gear games, but you'll find yourself just knocking every guard out and extracting them which makes some missions way too easy as you never have to worry about hiding bodies or guards waking up. 

The buddy system is pretty awesome. d-dog is a great companion and Quiet is very useful.

Gunplay is really great feeling in this game. Hitting a headshot is incredibly satisfying and feels just right in terms of difficulty, not too easy and not too hard. However there are so many different weapons of each type, as a person who knows almost nothing about guns they all blend together. There are half a dozen different rifles that all seem the same and have extremely similar names which makes it hard to keep track of them.

This is the kind of game I would have probably put 1000 hours into if I was still 15 and had all the time in the world to obsess over games. However as an adult I still got a great number of hours out of it and I only made it to the second act before it started to feel fatiguing. There is a whole base building mechanic and online battles that I didn't even really touch, if you find yourself really liking this game you can pour a ridiculous number of hours into it.

The story is secondary to the gameplay, you can ignore it or pay attention but it's one of those weird Kojima ones that people will either love or hate. 
I recommend playing this game, there is a good chance you will enjoy it a lot.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
