review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is the sixth and final main game in the Metal Gear Solid saga, but it's the third game chronologically in the Metal Gear timeline, a franchise comprised of eight mainline games.

Set in 1984, you play as "Punished" Venom Snake, as he and his "Army Without A Nation" seek revenge for the destruction of Mother Base 9 years prior to the events of Phantom Pain (Ground Zeroes).

The Phantom Pain is perhaps the greatest stealth game ever made. Unlike other games in the franchise, Metal Gear Solid V is open-world, giving you a multitude of options of how you conduct missions. You can infiltrate bases of operations any way you want to honestly. If you want to find a good vantage point to map out the area and get an idea of the soldiers in bases/outposts, you can do that. If you prefer to go in guns blazing, you can do that too. Everything you can think of is at the disposal of the player, and it really offers so many different ways to get creative. The enemy A.I. adapts with the player as well. Going for a lot of headshots throughout the game causes guards to wear helmets. Relying too much on smoke grenades, and guards will start wearing gas masks. Outpost shifts change as well, according to the time of day. You might see more guards at night, using strobe lights to search the area, whereas in the daytime, that wouldn't be needed. Sneaking into bases at night limits the visibility of guards, and shadows can be used as effective cover. The unlimited ways of performing stealth infiltration really is the selling point of Metal Gear Solid V.

The game takes place in Afghanistan and in parts of Africa during 1984. With being an open-world game, you would hope for cities or NPCs to react with, or a decent amount of side activities, but that's not the case here. The purpose of MGSV's open-world is to give players the freedom of how they want to go about missions. That's not to say the areas in which this game takes place don't look good, because they do, especially Africa. The rain forests are beautiful, but there isn't enough of them in the game. Some of Africa looks too similar to Afghanistan. Each setting provides weather patterns that can help you infiltrate bases easier. In Afghanistan, sandstorms will occur, severely reducing the field of vision for guards. In Africa, rain storms will mask the sound of Snake's footsteps, making it easier to move without being heard. While the setting of The Phantom Pain isn't bad, they can get bland and leave a lot to be desired.

Graphically, Metal Gear Solid V looks great. This really gets displayed out in the forests of Africa where there's a lot of vegetation and in the facial animations of the characters in the game. The Phantom Pain has some of the most cinematic cutscenes I've ever seen in a game, and the graphical detail makes them all that much better.

The gameplay itself is nearly flawless. The game rarely stutters, and I don't remember ever running into any bugs or glitches. It's extremely optimized and very smooth overall. The gameplay picks up where Peace Walker left off, and it improves on it in almost every way. Instead of the usual level system broken up by interjecting cutscenes, The Phantom Pain is much less linear, as it focuses on mission by mission gameplay. You can have your helicopter drop you in at a landing zone close to your mission objective, or you can use vehicles to travel through the open-world to get to where you need to go. Side-Ops are completely open as well, functioning similarly to Main Missions. The Mother Base building system is also brought back from Peace Walker, except this time you can actually visit Mother Base and all of the soldiers you have Fulton extracted in the field of operations. Expanding Mother Base and developing weapons is determined by GMP, the form of in-game currency that you accumulate by completing missions, acquiring materials, selling materials, achieving in-game tasks, and sending your soldiers on deployment missions. Development of weapons and Mother Base platforms also depends on the current level of your different teams of your army (Intel, R&D, Medical, Combat, Command, and Support). In almost every way, Peace Walker's development and Mother Base systems have been improved in a better way.

With all of the positives, there are a decent amount of negatives in regards to Metal Gear Solid V, and that focus is primarily in the writing and story as a whole. Traditionally, Metal Gear games will focus on the story of each game. You have a level, you progress through the level, and it triggers a cutscene (usually a lengthy cutscene). In Metal Gear Solid 1-4, the games ranged from 12-20 hours, so there was a lot of exposition dumps and story to tell. In The Phantom Pain, you're in an open-world. You're given free reign of what you want and how you want to accomplish missions. Rarely, will you see a Side-Op that has a cutscene attached to it. There's over one hundred Side-Ops in this game. The main story alone has 38 total story missions. Many of these don't relate to the main story at all, and if they do, it's vague to the plot most of the time. Take a game like Metal Gear Solid (1998). There's about three and a half hours of cutscenes in that game. That's a decent amount of time for a game that's only 10-12 hours long. Now take The Phantom Pain (at which I finished the main story after 67 hours), and that has about four hours of cutscenes. The story is there, but it's so spread out, that a lot of times you'll forget what's going on to begin with. Another thing to factor, in every Metal Gear game, including the first one from 1987, a lot of the game's story is told through Codec calls. Metal Gear Solid V completely scraps that for optional cassette tapes that you can listen to while playing the game. This is somewhat effective, but the organization of the tapes is a mess, and it really breaks the feeling that this a Metal Gear game at all. The story is about revenge, getting back what was taken away, but a lot of times Snake is ordered to do something trivial, like extract a skilled soldier. Cool. The boss fights that everyone has fallen love with in this series are almost completely absent. I believe there are six total boss fights. Six. In 70 plus hours, you have six boss fights in a Metal Gear Solid game. None of them are memorable, except for the last one, and it's a shame, because there could have been a lot of standout fights with the characters given to us in this game. Lastly, in regards to the story, it is there. Is it incomplete? Probably, yes. Is some of it unnecessary sometimes? Yes. Are there memorable moments in the main story? Absolutely, yes, and it's a shame, because what's presented in cutscenes really does look fantastic. After all of that though, there is a full story in this game (with one loose end that isn't tied up, thanks Konami), you just have to look for it more than you should have to. A true phantom pain.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom is a must-play for anyone who is a fan of the Metal Gear series, or for anyone who is remotely interested in stealth games. It stumbles a lot on itself in terms of story telling and the way the story is presented, often times not feeling like a true Metal Gear game at all. The story isn't terrible, it just feels like an investigation for information far too often, and it leaves you wanting more. However, the gameplay alone makes it a phenomenal game. Graphically impressive, and mechanically the best stealth game of all-time, Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain, is a great game.

review_text: The one word that comes to mind when describing MGS V's gameplay is freedom. Freedom to approach each and every mission how you see fit. Do you want to start off as a ghost, stealthily crawling in between patches of tall grass, but pull out a rocket launcher and every explosive under the sun when you get spotted? Fair, more power to you. Or maybe you want to go non-lethal, and tranquilize enemies, for fear of shedding unnecessary blood. That's your choice to make. MGS V gives you the tools to make your Venom Snake the kind of soldier you want him to be. The narrative is much the opposite. The story of MGS V is not one of freedom, but of prisoners. Soldiers imprisoned to their pasts, the deeds they've done and the deeds done to them. Its a tale of arms races and men becoming monsters in their quest to free themselves of their past. It is also a narrative that is imprisoned by the development process not being allowed to fully finish everything it wanted to, but even in spite of that, it remains a fulfilling story. MGS V is yet another hit by Kojima, and we can only hope that one day he and Konami will work together again for a return to the series.

As a big fan of the series, I can definitely say that MGSV:TPP truly is the ultimate Metal Gear experience. It is likely my second favorite in the series behind MGS1. If you haven’t played it yet, I highly recommend it.

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is an incomplete experience. It is fleshed out, enticing, and thrilling in some places while feeling lackluster and almost comatose in others. The final act of the story legitimately wasn't finished, leaving a gaping hole near the end. However, being incomplete doesn't make it bad. The story will feed you breadcrumbs to keep pulling you along to the next big payoff and it's about as free as a stealth sandbox can get, letting you approach any situation pretty much however you want. The game has a lot of secrets and a lot of shenanigans that it won't show you unless you experiment to figure them out.

A few more years down the line, I can confidently say that you should not buy this game through Steam. Buy a key of it, preferably through a grey market vendor if you're willing to, to make sure that not a single penny of your money benefits Konami in any way, shape, or form. Once you've had your fun with the game, mod the game and have more fun. Completely obliterate any and all sense of tonality or seriousness left in this Kojima experience. Some recommendations:

(You must have Snakebite to mod the game)
- Infinite Heaven, a mod menu that allows you to tweak pretty much any part of the game to meaningfully alter your experience. It is also compatible with multiplayer, as it toggles off during FOBs.
- The Man Who Sold The World reverts Venom Snake's appearance to something more similar to Ground Zeroes or Peace Walker, depending on your preferences.
- No More Timers, as a legitimate gripe of mine with this game is the strange, out-of-place development timers for equipment.
- Morbid's SIde-Op Expansion. This will give you a lot more to do while also letting you mess around more in the story; see, since a lot of unique skills can only be obtained by extracting people from story missions, it discourages most play-styles aside from non-lethal stealth, ghost, or non-lethal loud on your first run of that mission. However, Morbid's Side-Op Expansion adds many of these unique skills into side-op missions. This isn't a get-out-of-jail-free card, though, as these side-ops can be brutally difficult in the early game. They're mostly around to help you mop up anything you missed in the mid to late game. Regardless, they're very nice.
- Cuba's Quiet Redesign. While I eventually came around to Quiet's design, I also just don't really like the amount of gratuitous fanservice it brought to the game. If you're alright with that, then you can go without this one. If not, then this mod tosses aside a bit of lore to make her fit in more with everybody else on Mother Base (along with some pretty neat-looking alternative costumes that can be installed with or without the redesign).


TL;DR - good game, buy a key and enjoy

This game is difficult to review. On the one hand, it's a Metal Gear game. Story, stealth and gun mechanics, graphics, and sound are all top-notch. The only problem is that this isn't a stealth game. It isn't even a shooter.

It's a base management sim. Think Peace Walker but worse.

In order to do anything (and I mean *anything*) in this game, you need to do tedious base management. You need to always be online, always sending out squads for combat missions, always scavenging supplies, and periodically returning to Mother Base to raise morale and stay clean. Each deployment costs money depending on the gear you use, so the game actively punishes you for using better equipment. Mods are a necessity here; otherwise, you'll be constantly fighting against a litany of resource constraints, some of which are normally locked behind online play/PvP.

Let me put it this way: at the time of reviewing, I've spent 75 hours playing. Almost all of that has been grinding. I have gotten nowhere in the story, and my base is only halfway done. Without mods to basically cheat, I would have accomplished even less. That's right; this is a game that takes 100 hours just to get *started* with the story. Anything less will mean facing enemies with underpowered equipment.

Play this game. It's gorgeous in its mechanics, its story, and its overall design. Just please, for the love of gaming, play it with mods unless you think MGS should be Rollercoaster Tycoon.

Pro gamer move there Kojima.
The controls and stealth mechanics are mighty fine, very well done, and it takes a lot of patience for every mission. I gotta admit that after a while playing it, the game would tire me enough to just decide going in guns blazing. So, it's pretty well made as an open world stealth game, but it keeps contrasting itself with full blown action missions where you have to fight zombified unkillable soldiers or gigantic mecha warriors. All things considered, this is a very good game but it does have it's shortcomings and stupid cliches. There were times when it made me mad enough to go out and say that this is overrated as hell. review_text:
As "Big Boss", the leader of the private military force "Diamond Dogs", it is your job to rebuild the organization to its former greatness. You have to start small, and do this by performing a number of different missions in the field, ranging from assassination to gathering information.

You first do these missions in a large area of ​​Afghanistan, before later moving to Africa. Both lands are sparsely populated, and enemy forces have taken control of the areas.

We got to experience a lot of the updated and modern game mechanics already in last year's Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes , and they work at least as well in The Phantom Pain. The switch between running, sneaking and eeling on the stomach is responsive and intuitive, the animations are great and you have total control over the movements of "Big Boss" at all times.

Take, for example, one time I made a gross mistake, and was spotted by an enemy standing halfway around a corner of a house. When an enemy sees you, the reflex mode enters, which slows down the time so that you have time to react. The enemy was shielded so I could not shoot immediately. I threw myself on my stomach, turned around and put a perfect shot between his eyes before he had time to do anything. No other game in this series has given me the same feeling of total control over my game character as this one.

The shooting is well based on this sense of control, and for the first time, the battles in a Metal Gear game can withstand comparison with modern shooting games. In many cases, I would even say that it is better than many other games.

Patience is a virtue
Despite the fact that you have the opportunity to kill all the enemies you meet, this version of Metal Gear is also first and foremost a sneak peek. There are a number of systems that encourage the use of non-lethal solutions to neutralize enemies. One of these is that you can attach a balloon to the enemies, watch them fly up to the sky and then be picked up by a helicopter.

All soldiers can and should be recruited to your army, and you must therefore be careful with the number of lives you take, and rather save and send them back to the base instead. The soldiers get a job in one of several different departments at the base, and as you get the number increases, and you find skilled people, a department can go up in level.
When this happens you get access to new things. It can be anything from more information about the areas you move in, access to air strikes with combat helicopters or simply get the opportunity to develop new weapons and equipment you can take with you into the field.

Base building is an important part of the job of "Big Boss", and the developers have managed to give this part of the game relevance when you are out doing assignments. A little later in the game, the enemies adapt and get new equipment. They get better armor, helmets and night binoculars that can make your job difficult.

By sending a group of soldiers from your home base on a mission, you can sabotage inventory, disrupt deliveries and a host of other things. This can, among other things, prevent more helmets for the opponents, which creates a direct effect on how you play the game. Thus, the developers form close bonds between two parts of the game that can initially seem completely separate from each other.

The base building in the game takes a lot of time, but is essential for part of the progression in the game. It is never in the way, and you navigate easily to what you want to do with the help of a good menu system. Personally, I have spent far too much time hunting for the soldiers who have a good ranking in the world, as well as those who have unique abilities you need at home at the base. It's almost like a Pokémon game, where you only have to collect one more before taking the evening.

Friends in battle

Another thing you get access to a little later in the game is so-called "Buddies". These are helpers you can choose to take with you on assignments. In the beginning you have a horse, but you can later get both a dog two-legged robot called D-Walker. In addition to this, you can take with you the much talked about Quiet, the sniper lady who has appeared in screenshots and trailers for the game countless times.

Despite the distasteful figure design, Quiet is an exciting and interesting figure that is just the right Metal Gear screw. She is also an extremely useful friend to take on assignments, and has a number of useful qualities you take good advantage of, both if you choose sneaking or if you run in with grenade launchers and machine guns.

The assignments are divided into main assignments and side assignments. The main missions are the ones that mainly drive the story forward, while the side missions tell more about other things that are happening in the world. The story is presented in a more anonymous and not quite as dominant way as previous games in the series.

The amount of movie sequences is cut down considerably compared to the length of the game, and much of the story around is told via cassettes. You can put these on whenever you want, and are a good replacement for many of the long codec conversations from previous games.
I think the balance between story and game is at its very best in The Phantom Pain. It takes some time before it gets started, but the peaks in history are among the very best throughout the game series. It falls off a bit towards the end before it picks up again, and a couple of the missions you have to go through hold back the triggering movie clips unnecessarily much.

It may not be the very best story Kojima has told in isolation, but when you look at the game in the context of all the other games in the series, the story told in The Phantom Pain is very relevant. It tells a lot about how "Big Boss", one of the most famous characters from the series, develops into the character we know from previous games, and it does so in a very good way.

At the same time, it is not as easy-going and has far from as many humorous elements as the previous games. It is dark, heavy and tackles tough topics such as child soldiers and torture. It is a brave tale with a very satisfying ending.

Conclusion

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a fantastic game. It radically changes the formula one has become familiar with from the previous games in the series, and hits on almost all points.

The world you are in is full of choices. You can blow up, shoot and kill on foot if you wish. Or you can sneak in and out of enemy bases as a shadow no one notices, use sleeping gas and stun arrows and send enemies back to your home base.

The steering, both in terms of shooting and figure, is balanced and responsive. You have full control over everything you do at all times. The variety of weapons and equipment you can bring with you on missions is almost overwhelming. And with one of your friends, it no longer feels so lonely to do missions in Metal Gear.

This is a perfect farewell to a legendary game series. Thank you very much Hideo Kojima.

Metal Gear Solid 5 is a game where it truly feels as if you can approach any situation in any way you want. The game offers so many tools for so many interactions, from silenced semi-auto sniper rifles, to target-locking rocket launchers, to tanks and heavy machine guns; and that is just the conventional warfare. You can equip mechanical arms that allow you to electrocute all enemies around you or fire manually-controlled rockets. You can use a semi-auto grenade launcher that can carpet bomb entire areas in a single magazine. You can call in an attack helicopter or a literal airstrike to decimate enemy forces. On top of all of this, the stealth mechanics are some of the best out of any stealth game in existence. Simply diving behind cover and crawling out of enemy sight is so simple and smooth. Whether you want to go loud - blasting through enemies and destroying everything in your path - or go quietly - taking down enemies one by one without ever being noticed - or literally any variation in-between, the game will allow you to do that in the exact way you want.

Grab an enemy and use him as a meat shield to make enemies hesitate before you gun them down? Sure.
Steal an enemy car and drive into their base covered in C4 and blow them all up at once? Acceptable.
Attack an enemy stronghold with a machine gun loaded with rubber bullets and a rocket launcher that fires non-lethal stun rockets, allowing you to play loud and aggressive while simultaneously not killing a single enemy? Okay.

The systems in this game are so vast and dynamic, it's hard to talk about them in a single concise review. The game even contains a management simulator in the form of Mother Base, which rewards you with better equipment to use in gameplay. It is a constant feedback loop, where every action you make is always rewarding. The only major flaw is obviously the story - which is not only incomplete, but is also not as good as previous installments - but that doesn't change the fact that everything else in this game is so pristine, easily making it one of the best games of modern years.

Picture if Metal Gear Solid 3, and GTA got together and had a baby. It's two big maps which you go from place to place completing missions for yet another esoteric storyline (I'm not complaining, I love Kojima's way of telling a story) along the way you're gonna be constantly kidnapping soldiers off the battle field to stock your camp while you're doing so.

Gameplay is what you'd expect.  An action-stealth game, but this one being much more about action than stealth if you ask me.  Graphics are top notch for a game of it's time, and like usual, the fact Kojima made the in game movies use the game play graphics help to keep you immersed the entire time.

Audio is nice, there's a collection of music in the game (And ability to import your own MP3s into the game too) alongside some of the best voice acting I've heard from a game in a long time.  

Mod support is pretty good as Nexusmods has a collection of mods which can breathe some life into the game after you've put enough time into it, and find the game becoming stale.  For anyone playing this on an ultra wide monitor, you'll need a mod or hex editor to edit things to enable ultra wide screen resolutions, or any FOV changes.

Online for this game in 2021 is eh---There's a lot of hackers (90% of the people I encounter are hacking/scripting) and there isn't much Konami is going to do about it at this point in the games life so accept that for what it is.

If you think you might want to play this, I'd recommend it.  But I'd also say to wait until it's on sale.  I've seen it on sale multiple times for less than $10 USD and it you can get it at this price and you're a fan of the series I'd definitely recommend giving it a chance.  If you haven't played past entries in the series.  You may want to watch a recap video on Youtube prior to buying this because this series' plot can become very confusing at times.

review_text:
Is it a great game? Yes.
Is it overhyped by people? Most definitely.

Maps design:
In this game you only have Afghanistan and Africa, which both look similar with reused rocks, etc. That being said, it is a nice open world game, but at the end feels a bit lifeless. When doing side ops, you're basically playing free roam with challenges and with those mission, the map feels empty. You have a few outposts that are jokingly protected (a barracks has about 15 guards, but spans around 2500 square meters) and these outposts make it really easy to stealth everything (on the second map, africa, you have 2 outposts with cameras where their vision is piss poor).

Gameplay:
Pretty fun, a lot of variety to experiment with and interesting weapons (a water gun and a box to crawl in). This "experimentation" is ruined by the fact that there's a hidden karma system. This karma system grows out your "shard horn" the more evil things you do and permanently covers you in blood (yes, killing soldiers is bad), so to experiment with these weapons (there's a lot of them) you'll find yourself replaying "White mamba" mission where you save kids (they provide a decent good karma points). To be honest, having the horn out so much doesn't bother me and I like, but it's so jarring to see a completely bloody Snake every cutscene. It also ruins some great looking outfits. 3rd person shooting is kind of annoying with how inaccurate it is and when in "bullet time" switching to first person just becomes a hassle, i wish it was in the options somewhere (if i missed it my bad). 

Buddies:
All of them are unique and fun. I used all of them, but mostly DD and quiet. DD is nice when you're sneaking through an area and need to avoid enemies. Quiet is good all around, if you know what I mean. All joking aside, having a sniper under command is something I'd like to have in other open world shooter games.

Story:
I mean, the whole thing wraps up nicely, but leaves it on a cliff hanger (a bad guy steals something you wanted to prevent and you don't notice). Characters are a bit annoying with how they act, but I have to admit, this was my first MGS and will probably be the last. I know that big boss and others are supposed to be bad guys, but come on. How am I supposed to believe I'm fighting for the people and rescuing them, when every time I get back to Mother Base, I am either torturing or harming something. I go from saving kids, to torturing the same guy for about 3 times (last time the guy gets tortured he reveals some vital ending information, to excuse the torturing to the player, but he also contacted us for his rescue and to join our side, what?). With the karma system i am trying to be good and capture animals, use tranq bullets instead of normals on enemies, etc. just to come back to the mother base to harm my own soldiers. "Skulls" are presented as a force that everyone should be afraid of and that wiped out multiple platoons. They are the easiest things in game since they're just bullet sponges. Take a rocket launcher and shoot, then finish off with normal guns. If they come close, you can counter them with just one click, it's stupid (you're telling me I can use hand to hand combat on enemies that move as fast as superman, but i can't survive a bit of a bigger jump?). The sniper version are honestly easier, just lay down and snipe them, hell you can walk behind them even and shoot them up close.

The biggest problem I have with storytelling is with Miller. When you rescue Quiet, he aims multiple weapons at her and you, proceeds to complain about her being a "Skull" and monster. She is then permanently placed in a jail cell and only let out when you take her on a mission. Miller then openly accepts the "Code maker" that has signs of being a "Skull" and brings back the Sahelantropus that was controlled by someone even more powerful then the "Skulls". This Sahelantropus was "defeated" in the final mission of chapter 1 and his "creator" said he has no idea how they made it work, but sure, lets bring it back to our HQ.

Music:
Sublime.

Conclusion:
The separate points might be a bit negative. I think this is mostly because every time I heard of the game everyone praised it like it's a masterpiece. To be fair, it's opening was living up to the hype and that part of the game was the one that intrigued me the most, sadly the only part. If I went into this game blind, I probably wouldn't pick up such little things and would simply enjoy it. It's a 7/10 for me.

Disclaimer before anyone comments on the games I play and I have "no ground to stand on", yes I regularly play Destiny 2 and for honor (both games have multiple problems), but those games keep me intrigued and it's an interesting experience even through the grind. This game is the opposite where I find certain parts of the game annoying, but they're the core of the game. I had the same opinion with borderlands 3, a game with great gameplay, but annoying characters and story. I have yet to replay that game, because one of the core aspects of the game is annoying to me.

Upon release, I genuinely hated this game. I thought the story was the weakest out of the entire franchise, the switch to a nearly silent protagonist didn't work for me, and the "twist" was less of a twist and more of a "ok, now what?" (Nothing is the answer by the way)

Knowing all of this I revisited the game, mostly disregarding "Parasites, son!" story and focusing on the gameplay. And let me tell ya, the gameplay is probably the most well-rounded in the entire series. I do miss the more in depth CQC of MGS4, but outside of that the freedom this game presents to the player when it comes to gameplay is unmatched. 

It's a fun game. If you're a die hard MGS fan, I'd advise not focusing too heavily on the story. It's their, but that's about it. I miss cut scenes, I miss the characterization of Big Boss, and I miss being invested in the story. But gameplay wise it's the best MGS and because of that there's a lot of fun to be had.

review_text:
Metal gear solid 5 is the final entry of the critically aclaimed metal gear franchise. It's a game developed by industry god hideo kojima and his team of beautiful people with the purpose of being the "final link" to most of the franchises lore, with the incredibly dificult task of showing big boss' transformation from lovable hero to a extremely charismatic villain. This review will cover most aspects of the game and try to deliver my opinion on how sucessfully it accomplished it's task.

Now, on to the most important part of any game:

  --Gameplay--
 In the gameplay department this game knocks it out of the park, and in my opinion it is easily the peak of gameplay in the series, with only metal gear solid 3 coming close. Snake feels amazing to control, he's extremely responsive and feels just like the "best soldier alive" should. The game is littered with weapons and equipment to make your journey throughout it extremely entertaining. Each main mission has a multitude of ways to complete it, the guards are dynamic and will adjust to your gameplay style, forcing you to adjust aswell (ex: if you headshot alot they will start using helmets which block bullets, if you only play at night they will use NVG to see better etc.). The game (Like most japanese games) is full of secret mechanics and tricks that are never teached to you and are only up to you to discover, the guards are not allways the brightest but still great and the stealth mechanics are unrivaled. You've got more than enough content to satisfy you, an entire facility dedicated to make stupid ♥♥♥♥ for you to play with. It also has side ops, which are a bunch of little objectives spread throughout it's two open worlds which at best are extremely fun to complete, sometimes offer some much needed lore (paz's memories are a good example) and at worst are just a bit repetitive to complete. Each main op has a series of side objectives to do which force you to aproach the missions from whole diferent angles, resulting in one of the most replayable games i've ever played. Conclusion: The gameplay is the main focus here and it shows.

  --Story--
 Now this is a doozy. This game is known by fans to have by far the weakest story in the series. It is still entertaining, and the first act is pretty nice, but the second act is garbage. This is probably a good time to mention that this game is "incomplete", as there was content that was intending to launch with the game, but didn't due to time constraints. The story reflects that, with rushed plotlines and the whole second act as proof of this. It's sad though, since the first mission gives you both a completely wrong idea of the story quality in this and a really good story driven mission, with multiple subtle themes (ex: the first song you ear "The man who sold the world" originally by david bowie has themes that relate directly to the story (ENDING SPOILERS: [spoiler] it's about schizophrenic sensations bowie got because of his performances, and the song is normally assumed to be a song about a doppleganger [/spoiler].)) The main problem with the story was the promises it made, it was all about being the "final link" trying to wrap up a 20+ year old franchise of madness with notoriously difficult to follow lore. It promised to talk about men becoming demons, just to fall short on all these areas.

  --Characters--
 Dissapointing is the best word i can find for it. Snake is ok, but not NEARLY as charismatic as he's ever been, and this goes for everyone else. Metal gear is known for its perfect mixture of dark deep topics with ridiculous humour (ex: in peace walker, its revealed that the boss believes in santa.), and without the iconic codec call system, there's alot missing here in the likeable department. Most complain about the voice change for snake, but i personally don't agree with that, i think Sutherland was amazing for the role (still not as good as Hayter but thats some big shoes to fill) and snakes unlikeness falls completely on the script, not Kiefer. Ocelot is the strongest character here, and he is pretty watered down from mgs 3 (which is his best iteration imo). Miller was done dirty, and this game gives a completely wrong impression about his character, although the direction he was taken in is interesting, i miss the old Miller (and i think that was the whole point tbh). Quiet is cool, but is mostly there for fanservice, which is a shame.

  --Soundtrack--
 As with all MGS games, the soundtrack is very strong. Sins of the father (the woah ho song) is a complete jam and the game is packed with music tapes that you can collect and play freely that have some hits from way back when. It also features some extremely strong songs from the franchise that are bound to get your blood pumping. Overall, pretty good!

  --Conclusion--
 Metal gear solid V is pretty much the best stealth game released recently. It's gameplay and variety is unrivaled and even though most of the metal gear charm is missing, it still beats the snot out of most recent game releases. It shows alot of promise and is a very amazing game. I think if it didn't have the metal gear name it would be much more accepted, since a metal gear without story is something kind of ridiculous.

8.5/10 - Great, but its missing story and "meh" characters holds it back alot. Still please ffs try it out, its a great entry point into the franchise and its crazy amazing lore, and even if that doesn't interest you much its still a great stealth game.

review_text:
Summary:

   My personal favorite sandbox. Story is ♥♥♥♥. This is a ♥♥♥♥ metal gear game, but the best stealth game I've ever played. This game Vanilla is amazing, I've dumped hundreds of hours into it on various platforms, but it only reaches its peak in gameplay with mods. Infinite Heaven is the only one required, every other mod is optional. It is basically a command console that allows you to edit every facet of the metal gear experience. Thousands of different options. 

Gameplay:

   You are given two open world sandboxes to conquer. You will spend all of your time traversing the harsh desert of Afghanistan and the lush plains of Africa. During traversal you will fight a variety of foes, all of them are soldiers (with the exception of the Skulls, and the final boss). The unique aspect of this games difficulty is that it completely relies on your actions. It punishes repeated use of tactics, for instance if you consistently get head shots, the enemies wear helmets. You kill them with torso shots? Body armor. Use stronger rounds? Stronger armor. Every playstyle in MGSV will be counteracted by the AI, forcing the player to come up with new strategies to take the enemies out. 

Level Design:

    With few exceptions, there aren't really levels per say, but chunks of the open world turned into a highly scripted linear experience, meaning that for the most part, you aren;t having your hand held in these missions and you can take them on however you please.

Story:

   This story has a shoehorned villain, retcons, and just an overall feeling of emptiness. To be fair to the devs, Kojima was not allowed to work in unison with the dev team towards the end of the development. Konami had grown greedy, and in turn stopped having faith in Hideo's risky artworks. The whole story about the development of this game and the firing of Hideo Kojima is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and long so going into that would take a while. 
  In conclusion the story is just bad and takes a backseat in this sandbox masterpiece.

Rating:

9/10

Perfect gameplay that was robbed of a story.

This game is pretty fun, and pretty good. But it has absolutely nothing on older MGS titles IMHO. My memory of metal gear solid was an incredibly difficult stealth game, with a heavy emphasis on resource management. I cannot get over how forgiving and easy this is...

Enemy soldiers are completely blind.

BUT EVEN THEN if they see you you can just one shot them in the head with your silenced stun gun. The game also goes into super slow motion mode WITH auto-aim to help the most feeble of players.

BUT EVEN THEN if you miss every shot (some-how) and the enemy start lighting you up, you have an incredibly large health bar. You whip out your lethal machine gun, and just delete them. It's so easy, they die so quickly. We're talking tomb raider on the easiest, easiest difficulty.

Ahh but your weapons have limited ammo and the silencer has limited uses, right?

Yeah, and that would help balance things, except you can order an air drop that refills all your ammo and silencers to 100%. And you can order this air drop exactly where you're standing. 

Honestly, you might as well just open developer console and type refill_all_ammo

It's like playing with cheats. 

I found myself imposing my own limits. Can I take out this base without triggering slow-motion mode? Can I take out this base without using my stun gun? And you do get more points for this, and I think this is how the game's meant to be played. You create your own fun, create your own limitations and challenges.

This game is disappointing, overrated and pretentious like many Kojima games (cough Death Stranding), but that's not to say it's not fun. 6/10

This game is so disappointing. In my opinion. it is the worst in the MGS series (even worse than Twin Snakes) 
I am going to explain why is this a bad MGS game in my opinion
For TL;DR: Much less detailed than the other games, lots of flaws, decent game but bad MGS game
1. This game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ incomplete and 6 years later, nobody added a proper ending to it.
2. Most of the plot information is given through the tapes. (which was understandable in MGS:PW because it is a PSP game and you can listen to them while you are in the taxi or in an airplane) For me, Codec calls were very interesting to listen to in every MGS game, you could find out a lot of interesting details and additional information and the protagonist always had a reaction. But in this game, Snake almost does not have any lines and you are just listening to Ocelot, Miller and Code Talker. This is so frustrating, after 30 minutes of gameplay, you have to listen to 10-15 minutes of tapes to understand what even happens in this game. Yes, this can also be applied to MGS4 which has 12 hours of cutscenes, but at least they are sometimes entertaining to watch. 
3. It is an Open World game and both areas that they gave us just don’t feel alive. There is nothing happening outside of the missions, just outpost with guards. (btw this game can only render 12 guards on screen) So there is only one reason for the Open World to exist in this game, just to collect resources to develop new equipment or Mother Base.
4. Speaking about the Mother Base, does not feel alive. Yes, the cranes are moving there but they are not doing anything. They are just there to tell you that “There are things going on here dude”. There are some dialogues between the soldiers but there are so few of them. You can’t interact with the soldiers you recruited. Only base interactions like with enemies. You can’t train with them or something like that. If we had these interactions, if we could hear some of the soldiers’ stories, the infamous mission would’ve been more emotional. In the game, it feels like you are just killing soulless puppets (maybe it is different for you, but that’s how I felt) 
5. There is no diversity in this game. It is either extract a POW, eliminate(extract) someone or something, clear the outpost and clear the mines. And it gets repetative, there are more than 100 side ops and they are almost identical to each other. The only differences are, the location and the number of the targets.

These are the major points that I didn’t like, but there are so many minor details, for example: why didn’t Quiet just use a pen and notebook to write something so she would explain everything. Ocelot’s complete change of character compared to MGS1-MGS3 (Troy Baker is a great VA but he’s not playing Ocelot in this game and I understand that it’s mostly not his fault) and a lot more… (You can visit a Twitch channel OuterHeaven if you want to find out how much this game is less detailed that the others in the series)
In conclusion, I'd like to say that all MGS fans waited for this game for so long and the only thing we got is the phantom pain... literally.  This is a decent game, but it is not good enough to be a decent MGS game. If you want to have some MGS experience like back in the day, and you do not have your PS2 or PS3 to play the previous games, I can advise you to buy MGS2 on gog.com and simply download a fix. There will be a link in the comments on MGS2 gog page.

As someone who hasn't played the original metal gear solid games and only watched playthroughs, this was my first real entry to the series, and I am very happy it was. MGSV might not be the perfect metal gear game, but it's got solid stealth-action gameplay, dozens of different ways to handle each mission, and a damn good story, even with the cut content.

My primary complaint of this game is the absolutely horrendous checkpoint system, that is completely unpredictable and often puts players into a worse situation then they were beforehand, making deaths and mission fails even more frustrating than they already were. I suppose the reason for this system was to discourage players from always reloading after every little mistake, but I'm not sure this is the right solution for it.

Regardless, I completely recommend this game to fans of the series and new players alike.

review_text:
I'm really, really sad that I have to write this. I got MGS:TPP on the steam summer sale and was so excited to try a game series that i had heard nothing but good things about. I love stealth games and this series was one of, if not, the pioneer of the trend. 
However, by mission 6, i couldn't take it anymore. Where do i start?
For one, we have the fact that enemies who are knocked out (even with a tranquilizer), will wake up around 5-8 minutes after you put them to sleep. It doesn't always mean that the enemy will be alerted to your position, but it does mean that they might come back when you least expect it, or occasionally, radio help because you messed up the stealth takedown. Compare this to a game like hitman or dishonored, where if a body gets found, people will be alerted, but they won't be woken up. Not to mention that although Hitman penalises you for bodies found, they make up for it by having places to hide them.
Well reload an earlier save, right? Well no. You can't save manually in MMS:V. You can only save via checkpoints that the game gives out every so often. I understand that save scumming is a slight blight in stealth games, but the issue is that if someone wants to do an ultimate stealth playthrough (like i always want to do), the first slip up means they have to go back to a predetermined point. Not only is this annoying, but it discourages experimentation. I haven't used the lure/thrown magazine even once because i'm worried that it'll lead to the enemy finding me, and therefore just forcing me back to the checkpoint. I have never attempted to disable comms equipment, because i'm worried that i'll alert the enemy, then i'll have to restart the mission, or go back to a checkpoint/ 
Well, going back to a checkpoint isn't that bad, right? Well, you get a lower score if you do so. You can only get a perfect score if you go from the beginning of a mission, to the end, without reloading, or being seen, or using reflex, or anything. And that's something I think I could do. 
If it weren't for (again) the knocked out enemies getting revived, the surpressor on your pistol breaking, the occasional guard coming around the corner that there's no way you could predict and a miriad of other issues.
What finally broke me occured in the 6th mission. You have to get through around 3-4 checkpoints before you can even get to the mission location. Again, if you get seen, or you take down an enemy wrong, or use reflex at any of these checkpoints, you might as well restart because you're not going to get the highest score. 
'But it's not all about the highest score'. True, it isn't. People who go through with a lower score still can do impressive things. But i think i'm someone who strives for 'realistic' perfection in my stealth games. I get clean hands and ghost achievments in both dishonored games, and i get silent assassin in hitman in every mission. Personally, i don't think i can aim for anything higher then the top 90% score. 
And maybe that's where it stops being about the games flaws and it becomes about mine. Sure the game penalises you when you get seen or you have to use reflex, but i think most people don't mind if they don't get a near perfect score. But I do. And i think the mix of all the things above, plus a few others, combined with my high standards of what i consider to be 'personal achievement' in a stealth game, means that I just can't have fun with game. And it's a shame because i was so excited to try it out.
Obviously, if you like the game, kudos to you. This isn't meant to berate you. I just wish I could be better at the game and/or have a lower standard of personal achievement. 
I will likely pick up this game again, because i want to get better. But right now, i just feel annoyance.

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain

Hands down my favorite game. I feel if I skim on this review, I'll be doing the game an injustice. So this one will be lengthy.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
This game is a stealth game, but hey woah, wait!! - It's not forcing you to go stealth all the time. Instead, this game rewards you regardless of how you play. You can go loud or you can really take your time and play slow and stealthily or even fast and stealthy. You get rewarded regardless of your specific play style. Some missions require you to go loud and destroy vehicles and others are focused more on stealth. You get rewarded regardless of your playstyle with a matching animal codename which you receive at the end of each mission. Stealth yields the highest scores, however, once you learn the missions/maps and the entry points and develop the gear that helps accompany your play style, that just builds on the existing gameplay and feel of the game. Completing the side ops (there's 157 of them) yields not only benefits like soldiers for your home base, but also extra features like customization to your weapons, equipment loadouts and extra translations for different languages. All in the effort to make you go for better gear.

[h1]Story/Side Missions[/h1]
This story is amazing, however, you can feel the point in where Kojima and Konami had differences and Kojima was kicked. Around mission 46 onwards some of the missions were repeated but the difficulty is cranked all the way up to 11. Most of my difficulties when going for 100% were these missions. Total Stealth (being spotted is mission over), Extreme anything is massive damage received and some of the battles were rough. Once you complete a number of missions and you do go out to do them (you get a bunch of neat extra features) and all the while you upgrade your home base with soldiers extracted via missions or free roam. Fulton extraction, which is amazing in it's own right, is something that is hilarious if you extract a donkey, sheep or dazed soldiers. Their yells just make it hilarious to say the least as they are pulled up into the sky. The story in this game is amazing and has an insane amount of detail to it. True, it doesn't make sense in the beginning, but if you go through a bunch of missions and and you start realizing what's going on and the puzzle pieces start to fit together, it makes for a solid and gripping story which has a number of plot twists and heart-wrenching moments. From amazing highs to complete and utter surprises as rescuing Kojima himself from an enemy base, it really is something that I cannot stress enough.

[h1]Customization/Development[/h1]
Doing anything in this game, will eventually yield you resources and once you have enough resources, you'll be able to research new gear via the development option. This is, unfortunately but I feel intentional, real-time development time that you'll have to wait for your gear to be done developing and you can deploy with it into missions/side missions. The reason I feel it's intentional is because it then forces you to either go and look for new soldiers, try your hand at different approaches in missions or go for new skills or blueprints in certain areas of the map. This honestly makes for a very decent change of pace instead of rushing through equipment development in order to cheese the game. The higher the missions, the more you are nudged into developing more powerful weapons and gear to keep up with the increasing difficulty of the enemy forces.

[h1]Deployment Missions[/h1]
Once you have a number of soldiers under your command, you've got the option of sending them on deployment missions and they will then come back with either a bunch of goodies and a few injuries or they'll return with KIA's (Killed In Action) and/or a failed mission. These missions also have the option to disrupt the flow of weapons and gear for the enemies inside missions (it took me too long to figure this out and I think I rushed over a tutorial mentioning this). This includes: 
[list][*]directional mines - can catch you off-guard and alert nearby enemies if set off
[*]riot suits - massive pain if you play non-lethal
[*]gas masks - nullifies sleeping gas grenade effects
[*]shields - makes frontal assaults difficult
[*]armor - makes body shots with tranquilizers ineffective, arms or legs still work well
[*]helmets - prevents headshots with poor penetrative power weapons and tranquilizer rounds to the face
[*]flashlights - enemies have trouble spotting you when you play evening missions
[*]shotguns - gun goes *BOOM shuck BOOM* "Snake? Snake...? SNAKE?!"
[*]machineguns - this is emplacement weapons which I think also entails mortars, but I may be wrong
[*]decoys - inflatable enemies that really do, and I can't believe I'm saying this, surprise you and you whip out your weapon only to realize you got duped son! 
[*]surveillance cameras - they're more turrets equipped with a camera to spot you.[/list]

[h1]Hero/Devil Counter[/h1]
When recovering wildlife, which also happens to be an achievement on its own, you will receive GMP (Gross Military Product and the game's currency) and you will receive Heroic points. These points are in direct relation to the shrapnel in your head. Killing enemy soldiers, being spotted and being killed will net you demon points. Extracting child soldiers and wildlife will net you heroic points. Higher Hero points will make your "horn" in your head smaller, whilst demon points will make it longer. This spreads rumours of a "demon" killing and wiping out checkpoints. Speaking of checkpoints, that's also a way of increasing your heroic points and you also receive codenames.

[h1]Completion[/h1]
Going for 100% is a massive task. But that doesn't mean the journey isn't a memorable one. This game honestly had me in tears in a bunch of different missions. Brutality of war, the controversial matters of child soldiers in Africa and then of course, the meddling of country leaders in civil wars and gun trading. This game honestly had the biggest plot twists I've ever seen anything having a story in a game and I've only ever played MGS 3 Snake Eater on PlayStation 2 more than a couple of years ago. That was also an amazing game. The freedom this game gives you for doing whatever you want to do and how you do it really makes it amazing. The way to execute your missions the way you want to, it just does it so seamlessly. This game shouldn't deter you from trying it because it is focused on Stealth, rather you should really be trying this game because it does give you so much freedom. Give it a shot, you really won't regret it.

[h1]Graphix and attention to details[/h1]
This game's graphix is a solid 10 in my opinion, however, it doesn't support 144Hz. Bummer, but, it's so smooth that you won't feel the 60Hz and fps lock. The devil is in the details and I gotta say, there be a lot of devils here. Example of just what I mean: You have communication equipment that run on battery or some form of electricity (- Captain America) and you have a water pistol. Whatchugonnado? You gonna shoot that bad boy and watch the equipment fry like a chicken drumstick at KFC. What other game has this type of attention to details? You don't have a rocket launcher for a helicopter or tank? Crawl along the ground and make use of the terrain. Infiltrate at night. Wear appropriate clothing for the terrain and infiltration time. You don't have a decoy to stop a convoy? Have your buddy stand in the road and block the path. Enemies are transporting a prisoner you need to extract? Have your buddy D-Horse defecate on the road and make the vehicle spin out of control knocking everyone unconscious. The lists are endless and the game focuses a lot on these mechanics.

[h1]Final Comments[/h1]
Get this game. Don't think, just do it and once you have it - Play it. You won't regret it.

I consider MGSV my favorite game of all time. It's far from perfect, of course. I've probably played games that are more "flawless" for whatever that term is worth. On the other hand, I can count on just one hand the number of games I've played that hand me the keys to accomplish tasks however I see fit.

MGSV builds from a thousand different fundamental components -- simple on their own. Holding enemies up, different "down" conditions, hundreds of tools, commandable allies, etc. Then it plants these ideas in an open environment where enemies will respond consistently to your inputs, throwing a wrench in your best laid plans just often enough to keep things interesting, e.g. night vision if you keep infiltrating at night, helmets if you're going for a lot of tranq darts, etc.

Simply grabbing an enemy from behind can lead to numerous situations and outcomes. You can use them as a human shield, throw them out at their buddies, interrogate them, push them off a cliff... the list really goes on. All these simple parts combining into a whole totally unique to each player. Everyone will inhabit and interact with this world differently -- something really special that most games can't even dream of. It's not as simple as building a character in Skyrim; all that is scripted at the end of the day. i.e. intended by the devs. MGSV has a level of emergence allowing the player to use the tools at their disposal to make their own solutions. It's honestly beautiful.

This game is not for everyone. It's not even for a lot of MG fans. But it's definitely for someone, and if there's a small chance it could be you, don't let this one slip through your fingers.

review_text:
Yes, as you see I have a very small amount of playtime writing this review, but hear me out!

I have played MGSV to full completion on consoles and have decided to get it on steam as well. I have spent well over 300 hours on my rusty PS4 playing this which may not be a considerable amount for some, but it's still noteworthy that a singleplayer, story driven game can engage people for so long.

Firstly, this game's story is without a doubt my favorite out of the series and out of all the games I've played; however, it may not make total sense if this is your first journey in the Metal Gear universe. I suggest playing older titles or watching full playthroughs of them on youtube (they are great games for their era as well. definitely worth the time spent)

The gameplay is a big selling point for this game. Bringing the stealth mentality into an open world sandbox without causing something to break in the gameplay isn't an easy task; but the game manages to pull it off perfectly. Every infiltration requires careful observation, detailed planning and accurate execution since the AI is a force to be reckoned with in this game; hearing voices and noises, picking up small movement and reacting to unusual changes or behaviors in their comrades. It is worth mentioning that the game does not feature a difficulty selection, and offers a fluid difficulty system, whereby the world reacts and adapts itself to your actions in a meaningful way; which means that enemies don't magically become more accurate or harder to take down; but they rather employ specific tactics in reaction to your play style. This system is communicated clearly to the player and is so fun to deal with as you progress. The world never reacts the same way to player's tactics since there is so many! The freedom in this sandbox is near limitless; the sheer amount of ways you can carry out a mission, the wide variety of tools and exciting combinations you can discover is insane!

For a game from 2015, not only do the graphics hold up, they don't look dated at all! Sure, certain models or textures aren't on par with what we see in the industry today, but the photorealistic image processing in the Fox Engine utilized in the game never fails to deliver impressive and believable visuals. Graphics shine especially in cutscenes (which are rendered in real-time) where stunning camera-work and cinematography is the centerpiece; a common staple of Kojima games.

I was surprised with the stability of this game. I don't have a very powerful system; a 10 year old CPU paired with 14gb of DDR3 ram and a GT 1030. Yet I can still get a smooth, 60+ fps on 900p medium quality, with the game still looking impressive in all aspects. I should also mention that in my 300+ hours of playtime on PS4, and my experience with the PC version so far, I haven't encountered a single glitch once. The game is really well optimized with all things considered.

Now do I recommend getting this? Absolutely! Some of the best storytelling, cinematography and sandbox gameplay you can find is put together in this title, and I believe the opportunity to play this is something one cannot easily pass on. I'd especially recommend buying the Definitive Experience version, as it includes the MGSV: Ground Zeros and some exclusive cosmetics and missions as well. Bonus points if the game is on sale too!

review_text:
Memes about Quiet and Kojima's lame excuse for why she walks around practically naked aside, this is an utterly fantastic, flawed masterpiece.

Most of the flaw is in its story, which ironically is what Kojima is over-praised for in his games all the time, but I don't understand the complaints. Not because they're wrong, they're absolutely not, but the criticisms are things like "it doesn't really expand on the things we wanted it to" and I'm just sitting here thinking "none of the MGS games do that". Kojima doesn't care what fans want, he just wants to make another game how he wants it.

In fact, it's well-known he wanted to stop working on the Metal Gear franchise a long time ago, but it was his most popular creation and Konami simply wouldn't let him neglect it... and frankly, they were right not to, because even when he half-assed it, he somehow made [i]the best sandbox MGS experience I could imagine[/i]. Sure, it's not perfect, the plot goes nowhere fast, it retcons things and has pointless cameos from characters that frankly shouldn't be in this game at all, but it's just such a fun game. It's mission-based, so it's not a full sandbox experience, but I don't see that as a flaw, because it works pretty well and lets you get a more tailored experience while still having the feel of an open-world game.

There are tons of things to unlock, a very large checklist you can follow, you get several companions you can call in to help you out in missions with their own unique traits, and if you beat the post-game, you can use the multiplayer character you created at start-up as a bonus skin. Add in the fact that this game has decent modding capability (watch out for the thirst mods, they're everywhere and you don't want your parents to walk in while you're browsing the Nexus) and some online PvP elements you can interact with and you've got a long-lasting experience that I think shouldn't be overlooked.

...and yes, while the story has plenty to criticize, I didn't actually think it was bad. There are just a lot of great character moments that keep you engaged throughout. The game can be a bit divisive for some MGS fans, but as someone who has played just about every MGS game under the sun, it's probably... no, it IS my favorite MGS game. The gameplay elevates it above anything we've ever gotten before. I don't hate the old gameplay of the MGS games, but this is just on another level, and there's no debating that.

The popular narrative goes something like 'MGSV has great gameplay, but too bad they didn't let Kojima finish. Best gameplay and worst story of the franchise.' You'll see this repeated over and over like fans are afraid to have a unique opinion. IMO, both the gameplay and story are poor. 

TLDR; Boring and repetitive gameplay. The game feels devoid of purpose. Empty world. The story is lacking tonal variety, is poorly paced, full of bad decisions (I say that as someone who enjoys the weirdness of the franchise), and is clearly incomplete. 

Pros:
-Retains the awkward Metal Gear franchise dialog pacing, which sounds like a negative but I think is charming and campy.
-Looks pretty good, aside from the overuse and awful quality of blur.
-Some fun weirdness in the story.
-Aesthetic customization for playable characters, companions, bases, helos, etc. 
-You'll feel some attachment to Pequod, DD, and the other battle buddies.
-The online play is often neutral but sometimes fun. It's not a bad way to burn some time.
-Some mods can introduce a bit more excitement. Modding community is decent.

Cons:
-Takes itself way too seriously. Previous installments incorporated silly elements and 4th wall breaks. None of that charm is here. As a side effect I felt less dread during serious moments because the contrast wasn't there. The whole game feels flat in tone and personality. 
-The blur in this game is awful. It comes in hard at weird times and completely obscures what you are trying to view. It is constantly shifting. Sometimes it is soft, sometimes it is intense. It is also applied strangely - the blur seems to bleed into the edges of foreground objects. That's my one major gfx complaint. 
-The story is pretty incoherent, fails to give the enemy characters any significance, retcons everything, and feels incomplete. And this isn't just because the game is 'unfinished' - I would argue that many of the storyline decisions were poor from the beginning. Things like cramming characters into the story in clunky and stupid ways, the focus on trying to show the mundane side of Mother Base, and the complete lack of a civilian world. Cut scenes go from far too long and frequent at the beginning to almost entirely absent by the middle of the game. I won't dive into the story flaws too much because so many people already have.
-The fan service is cringe and overtly try-hard. Some folks can forgive the awkwardness of it because they enjoy that kind of thing, but it really makes all the game's failures feel worse.

THE WORST OFFENSE OF THIS GAME IS THAT IT IS BORING. The open world feels empty and devoid of purpose. There is no civilian aspect and no culture to the lands themselves. The world actually has little playable area beyond the roads and intermittent installations, so there is no point anyways; this world exists primarily for the purpose of traveling from one mission to the other. You will see the same installations/bases over and over. Your character has very little at stake in most of what you will be doing - they're typically just 'jobs.' You don't feel like you are accomplishing anything. The jobs themselves are incredibly repetitive. While progressing you spend most of your time traveling between missions, goofing around in the iDROID, and either extracting or killing targets in copy/paste missions (in that order). Outside of the story there are many, many tasks included in the moment to moment gameplay that are totally mundane and often pointless. This game has absolutely no respect for your time. 
 
Sure you have a large arsenal...but all the weapons within each category feel kind of samey. Even the mechanics here suck. Want to try to take absurdly long sniper shots? Nope, there is a 362m distance limit, beyond which your shots vanish and never make impact. ADS looks really awkward, but the recoil and sway mechanics are satisfying. You have a variety of vehicles...but they are all slow and you can't do much with them anyways. Most of the 'fun' people talk about is sliding around in cardboard boxes and hiding in dumpsters. It's like playing a premade Gary's Mod map solo and without any building tools. You goof around for a little bit and then you get bored.

review_text:
What a thrill... jk, I wish though.

This game was my introduction to the Metal Gear Solid series a couple of years ago when I bought it on console. What transpired after my first 100% completion of this game was a full immersion into the Metal Gear series as a whole. Being the "Ghost Recon" of the series really, MGS5 is a nice lil entry-point for newcomers to the series to come into. Everything "Metal Gear" is there from great cutscenes (they do feel short and few in this game compared to others however), "figure it out" based game design, and the stealth (as easy it is in this game to just Rambo through everything).

You are also constantly working on your Forward Operating Base: trying to swoop up hundreds of soldiers from the field, hunting for S-ranks, managing deployment missions, and doing events to get more staff. Basically one of those Facebook or MySpace micro-management games but built into your Motherbase so there's a sense of a greater goal with doing side-ops or wandering around in free-roam when off-mission. But if you dislike that kind of thing, it is a very primary part of the game that you have to get around in order to unlock missions or to get the equipment you need to finish missions easily.

If we look at the game itself without comparing it to other Metal Gear games, it is amazingly fun to me. Yes, the maps feel mostly empty with a set number of enemy camps and bases scattered along the main roads. There is not much in the way of those who love exploration; but, I felt as if this was a perfect setting for a realistic combat scenario out in the field. The movement itself is very slick between keyboard or controller, never really turning on a dime or being able to change your vector of direction quickly; so, there is a very real detriment to carelessly moving around and not paying attention to how you are moving yourself. The gunplay feels great from first person or the shoulder. They have a nice lil selection of guns, lacking somewhat in the explosives department. Stealth can be a little iffy at times if you're not playing on the hardest difficulties and you'll find yourself doing some stupid crazy stuff late-game if you're not challenging yourself. 

But this game is really a "find a way to do it and enjoy it yourself" type of game. It's preferred to be stealthy and they definitely design it that way; but, they also give you lots of tools, vehicles, and fun lil gadgets to go in there and blow everything up if you want. Or you could be a ghost of war, undetected and stealing soldiers everywhere you go to work for you. I'd definitely buy it, if not for being a metal gear game; but, just for being a pret good game.

If you dislike it because it's not "metal gear" enough for you, well... help me petition for a Snake Eater HD PC port then.

review_text:
[i]I have finished this game previously on the PS4. This analysis will consider my previous experience with the game, and some new opinions I've formed when playing it on PC and after gaining some maturity.[/i]

 As with most long-time fans of the franchise, my opinion on MGSV:TPP can be summed up as "It's a great game, just not a good Metal Gear game". For the most part, this holds true: While MGSV doesn't disrespect any of the previous lore established in the franchise, many design choices reinforce a radically different  style of gameplay that feels too far from the other games to make an old fan feel "at home". In earlier games, the moment-to-moment gameplay consisted of constantly being aware of one's surroundings, enemy patrol patterns, and approaching every scenario like a puzzle to be solved. While this still exists in TPP at some level, the open-world gameplay makes stealth feel much easier by allowing the player to attack from great distances with virtually no penalty, especially using the tranquilizer rifle with the silencer. So tough decision-making situations aren't as difficult, intense, or frequent. 

 This ease in gameplay is further compounded by the new inventory system, regenerating health, and virtually limitless resources - While the player isn't able to hold as many weapons, the ones they can hold are like swiss-army knives. The previously mentioned tranq rifle can do basically everything short of knocking out non-human opponents. Even when you're out of ammo, getting it back is as easy as ordering a supply box from the Mother Base - which can be done anywhere, anytime, for a negligible deduction in in-game currency (GMP). Since health regenerates now, damage is only something to worry about in the most extreme of situations - Like fighting gunships or bosses, which rarely happens.

 That is not to say that TPP never does, or can't feel like Metal Gear games of old. Playing the game without reflex mode (a new mechanic that slows down time once an enemy sees the player) and attempting no-detection runs does approximate the feeling of sneaking through rainforests in MGS3, and some missions in the game are particularly tough. But these moments are rare and it makes the rest of the game feel all the more alien once you're back to fultoning animals for an NGO.

 This dissonance with the rest of the franchise can be pinned down to those elements: The excessively open-ended gameplay, a severe reduction in difficulty, and a huge amount of side-missions that aren't particularly interesting.

 With that said, is TPP a bad game? By no means. The controls are tight, combat is smoother than ever, and graphics are still beautiful 6 years later. It is definitely an enjoyable game that I will finish again on PC. But I can't recommend it as a starting point if you're new to the franchise. Play in order of release instead, preferably beginning with MGS1 (the MSX games are great, but hard to come by on PC).

8-9 out of 10, buy on sale and go for the "Definitive Experience" pack. Contains GZ and all the DLC.

review_text: I've been a huge Metal Gear Solid fan and I've managed to play the entire series. This one is definitely the most ambitious and fun gameplay-wise. Whereas previous Metal Gear Solid titles felt a bit more cinematic and featured extensive cutscenes, this one places far more emphasis on the gameplay--which is a welcome change. The tools and choices given to the player on how to go about completing the missions and objectives are so incredibly vast the game never gets boring or repetitive. The open-world concept and much larger level design compared to its predecessors really open up a lot more possibilities on how to approach enemy strongholds. Metal Gear games have always revolved around stealth, and this game is certainly no exception. I'd say the game is the most fun and challenging to play utilizing both stealth and non-lethal takedowns. The game also actively rewards you for playing in this fashion as it is typically more beneficial to extract valuable soldiers for your base and you earn way more points for utilizing stealth and/or not killing anyone. That being said, this game also empowers the player with a vast arsenal of powerful lethal weapons and techniques for killing a whole base of soldiers if that's what you'd prefer doing. The game never tries to hold your hand every step of the way or make you feel stupid for your decisions. Often times there are multiple ways to accomplish goals, many of which are never explicitly told to you. The emphasis on player experimentation cannot be stressed enough and I think that's what sets this game apart. The game can be quite challenging at times, but part of the fun is replaying a mission using a different strategy that best suits the situation. Overall, this product is a master-class of game design and such a strong finish to an already outstanding series. I hope they bring the Metal Gear Solid HD Collection to Steam.
