review_text:
The Phantom Pain: Abundant gameplay, mediocre storytelling, boring open world

MGSV: The Phantom Pain is the only MGSV I ever played. Before I played Ground Zero, the demo of Phantom Pain, and Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance, an ACT title. Not having much knowledge of the previous story, I won't go deep into what was going on before and focus on the Phantom Pain itself.

Ground Zero is not a good narrator of the previous story, and The Phantom Pain does not require you to have a full understanding from previous. Viewed it as a fresh start, a man waked up in the hospital and recruited his crews, becoming a powerful mercenary and warlord taking his vengeance. Plus, with some persons he meets, his adventure is a little bumpy, yet not affecting the main story a lot.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

The Phantom Pain is a really fun game to play with abundant gameplay. As a third-person stealth game, you can choose to go stealth without a kill, do stealth kill, go into hardcore fight and massacre or even call airstrike to your enemy. You have lots of ways to play, along with huge weapon and gear choices, and very differentiated buddy you can bring. Depending on what weapons, gears and buddy you choose, what style you like, and what objective of your mission, you have lots of options on your missions, being the reason why I say this game has abundant gameplay. Other than that, it has a looter/farm game mechanism and a big upgrade system, both of which are very easy to master. If it is what you like, you can really lose yourself into it.

However, it has drawbacks. Side op missions are very much similar. They are not easy to get tired of, with abundant gameplay, but indeed they are repetitive. Worse still, this game has two chapters. But after Chapter 1, the dev clearly ran out of budget, causing a very imperfect and incomplete Chapter 2. Basically, missions of Chapter 2 just repeat missions in Chapter 1, with an upgraded hardcore difficulty. They are hard and most of them are far from being enjoyable, given the fact that this game is not really designed to go into hot battles (fight mechanism is not perfectly designed so it is not handy) which you are forced to get into quite often.

[h1]Storytelling[/h1]

Hideo Kojima is a talented director. He is indeed great at creating immersive scenes, making stunning visual effects, and showing intense emotions. Particularly, the Prologue is a work of genius in showing the intention in a meticulous and immersive way that I have never seen in any other games. He shows players lots of cool stuff as well. I guess it is every boy's dream in childhood to have his own secret base and here you have one.

That being said, Hideo Kojima is more of a Michael Bay type of director, who is good at visual but not good at the story. With all due respect, he is not a good storyteller and scores low in the script. The script has some interesting ideas, but it is a mess and the story is incomplete. A significant part of it shows unnecessary and unimportant details, which are useless for the story. There are some logical loopholes in the script as well. For example, [spoiler]why Snake doesn't kill Quiet when they first met, just because she is a girl?[/spoiler] It doesn't make sense as you don't see a very solid reason for it. Another example, [spoiler]why Paz is not dead? I remember she was killed by the bomb from her stomach in Ground Zero.[/spoiler]Anyway, the script is not perfect. As for storytelling, it is bad. For all the characters, there are no characters that are really impressive. You don't see emotions from the characters themselves, but from the scenes and plots created. Such as, [spoiler]in the quarantine area where Snake is forced to kill his comrades,[/spoiler] it is designed to show emotions not from the character but from the environment. It is executed very bad and the emotion seems fake. The only good and genius emotion expressing I have seen in the game is [spoiler]in the part where Quiet[/spoiler] Other than that, the part where [spoiler]Skull Face brags about his plan in a truck[/spoiler] is really bad. Why there is music in the middle? Make it as a CG is so much better.

[h1]Open World[/h1]

It is a boring open world. It is said that the best open-world game so far is the Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, which I did not play. I don't really know how to judge an open world, but as far as I can tell, this game is not a good one. The world is featureless and not impressive. There is no interesting place on the map and you have no desire to explore this static world where everything stops when you are not around. 

There are lots of outposts that block your way and restore when you leave, causing lots of unwanted and annoying crossfire. This design is very much the same as Far Cry 2, as the thing I hate most in Far Cry 2. Luckily unlike Far Cry 2, you can choose to take detour or stealth to avoid the fight. And there is another annoying thing like Far Cry 2 that I hate so much. There are lots of mountains you can't cross in the map, forcing you to take a much much longer way to take a detour. It is super annoying cause you can somehow get lost reaching dead ends and it causes you so much time.

This open-world is like a sandbox, with fortresses (levels) scattering in between. The level design is nice, each fortress has a unique design so that you don't simply repeat your strategy in getting into a different fortress, making the game much more interesting.

[h1]Other things[/h1]
Decent graphics with great optimization.
Beautiful music.
Invisible wall sucks.
Control in indoor activity is not very handy due to easily getting stick to walls or obstacles. Plus, the butt of Snake is very big (camera zooms in), blocking my sights.
Fast travel is needed.


Despite all the drawbacks I talk about, MGSV: The Phantom Pain is essentially a good game worth recommending. Otherwise, I won't play it for so long. Play it and see it for yourself.

review_text:
Full disclosure, I've never played a Metal Gear game prior to this one. So I have no idea as to how it compares or even relates, beyond a nigh-impenetrable block of lore that's equal parts compelling and retarded.
But the gameplay though, THE gameplay. It lies somewhere between poe-faced stark realism and absolute ridiculousness. To wit: I'm so used to dealing with AI that, despite having a light machine gun, will still fire at me in controlled bursts like a sensible person. So imagine my surprise when I was busted by this Russian Rambo fella and that commie bastard unloaded on my ass like a lead dispensary. I hear it's a regular thing for MGS AI to act in surprising ways, counter to other games, and it's on full display here.
And then on the other foot, you can not only hide in a cardboard box, but you can put a picture of some anime girl on it and these dumbasses will come up and ogle the box like a 14-year-old. You can tell your horse (you get a horse) to poop, and it does. And if a jeep drives over it, the jeep will lose control and spill off the road. It's fantastic. Also you can attach what is ostensibly a fulton extraction device to an unconcious soldier, a gun emplacement, a wild animal, a vehicle, a shipping crate, what have you; and watch it pause for a moment and rocket into the air. And if it's a person, with an accompanying and totally understandable shriek of terror. It's not yet ceased being funny.
There's a pretty complex base-building mechanic, which is what all this fultoning serves. It ties directly with what resources you can have and deploy in the field, and so it synergizes well with the primary gameplay loop of sneaking, killing or knocking out, stealing ♥♥♥♥, rinse and repeat.
The endgame is pretty elaborate too, though with the usual dumb Konami ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fare behind LONG waiting times that you can skip with microtransactions, on top of in-game resources that seem to exponentially increase in the endgame. You can also raid other players' bases and steal materiel and personnel, and I would've loved to see it in its heyday, because if the defending player is online, they absolutely can jump into said match to defend it. At that point it's super one-sided and terrifying, as you play a game of cat-and-also-cat with a human player, doing ♥♥♥♥ that decidedly isn't AI-like. On the one hand, you're about boned if it happens, but on the other hand, on the rare occasions that they showed up (and it IS rare nowadays), it was an absolutely terrifying and engaging affair.
Now, the story, from an outsider's perspective, is a complete mess. It doesn't help that it's all Kojima-y, who seems like he's VERY close to understanding what humans are. Like David Cage, if you splashed in a little bit of hallucinogen. It took hours of reading the MGS wiki to understand what in the hell they're on about, but y'know.
Anyway, to sum it all up: dumb story, superb and occasionally meme-worthy gameplay, meh endgame, practically nonexistent meta, get it.

This was my first entrance into the Metal Gear Franchise. I have been left confused, shocked, amazed, immersed and mindblown. 

The story is all over the dang place and I've been watching and re-watching videos on YouTube just to get a grip on this rather interesting timeline of events that I still found to be enjoyable. The gameplay is where it shines. The open landscapes, stealth mechanics, combat, weapons, heck even the base management is enjoyable. Being able to take on a mission however you want gives an awesome dynamic. Being able to extract enemy soldiers and equipment with a Fulton Extraction System (Yes it's real, read up on it. It's quite interesting) is always amusing and satisfying. Don't even try driving the tanks and IFV's though. I don't think Kojima will ever figure out good driving physics. :p

Let me start by saying that this game is both addicting, and agonizing.
Not only do I absolutely love Kojima's storytelling, but I marveled over the limitless feeling of the game. You can customize so much about your weapons and gear, much like previous installments, but you also build up a base for you and your on-hand army of mercenaries, forge bonds and functions with four different allies that you take into combat, and have access to an open world filled with opposing forces, animals to rescue, resources to collect, ruins and bases to explore, weather systems, and some interesting new threats.
As I originally stated, this game is agonizing though, but not for the usual reasons you'd find a game agonizing. This is, as far as I know, the last Metal Gear game Kojima will have ever worked on. 
This isn't so much a problem in function, so much as it is in vision. Most people can't repeat stories in the same way the original storyteller did, much less continue from where the last story left off with the same momentum and passion. That's not to say Konami can't do it without Kojima, but I know they haven't inspired any confidence after Metal Gear Survive.

Don't get into this game expecting to finish it.

On a mechanical level the game is wonderful with countless ways to approach each mission.  The sheer variety of ways you can either take-out or sneak past an enemy are staggering to the point where I feel that in my 40 hours of playing the game I barely scratched the surface.

There are three things that heavily detracted from my enjoyment:
The real-time wait times.  If you want to improve your home base you'll be given a timer you'll need to wait to expire in real-time.  Personally, I think that is a mechanic best left in money-grubbing mobile games.

The second is the god awful, nonsensical story.  I won't attempt to try and explain it because I can't; suffice to say you will spend the first hour of the game crawling on your belly (you don't have a choice, your characters legs are atrophied) and running away from a physic mental patient and a man who can summon flaming unicorns.  Later on full-scale building-sized mechs show up.  

Finally, the repetitive nature of missions.  While you have in your arsenal a near limitless bounty of gadgets and weapons, by the time you reach the second map you'll have been asked to extract the prisoner from the enemy camp so many times that I personally chose to stop playing at Africa.

Its an incredible game with a solid engine, I just feel the story/gameplay director wasn't competent.

review_text:
Pros:

*Improved CQC

*Weapon selection

*Tactics

*Computer combat AI

*Improved characters

*Use of alternate characters other than Venom Snake for game play

Cons:

*Repetitive menial tasks to gain GMP

*GMP (gross military product) is bound to online/offline. If you use GMP to research an item, offline GMP resources are used first, leaving you in the red if you do not remain online. Basically, forcing a player to remain online if they do not want soldiers to desert mother base, lose soldier platform levels, and the ability to research items.

*Cut Scenes do not use selected character; cut scene default is Venom Snake

*Head shrapnel is unrealistic. Real soldiers would be forced into retirement.

*Antagonists lack substance

*PVP is dead. Only seen 3 in there and they were game veterans using gimmicks to win a match.

*NPC auto-missions are capped by PVP. Forward bases of operation are required to achieve more beneficial NPC auto-missions.

I've played this game for a fair amount of time. I enjoy the open world aspect very much. Researching weapons or gear. The buddy system is fun (DD is my favorite buddy). NPC Buddies fulfill a specific role in the game. A horse for travel, a dog for stealth combat, a chopper for air strikes. I enjoy the deployment of vehicles, weapons, gear, and buddies in the field. Air strikes are fun too. As to the possibility of others enjoying this game, I can not say. I've been a fan of Metal Gear since the Nintendo console. Close quarters combat, weapon selection and tactical abilities have all improved over the years. As for the story characters, not so much. I found myself ignoring much of the story line to enjoy the game mechanics. 

The only major drawback I find in this latest and (supposed) final rendition of Metal Gear is the Online and PVP system. Some of the online auto-missions are bound to FOBs (forward operating base). You may think it is not a problem until you try to maintain a FOB. It is difficult to maintain a FOB when other players are destroying what you have built online. Now compound that with the fact everything you obtain online remains online and your offline GMP is used FIRST, with no way to transfer the online items to your offline resource pool. Unless you remain online indefinitely, your GMP will fall in the red. You'll lose research soldiers, access to GMP, and resources gathered while online all for research. As of now I have over a million GMP and resources sitting in my online pool because of the lack of combined resources while offline.

I recommend this game if you like stealth, CQC, and are not dependent upon PVP for enjoyment. I suggest you read the game forums for a more in depth explanation. Ultimately, only you can decide if this game is good for you.

Hideo Kojima's Magnum Opus, this game will go down as one of the GOATs in gaming.
Update: Ironically, Kojima wanted to push nuclear disarmament but essentially encourages nuclear proliferation especially with it's preachy cutscene at the end that appears every year and can't be skipped.

I cannot recommend this game enough even if you've never picked up a previous Metal Gear Solid game. The excellent stealth gameplay, level of open world freedom and some of the most immersive environments ever that really make you feel like you're in Soviet-Occupied Afghanistan or a nuclear-armed South Africa splintered by civil war. The game is great at making believe you are a soldier in the middle of a conflict from the suffering and loss as well as the reality of some of these people are simply young men (sometimes children) who are following orders, there are times the conversations that I encounter in the game are so engaging I have to stop and listen. The level of detail really captures the tone many people especially combatants had felt during the nuclear arms race. You have to remember that during this era nations and organizations wanted to secure their existence on the global stage by securing the closest thing we have to a a real-life doomsday device. You will also be thrust in this argument with the choices they can plan to make. Deciding to either be a hero that seeks to disarm rogue nukes or a villain securing their position of power by amassing nukes. The amount of detail Kojima put into this game really encapsulates the level of tension involved during the Cold War through the eyes of an elite espionage agent. 

On a side note, Konami is a despicable company that forced Kojima to not be able to work on the Metal Gear, Silent Hill, or Castlevania franchise anymore. They were even petty enough to cut off Kojima's ability to buy health insurance for his employees by blacklisting his company through a health insurance subsidiary they own. Only buy games published by Konami during sales or even from other means.

review_text:
Metal Gear is one of my favourite series. I've played MGS 2, 3  and Peacewalker. This is my favourite out of them all. MGSV takes all the base building and item development from Peacewalker and polishes it. It takes the stealth features honed from each game and refines it. It adds an open world environment for good measure. The story is up to the usual MGS standard: conspiracy wrapped in conspiracy. There are twists you may see coming, or others you do not. 

Gameplay:
Finally do we get the ability to prone crawl and crouch move. Decide what degree of stealth you need. Or throw caution to the wind and sprint. 
There are a variety of vehicles to make movement easier: ranging from jeeps to tanks. 
The open world means gameplay is not limited to missions. The very same map you play missions on can be explored. 
Companions. There are various companions with their own bonuses and equipment. Also a dog companion you can pet. Need I say more?
Base building: Unlike Peacewalker you can walk around the base. When you add a platform you can walk around it. You can also assault your employees (Non-lethal weapons only)
Kidnap soldiers you find on the field and make them work for you. I jest: you can extract people you meet in game to your base. They will then add their talents to Mother Base.
Eliminate your way: Want to slaughter everything in your path? Here's a wide variety of lethal weapons ranging from machine guns to rocket launchers. Want to fight non-lethally? Here's many rubber bullet and tranquiliser weapons. Or just CQC them. CQC is MGS talk for Close Quarters Combat, or slamming your opponent against the nearest object as violently as possible.
Intelligent enemies: MGS AI is generally good. Enemies investigate noises, and report things to command. They will flank you during combat, and bolster their equipment to combat your tactics. (For example, they may deploy helmets to protect soldiers from head shots if you're good at hitting their heads.) They also report to command: if a soldier finds a dead body he will inform the rest of the base and put them into alert. 
Many tools to help you: from the classic cardboard box to a binoculars that marks enemies you have lots of tools to help you. 

If you care about story order, this game takes place just after Peacewalker. It contains spoilers for MGS 3 and Peacewalker. Both are very good games and I'd recommend playing them. But don't let that stop you: MGSV knocks the gameplay of those two out of the park.

Overall I feel this game is a fitting send-off for Kojima. I cannot possibly capture all the nuances in this review. I got it for around ten euro in a sale: it is easily worth several times that.

Played for several hundred hours and more than half a dozen play-throughs on PS4, one of the first games I bought when making the transition to PC.

Both Ground Zeroes and Phantom Pain are two of the most divisive games in the franchise, and rightly so. The treatment of Kojima by Konami and his eventual departure from the company show heavily in Phantom Pain's narrative and design. You can pretty much tell exactly when things got bad. 

The controls for PC are quite a culture shock for someone who's only ever played on consoles, and I had to resist the urge to plug in my controller. I rebind the (Walk/Run) key assignment to the Spacebar and the (Dive) button to the "T" key, as trying to move with WASD and hold the CTRL key is nigh impossible unless you have a digit growing out of your wrist... 

Other than the minor nitpick of swapping the keys to more my liking, the PC versions of this game are the way they're meant to me experienced. My laptop maxed all the graphical settings out, and beholding the visual masterpiece that is the FOX engine's horsepower brought a tear to my eye. Truly a very well rendered and realized game world.

I'd recommend grabbing this on sale, because Konami deserves as little money for their awful treatment of Kojima as possible, but other than that I whole-heartedly recommend this game if you like action/stealth shooter adventure games. It's definitely different than any other MGS game in the franchise, in both good ways and bad. But it's worth a playthrough, both for series fans and newcomers alike.

Cheers.

review_text:
Possibly my favorite game of all time. 
I could spend hours, days even, talking about Metal Gear Solid and this game in particular. How it feels to run around as a random mercenary in his appropriately camouflaged undies, terrorizing the poor PMC conscripts of central Africa with your highly customized, shotgun-shells-firing assault sniperrifle which you exclusively use to point at people's back so they go "Oh shi.., don't shoot", only for them to watch helplessly as you proceed to attach a self-inflating balloon to some random cargo container before riding it back to your mobile home, a neon-pink Apache attack-helicopter that you outfitted to blast ghetto music to weaken the enemy's morale.
The game is wild. And it doesn't lie about "offering you tactical freedom to carry out open-world missions."
If you need a TL;DR about it, this sentence is all you need: it's the single best description to what MGS:V is at it's core. 

It is - ultimately - one of the most flexible and solidly executed pieces of work ever in terms of raw gameplay. Every single weapon, item and tool has it's merits. Everything has one to several hidden mechanics and applications waiting for you to explore them. The gameplay is, in my opinion, the pinnacle of action/stealth thus far. Period. 
Going on a nuclear rampage with your self-replacing, exploding rocket arm is as legitimate as crawling past unaware guards in a sandstorm at nighttime while wearing camouflaged fatigues. The choice is yours.
The gameplay is rewarding, intricate and smooth to no end. MGS:V-TPP falls flat in many ways, but gameplay is none. If TPP has anything, it's gameplay. And in times where developers like to put out unfinished half-assed attempts at games, TPP at least got this done. I respect that.

The progression is ... hm. I like it. Many other's don't, which is fair. You have to find and unlock blueprints for new weapon designs while increasing both your physical resources in terms of money and materials as well as your army's numbers to develop them - and you need enough resources to deploy them in the field. It's an interesting mechanic that adds depth to the game - which is why I personally enjoy it.
 
Also, the PC port is amazing. My potato garbage dumpster fire craptop could handle it with ease while still having it look good visually. 

Where there is praise, there are also negatives ... which are mostly everything else, to various degrees between neutral and bad. 

The story, oh dear... Story is one of the most important aspects in every MG game, and this one really doesn't hold up in that regard. 
I believe it's common fact by now that the story isn't finished, and you really do feel it. The story lacks from serious communication problems. Sometimes, you just don't know what's going on even though the game practically shoves it into your face. Some elements on the other hand are so stupidly subtle that you don't even recognize them unless your perception check happened to hit an imaginary number. 
It's too much talking and too little telling, effectively. Unlike in older Metal Gears, where exposition was tied to critical information, everything here develops in a sort-of linear fashion with story missions happening in the order you choose them. All of which deliver a lot of talk, but don't tell you a lot.
 
The game's tone is jaded and gritty, which works for the story it tries to tell, but ultimately felt exhausting to follow for prolonged time. Take a shot whenever Miller mentions revenge or Cipher. You'd be the one in a nine-year-coma even before the game has really started.  
TPP only really hits the nail once in terms of atmosphere. Once. Which is the sad negative record of the franchise. 
Ironically, MGS:V - Ground Zeros is a far better Metal Gear in this regard, as it tells a story while featuring the grim, oppressive atmosphere, sense of urgency and permanent feeling of anxious paranoia which every Metal Gear tries to achieve to various degrees. TPP, however, has an interesting but mediocre story to tell and outright fails at the story-telling aspect.
The dev team and the community (myself included)  came, after their collective hand-wringing, to the silent cope that the feel of having it unfinished is what "The Phantom Pain" ultimately truly means. It's up to the player to decide that.

The biggest issue I personally have, going along the lines of "phantom pain", is that I see wasted potential. The game, and I'm not exaggerating with this, has the potential to be one of the best if not THE best game of all times. Sadly, you are restricted to two different sandboxes == maps that allow you a lot to try but not much to do. The online experience does provide another aspect and experience to the game, but it's fairly hard to get anywhere without having another friend on standby. You can invade their Forward Operation Base, or they can invade one of yours. Nothing else. No coop, nothing - which is an incredible waste; MG:Survive did it in the same engine. Why not implement it into the original game, too? 

One particular thing that you need to consider with this game is it's repetitiveness. The basic cycle, while enjoyable and extremely flexible, at one points boils down to scout - infiltrate - reach objective - exfiltrate. It requires you to set your own goals, which gatekeeped a lot of people I feel. Paired with the progression mechanic I mentioned above, the game is prone to feel like a grindy chore at times where you'd only try to accumulate resources to unlock the next thing. And here it is at this point - the point where people feel like "so I just go in, tranq everybody, go out and that's it?" - where many players dropped the game.
In order to enjoy it, you need to set your own goals. Be prepared to do so, because once the fresh feeling of the first 5-10 hours wears off, you will need it. 

So yeah. That's MGS:V. There's still so much more to talk about, but I've edited this review already once and I don't want to go on eternally. Browse other comments and form your own opinion, but I do recommend giving it a go either way.

At the end of the day, the game is what it is. An amazing, stupid, powerful and strange little sandbox that could've been much more, but also could've been much much worse. 
It's best to enjoy what we have instead to mourn what could've been, in my opinion. 

So, all in all: 
MGS:V - TPP is not a good Metal Gear, but a good game. 
I found it best to enjoy it once in a while instead of playing the fück out of it. Keeps it fresh and allows you to relax while sneaking around unaware Soviet goons while wearing a stupid cardboard box over your head. 

Utterly recommended.

review_text:
This is one of those games which I would really give neutral review if that was an option. Some missions in this game are really well thought out, and some are just really boring and repetitive. This game has mostly really confusing story. In fact this whole franchise has one of the most confusing and complex storyline out there to understand. 
At the second chapter this game hits a new low. it reintroduces SAME OLD missions and just makes them harder, barely adding any new content you to play and understand better the lore behind this game. I actually think that chapter 2 is mostly old missions which many of them you are required to beat to get the ''real ending'' after chapter 1. Even after this real ''ending'' this game has still a LOT to explain about certain events and characters, but the game just ends. I have heard that konami had cut content from the original game and didn't give kojima enough time/resources to finish this game properly. So there's that. 

Now about the gameplay... I think that this game has solid and fun gameplay with really nice weapons and vehicles, but I must say that vehicle physics are awful in this game. Vehicles and weapons look really nice and they become super helpful especially at the end of this game. Stealth works quite well and you have good control over your character and items you handle.

AL is bad tho, because sometimes AI can't see/notice you even at a close distance without cover, But sometimes AI can see you at a great distance. This is really annoying because you are not entirely sure how the AI ​​will react to your movements and at what distance.
visually the game is spectacular. The game also has good sounds and voice acting, and the animations are well done. The cutscenes are well made in this game in my opinion, although sometimes certain cutscenes can be quite ''cheesy'' and ''scripted ''

I also think  that there's way too much fanservice and grind. I've already explained this  grind aspect earlier in this review but here's some other things wrong about that grind. For example if you want good weapons and enough resources to upgrade your base and arsenal, you have to do quite a lot of side quests and other extras. I don't mind if the grind is '' fun'' but I mean it's mostly really boring grind that you ''just have to do''.
Now about fanservice... I mainly mean Quiet, because I think the reason why Kojima put her in this game was to create some sort of '' waifu '' -like character that the player could cling to because of his ''appearance''. Quiet constantly plays a certain kind of shy but at the same time tough (in my opinion) half-naked woman in the game, which you can take on tasks and missions. Quiet does add certain aspects to the story, but I think there were a lot of plot-holes in that character, especially at the end. For me the fanservice was too over the top in this game and ''cringey''. 

In my mind this game is fine if you can get past these things in game. HOWEVER, this game IS NOT 10/10 game, because some people say that this game can be and is 10/10 game. For me that's just too big rating for game like this. It has OK-ish story, which is really confusing and hard to follow, repetitive story missions and side missions, really awful grind and fanservice. Even AI can be iffy in this game sometimes and for a stealth game you must have a good AI to let player feel like they are in fact playing proper stealth game with good and smart AI. This game has some of those aspects, but not all. 
Sometimes I felt that these negative aspects are just too overwhelming to me to give this game thumps up, and sometimes I felt like this game has it's downsides, but it was still interesting enough for me to beat this game. However, I will give this game thumps down because I feel like this game has too many major negatives to give this game a thumbs up. If Steam had neutral review option, I would give this game a neutral at the moment I am writing this review.

Rating: 7/10

You will like it or hate it.  Personally, I like it.  I don't mind doing the grind work.  Doing the side missions to nab a few good soldiers and prisoners that will help me with the research and development, combat deployments for more resource gathering.  Some people won't like this format because its really not story driven so it feels pointless and waste of time.

 The game is not like the Witcher 3 where you go through all the side quests to get better gear for yourself which gives you immediate satisfaction.  MGSV is more like gathering resources so in the long run, if you need to research a gear that you need in mission, you can research and deploy it and also grow your army for deployments to earn money or resources.

Story wise, the MGS universe is weird, sometimes convoluted.  In fact, I never paid attention to the story of any of the MGS games.  I really don't care.  I just like the game play.  If you ask me to recite the lore chronologically, I can't do it.  I can't keep track of Snake's history.  I am not a prude, I like how Quiet looks but you have to admit, Kojima's mind is weird.

Game play, I am sticking with the PS4 controller.  In my opinion, the PC controls are terrible.  If you can play on it, more power to you.  I always felt more comfortable with a controller for 3rd person games, I stick to keyboard and mouse for first person.  Search online for the PS4 controls, the game only has the mapping for xbox controller in the menu.  

The common complaint people have about the game is the travelling.  Yes, it is a waste of time so it is important to keep track of your main and side missions and do them efficiently so the distance between each one is short.  

As you go along, destroy the air radar defenses, it will allow your helicopter more places to land to pick you up.  Other wise, you will have to do alot of galloping on your horse.

Game world, its Afghanistan, its a desert so naturally, it will fee samey.  So once in a while, fly back to mother base.  When you go back to motherbase, do some more research and commission base expansion if you have the resources.  Also when you go back your army's moral will increase.

To break the samey feeling, try different ways of infiltrating.  Sometimes, going through total non lethal gets boring.

Now, even though I like this game, I don't think I will finish it before another game grabs my attention. But I am fine with that.  I can always go back and I will when I get an itch to play it.

review_text:
You know how every school has these cool kids, with whom practically everybody wants to be their friends? When you finally get the chance to befriend these cool kids, you don’t find them as great as you’ve heard. They’re nice and of course, cool. Yet, despite popular opinion, you can only see yourself as their acquaintance. For me, [I]Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain [/I] is that group of cool kids.

The [I]Metal Gear Solid [/I] series is undeniably cool. If it were not, it would not have stood a chance given the ridiculous names of its games and characters, the convoluted yet intriguing storylines, and the outlandish mix of military action, stealth, science fiction and fantasy. A game, let alone a game series, with these qualities should not have worked. Yet, under the meticulous direction of Hideo Kojima, it improbably did.

Up until [I]Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes [/I], I’ve never played a [I]MGS[/I] game as I am primarily a PC gamer. [I]GZ[/I] allowed me to finally appreciate Kojima’s craftsmanship and artistry firsthand on the PC, and [URL= https://steamcommunity.com/id/CharlieLima79/recommended/311340/]I really enjoyed it[/URL]. Needless to say, [I]GZ[/I] got me excited about what [I]TPP[/I] would deliver.

[U][B]What I Liked[/B][/U]:
[I]TPP[/I] has stunning, photorealistic graphics. The stealth action in the main missions are intense, with each set piece designed to encourage you to devise your own plans for infiltration and exfiltration. The cutscenes are cinematic and of high production value. [I]TPP[/I] is without a doubt an ambitious and loaded game that invites you to spend time with it, bit by bit.

[U][B]And Yet…[/B][/U]:
It pains me to profess that [I]TPP[/I] is not the game for me. If it just features what I just mentioned, it would be easy for me to praise it to no end. Instead, what I experienced was a bloated stealth action game that also includes open world exploration, base-building, resource gathering and management, and online multiplayer. Because I’m not a fan of the latter three, I found a good part of [I]TPP[/I] tedious because base-building, and resource gathering and management are obligatory.

[U][B]But First…[/B][/U]:
Let me state unequivocally that the stealth action in [I]TPP[/I] is spectacular. It has been fine-tuned for optimal challenge and excitement. I love this part of [I]TPP[/I], and I wish there was more of it in the first 20 hours of gameplay, during which I completed the prologue, the first 8 main missions, and at least 10 side ops. Yet, I feel like I’ve spent more time than I had liked on tasks that are superfluous to the stealth action gameplay that I expected.

I want to describe a few aspects of [I]TPP[/I] that irked me most, ones that I wished I knew about before purchasing it. If you believe I’m wrong, or at least you can accept these shortcomings anyway, just know that I’m still recommending [I]TPP[/I] because the stealth action bits are truly fun.

[U][B]Open World[/B][/U]:
As an open world game, [I]TPP[/I] is disappointing. With the setting being a rocky, hilly desert in Afghanistan, there are hardly unique locations to explore like in most other open world games. The wide, mostly barren landscape is dotted with small outposts and makeshift bases occupied by enemies, joined by pretty much a single road and the occasional slightly hidden canyon path. With your enemies ready to shoot on sight, open world exploration is hardly a carefree experience.

You can travel from A to B by helicopter as means of fast travel, but it’ll cost you money and is actually not that fast. There are a lot of cinematics that accompany this fast travel, likely because the game uses them to hide its loading times. After watching these cinematics several times, the whole process got tiresome. 

[U][B]Pacing[/B][/U]:
Many open world games have uneven pacing, mainly because the players are likely distracted by all the side missions and hidden discoveries that the games offer. Given that, open world games should have main missions that are varied and that will move the story along at a brisk pace. Unfortunately, [I]TPP[/I] does not.

The prologue/tutorial of [I]TPP[/I] is exciting, with hardly any moment for you to breathe or let the chaos sink in. It’s a grand way to open up a game, but that was the last time I experience that type of excitement 20 hours into the game. Once the proper game begins, the pace is much slower. I was constantly waiting for the next big action set piece, but it never came.

This game is also very repetitive, and its side ops feel like work because in many ways they are. Side ops are obligatory because you need to collect resources in forms of personnel, blueprints, and materials to build your private army, develop new weapons, and expand your Mother Base. In the first 20 hours, I revisited the same locations 2 to 3 times. Although the time of day, weather conditions, and enemy patrol patterns might have differed, I was still in the same locations and not visiting anywhere new.

After my first 15 hours of playing [I]TPP[/I], I found myself still in the Afghanistan desert. It’s only then that I realized I’d be stuck in Afghanistan pretty much forever. (Perhaps it’s a sly commentary by Kojima?) I was still sneaking into outposts occupied by Russian armed forces to clandestinely recover X (usually weapons or weapon blueprints) or extract Y (usually a prisoner or a skilled person who can benefit my private army).

You would think, for a game that has 31 main missions, over 150 side ops, as well as post-game missions, there would be more to see 20 hours in. Yet, given all the time and effort I’ve invested, I’m reportedly at 7 to 8% completion. For game that has this much content, a little more variation to its gameplay and setting to keep things interesting would have been appreciated. At the very least, [I]TPP[/I] could have moved the story along.

[U][B]Too Much Other Stuff[/B][/U]:
The repetitiveness is made worse by all the other stuff that you can/have to do in the game. In between missions and side ops, I found myself:
[LIST]
[*]searching for fuel, minerals, rough diamonds, etc.
[*]building new platforms to expand my Mother Base
[*]reassigning staff in my army to optimize efficiency
[*]researching and develop new weapons
[*]listening to many mission cassette tapes so the game can fill me in on [I]MGS[/I] lore and world history
[*]picking herbs
[*]rescuing wild animals
[*]stealing music cassette tapes
[*]collecting posters
[/LIST]
That’s right, all of the above is part of [I]MGS[/I]’ tactical espionage action. Fun.

The game also encourages you to return to Mother Base regularly to boost your soldiers’ morale. You do that by going up to each of them so they can salute you. The soldiers are scattered throughout the many platforms that you can build, which you can “quickly” travel to by driving or by hailing a helicopter. Tactical espionage action indeed.

[U][B]Final Thoughts[/B][/U]:
In the end, [I]TPP[/I] is not the game I expected. The fantastic core stealth game is surrounded by too much clutter for me to enjoy it properly. I now find myself appreciating [I]GZ[/I] more because it’s a leaner, no-nonsense stealth action game. I also find the level design of Camp Omega in [I]GZ[/I] to be more stellar than what I’ve seen so far in [I]TPP[/I].

Now that you’ve taken time to read why I like and dislike some parts of [I]TPP[/I] (thank you), I hope you can make an informed decision about whether or not to buy or try this game. Chances are, if you’re an [I]MGS[/I] fan, you’re likely to give it a go anyway. However, if you’re unfamiliar with the game series or are new to it like me, I hope you’ll enjoy it more than I did.

I've played MGS2 on the second hardest difficulty, MGS3 multiple times, pieces of MGS4, I've beaten Ground Zeroes in less than half an hour at a game shop. Point is, I'm familiar with the gameplay and the overall lore and the discussion surrounding the series.

Here's my problem straight up: This game is a 10/10 if the story shuts the hell up.
The open world aspect is decent. Not impressive but functional which is good amidst this era of broken AAA game releases.

The third person shooting mechanic is probably the best system ever made behind Vanquish, and definitely better than Spec Ops: The Line. However, gameplay can a bit dull and repetitive especially after hundreds of hours of playing. You'll be shooting a lot soldier because this is a Metal Gear game. Half of the bosses in this game are just giant ass bullet sponges which are "fun" to deal with. Gosh, the progression system really wants you to grind and wait for hours even days just to unlock higher level equipment, it is designed to slow down your engagement with the game, which in hindsight is kinda frustrating, and why I stop playing the moment the game hit the credits. 

The narrative is disposable. The theme of the story is understandable, and you can see it through gameplay stats and objectives but I just don't care. The way the story ideas represented were unintuitive. They're mostly not stories, they raw research notes, Discovery Channel lectures, and boring ass audio logs. Even the cutscenes aren't really impressive. Some of them are just unsatisfying melodramatic nonsense. The political intrigue are just facade for superficial effort to make the story seems deep.

This is another case of having a lot of good story ideas executed poorly.
I recommend it if you want to play a great diversely flexible third person shooter.
Don't play this game for the story, you'll hate yourself.
Don't even play this to see Quiet's body.

review_text:
[h1]"Why are we still here? Just to suffer? Every night, I can feel my leg... And my arm... even my fingers... The body I've lost... the comrades I've lost... won't stop hurting... It's like they're all still there. You feel it, too, don't you? I'm gonna make them give back our past!"[/h1]
METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN is an open world third person stealth (optional) game. It is a combination of a movie and a video game, it got hours of cutscenes and the lore is more complex than any other video game or movie i know. I am not a big fan of lore in games and sometimes i just skip it and go straight after the gameplay, but it is not the same for this game. It made me read lots of long wiki pages on some characters, organizations and places (Do not do the same before completing the game for your own good. Spoilers are not fun).
The gameplay is great, as i mentioned earlier the stealth is optional and it can be played and enjoyed by loud and ruthless players too. It is a really long game so it is worth your money 3 or 4 times more than the average AAA title without counting replayability. There are a lot of options in weapons, vehicles and backup and you can choose one of the 4 available buddies to help you in your mission. Each buddy has different abilities that you unlock by increasing the bond level (which is also pretty easy, just don't let them get hurt and order them to do stuff a lot). The enemies also get small upgrades along the story, you have to change your techniques if they don't work anymore and i find this a great way of stopping the gameplay from being repetitive. I personally finished all the main missions and a few side ones in 100 hours and still have some other side missions and new difficulty ones to do. There are FOB raidings too, pretty much the only online part that is still alive. MGS online seems dead, couldn't find anyone to try it out with. FOB missions are about invading player bases for stealing resources and crew, its cost is that if you fail or get spotted the one invaded knows who you are and can invade back.
The graphics are pretty damn good and the optimization is great, i ran it on almost max settings with stable 60 fps (capped) on GTX 1050 4GB (laptop), i5-8250U and 8GB RAM DDR4. My laptop didn't even make a lot of noise and it didn't get very hot, so if you got a similar system i bet you can run it on max easily. The soundtrack is nice and there are featured licensed songs released in the early '80s, which is good for the game's atmosphere, since that is when the story takes place. There are a lot of menus in this game, they look good and have satisfying sound effects.
 
There are parts i didn't like too. The helicopter takes too much time artificially. After doing a mission you are all bloody and want to go to Mother Base and take a shower. You have to call the helicopter, wait for it, get in, wait for it to traver long enough so you would close its door, wait for the game to load and press a button, use your idroid and go to mother base, wait for the loading screen again to press a button, waiting for it to get down and FINALLY getting out of the helicopter. It takes too much time and you can't do something else meanwhile, because you still need to press a few buttons. If you want to get to other platforms of the Mother Base you have to drive there in a vehicle. The road is too long and again, you can't do other stuff while doing it, maybe listening to cassettes at best. There is no reason for them to be this long, i think the road to other platforms should be at least half as long.
The upgrades take too much time. I understand it would be ridiculous to upgrade weapons instantly, but it goes from instantly for low tier to 18m, 36m, 1 hour and a few minutes, a few hours and to my surprise, one weapon that i didn't really need, but that i upgraded only because i had money made me wait 4 days. If i really wanted that gold tier heavy machine gun i would be pissed off badly.
The DLCs are ridiculous, at how much content there is in this game they are almost nothing and shouldn't cost money, yet they do. I never used the suits, i have them only because the bundle that included Ground Zeroes had them too and was only a few dollars more. Honestly there is no reason to buy them, you're wasting money.
The main story wasn't finished, Snake gets robbed of his secret weapon by an annoying brat and you don't get to see him again. If that scene wasn't in the game i would consider it complete, it's like starting a new chapter and leaving it after the introduction.
You see credits everywhere. Even if you don't want you will remember Hideo Kojima's name. At the start of every mission you will see his name credited, then some other credits for the people that made the missions. I think they did a great job making this game but i'd rather have all the credits at the end of the game only. I guess it's just his ego.

review_text:
The man who sold the world. Kojima has once again crafted a masterpiece of both a story as well as introducing the idea of a bigger threat then your traditional nukes and looks at language. Now some may see this game as unfinished as the situation between Kojima productions and Konami went for a deep s*** around the time this game was getting released. However if you are willing to look past all that you will find a well fleshed out story that connects in interesting ways to the previous games.

At the games core this is a third person shooter with your usual mixture of cover, shooting and stealth mechanics. This game provides players plenty of ways to both play it fast and loud or quiet and sneaky. What's great is the amount of freedom this brings to the gameplay in that you can adapt to the situation on the fly without the need to worry unless you are going for the S ranks in which case the sneaky way is your best friend but still. The option to go loud is there if you feel you must go that route. Just be ready as cover isn't always plentiful out there in the wild open world map. So make sure you are ready if you choose to do that. One of the unique things is that this game allows you to take along a buddy so to speak in missions. Now these have to be unlocked over the course of the game and you cannot take a friend along. These buddies take the form of a horse, a dog, a sniper and a robot. All of which can be custumized to an extent. You can also take people and animals home back to your base via ballon. Which lets say can be quite funny at times.

At the end of the day this game can be quite fun and for what you pay you can easily get around 50hrs+ in terms of gameplay and missions to take part in. While some may feel this game in incomplete it does have plenty of a moments that  may stay with you after the credits have rolled. Highly recommended.

        [td]10[/td]
	[td]They nailed this one TBH. Whether it is how responsive and consistent Snake's movements are. The horse riding. The shooting and CQC. Despite not having a difficulty setting, the game gives you ways t play it on Easy mode, such as using Quiet, chicken head etc. It is up to the player of how they want to play the game, and how much they want to be challenged which was a very organic way of implementing difficulty. The AI is one of the best I've seen too. 10/10 on the difficulty balancing.[/td]
    [/tr]

        [td]9[/td]
	[td]There are a great many ways to tackle the same situations. Say there is a mission where I needed to disable some communication satellites in a base. I could sneak up and take down enemies one by one, also selecting the good ones for the mother base, which is a place where you develop more resources, etc. could methodically disable the satellites and get out of there without being spotted. Or could just land on a helicopter in front of it and blow satellites up with a rocket launcher and get out of there as fast as possible. This is one of the missions where the aggressive approach works better than others but you get the point. There is no lack of accommodation of player agency in the gameplay. But the game never forces a player to play a certain way, which could be seen as both a positive and a negative. On one hand, you are free to choose your own approach - on the other, you might go through the whole game without ever knowing about things you could have done. But then there's a bunch of issues I have. The motherbase interface leaves a lot to be desired. The troop management is convoluted but at least can be gotten used to. review_text:
In spite of a flawed, incomplete, and inconclusive ending, MGSV is the logical evolution of the franchise's formula that gives you more freedom and options than any game prior. Each mission zone feels less like they're a spot in an open world map, and more like a microcosm of the MGS gameplay loop. It's hard to even perceive MGSV as an open world game because there's only two maps, and the way enemy NPCs and structures are set up in hot zones makes it feel like I'm playing a prior MGS in condensed bites.

However, because this is a Kojima joint, it's got his token style of over-the-top sci-fi military fantasy that's been an obvious staple since MGS2 (when things got the most obtuse they've ever been). The first Part's villain is undercooked in spite of his charisma, and I feel that his VA is miscast. The second Part has no villain, and it was meant to but Konami is a troubled entity to say the least. The new Metal Gear Sahelanthropus has stylistic cues that reach both forward and backwards (because this game is the final prequel), but some of the tech that's in it feels like a pseudo-retcon because it never shows up again. The big twist at the end feels like a convoluted attempt to make the canon of two MSX2 games made in the 1980s more sensible, even though most people don't care.

If you can get over the hamfisted, excessive script, MGSV has the best gameplay in the series.

review_text:
MGSV is an absolute masterpiece of a game, and totally deserves all the praise it gets. It's fun, it's really weird, and it will keep you busy for many hours without getting stale. There are a few areas to complain about, mainly a few BS missions and an unfinished second act, but all that pales in comparison to the good on display here. This was my first Metal Gear game, but I found it actually quite approachable as a newcomer to the series. This is a must-play for pretty much anyone.

Visually the game is top-notch. It goes for ultra-realism, with great facial animations, lighting and textures. The fact that this real-looking world also includes things like giant robots and ghostly soldiers just adds a kind of quirk you don't get from other games. The audio is also very good, and it can help you out a lot when you're trying to make your way around undetected. The visuals and audio combine to make the kind of atmosphere where you're transported to Big Boss' shoes and can just enjoy inhabiting this world. It's hard to describe, but when you're out in the countryside (probably doing silly things like sleep-darting wild donkeys) and are scoping out the base you want to infiltrate, you really feel like you're there and part of it.

Now, the gameplay and feel are really where this game shines. It's so polished it's ridiculous, with all kinds of little systems and details in play that can impact the way you play. Maybe you usually do your missions at night, and like head-shotting guards with your sleep darts. Next time, they might have night vision goggles and helmets. Sneaking around feels great, and it's fairly forgiving if you make a little mistake. If you're seen, you have a few seconds of slow-time to respond appropriately, usually with a sleep dart to the face. That said, it's not always a walk in the park; timing and boldness pay off big time. There are a few parts where your approach needs to differ completely based on the mission, and sometimes it takes some trial and error before you figure it out. Some of the story missions were quite challenging, too. Aside from the stealth, there is a pretty involved meta-game of building up your base, supplies and private army. You collect objects and people with a "Fulton" device, which attaches a powerful balloon to the object and shoots it into the sky (hilarious when you do it to people). There is a whole multiplayer segment of the game which I mostly stayed away from, but some people can spend hundreds of hours just on that. The possibilities in this game are vast and various.

The story, while often totally absurd, is generally very interesting. It immediately hits you with mystery after mystery in the opening segment, and just when you think you're maxed out on WTF, it dumps your into this huge sandbox and says "go play!" Eventually the plot opens up a bit and you learn your place in all this chaos, but it's teased out in a way that keeps you pushing to know what's next. The story does of course falter in Chapter 2, in that most of the "story" missions become re-treads of previous missions with challenging modifiers, but these are actually optional. There are still a few new missions, and I enjoyed them. A lot of the story is told through audio tapes, so you can actually get parts of the dialog while you're still out doing things, which is nice. Some people say the story is bad, and I can't really judge based on other Metal Gear games, but I definitely enjoyed the characters, the ridiculous and cinematic cutscenes, the weirdness, and the general direction of the plot.

My biggest gripes were just a couple of sticking points. There is one part that involves going through your whole army list and separating some of them out, one by one. Since I had like 800 guys by this point, it took me a solid 30+ minutes of just scrolling down and occasionally hitting a button. It... was... terrible. Also, if you leave a mission area by mistake, there is no confirmation given and you can pass the point of no return very fast. I was running away on horseback from a giant robot at the end of one mission, and accidentally crossed over the invisible line. It abandoned the mission instantly and I lost a good 90 minutes of time I put into sneaking around. That really made me mad. They didn't ruin the experience, but things like that occasionally just made me question some of the design decisions.

Overall, MGSV holds a spot among the best open world games, stealth games, and video games in general that are out there. If you're on the fence, just take the plunge. I am very glad I took the time, and you will be too.

[b] A Love/Hate Tragedy [/b]

[b]As far as Single Player Gameplay goes, The Phantom Pain is the best Stealth Action Game Out there.[/b]
The Variety in ways to complete missions is awesome. It is rewarding to replay every mission to get all unlocks and to find little holes in the defences and such on your own.

The two and a half worldspaces are phenominal. Afghanistan and Afrika are athmospherically enticing and one wanders off easily between Missions. The level of detail that went into the design is admirably minute.

Storywise the Phantom Pain can be considered a wrapup of all loose ends in the Metal Gear Universe, including one last big deception unveiled.

[b]And then there are the FOB's....[/b]
FOB's are unlocked as part of the main story and are seemingly an extension of the singleplayer gameplay. 
Only that they are not.... The forced upon PvP gameplay is one huge cycle of revenge among participating players. The ugly, abhoring downside is, that the game frequently shifts 90% of your ressources to the FOB's online account, where it can be easily stolen by other players. Additionally the the FOB's No. 2,3 and 4 are [b]hidden behind a soft paywall of ingane currency[/b]. And a rather substantial one at that.
And god help you if you ever develop a single Nuke, even if you only wanted it for the achievement, to unlock it and dispose of it. Now in 2019 this game has only really good players left and they know no mercy. If ever there was a toxic playerbase...
[b]And the Cheaters...[/b]
If all of the above wouldn't be enough KONAMI does not protect you against cheaters.
Even reporting them is more likely to get you yourself banned, rather then the cheater. This has been documented, sadly!

If you can ignore half of the game being unplayable, enjoy being thrashed regularly by demigods of infiltration or you like to be robbed of everything you played so hard for, then this is your game! 
[b]Otherwise leave it![/b]

review_text:
This game is simultaneously the best Metal Gear Game and a somewhat bad Metal Gear Game. 

From a gameplay perspective, this is one of the finest stealth action games ever crafted. The systems that make up the base game such as sneaking, combat, cqc, pretty much everything that makes a Metal Gear game good are present in tight form. Add onto that an enormous tree of new toys that can add variety to your game, and you have some satisfying as hell stealth gameplay. There's also a base system that incentivizes silently capturing strong guards instead of just going in guns blazing. Really fun, 10/10.

From a story perspective, this game is one of the worst Metal Gear games. It is clear that this game is unfinished with missing final missions that could help complete the story, but are unfortunately absent. While the moment to moment storytelling is still cinematic and interesting, the overarching plot doesn't really go anywhere. Without spoiling specifics, this game really ends for no reason. The final mission shows up randomly and doesn't have anything to do with plot events occurring in game.

Now it is totally possible that Hideo, being the mad genius that he is, purposefully left out the final chapter of this game after having teased it in earlier trailers. Much like how the ending of Metal Gear Solid 2 left you wanting for more at the time, but in retrospect has been analyzed and shown for the incredible ending that it is. It would make sense, as the themes of this game involve feeling the pain of something lost that once was there (I mean the game is called The Phantom Pain, in allusion to the feeling that amputees still have even after their limb is gone). It's possible that Kojima knew of his inevitable firing from Konami, and wanted the player to feel that emptiness in the gameplay. I'm sure in 10 years we will all have some newfound appreciation for this game and its themes, but for those just wanting a surface level story, the game leaves me wanting.

I'd recommend you play this game for the gameplay alone, as it is possible the single best example of freedom in a stealth game ever. Ignore the story, or pay attention to it once and then leave it alone as you do missions and you will certainly have a great time with this game. 

I give it a Perfect for the Gameplay, and an Almost Good for the Story.

[h1]Mistakes only make it more fun[/h1]

[b]The Good[/b]
[list]
[*][b]Absolute Game Play[/b] - As I said, 'mistakes only make it more fun'. I enjoy the game best when I screw up and everything turns to crap. I start to improvise and am always impressed on what the game lets me get away with. This is when the MGSV shines.  
[*][b]Deep Armory[/b] - I was impressed with the selection of weapons and tools you're allowed to choose from and bring into a mission. This contributed to the fun I had in the game, as I got to experiment with the toys they let me have.  
[*][b]Mission Design[/b] - Strictly talking about the main missions and a few critical side missions, their design delivers maximum fun. Having me move to places to complete my objective, or an event/ twist that completely flips my situation are more than welcome. 
[/list]

[b]The Bad[/b]
[list]
[*][b]Chapter 2[/b] - I'm currently working on Chapter 2, and I noticed that its got me repeating missions at higher difficulty. So I did some research, and learned that Chapter 2 contains 19 missions, 12 of which are repeats. This feels like padding / fillers. Seems like they were trying to hit a certain amount of hours of game play for chapter 2 to make it out of the door. Luckily the game play is really good so maybe, I just might do these to get to the stories of some of the other characters in the game.
[*][b]Vertically Challenged[/b] - MINOR ISSUE here, I think the level design could do with a bit more of vertical design. The entirety of the game will have you infiltrating wide flat spaces. To be honest though, I would imagine facilities of these nature, to look like how they're designed in the game, flat and wide. So why ask for verticality?? - To vary the game play and challenges of course! We've got giant robots, psychics, and a living burning man, so might as well get liberal with some of the level design. 

[/list]

[b]The Recommendation[/b]

Given that Chapter 1 is a bigger part of the game, and Chapter 2 is just a handful of missions with most of which are re-do's, I'd give this game an 8/10. I can look past recycled missions because of good game play, varied mission designs and generous story telling. 
[b]8/10[/b]

[list]

It'll probably be a Gem for die-hard Kojima's fanboys, but for the people who care about anything other than the producer's name, it'll get stale really fast. The game feels as it's about to collapse under its own weight at any moment.

The story was written awkwardly heavy and it keeps shoving every useless detail down your throat as if the writer felt he was too much of a genius to not get noticed for his attention to detail. Unfortunately for him, his details kept contradicting themselves while going against the original lore. In the end, it feels like they just wanted to rewrite history just so they could organize the lore's timeline. It's a poor job and you can notice it quite easily even if you're not familiar with the early game's story.

The gameplay can be quite awesome at first, then you start to realize how stupid the AI is. You can stealth pretty much any mission, you can also JUST RUN TO THE OBJECTIVE. Most enemies won't be able to kill you if you keep running...

Corny and ridiculous gadgets like the Fulton Extraction, Rocket fist and a Inflated decoy (modeled after yourself) makes the game feel like a parody of itself. While some are optional, most missions force you to use some of them.

By the way, it has more cutscenes than Detroit Become Human, except they're way more insufferable as the exposition narration, cringy deliveries and ridiculous dramatic takes/pauses makes them game feel cheap and bland, sometimes is just impossible not to laugh as the ridiculousness reaches sky-high moments...

Overall, the game is fun if you don't take it seriously. Other than that, get Ghost Recon Wildlands or something better...

I have to say although the story was confusing as heck because it slots into an already existing timeline I know nothing about, it's a solid gameplay experience and whilst I originally played it on my PS4, it was good enough for me to grab a Steam copy too.

There is also a cover system where you can hide behind walls/crates/trees or hide in grass or ditches/trenches or even just in a port-a-loo. Classic CS:GO move. Moving around was fluid and felt natural. There's nothing I like more than sprinting at an enemy and then diving into prone whilst headshotting him with a tranq dart. Classic COD move.

Controls are great for controllers, keyboard however was another story. This game has its own unique style of keyboard assignments. I say this because it's the only game I've played with this keyboard layout and it took some time getting used to, especially in the menu..... Especially (in italics) in the menu.

Sound was good. Good soundtrack too.

Ok I'm done.

review_text:
TL;DR: Game is great, something everyone should sample. My personal issues with the game lie within somewhat abrupt ending and some problems with game design. A strong 7/10 even if I'm being rough on the game.

 Level design feels great. There are a lot of different ways to go about solving majority of the missions -- go in guns blazing, sneak, let your allies do the work or all at once. Weather and time of day will play a huge part in how you approach the mission, and I enjoyed how seamlessly it's integrated. The freeroam world often sadly feels like a filler. You can collect animal species and capture outposts, but personally I saw traversing the map as a nuisance rather than a feature. This opens up a lot of grind for post-endgame though. The control over character felt very fluid once I got used to the keybindings. The terrain interaction is another issue. Often you can't get up some slopes that should be passable. You'll see a lot of this in the wild, restricting your movement or limiting your options. Shooting felt a little off for me as well, which is why I resorted to CQC and buddies majority of the time. I absolutely loved how customizable everything feels by the way, feels like there's almost too much to choose from. 

Story. Not going to spoil anything too specific. The story finally got its claws in me somewhere after the tenth mission, and kept going pretty strong until the end of chapter 1 which was an entire story on its own. It felt really packed and tight. Chapter 2 had some really memorable moments that I will absolutely cherish, but the story just... ended? You get a bunch of recycled challenge missions during chapter 2 and the new story missions are pretty much drip-fed to you which I heavily disliked. It's just a shame The Phantom Pain didn't get more closure as a whole when it came to the storylines. That being said, I love the method of telling the player (extra) background story in ambiguous cassette tapes, filling in gaps where necessary. The cutscenes are also amazingly directed, camerawork especially stands out. 

Furthermore on the cassette tapes - I'm a sucker when it comes to 80's music and you can actually collect some of the hits in the vast open world and listen to them while playing. Thought that was a pretty cool addition to have. The soundtrack as a whole really suits the game and is totally worth listening on its own. Shortly on other aspects of the game - graphics look good, the game also ran really well on my rig that was bottlenecked by my CPU. The locations didn't look exactly stellar, but were quite memorable. There are microtransactions to buy some in-game currency. Overall they don't impact your experience too much (I had no use for them whatsoever) and you sometimes even get them for free so I didn't almost bother to mention it.

Overall I was really amazed by the possibilites and the worldbuilding and gripped by story, It's a shame a lot of what I liked fell off towards the end though and caused my last 10-15 hours to turn into a slog. In the future I'll probably look at the game in a very positive light though as those flaws don't really distract from the whole experience as a whole, so there's that.

review_text:
MGS:V is a great example of a AAA game made with heart and love. I've played this game on and off for a while and very little of it disappoints. That isn't to say it doesn't have problems of its own despite this.

For one thing, combat is a little awkward, and stiff. This game was designed probably intended to be played on the controller, and the autoaim seems to cause problems for anyone playing by keyboard and mouse. Sure it delivers better movement and control over the game, but the stiff aiming makes it difficult to play out as that sort of action man. The controls are good, and even great sometimes, but they suffer from being intended for controller. Driving around in any vehicle that isn't the horse or the D-Walker is problematic, and I never can get around to making smooth turns or maneuver around common obstacles like rocks or tree's that are littered all over the maps in the game.

The gameplay besides that is great though. Carries a fun loop of going to the objective, checking everyone to decide which character gets to be in your personal army with their special skills, before going in and doing all that before completing the objective. It's organic, natural gameplay in a way surpasses MGS:3 in its own competing strength. The stealth itself is very fun as well, smooth and enjoyable. Though I wouldn't recommend trying to get an S rank on every mission you encounter the first run through. It requires a perfect stealth with no kills, and you'd have to have good knowledge of the mission to even attempt this safely. It is however very satisfying, even in the second or seventeenth run through. Though again, charging in with combat in mind is still awkward on its own due to the aforementioned PC controls.

And as someone who's never played an MGS game, this game is good as a primer to the proceeding events of the story... I think. I dont follow overly complicated story lines, and I wouldn't recommend thinking too hard about it unless you want to undergo the insanity that is Hideo Kojima's writing. It isn't terrible, it gets interesting up to a point in the early twenty missions, but from what I've heard in what I played, it's even weaker than every other MGS game released. As far as I understand, this game was sadly affected in a negative light due to Konami completely ruining Kojima and having some of the story cut. The story boards and voice acting can be found online for this sort of missing chapter of the game, but if you're here for story, I advise you be warned for it to cut halfway through.

All in all, the game itself is wonderful to play rather than invest in. It's core loop is fun and creative with how it plays. The stealth action and the base management all compliment each other, and even features base raiding down the line once you play enough of the game. Even with a cut story, it is something I'd recommend. It's sales usually go pretty low, which makes it worthy of a buy down the line. It's hard for me not to recommend this game, because when I end every session feeling like I did something significant and accomplishing with a smile on my face, then it is worth.

Metal Gear Solid 5: The Phantom Pain.
The last of it's kind probably, while simultaneously being the only of its kind. Because while it might be the last Metal Gear we will get it is the only one who has brought these kinds of features.

Until I miss that feeling of clear direction that makes me want see what happens next, I'll play MGS5 but for that moment when I don't care too much I'll enjoy every moment of it.
There is something about running a warzone using the Fulton surface-to-air recovery system to steal everything and everyone that I can get my hands on that is satisfying, like an adventurer who is hoarding too much loot except the loot get sent to your lair. 
I liked to change up the tactics because of the feature that makes enemies change their gear and tactics because you used to attack their bases a certain way too many times. 
These things I'll remember because they were just fun gameplay.
Moreover I liked the story, I mean the pacing is not great because of how the game is structured but for me it was fine.

review_text:
[b] Positives [/b]
+ Outstanding gameplay - I think it's second to none in the stealth-action genre. The amount of true freedom to tackle missions is on par with or better than Zelda: Breath of the Wild, rivaling Hitman's legendary sandbox design laser-focused on player choice. Getting the elusive 'S' rank on missions is also a rewarding experience that makes you feel like a Boss!
+ The controls are on point. Snake handles like a dream, and the animation transitions are godlike!
+ Smart and challenging AI. How the AI adapts to your tactics, is a thing of beauty that makes sneaking past exhilarating, as well as satisfying!
+ The Fox Engine is a total gem. The day-night cycle, dynamic weather, lighting, draw distance, along with facial animations are among the best-of-the-best. The game still looks spectacular, and it has been over 4 years since release.
+ With the Mother base, building a private army is neat. It does take constant management to get the most mileage.
+ The soundtrack, along with selection of collectible in-game music are quite superb.
+ Impeccable PC optimization. Moreover, zero bugs in 600+ hours of playtime! Quality control from Kojima and team have never been less than extraordinary, so no surprises here.

[b] Didn't bother me much [/b]
= The open world/sandbox is a bit barren, chiefly the first region. There aren't various different adventures waiting around every corner. It does gets a tad better with time, and there are memorable locations along the way.
= If you came in to get many answers on the Metal Gear saga, you'll get very few.
= Boss fights could've been better. Although there are some good ones, I've witnessed so many solid boss fights in the series that I expected more quality and complexity.
= Side ops are numerous, but they are repetitive with recurring themes. The plus side is, you are not graded during these missions, so feel free to experiment. Option to go full-ninja, or full-Rambo (or anything in between) on those chumps!

[b] The not so positives [/b]
- Game is unfinished towards the end. Be prepared to read up on the internet for info on the unfinished episode that attempts to tie up a crucial story arc. If only Konami cared.
- The "time-gating" mechanic aka waiting for real world time to elapse, in order to develop items, is plain stupid and a poor excuse. Optional, but there is a lot of grinding involved, if you choose to do the online FOB missions. Oh, did I mention that microtransactions are available on this mode? (Thankfully the only place in the entire game.) Absolutely deserves plenty of F-Konami rants for their atrocious decisions here.
- The twist at the end was bittersweet. [spoiler] Kojima and team's effort to retcon makes sense for Big Boss' journey/Metal Gear lore. However, it still was disappointing when the truth was revealed.[/spoiler]

[h1] Overall [/h1]
Had a blast, and the S++ gameplay keeps me going back for more! There's so much this game does effortlessly right that the positives far outweigh the negatives. RIP Metal Gear franchise, you were one of a kind.

"You're pretty good!"
[b] 9/10 [/b]
