This is undeniably a great game. The opening mission was fantastic, the gameplay is smooth, the graphics are great, and it's a typical Metal Gear storyline.

This review is just to serve as a warning to potential players. If you're like me and have played the other games in the series, you should know the are some somewhat annoying additions to this game that may deter you from playing like me. I am a huge fan of the Metal Gear series and loved the first 4 games. 

The most annoying thing is the mother base, which reminds me of the HQ area of XCOM. On missions, you have to use a device to capture soldiers or people, who will join a team under your employment. You can then assign those people to various departments and they are a requirement to research new abilities and items to use. This may sound awesome to a certain type of person, but it ruined XCOM for me, and ruined this game for me. I don't want to be boggled down by micro managing and staring at menus in a base when I could be out on the field. The appeal of the Metal Gear games are the ridiculous storyline and stealth action. There's no action in deciding Corporal Roberts should be on Research and Development so I can learn how to make cardboard boxes. I've heard people compare this game to Peacewalker, one of the only Metal Gear games i've never played, so maybe this isn't new to the series, but it was new to me. 

This may sound petty or small to some people, but it was a dealbreaker for me. Again, this game is great, i'm sure of it, but i'm not recommending it to the demographic of players that are like me and wanted a game like the first 4 games. I wish I would've read a review like this before I bought it.

review_text:
Casual fan of the series since MGS 1, received this via a giveaway.

To start with, the game runs surprisingly well on my dinky HP laptop, a 5-year-old, off-the-shelf model with no real power to speak of (i5-5200U 2.2ghz, Intel HD Graphics 5500, and a piddly 6gb RAM) . Now I obviously don't run the game with the settings anywhere close to their maximum on this machine, but what I do use is good enough to play the game in a satisfying fashion. There is some rare slowdown, mostly during cutscenes--like Big Boss's flashback to the Mother Base attack early in the game--that don't use the game's own engine, but aside from that it runs quite smoothly.

While there is some truth to claims that the game's structure is repetitive and grindy, I actually don't see that as much of an issue, particularly as the early missions are completed and the game's full features--mostly in the form of a base with increasing capabilities, and more responsive enemies--unlock and come into play. And being able to repeat missions at any time for increased rank, funds and resources, or staff is more interesting than "one and done" that I'm used to in other games. Further, as you develop better weapons, you'll have steadily expanding options for HOW you go through a mission that makes repeats not quite as dull as they might first seem; full stealth like a ghost, long-range headshots for everyone, one punch man, all-out assaults, and more are possible.

Above, I made mention of responsive enemies. What that means is that, as you play missions in a certain way--always at night, always using tranqs or headshots, etc.--the enemy forces will begin to respond accordingly. You'll start to see guards with helmets and body armor, NV goggles and flashlights, and even gas masks, all as a result of how you choose to hit their bases. It's a neat feature, in my opinion, that keeps you from settling in to brainlessly hit every single mission with the same tired bag of tricks.

I haven't done more than casually poke a toe into the online side of the game, but doesn't seem terribly lively and I haven't gotten to the point where game's FOB missions are available, so I can't comment on those either.

For those who somehow don't know this detail, MGS V: TPP has a prequel in the form of Ground Zeroes, and I very much recommend that game as well. Not only does it offer a fuller exploration of how Big Boss and the others came to be in their current circumstances, but completing certain tasks in the game's small collection of available missions will unlock useful bonuses in this game.

review_text:
In a long line of Metal Gear Solid games filled with mind-straining amounts of backstory (and forward-story), this game delivers a wonderfully refreshing style of gameplay packaged in an open world set between Afghanistan and South Africa and in the timeline between MGS3 and the original PSOne MGS. While still being and emphasizing a stealth game at its heart, it opens up a massive variety of play-styles and approaches to its missions that let you toy around with a ton of weapons, devices, buffs, buddies, and support elements while maintaining a challenge that encourages you to try different strategies to overcome a plethora of enemy types and enemy weapons. There are many satisfying ways to eliminate targets and complete objectives.

Also, there is a Metal Gear.

10/10 would play again, currently AM playing again, and will probably come back to again in the future. 

P.S. The online tie-ins to the single-player campaigns and the accompanying tutorials are annoying and unnecessary.

review_text:
I personally have had very little experience with the Metal Gear franchise previous to 5, most of my exposure was sporadic gameplay of the PS1 game as a child and indirect internet exposure. Recently I acquired a grippling interest in the franchise, chiefly because of the name pattern of the characters that I found very interesting and aesthetic (Solid Snake, Naked Snake, Solidus Snake, Revolver Ocelot, Big boss, etc), previously I thought MGS was just a generic stealth game with a special forces guy infilitrating places and blowing things up on a shallow backdrop setting with obvious bogeys and good guys, I don't need to explain how wrong this notion is. I ended up loving this game so much that I spent hundreds of hours to get the sweet 100% for it (Backup-Backdown Extreme almost induced me into writing a negative review for MGSV, I really want to erase the 10 tries I had to go through that mission to do all it's tasks)

I picked up Ground Zeroes first, it was an absolute blast. The gameplay was breathtaking, the cinematics were on-point. It was a short scenario with around 2 hours worth of gameplay give or take (with several more in the side ops). But I swear to god no game out there has put me "in the scene" as much as Ground Zeroes did. I followed up with getting the Phantom Pain, my start with these games was admittedly somewhat slow, I kind of got bore-bogged in Afghanistan and took a while to slog through that, but once I did, I could not consider myself anymore luckier. MGSV: The Phantom Pain subsequently proved to be one of the funnest games I ever played.


[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]

MGSV has some of the best gameplay I have ever got the pleasure to experience in a video game. The gameplay is extremely nuanced, vibrant and varied. The open world is extremely malleable and can be approached from too many angles/directions for me to describe right now. You start off light, only a few selection of clothes, weapons and equipment. Over the course of the game you'll go from mounting a horse and tranqing people with a low-end WU.Pistol to wearing parasite suits that allow you to become invisible or indestructible, riding a walker gear that can carry flamethrowers, fulton-extract people through metaphysical wormholes, utilise a rocket launcher that can fulton people and throw balloon decoys of yourself that speak short lines like "Kept you waiting, huh" to distract enemy guards. You can slide in cardboard boxes with posters of nude models (or anime girls) on them, you can order your d-dog to stun people with an electric bat, you can call down a thunderstorm that stuns everyone in a 50 meter radius with the highest level stun-arm, you can call weather-modification to induce rain, sandstorms or clear weather, you can also call fire support with chaff that cuts enemy comms, sleeping gas, conventional bombardment, etc. The game is just loaded to the brim with sandbox stuff that you can do and has an amazing and interesting backdrop that is your mother base (struts in the Seychelles that your private army inhabits, you can develop them over the course of the game, fill them with your soldiers that you either kidnap, rescue or recruit, fill them with vehicles and weapons and security cameras to defend them from intruders, and you can visit them and see all this growth in real-time). The controls are amazing (some of the UI and IDroid controls are awkward and stupid, but everything else is fine), the engine is one of the best I have ever got to enjoy, all of this converges into a massive game where you can do a great deal of actions and things and you keep getting even more new toys to play with as you progress the game through development or mother-base growth. The boss fights, as few as they are, are amazing, the Skulls are some of the coolest enemies ever presented in a video game. There are countless mechanics you will discover only after hundreds of hours of playing and cracking all the secret stuff (holding up people with guns, CQC chain take-downs and gun-steals, air-dropping boxes on top of enemies, etc). Your mother base is composed of staff you extract from the battlefield or those that volunteer to your ranks, so a lot of the gameplay involves extracting materials, equipment and soldiers (given they have good stats) to growing your mother base This element might seem tedious to some and fun to others (such as me), so ascertain this is the type of gameplay you are searching for (although you can largely ignore this element of the game, but you will be punished by having the ability to develop less weapons, items and equipment to utilise in the game.


[h1]STORY/LORE[/h1]

This game is widely criticised for having an unfinished story, which I can corroborate. But I still do not feel like it deserves all the flak it gets. The story is there, it's kind-of complete, it has a brutal plot twist in the end, I personally enjoyed it and found it really good (I really love plot twists, so it's subjective). The characters are also one of the biggest carrying weights of Metal Gear Solid V: The -Phantom Pain-. This subtitle almost tells the story on it's own - this game is about the phantom pain, experienced by Venom Snake for losing his arm and his former self, experienced by Kaz for all the limbs he lost (and all the comrades he lost), and finally, experienced by the player, for the big boss he lost. Phantom Pain is this game's story and theme. 
You start-off as Big boss, bed-riddened in a Cypriot hospital, hidden away for the duration of his 9-year long coma after the events of Ground Zeroes, you escape the hospital with the help of a certain Ishmael as Cipher, MSF's old enemy, learns of your where-abouts and attacks the hospital and kills everyone. From there, you go on to rebuild your old Mother base, as things progress, you will find some shocking surprises regarding the origins of your own protagonist, Venom Snake.
I would normally write alot more on the story, but I will not dilate any further on this as I will enter heavy spoiler-territory.

[h1]VISUALS[/h1]

The Fox engine needs no more praise than it receives, it's one of the most breathtakingly cinematic engines, as cinematic as it can get. The lighting alone is stupendous, the textures are (for the most part) amazing, the level of detail on alot of the world is commensurate. But it does feel like there is definitely some level of down-grade from Ground Zeroes (especially in the textures & lighting areas), but overall, it still looks amazing enough that it's easily going to hold up on the visuals department for the next few years. It is easily one of the most beautiful games I have ever enjoyed, and Kojima made no expense or hesitation to make it as beautiful and realistic as possible.

[h1]PERFORMANCE[/h1]

The performance of MGSV is one of it's highest and strongest points, despite being a Japanese console port (which are notoriously under-performing or gimped in some way or another, Nier;Automata and Dark Souls PTDE as examples of this), MGSV has exemplary performance with dips being a rare rarity. I can alt-tab and tumble around in my browser tabs while the game is running at borderless window @ 1440p and be able to tab-back and resume playing seamlessly, in my book, that is a standard for solid video game performance.

There are very rare framerate drops in the games with the usual suspects behind them (Severe dust kick-up, usually from fultoning a cargo container), otherwise, I have absolutely nothing to complain from this game's performance even while playing it supersampled at 4K, a resolution higher than my monitor, and it runs at smooth 60 FPS at all points of the game that matter.

review_text:
I first picked up GZ in September 2019 and after beating it, I picked up TPP. The game is amazing! The intro had me sooooooo hooked! My heart was racing, my assh0l3 clenched, my eyes wide open and my brain thinking, "Kojima is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ genius! I'm gonna have a blast with this game. This is epic, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! My first Metal Gear game and it's such a blast!" 30 hours in- the charm was gone. I was sick of the desert and the sand. I was tired of the same copy-paste missions. I had no idea what I was even trying to achieve half the time by scrolling mindlessly through the entire complexity-ridden list of Motherbase chores and I haven't had the same adrenaline rush I got at the beginning of the game in days. I felt disappointed and lost.

Don't get me wrong, I love the game. The graphics are groundbreaking, the AI some of the smartest I've ever seen, the story had a lot of potential, the environment was breathtaking at first and the level of realism put into the game is mind-blowing. Yet, something feels missing. It's like they hooked me into the game with that nail-bitingly well-done prologue but seems like they spent 80% of the development time and resources into designing and polishing that prologue and the rest of the game is basically you jumping between the Motherbase, Helicopter and enemy posts. Same stuff all around- infiltrate the enemy outpost, retrieve something/kill or extract someone. It's gotten to a point where I've memorized each and every outpost's layout. In the beginning, I was getting A ranks on my first tries. But now even if I try not to, I end up getting S ranks. My last mission was to infiltrate the same outpost I've infiltrated for numerous side missions before. So I decided to ♥♥♥♥ around and explore. Alas... before I knew it, I had pacified the enemies in the immediate area (because they were so closely bunched together that if one of them sees you and you put him down, the others come looking and then you have to basically pacify everyone or they raise the alarm). With this done, I had no choice but to extract the VIPs I had pacified earlier before they woke up and sounded the alarm. 15 minutes was all it took. And bam! Just like that, another main repetitive mission was over. No cutscenes, no story, nothing special going on to drive the narrative further. And I've got three more missions like those on my to-do list right now. It's not even fun. The open world was meant to give you freedom of approach for your missions and for exploration. But every game mechanic so far just limits this in its own way.

- You can't kill enemies because otherwise that lowers your ratings and gives you demon points and changes your character's look.

- You can't explore or be patient about your stealth approach if you wish to pacify enemies because they wake up or are woken up and sound the alarm, making it difficult for you to complete the mission

- Suppressors get worn out fast and you can't even find replacements in the enemy outposts.

- You can't explore even in free mode because most of the map is unscaleable mountains and the roads which you can explore are filled with enemy outposts and patrols every few meters.

- What little you can explore is basically either bland and dead desert or just some vegetation after a few levels anyways.

- Not much do in Motherbase or in the Helicopter either (excluding Staff/Resources and R&D management which is unnecessarily cluttered and gives me migraines).

- AI sometimes reacts unpredictably (turning on generators from 4 walls away while doing the animation as if they're right next to it, running in the player's direction for no reason at all even when you're completely still and no one is suspicious or alarmed, reacting to deaths of fellow soldiers for which they're directly responsible (mowing them down with their truck, losing them in a mine placed by themselves) and blaming it on the player who is hitherto a complete ghost btw, sometimes reacting to loss of resources and other times not, some times spotting a player helicopter flying right above and other times not, etc.).

So despite a passionately carved and extremely detailed open world, millions of lines voiced by expensive voice actors, countless lines of code written to make the graphics so wonderful, there's not really much to the game in the way of content. Most stealth games I know of (Splinter Cell, Dishonored, Deus Ex, Hitman) reward patience and encourage exploration yet this game only seems to condone speedruns. If you avoid exploring (by avoiding enemies) and run straight for the mission objective and exfiltrate right out in record time, you get rewarded. If you ♥♥♥♥ around, take your time, carefully mark enemies, sabotage equipment and pacify guards to give yourself an edge, you get punished for it. I've never seen a game which is so confused about what it wants to be- an open world game (which are known to condone exploration) or a stealth game (which are known for amazing level design, and for rewarding patience and planning) or an RPG game (which are known to have a good story at least).

I love this game for it's (mostly) flawless mechanics, weapons/gadgets variety, multiple playable characters ability, buddies system and amazing graphics but... it appears Hideo Kojima was given an unlimited amount of time and money for this game and he just squandered it all on the first few minutes of intensely directed cutscenes and left the rest of the game to a braindead, uncreative team of interns which basically copy-pasted similar missions across the same three or four enemy outposts. 160+ hours in, 62% of the game finished, story completed and I still have a bad taste in my mouth. And not just because of the gameplay shortcomings. I've never played any other MGS game before yet I can already tell it's one of the worst story-wise, not just as an MGS but as a game. UI/UX is acceptable at best with it's overwhelming information overload at times which you sometimes need to catch up in the log section of the iDroid, which by the way doesn't pause the game, and it's a curse when you're on a mission because the game is already unforgiving as hell. The rest of it is just artificially inflated to somehow justify the outrageous pricetag they arbitrarily came up with. The endgame is basically a copy paste of the entire first mission (the prologue hook which was really well done) except with the most anti-climactic twist of all time at the very end. What a waste.

Let's be honest, this is a poorly-written Japanese Gundam anime whose most of the content is boring, repetitive and filler in nature, falsely advertised as a bold, realistic open world game which doesn't shy away from exploring the harsh realities of the real world like the child soldiers of Africa, terrorism and the rise of PMCs. In game, however, none of this actually makes sense and forced narratives masquerading as lore ask you to believe nonsensical made-up ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that even a 5 year old would laugh at. I only played for so long because I wanted to get my money's worth. And as for the cultists, well, I guess they'll have a lot of catching up to do with the world now that it's clear that Kojima won't be making another MGS. They've been living in a bubble believing MGS has some of the greatest moments in a videogame by far. I've seen some of them being "blown away" by some of the most underwhelming scenes or plot twists I've seen in a videogame cutscene. Welp, it's time for them to wake up and smell the coffee, I'm afraid! The world's been churning out a lot of quality content while they replayed all the MGS titles over and over again fuelled by the cult's confirmation bias of MGS being the best videogame series to have ever been produced.

review_text:
Yes, I am very well-impressed with MGSV. This is definitely up there with Mad Max, Wildlands and The Division in terms of immersive third person open world gameplay. It's slower-paced, for sure, but strategising and working out where to go and what you have to do in each mission brings that extra sense of realism and immersion to the table. It really does a sterling job in making the player believe they're in the thick of a full-blown major military operation. It is also pretty challenging stuff at times which is also a refreshing change.

Progress comes in the form of resource gathering while out-in-the-field and then spending said resources on buildings and upgrades to weapons and armour etc between missions. You have a "mother-ship" consisting of departments manned by personnel that you also collect (by attaching a fulton balloon to them) while out and about.

The environment is mainly the desert or barren landscapes which is rendered well-enough and you can carry only two weapon types at a time with two added devices/gadgets. As mentioned, gameplay is slow-paced. This is a thinking-person's third person shooter where thought is always necessary for completing tasks successfully. You can't go in all guns blazing. MGSV, however, is not open-world in the strictest sense. Missions are listed in a menu while your character is resting between missions in his helicopter or visiting the mother ship. You pick a mission and are then air-lifted into a specific area of the map for you to start. You get a handful of objectives which will usually take multiple "runs" to complete. 

The Cons:

1) I found the roster of soldiers who work for you - and how to employ them - very confusing. They are graded A-E but I found the UI to be cumbersome and just had the AI assign them their best roles. I am still quite unclear as to how that system really works.  

2) The map is badly rendered, hard to decipher and totally dull and boring. I know it's supposed to be a realistic satellite-style map but surely, for the sake of better gameplay or user-friendliness, realism has to sometimes be compromised to make way for something aesthetically pleasing.

3) It's capped at 60fps and I have a 144hz monitor. YES, 144hz monitors ARE made for a reason and IT DOES make a noticeable difference.

4) An over-complicated UI with some bizarre key-bindings. 

So there you have it. Despite the noted flaws, MGSV is still a top-of-the-range third-person open world shooter and proudly sits in the Top 5 of that genre (which are):

Honestly, I enjoyed this game at the start. Fantastic, fun, doesn't always take itself too seriously. But holy crap did this game fall off at the end. 

All the little things really just start to get annoying. For some reason quick saves are just too asinine and will ruin all enjoyment of the game, so they don't give you quicksaves, just checkpoints, which for most missions don't happen in the middle of infiltrating a base. A lot of us don't want to keep replaying 10-20 minutes of a mission to get the coveted S. Yes i understand you don't need to achieve these ranks, but come on. A lot of us do and we don't want to dedicate the majority of our free time to do it. 

The sliding mechanic to stop players from reaching areas purposely put in the level design is insane. Snake can't climb up some small slopes or rocks, but can sometimes sprint up an almost sheer cliff. Very annoying, especially when you're trying to be stealthy and all of a sudden you're sliding and now standing up and being spotted. 

Random death pits. Why.
But seriously, why put parts of the level in death pits? It's a game, if you don't want players to go there, at least give them a fence or a warning that they will die if they go in there. With no checkpoints and no warnings, sometimes you lose 20 minutes of gameplay because you thought the little river 6ft below you was walkable terrain. But nope, you die the instantly and restart. Fun.

And then FOB's. Not only does it take an insane amount of resources to develop your FOB, but you can't even get close to the amount you'll need without playing multiplayer. I don't want to raid people and take their hard earned stuff, but I guess I have to if I want to 'enjoy' the game they way it was intended. And none of this would matter if weapons weren't locked behind such high level team criteria. I totally understand why they don't want you to be able to unlock high tier weapons from the get go, but come on, don't shove multiplayer down our throats for a game completely centered around single player.

I loved the game at first, but I really can't bring myself to play it anymore without getting mad at this stuff.

review_text:
So MGS: V was the first game in the series I played. I watched the other games to get the story and such, but gameplay-wise, this was my first delve into the world of Metal Gear Solid. And I can say that it was an overall positive experience.

The gameplay itself is smooth, responsive, and fun. I'm terrible at stealth games (I get too impatient, or just throw a wrench into a multistep grand plan that ruins everything) and even I had a lot of fun with sneaking around as Snake. There's so many options and tactics to use in MGS:V's Far Cry-esque gameplay loop of: Find outpost > plan approach via marking enemies > tackle it from any way you can.  It was quite fun... for awhile. I'll admit I burned myself out on it because of a few reasons:

1. Every time I got caught, I felt like I lost the mission. You don't lose, and in fact it's quite easily recoverable, but I still felt like I failed each time. And I'm pretty sure I died at least once on nearly every story mission, which sucks as you see it penalize you in the score at the end of each mission for it. I honestly think if there was an option to skip the post-mission grades and credits, I'd be a lot more satisfied with my own gameplay.

2. I tried to do a TON of side-ops in between story missions, and these become kind of tedious after a few hours, and ultimately made me end up liking some of the main story missions less because I had spent hours prior doing essentially the same thing. 

3. The game doesn't do an amazing job of explaining just how vast of an array of options you have, which led me to fall into the trap of doing the same, path-of-least-resistance stealth tactics for the first few hours of the game. Combined with the feeling of getting penalized for screwing up anything than perfect stealth, and I had to force myself to experiment with cool little stealth options/tactics/items beyond just interrogating and throat-slitting enemies.

Other than the few gripes above, the rest of my gameplay experience was pretty darn good!

Story-wise, however, it's... a bit of a mixed bag, for me. Snake doesn't talk much, leading to awkward cutscenes where he SHOULD say something in Kiefer Sutherland's gruff voice, but just... doesn't. Like, not reacting to major plot developments is just jarring. Especially when it's not this is a blank-slate character; he's established!

The story itself is pretty... predictable if you've seen any of the other MGS games. There's a few character reveals and developments that were so obvious I had tricked myself into thinking this was gonna be some crazy multi-layered plot twist but... nope. The game is not subtle about it's main plot points.
The plot elements are a bit long-winded and silly to take in through the hours of cassette tapes you have to listen to in order to flesh out the rather lacking mission stories (meaning the vast majority of story elements are not given while you play... they're given as background loredumps). 

And I'm sure you've heard the infamous news about this game: it isn't finished. And it sucks. Major plot threads just abandoned. Literally left flying off into the distance. "I have to go now, my planet needs me," style. At least you can look it up online to watch the unfinished cutscenes.

Another gripe I had is with Quiet. Sigh... Kojima... If you've seen any of his games, you know he's not subtle with how he ogles practically every single woman in his games, but like... It's never sat quite right with me, and it's frankly disturbing in this game. To the point where I would be so embarrassed if anybody walked in on a cutscene that featured Quiet. And I can't get over how he thought he roasted everyone who was like, "This is too much" by saying, "You'll regret you're words and deeds" when he reveals why she's a half-naked bikini sniper... but it's not even a good justification (especially when other characters in the series were revealed to have had similar ...circumstances as her, but shocker, they were a male and as such weren't delegated to be creeped heavily upon. It's a shame really because her story arc is pretty good.

The game's visuals were absolutely fantastic. I love all of the cinematic lighting effects to highlight things in cutscenes, the way the search-lights, headlights, and sun all produce lens flares that also have sound cues. The facial capture is great, and the vast majority of the motion capture is great. The voice acting is all good, though I will admit I thought that it was a bit jarring soldiers didn't have fully voiced interrogation lines (once you get a translator, I feel like they should say their lines to you instead of just grunting and groaning at you. Shoutouts to the one voice actor for random russian soldiers who sputters like Grandpa Simpson when you interrogate them). My game ran at perfectly, never even dipping from 60 fps during intense battles with a ton of effects going on.

Overall, the game was fun and I do recommend at least giving it a go. The main chunk of the gameplay is fun enough to overlook the gripes I had with it, and though the story is overall just alright, it is a fun romp to go through. If you enjoy Far Cry, Assassin's Creed-style open-world stealth-action games, you'll probably like this one too!

Probably my most anticipated game of all time and it did not disappoint! 
I think the game-play here is probably the best I have ever seen, everything has a purpose and can be used for our advantages. The game is very well optimised and I hardly ever came across a bug. The attention to details is insane like if you infiltrate the enemy base at night they start wearing night-vision goggles or if you start using snipers for head-shots they start wearing helmets, thus the game organically gets harder as you progress. The enemy AI here is insane as well(probably the best) which makes you feel like you are infiltrating the base for real. 
Now the cons - The first thing you think about when you hear Metal Gear Solid is the story and those movie like cut-scenes the story is good but not MGS level plus it is incomplete due to Kojima-Konami fight.Also I think a lot of main character were under-used like Ocelot(there was not a single action scene with him except the prologue). I think the story-line should have been more significant which contributed to MGS saga, rather than focusing on skull-face the focus should have been on cipher and characters like EVA should have been included! Also I rather feel sad saying this but the PSP released MGS: Peace Walker did a lot of thing better than this new generation MGSV like - Story, Side-ops(which were varied and challenging not repetitive like MGS V), managing staff and sending them for missions was also done better than MGS 5. The blame is obviously on Konami for messing with Kojima and not letting him complete the game.
Having said that I am very passionate for this franchise and it wasn't able to deliver on the story-front but in terms of game-play this game is the king , it is so fleshed out and there are so many ways to approach this game its insane. This game is worth for its gameplay alone!
P.S. - If you love MGS lore don't miss the cassette tapes!

review_text:
Would I reccomend this game?
Yes, absolutely, but there are a few things you should know going in.
First, this game is desperately unfinished, it’s very clear when Kojima left development and it got an “ending” stapled onto it.
If you’re at all familiar with the MGS franchise, everything that happens in this game probably won’t surprise you. I’m only moderately familiar with the timeline, so certain things didn’t make sense to me, and other things that were probably obvious were complete surprises.
Without spoiling anything, the game is sorta building this mystery around some key characters, then without warning, and not in a cutscene (well, not really anyway), a key character basically explains the story to you in a none-too-subtle “We desperately had to wrap this up and we didn’t know how” kinda way. Which then culminates in a mission that might feel like the end, but isn’t happens, and the game moves onto chapter two.
Chapter two is basically just a bunch of challenge missions locking off a few key story events to wrap up a few dangling plot threads. Which felt cheap to me, since they just recycle old story missions with some arbitrary difficulty ramps. It’s disconcerting because I definitely felt the game was building to something, but then the game just kinda pads itself out for a few hours. A few key characters stories get quickly taken care of, then boom, game over, please come again, maybe give us a few bucks and buy our asset flip “Metal Gear Survive”.
It’s a fun game for sure, I sunk about 50 hours into it and I mostly don’t regret that, but it’s a lot of buildup for no payoff. I can’t think of many other games that feel as distinct as this, and the pseudo open world benefits the series. I felt like I had a great deal of control over how I approached objectives, and the game didn’t really railroad me into pure stealth or pure action. It’s kinda like Batman or Deus Ex, where slipping up on the stealth doesn’t mean game over, and while Snake isn’t a bullet sponge like Gordon Freeman, it’s 100% possible to fight your way to your objective.
The gunplay is different than most 3rd person action games, but it feels very clean and to the point. The stealth is top notch, and the addition of an upgrade system allows you the freedom to approach things very differently as the game goes on.
The fulton mechanic is pretty neat too. If you upgrade it enough, you can basically extract anything from the battlefield, which can drastically change how you approach missions. Here’s an example.  A late game mission had me destroying a few convoys of armored vehicles and then a chopper. In a similar previous mission, I might have laid down mines or C4, but now I just waited on the side of the road, ran up to where the cannons couldn’t hit me, and extracted them without ever firing a shot. And that’s a totally viable strategy. The game recognized I had done that and I got a personnel bonus for all the tank commanders. The game is surprisingly fluid in how it allows you to get things done.
If you’re looking for the TLDR, yeah, buy it when it’s on sale or something, but basically know you’re definitely there for the journey, not the destination. It’s a unique game that you won’t really get anywhere else, it’s just sad that company politics robbed us of what might have been an outstanding overall experience.

This review was made by [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Baby-got-DLC/]a friend[/url] that i family share and can't post the review himself if he doesn't own the game. Please follow his [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/35565038/]curator page[/url].
 
[h1]"Why are we still here? Just to suffer? Every night, I can feel my leg... And my arm... even my fingers... The body I've lost... the comrades I've lost... won't stop hurting... It's like they're all still there. You feel it, too, don't you? I'm gonna make them give back our past!"[/h1]
METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN is an open world third person stealth (optional) game. It is a combination of a movie and a video game, it got hours of cutscenes and the lore is more complex than any other video game or movie i know. I am not a big fan of lore in games and sometimes i just skip it and go straight after the gameplay, but it is not the same for this game. It made me read lots of long wiki pages on some characters, organizations and places (Do not do the same before completing the game for your own good. Spoilers are not fun).
The gameplay is great, as i mentioned earlier the stealth is optional and it can be played and enjoyed by loud and ruthless players too. It is a really long game so it is worth your money 3 or 4 times more than the average AAA title without counting replayability. There are a lot of options in weapons, vehicles and backup and you can choose one of the 4 available buddies to help you in your mission. Each buddy has different abilities that you unlock by increasing the bond level (which is also pretty easy, just don't let them get hurt and order them to do stuff a lot). The enemies also get small upgrades along the story, you have to change your techniques if they don't work anymore and i find this a great way of stopping the gameplay from being repetitive. I personally finished all the main missions and a few side ones in 100 hours and still have some other side missions and new difficulty ones to do. There are FOB raidings too, pretty much the only online part that is still alive. MGS online seems dead, couldn't find anyone to try it out with. FOB missions are about invading player bases for stealing resources and crew, its cost is that if you fail or get spotted the one invaded knows who you are and can invade back.
The graphics are pretty damn good and the optimization is great, i ran it on almost max settings with stable 60 fps (capped) on GTX 1050 4GB (laptop), i5-8250U and 8GB RAM DDR4. My laptop didn't even make a lot of noise and it didn't get very hot, so if you got a similar system i bet you can run it on max easily. The soundtrack is nice and there are featured licensed songs released in the early '80s, which is good for the game's atmosphere, since that is when the story takes place. There are a lot of menus in this game, they look good and have satisfying sound effects.
 
There are parts i didn't like too. The helicopter takes too much time artificially. After doing a mission you are all bloody and want to go to Mother Base and take a shower. You have to call the helicopter, wait for it, get in, wait for it to traver long enough so you would close its door, wait for the game to load and press a button, use your idroid and go to mother base, wait for the loading screen again to press a button, waiting for it to get down and FINALLY getting out of the helicopter. It takes too much time and you can't do something else meanwhile, because you still need to press a few buttons. If you want to get to other platforms of the Mother Base you have to drive there in a vehicle. The road is too long and again, you can't do other stuff while doing it, maybe listening to cassettes at best. There is no reason for them to be this long, i think the road to other platforms should be at least half as long.
The upgrades take too much time. I understand it would be ridiculous to upgrade weapons instantly, but it goes from instantly for low tier to 18m, 36m, 1 hour and a few minutes, a few hours and to my surprise, one weapon that i didn't really need, but that i upgraded only because i had money made me wait 4 days. If i really wanted that gold tier heavy machine gun i would be pissed off badly.
The DLCs are ridiculous, at how much content there is in this game they are almost nothing and shouldn't cost money, yet they do. I never used the suits, i have them only because the bundle that included Ground Zeroes had them too and was only a few dollars more. Honestly there is no reason to buy them, you're wasting money.
The main story wasn't finished, Snake gets robbed of his secret weapon by an annoying brat and you don't get to see him again. If that scene wasn't in the game i would consider it complete, it's like starting a new chapter and leaving it after the introduction.
You see credits everywhere. Even if you don't want you will remember Hideo Kojima's name. At the start of every mission you will see his name credited, then some other credits for the people that made the missions. I think they did a great job making this game but i'd rather have all the credits at the end of the game only. I guess it's just his ego.

review_text:
This game is something special, it brings the best mechanics a good story* and ideas which I think we rarely see in today's market. I highly recommend it, it is close to flawless.

I see this game as the spiritual successor to MGS2; Both games were heavily criticised when they were released, but their stories and their messages are the most impactful of all the MGS games. The two games also changed the gameplay quite a lot compared to their predecessors. These two games are my favorite games of all time. It's sad there is no MGS2 on steam, but here is why MGSV is the best MGS game of all time.

The story:
The story takes place after the events of MGS3 and MGS-Peace Walker. I recommend you play these games first. But here's a short take away [heavy spoilers for the aforementioned games]: [spoiler]Big Boss aka Naked Snake aka Jack kills his former mentor The Boss, in order to save the relationship between the US and the Soviet Union, sacrifices herself. Snake, left feeling mistreated by his government and leaders, leaves the US and forms his own private army. The army is meant to serve the good, but ends up being nothing more than the tool of those who can afford them. Kaz (one of Snake’s companions) works for an ideology close to marxisme, but it is the soldiers being oppressed by the higher ups.[/spoiler]
More importantly the phantom pain is a direct sequel to Ground Zero, playing this game is a must.

I highly recommend that you read the book Moby ♥♥♥♥ to get the full story. Without spoiling the story, the story of MGSV parallels the story of Moby ♥♥♥♥, which is a story of descent into madness, how Snake and his crew falls into madness mirrors how we in the quest for peace (a big theme in MGS) end up doing the opposite. [spoiler] The crew fights for the liberation of soldiers, but end up being used by those who can afford them [/spoiler].
MGSV also uses the song ‘The Man Who Sold The World’ by midge ure to great effect, a song about two identities with one body in common, like how the song is a cover a song by the same name by David Bowie.

A big theme in MGS is identity. This came continues where MGS2 left off on the topic of identity. It raises the questions: Who am [b]I[/b]? Am [b]I[/b] fighting for others when [b]I[/b]fight for [i]myself[/i]? You might end up asking yourself these questions when you are hit with the twist.
A big question is: where do we as humans come from? Is our identity our gene, that we inherit from our parents, or is it the meme that we affect how we live our lives and how society shapes us. 

The story has, however, taken a bit of a back seat when compared to other MGS games. And this game’s story is not super crucial for the overall story of the series. The story and themes are still far better executed than other games on the market (even though the game has been out for over five years now)

In between the story you are treated to the greatest gameplay the series has to offer. Throughout the series, I feel like you have always been on some sort of rail; not being able to do everything that an almost super human should be able to do. However MGSV  nails something as basic as walking. Everything you do has a certain weight, yet every action is performed rapidly. 
With all the ways you can move, a great many ways of engaging enemies is possible (sneaking, guns blazing and more). All of these ways to engage let down a path of almost exclusively sneaking, mostly defeating the sandbox because I could run around doing everything the way I felt was correct, however the game does shake things up, when you are forced into combat-only missions.

This game is genuinely a masterpiece. If there was a game to end a series on, I’m happy it was on this one, it takes all that made the series great (great gameplay, action and a politically charged story). This is the ultimate Metal Gear game.

I am late to the party on this one, but I swear to God I have never played a game less deserving of all the accolades it received since Watch Dogs.

The story just does not work on any level. As a main entry, it's freaking confusing since a lot of characters are from the HANDHELD GAMES! As part of the MGS lore, it constantly contradicts previous entries. And as a standalone narrative, it is completely unengaging and pointless. It is woefully lacking in narrative flow, since it plays out with you doing unrelated missions until the game decides to drop a cutscene on you. You end up with a sense of aimlessness as you blow up this tank or rescue this prisoner, not knowing how any of it relates to your goals or your adversary's.

Characters either have no personality (Quiet and Code Talker are prime examples) or are ridiculously annoying. Huey and Eli are especially grating, between the former's complusive lying & hypocrisy and the latter's whiny angst. Heck, "Snake" in this game has no agency whatsoever, only existing in the story to do whatever Miller and Ocelot tell him to do. That's not to mention how Ocelot and Miller, MAINSTAYS OF THE FRANCHISE, are relegated to dumping exposition on you for the majority of the game.

The gameplay is mechanically sound, favouring stealth gameplay over run-and-gun tactics. There's not really much to say on that since I don't really have big complaints about it other than cover is too sticky, which is troublesome when things invariably go sideways and you need to sprint. It's especially an issue during Mission 45, which is an absolute dumpster fire of level design. Also the lack of vehicle stealth. Are you driving a tank? Too bad! They know it's you.

By far, the biggest offenders are the level design and mission structure. The decision to make MGSV sandbox was absolutely the wrong one, as it introduces so much dead space into gameplay by forcing you to traverse an empty map for minutes at a time. Just to reach a mission area. Most of the camps and outposts scattered throughout the map are also fairly repetitive, and are positioned such that it's pretty cumbersome just to avoid if you don't want to deal with them.

In terms of mission structure, its biggest weakness begin to rear its head in Chapter 2, which basically forces you to play hard mode by recycling Chapter 1 missions, but making them harder (which by this game's standard is stripping you of gameplay mechanics you have grown used to). There are few original missions in this chapter, and the ones it does have are incredibly uninspired. Except Mission 45, which is specifically designed to be the worst MGS mission of all time. It forces you to use these controls, so finely tuned for stealth gameplay, to participate in wave defense. With tanks that can withstand 3 rocket blasts. And can kill you in one hit. And come in waves of threes at a time. And you cannot abort the mission once you start. Because whoever made that level tortures Satan as his hobby.

I have genuinely never felt so much like I wasted my time. Avoid like the plague.

The story, despite an abrupt wrap up with clear missing pieces, is an unbelievably strong atmosphere and tone. Total bro stuff, starting a for profit military with no borders to search for revenge against those who destroyed what you had in the past. The supporting cast is great, and the ties to the past metal gear games are lesser than previous entries, although you will run into of plenty of names you might not otherwise recognize. I played this before any other metal gear game, and I got through fine aside from a wiki lookup or two.

As I have now gone through the entire franchise... I don't know if my love of 5 correlates to my enjoyment of the others. The gameplay is clearly a perfection and continuation, but taking away the semi-linear structure and biasing your time towards actual gameplay really doesn't make this feel like a Metal Gear game. There is so much merit and accuracy in calling this an ok MGS game, but an amazing game on its own. It's not bad at all, and has a lot of good purpose and fulfillment for the bigger picture, but could've served a lot more.

I don't usually consider immersion to be that highly valued in the games I enjoy for me, but my love of this game is heavily associated to how much I was enveloped by it during it's initial release. I was in high school, moving over from a genuine puppy love of Splinter Cell Blacklist, and I reallllly found this game to be an absolute perfection on my favorite genre at the time, stealth games.

Stealth hasn't died, by the way. It has more confidently blended with action games in games like The Last of Us and Helldivers 2, and the Hitman franchise had a bombastic trilogy that basically saved IO Interactive. Some indies touch on the classic stealth first design of the past, but the main pain point is watching the biggest players, Metal Gear and Splinter Cell, grow old and lose the limelight. MGS4 seems like a more fitting send off for the story, but this game plays way better than it and the rest of the franchise.

Catch it on sale, love it dearly. There's a reason my hour count is what it is.

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is one of the greatest scams ever pulled off in the history of videogames.

First there were trailers, with promises of open-world gameplay and freedom unprecedented in Metal Gear franchise, or any other game for that matter, and an epic conclusion to the story of Big Boss, the missing link of the Metal Gear saga. And these trailers, man! I still have chills watching one with Mike Oldfield’s song to this day, even with the context of that game.

Then there was Ground Zeroes, the glorified demo and a piece of misleading marketing, but a damn good one. Actually, it was not just “misleading marketing”, I am willing to say, that was a demo for a game which was never made. 

I am not easily separated from my money, but I decided to bite the bullet, and that was actually a great time. I really tried very hard to squeeze as much value from that game as I possibly could, but I think I’ve got my money's worth. And my hype for the Phantom Pain was through the roof. 

But, as I’ve said - I am not easily separated from my money. So I’ve waited for the reviews, and wouldn’t you know - these were perfect 10s front to back. Everybody seemed to think that it was a perfect stealth game, everyone pointing out the intricate guard AI, the multitude of systems interacting with one another, the amazing technical performance of FoxEngine on PCs, and so on, and so forth, just barely mentioning some problems with the plot. There were, of course detractors, trying to put the spotlight on some massive  problems this game carries. But then, there were also amazing gameplay videos by guys like videogamedunkey, who just had a great time messing with the guards. 

So again, I’ve gave in. After 30GB download I’ve sunk into the game for 10 hours straight. And what those 10 hours are! The opening, with its downright psychedelic atmosphere, the first missions, where the stealth sandbox opens up, and the plot gets its gears going. The introduction of its various systems just blew my brain away. “This really is the best Metal Gear Solid game Kojima is a GOD!”.

But then, around the ten hour mark, a weird feeling started to set in. Suddenly, the story cutscenes became few and far between. Sure, there were a multitude of ways I could approach every mission… But all of them were inferior to tranq pistol + tranq sniper rifle + stun gun and just headshotting/CQC slamming every guard. Sure, the guards would “change their tactics” which meant “they wear helmets/night vision now”, but effects of that felt negligible at best.

Suddenly the realization hit me - I was scammed. The game is super unfinished, not just from a story perspective (by the way, you gonna love the “twist” of the “real” ending), but on the game design front. There are a multitude of systems, sure - but you can ignore most of them safely, and just do whatever you feel like. 

They say that given the opportunity players will optimize the fun out of the game, and after playing MGSV, I can confidently say I’ve experienced that myself. I understand that some players (like aforementioned videogamedunkey) find freedom this type of sandbox provides liberating, and can pull a ton of fun from such experiences. And the game is a masterpiece from a technical perspective, FoxEngine is really that good. 

Hoverwer, I won’t be finishing the game for its devs, and imposing challenges on myself just so I can have some fun. It’s not my work, I’ve paid for this game to play it, not the other way around to test it. 

It is a scam, a front loaded production, a ten hours game stretched to last for days. And we helped to make it what it is, hyping the game mindlessly. We are all guilty. 

Maybe that was the true Phantom Pain?

It's like a metal gear game, except you have to walk for 5 minutes between anything interesting.  Even in the supposedly curated missions, you will go to one location, then have to walk somewhere else kilometers away.  That's in addition to the normal stealthing around, so the game's pacing is terrible.

Bullets don't go where you aim, which is really annoying in a shooter.  Additionally, eventually guards get body armor, and there's really no way to tell until you shoot them.  There are probably some fun guns in the game, but they're locked behind base-building.

Stealthing around is actually fun, but frequently missions require you to just wait around without getting caught, while some guy takes 20 minutes to go visit stuff around the map.  I frequently got caught just playing around because I got bored, because that's boring.

Finally, you put up with all of that for a piecemeal, mediocre story without a satisfying ending.

There's a reason Kojima got canned.

review_text:
Alright, just in case you guys weren't aware, if you played this game at ANY point and built up an FOB, you'll find yourself with a ton of GMP over time. Stopped playing for 2 years and returned, only to find out that my FOB on the old savefile ended up making me like 11 million GMP and tons of resources. 
With that out of the way, I CANNOT see this as an MGS game so much as a "Mercenary Army Man" simulator with incomplete elements from MGS sprinkled in. That said, the gameplay makes it into a FUN Mercenary Army Man simulator. There is no end to the amount of shenanigans you can get up to clearing bases silently while taking their best dudes as your own. The gunplay is absolutely fantastic, as is the weapon customization system(retro tacticool is best tacticool, I challenge all dissenters to a boxing match). Kojima did a great job with making you FEEL like a proper mercenary as seen from a 1980's Soldier of Fortune magazine. Only trouble is though, if you end up shooting it out with rival mercs or pinko red bastages, the game basically says "you're not supposed to do that, but we can't stop you", You also miss out on nice bonuses when you're mowing down S+ everything guys by the truckload, as fun as that is. 
Personally, if this rendition of the MGS series were to continue as a standalone game focused on the mercenary stuff, I would be beyond happy. Only things I'd really do are 3 things: make it feel like less of a punishment to get into fights, expand on character customization to include different outfits and gear, and finally, expand the buddy system so you can effectively control a squad. Unfortunately, it's become obvious that you cannot trust Konami to do ANYTHING right, and as sad as I am to say it, I hope this sleeping dog gets left to lie.

review_text:
A lot has been said about this game, about the final chapter of one of the most long-running and narratively complex videogame series in history. After playing through all the story missions and the vast majority of side ops, having spent a lot of time with side objectives, base developing and a good amount of FOB missions, I think it's time for me to give a verdict as well. But first, I'm gonna leave a brief list of what are in my opinion the best and worst aspects of this title.

PROs:

+ Varied, smooth and engaging gameplay, by far the best that the series has ever seen. It seems like the series has fallen for the "open-world" meme at first, but you soon realize it's more of a hub system with different operation zones that can be freely explored or faced mission-per-mission, at free will.
+ Lots of freedom in approaching mission objectives. There's never a single way to reach a mission goal and the player is encouraged to experiment new tactics.
+ Tons of different equipment, items and customization options available.
+ Micro-management of Mother Base is simple and efficient.
+ The plot contains interesting insights and food for thoughts, like the role of language in defining individuals and such.

CONs:

- Extremely grind-based resources management, with lots of options tied to online play. If you don't participate in events or online rankings you're gonna have a really hard time farming all the materials you need for base and items developing and you'll be on shortage of GMP for most of the time.
- Related to the grinding for resources, there's the massive waiting time needed to develop all the advanced items. That can be shortened by spending in-game value. A cheap trick to lure people into online play and spend real money to get MB points. Awful.
- Said online play only consists in trying to capture another player's base, which practically means repeating the exact same task again and again while remaining confined in the same base all the time, since FOBs can't be customized in any way. Then there's MGO, but I doubt anyone actually plays the stealth version of Counter-Strike.
- Ranking system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up and can really ruin the whole need for stealth approach for some missions. Since it takes into account the time as well as the player performance, sometimes the best approach for getting an S rank is just taking your chopper and heavy equipment, get right in the middle of the enemy base, kill everyone with the gatling and finish any survivor with heavy firearms, then snatch your mission target and get away. Sometimes you don't even have to leave the chopper if the mission objective is about eliminating a specific target, so you just get there, make a mess with the gatling and go away. Boom, S rank. It's ridiculous for a Metal Gear game.
- Badly explained briefings. Sometimes the explanation of the mission objective is so vague that you don't really have an idea of what you're going to do until you actually start the mission, which can lead you to bring the wrong equipment or choose a wrong deployment zone. At that point, it's better to just restart the mission from the beginning.
- Lots of useless side objectives meant purely for wasting the player's time. What's unnerving about them is that they're not explicitely pointed out until you finish a mission once, and even then you're often forced to replay the mission multiple times since a certain objective cannot be obtained without missing another.
- Main missions are for a good 80% either completely disconnected from the story or lowly relevant, which makes a lot of the game's content feel like little more than a filler. Even worse, after a certain point the game forces you to replay the same old missions with higher difficulty in order to unlock the final episodes. It's clear that they needed to dilute things and make the game longer, but there are more subtle ways to do it.
- Stupid enemy AI that makes them unable to see a man crawling 10 meters in front of them or to notice a vehicle passing at full speed amid rocks and dirt a few meters outside the main road. Metal Gear guards have never been a particularly good example of brilliance, but that is no excuse. Funny enough, once you've been spotted everybody seem to miraculously get their sights back and it becomes extremely hard to hide since they'll start shooting immediately at the minimum movement while in evasion mode.
- Excessively long waiting time when using the chopper, especially to move inside the Mother Base. I don't know if this was intended to mask loading times, but it's very annoying in the long run.
- Lastly and worst of all, the story is rushed and chopped in half. Some aspects of the plot sound ridiculous even for a Metal Gear game ([spoiler]like Skull Face's motivations being nothing much than a personal revenge directed against the whole world, making him a rather pathetic character[/spoiler]) and the fact that lots of important revelations have just been left on cassette tapes instead of being properly presented with a cutscene etc leaves a giant void that makes the whole game feel empty and soulless. The last mission is a big ol' explanation of what actually happened - which is YET ANOTHER RECYCLED MISSION - that is thrown in the middle of a bunch of secondary stuff and leaves important events unresolved, as if they never happened. [spoiler]Eli going away with a psychich friend and stealing a giant bipedal weapon? Nah, let's just forget about that.[/spoiler] It got so bad that Konami eventually had to make an extra scene on the special edition blu-ray (PS4 only, haha) to try and explain all that stuff a minimum. You can find it on youtube as the infamous "Episode 51".

After playing this game myself I understand why people got mad about it and I can't put the blame entirely on Konami either. They might've been making pressure on the developing team, but if Hideo Kojima invested half the time he wasted writing useless missions and implementing tons of utterly redundant equipments into actually writing a decent ending, things would've been way different and long-time fans like me wouldn't have felt so disappointed. The whole development planning of this title was lacking in every possible way, which is easily proved by comparing the amount of resources invested in making the intro and the useless pieces of equipment with the downfall of writing and mission variety from the end of chapter 1 onwards. It's almost as if the game's ending was left out of the schedule while waiting for Kojima to finally get his ♥♥♥♥ together and think about something to write. It's embarassing.

MGSV might be a neat game gameplay-wise but it's a disaster as storytelling and fails miserably where it was expected to excel the most. I have no idea what the hell Kojima was thinking about to leave a game in this state, he must've been tremendously burned out for sure but that's no excuse. Metal Gear deserved a better swansong than this.

♥♥♥♥ Konami always, but dear Hideo, you shat on your heels too this time.

Pessimistic Review:

Metal Gear Solid V is the long awaited prequel to the first Metal Gear game and a story line sequel to MGS 3 and Peacewalker. Overall the game received universal praise from the mainstream gaming media but in general I feel like a lot of it was reactionary in nature and the praise doesn't look in depth at the mechanics and the most important part of the Metal Gear Series, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story.

To start off with, I feel like the mechanics in MGS V feels fantastic to use and control, you really do have a lot freedom with how the main character, Vemon Snake, can move. But the main issue is the game is entirely open world so the polished controls aren't always complemented by good level design or good enemy placement. (For me) It offers either no challenge in some areas or way too much in others, the issue isn't that there it's any middle ground areas and that they are few and far between. This gets even worse with the upgrading and Mother Base building mechanics that are thrown in as well. In certain areas of the game you are either way too good with all the weapons you have or you are way too weak with the lack of decent upgrade further enforcing this idea of either too easy or too hard. Now, others claim that the way you play the game in MGS V crafts the difficulty for you, but I somewhat disagree. In open world games such as these, players are dropped into the game with almost complete freedom and test out most of the mechanics and or weapons of the game, but when they find a system that works for them they usual stick to that system for the rest of the game as it is usually the easiest for them. Now, that might not be a problem if the developer of the game makes varied level design to complement the varied weapon choices so you have to use other weapons to tackle different threats but they don't in this game. So, the player sticks with the same weapons until they are sick of playing the game due to their own lack of change, the main issue is whose fault that is, the player or the developer. In this game I would state the developer but that is up for interpretation.

I usually really like the story of a Metal Gear game but MGS V is one my exceptions for this rule. It has some of the worst story telling in the whole series but to be fair the series has somewhat of a high standard. First of all, it doesn't seem to cover up the plot holes of some of the previous games and actually makes it worse by adding new plot holes all together. Now, you might think that isn't too bad at first but when you have 100 hours + of gameplay and one of key selling points of a MGS game is it's story the Missions might ware on you quickly, as most of them are pretty generic with some amazing exceptions. You also might think that they are leaving plot holes for the next MGS game but this was supposed to be the climatic finale to the MGS series that answered all of our questions we had. Instead, the game added a bunch of new character which range from "Good" and "Weird but enjoyable" to "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ James Bond Villain #543" and also ruined (ruin is a strong word) some old characters by changing their character motivations and personality (looking at you Ocelot) for little to no reason. Overall though, the biggest sin this game commits story wise is the final chapter that was never finish. Look, I understand Kojima was rushed through development by Konami and due to the fact he had a big vision for the game he never was able to complete it on time, but that does not give the game a pass at it's certain state. I am not blaming Kojima, the blame solely rests on Konami but the issues with the game's story still stands. 

Overall, would I, an obsessed fan boy of the series recommend the game? Depends, if you are an obsessed fan boy like me, please take this game lightly and you'll love it. For everyone else, the game is pretty good with some holes in the gameplay but it's still super fun. 

Optimistic Review:

It's a fun game with good charm and fun gameplay. Would recommend, 10/10. Love yea take care.

review_text:
Were this game not to include Chapter 2, and had a better base building mechanic that doesn't halt all progress to a grind, then it would easily be a 10/10.

But so much of this game relies on online mechanics and events and waiting, in the end just playing this game to progress suffers.

Otherwise, this game plays near perfectly. Despite what others say, the story is good and well directed. Some might not appreciate the retcon, and there are a couple of plot holes, but saying this isn't enjoyable or doesn't have a message is shortsighted. The opening few hours are intense, and while the story is sparse, whatever is there keeps that same intensity. The only reason they feel sparse though is because some missions are a bit, now thankfully for most of the first chapter, the game is really enjoyable and doesn't get repetitive. There is intensity and new mechanics introduced bit by bit. 

By the second chapter however, it gets boring. Things start repeating themselves and there is about 15 hours of just doing side ops to advance story missions. Then if you want to unlock the true ending, you need to grind out your base to maximum level, and even if you somehow had the appropriate material, this game wants you to wait hours of playtime before progressing each level. It's unnecessary padding that it boggles the mind how something like this was accepted. Reviewing this in 2019, I don't know the context, but it feels like they were pushing microtransactions. And this is why I can't give this game a perfect score. It gatekeeps its good content behind a grind.

Anyway, I still definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes stealth games. Just keep in mind that later on it will drag and it's okay to take breaks or even stop playing. 

8.5/10

review_text:
As someone who'd never played a Metal Gear title before this, I cannot recommend this game enough, especially if you think of yourself as a creative person. This game rewards creativity in a way that no other title (in the world, as far as I'm aware) does. If you come up with some crazy solution to a problem and wonder, "Will this work?", the answer will almost always be yes. The more "out there" your ideas are, the better your experience playing this will be. 
So don't sneak through levels. Slap a sticker of an enemy soldier on your cardboard box and MARCH through as if you're one of them. Or lure guards away from their post with a picture of a scantily-clad woman. Power move.
Don't just run-and-gun through levels. Find a good toilet and rig it with enough traps to incapacitate everyone who walks into it. I promise it's a lot more satisfying.

Just as good as the creativity aspect of MGSV is its difficulty. The game never feels too easy, but at the same time never feels unfair. Enemies will, over long stretches of time, learn your techniques and adapt to them. This would suck in any other game, but MGSV gives you enough options that even these adaptations feel fair to play against. (If sleep darts stop working on a certain enemy, for example, you can still lure them onto mines, distract them with lewd posters, or make them so paranoid that they'll investigate anything, even if you're nowhere near it.) It's hard, but never punishing, which is probably what makes this game so easy to get into. 

I should probably mention that the story isn't great, but isn't bad either (7/10). Online play is weird, but can totally be ignored. Soundtrack is absolutely outstanding. Wholeheartedly recommend, even if you're not normally a fan of stealth games.

40% of this game could be considered an actual game, the rest is microtransaction hell. It's in no way a part of metal gear solid.
And hey, it's Konami, so i'm allowed to bash it every way i like.

PROS:
Good amount of stuff to do

Stealth felt rewarding and challenging

CONS:
The game didn't manage to keep me for even 100 hours before it started to piss me off.

Extra acid in the face for making me play the long ass prologue twice over the course of one mission list.

After finishing quiet's "storyline", i can safely say that this is one of the most useless supporting characters there ever is. She's never truly developed, pointless as a buddy in comparasion to D-Dog, and leaves after a mission. You can get her back, but why the hell would you? The only reason she's even in the game cause the creator is a pervert.
Good riddance.

The fact that Emmerich wasn't publicly gutted after all the crap he's done made me furious. One of the dumbest moments of judgement i've ever encountered.

About 30-40% of the time spent was during unskippable flight chopper scenes. Wasting time is just about the biggest spit in the face you can receive from the game, so i'm returning the favor.

There is a mission that is nothing but retrieving an item, but it's location is randomised between 3 spots. For a game that's about espionage and planning, that's kind of low. It was after beating the main game aswell. What a lazy dev.

After the final fight the majority of upcoming missions turn into reruns of the previous ones, but with a modifier applied to them. Be it literally no weapons or gear at the start of it, or removal of reflex mode ( which game pretty much teaches you to rely upon in most cases ), and force faliure upon being spotted. There are some unique missions after that, but one of them is like in the point above, just a fetch quest. By total mission count that's 30% of them being those reruns.

Game's unfinished. You can tell that by missions 29-31 with "To Be Continued" in each one that the dev was getting rushed.

The sole existence of helmets in this game made me go lethal for freeroam and most of the FOBs. The hitbox is trash, penetration doesn't exist, and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ANIMATION OF ENEMY SPOTTING YOU WHEN HE PUTS HIS HANDS IN FRONT OF HIS FACE deserves it's own mention. That combination made me hate the non-lethal approach with a deep passion.

FOB and any online content is basically them trying to goat you into buying MB coins. From massive timers, to resource insurance. This can get a negative review already based on this. Timegates and microtransactions in largely singleplayer game.

The traversal is infuriating. They copied outpost system from Far Cry 2, which is the last thing they should've copied from there. They could've gone for the atmosphere, but no. Constantly respawning outpost guards that prevent you from silently driving up to the base, each time. A massive waste of time.
Other point is that landscape is riddled with rocks and impassable ridges. If that's their excuse to force me to use a horse, i'm still not doing it.

Most of the guns feel pointless. Stun duration on rubber bullets is pitiful, i've only seen one sniper that can get a supressor with tranq rounds, and the only good jack-of-all-trades AR is the starting one. And there's litterally no point in any other sidearm besides WU Pistol. And CGM trumps everything in the launcher tab.

They hid a way to attach a medium supressor to a gun of your choice behind a side op for master gunsmith. This needs to be a story mission, not an optional and almost hidden thing.

Pretty much any online(yellow) blueprint asks you to waste up to 4x of the previous tier's resource value to use the gun even once. Which is just another way for the dev to force you to go for FOBs.

These is an enemy type that has full body armor and a full face protection helmet. If you're going to middle finger my attempt at stealth that hard, i'll return the favor.

For the whole moral points(lol) penalty and turning you into a massive red flag on FOB invasion list, nukes are essentially worthless since the only thing they do is prevent you from getting raided by people without Hero's codename. Which is obtained simply by having enough heroism and finishing the game. Which is not that hard to rush through once you know what to do. Or use mods.

Speaking of morals, this game is about revenge and private military forces. And it punishes you to use a gun to kill someone. *slow clap*

They really don't want me to touch stealth in any way. They are working against the core concept of their own game.

And without being threatened by other people 24\7. And shooting is fun and rewarding. And you can get a military vehicle without any hurdles just by casually stealing it, even if it's a tank.

review_text:
MGS5 is the end result of the design that Kojima was fooling around with starting with Portable Ops on PSP, continuing through Peace Walker and Ground Zeroes. It's a game built around assembling a team, taking on missions, and growing your influence - a prominent part of the storyline of the series. 

I really love this game. It's a lot of fun to explore, take on missions, experiment with the different weapons and tools, and make it your own. There are a ton of different ways to approach each mission and the game actively encourages you to do so - of course the scoring system emphasizes stealth but that is only one way. The base building is a lot of fun and very addictive. It's easy to lose hour upon hour into this game. Most stealth in videogames has moments that feel arbitrary and frustrating, but MGS5, like the older titles, has an AI that follows a defined logic that is easy to understand and makes the game very transparent and logical. 

Hardcore MGS fans didn't like this title and I understand why. The story is rather threadbare and for some reason Snake barely speaks. It's incredibly weird by the standards of this series. Most of the story is delivered on optional cassettes from your underlings. The bad guys in the game are weird and don't make a lot of sense, and the main story missions (which pop up every 6-7 main missions, and are the ones tied to achievements) are far less fun than the other ones in my opinion. However, in spite of this, it's most definitely a MGS game and full of the characters, moments, and level of detail that are part of the series. 

I think MGS5 is a far more approachable and accessible game for a broader audience - it's probably the only title in the series I can say that about, except for the first title arguably. I think it's easy for a newcomer to pop in and pick things up. The game also runs great - it isn't the most advanced title graphically, seeing as it was designed to run on an Xbox 360, and scales really well - I have a powerful PC and can play it at 4K and 60fps maxed without any problems. There's a ton of content, it's a lot of fun, and it plays great - an easy recommend. Give it a try!

If you take a look at my profile, you'll see that this is a game I put a lot of time into, as I fully completed the game, leveled up the normal badge to max, and crafted the foil badge, all because I loved this game so much.  Do I think this is the best game ever, especially in the Metal Gear series?  No.  However, I had a great time with this game, as I do with most stealth games.  I always feel a great joy in infiltrating enemy bases without being noticed, and I love the thrill of being chased (at least, when it's not just a complete failure of said infiltration).


TL;DR

If you enjoy stealth action games, Metal Gear Solid V is definitely one to keep in mind, but if you're looking for a story to get into, then you're going to have to study a lot of other material to understand exactly what's going on in this game, and then possibly be disappointed at the end.
