The question is, what do you buy a game for, story, or gameplay? No Metal Gear fan with taste honestly thinks the writing of the series was Pulitzer material- if anything, Kojima's style of "filmmaking" seems to fit into the archetype of filmmaker whose films aren't Oscar nominees, but still have their charms and their devoted fanbase. The reason I point this out is because to play a game plastered with the text "Directed by Hideo Kojima" meant you were getting a game with cutscenes with a cinematic flair, and a very specific kind of cinematic flair. This leads us to MGS5, which is inconsistent with the rest of the series, in that his style takes a drastic change. Kojima here takes a straightforward approach to cinematic direction and- inconsistent with his prior series entries- avoids delving into bonkers conspiracy theories or anything approaching silliness; everything is serious, subtle, and everything (but for one endgame reveal) is exactly what it seems. Thus, inconsistency in tone versus other entries of the series would be an inevitability of MGS5 for its intended direction. And the inconsistency could be forgiven, if the story could pull it off, and opening the hood reveals nasty details that make strong arguments. Peace Walker's mission-based structure segmented its plot and focused entirely on that point, on that mission the player conducted, and jumping off from this structure, MGS5 segments the plot further, and unlike Peace Walker, all of the missions leading up to the main antagonist of the game has a sense of disconnect from the main plot: in MGS1, I destroyed the tank because it was preventing me from getting to Hal Emmerich who could tell me how to destroy/disable Metal Gear, but here I'm eliminating the tank unit because... uh... to wrest power from the Soviet forces to enact a paradigm shift in power to disrupt Skull Face's operational capacity? A far subtler objective that plays into a subtler narrative flow, sure, but the game gives you a myriad of missions that play into the exact same "because"; contrast to MGS1, where the plot and objectives constantly evolve, change, and despite being inconsistent, keep players on their toes. 

But that just plays into the drastic shift away from the other entries in the series: it doesn't TRY to be a tightly-focused thriller with a sense of place, it tries to be an open-world game. Completing a majority of its missions means you go a safe distance from the area from the objective, go by car, horse, or foot to the outskirts of the area of the objective, observe and plan around it, then bust in and complete the objective, and then exit the mission area. The game then expects you to wait a lengthy period for a helicopter extraction to get out of the area, and here's where the game loses that tight focus. Waiting sucks. Loading screens suck, and being forced to wait through 2 loading screens and 2 helicopter rides to get from one area of the mission to another, sucks. It creates far too wide a period of silence from completing one objective to beginning another. It would be one thing if the majority of the game was played on the entirety of the map, going from one location and objective to another, gameplay uninterrupted, but because of the game's "Mother Base" you have to return to, the gameplay is repeatedly interrupted, by its intended design. It's not to say it's insuffrable- it never destroyed the experience for me, but the accumulation of the wait times and load times becomes taxing. Perhaps it was done out of a desire for players to play maybe one or two missions per session and easily organize their play sessions, but nothing about that would have required the helicopter. Another weak consistency is the consistency of which the game itself is played. The majority of the missions boil down to: destroy a target, extract a target, extract an item, and then proceed to evacuate. Contrast to the objectives of MGS2: disarm the C4 in all areas. Sneak around as an enemy soldier. Identify one hostage from all other hostages. Escort a character through an underwater area. Nothing about the open-world design philosophy prevented the game from having more variety in its objectives. On the contrary, an open-world style begs for creativity, and "Extreme: destroy the tank unit with no checkpoints and tanks having 2 or 3 times the HP as before and their shots kill you in one shot" is not the realization of what the "open world" genre can do. 

The theme of the game is "being wronged, having things taken, not being complete", which I'm not sure is Kojima giving a tongue-in-cheek statement about his leaving Konami, or a statement about the incompleteness of the game, or what he was intending from the start before he knew he would be leaving Konami. It's not that you don't get play time out of it, but vital areas of the end of the game are conspicuously unfinished, such as the infamously-missing Mission 51, or what was intended for the "second chapter" of the game as a whole. Maybe Mission 51 WAS the point of Chapter 2, or maybe there was supposed to be further development, the hints of which were never publicly revealed, and like the protagonists of the game, we'll likely never get a definitive, satisfying answer that will fill the void. A "Phantom Pain", if you will.

The game has a purpose to deliver its story in multiple "chapters", but 70% of the game's story content/missions are delivered in Chapter 1, and Chapter 2's missions have no focus whatsoever, no mission or villain to give the nonexistant plot threads any centralization. The point is, the game shouldn't have defined its story by chapters but defined itself by a SINGLE story revolving around Skull Face, the Chapter 1 villain. Perhaps Kojima wanted to accentuate just how much of the game he wanted to make by purposely designing as such, or perhaps the game was rushed to get out the door and was lazily included. Either way, the game is ultimately unfinished, and there is no satisfying justification for that, executive meddling or otherwise.

In MGS1, the graphics aren't that great and the aiming/combat was terrible, but the game kept the player, the plot, and the gameplay all inconsistent and focused, and had a complete story from start to finish. Here we have the opposite: the game looks great, has fantastic combat, arguably the best gameplay in the series, but the game's boring consistency and unfocused plot with very vital threads left untied. MGS1's ending left me exhausted, but with a sense of closure. Closure, in MGS5, is nonexistant. The game has no stopping point, no credits that lead into a repeat playthrough; the game just lingers there, your base's GDP rising and the side-missions staring at you, and as you look at the blue user interface, after completing another post-chapter-1 mission, you wonder: is this when the game ends? To ask yourself that, knowing despite what's there being there, and what's there being really really good, is a really bitter feeling. 

At the end of the day it's an experience worth having, and at $19.99 it delivers a lot of content for its asking price, but it's not going to leave you with a sense of closure the way other titles in the series do, for the Metal Gear series, or even for itself as a standalone title. That's the true Phantom Pain.

review_text:
Is this the best Metal Gear game of all time? Probably not. But I must give credit where credit is due. This game IS one of the best games ever created. And, this game came VERY close to becoming my favorite game of all time. My favorite genre is a blend of mystery, conspiracy, and espionage. I enjoy games with both memorable visuals AND sound. That means that the music, sounds, and voices in games are just as important as what is being shown to me. 

This game has conspiracy, mystery, and espionage. It has amazing and impactful visuals. It has an AMAZING 80s soundtrack as well as a superb original soundtrack, and well scripted vocal performances. But my previous favorite game manages to do all of the above, only a tad better. Deus Ex Human Revolution is the absolute best mix of the elements described above and it manages to do them with one thing that MGSV lacks: PACING. 

Many will disagree with me, but I thought MGSV's story was awesome. It is weird, quirky, and explains things with outright fantasy, but that is what gives it character. I didn't ask for a story that was 100% scientific and factual. I want a story that takes real life and mixes it up with different thematic elements. And MGSV delivers. But the one thing it fails to do well, is pacing for the story. There are countless main missions that do not AT ALL deserve to be story missions. There are also a few side missions that should have been main story missions. 

One simple change to the game could have made it so much better in my opinion: moving all of the main missions, not essential for the story, into the side missions category. Yes, certain main missions give minor points for understanding the story, but overall aren't completely necessary for story progression. This would allow the main missions section to comprise of only essential story content. 

If the Phantom Pain had included Ground Zeros mission as a part of the game (as part of a flashback mission or whatever), had a main missions section comprised of ONLY story content (and made the filler missions as side missions), and if there had been an ability access a cutscene player, this game would have surpassed my favorite game of all time, Deus Ex: Human Revolution.

That being said, this is my first Metal Gear Solid game but I can honestly say, it has become one of my favorite games of all time. I know fans of the series were greatly disappointed with it, but coming from someone who is entirely new to the series, this game is seriously unbelievable.

It has some of the best gameplay I've ever seen in gaming and the stealth and combat functions are extremely in depth. THERE ARE NO OTHER STEALTH GAMES LIKE THIS ONE. Some may not agree with me but I think the FOB mechanic is a good unique addition to the game. The rewards of having an FOB outweigh the losses in my opinion. It gives the game new life and meaning to play with other friends and invade their bases. The FOB mechanic is a little confusing at first, but I actually like it. This also is one of the few games I own, where I feel inclined to 100% it. 

Having beaten this game 100%, I feel a never ending emptiness. There are games that I played before Metal Gear Solid V and those that I played after. And the ones that I played after seem like distractions from the potential time I could spend in MGSV. As unbelievable and saddening as it is to say, it is also true...

review_text:
Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain was supposed to be the last Metal Gear game, consolidating all the years of Hideo Kojima experience into a brilliant game for the books. And you can see that the game has that potential. However, probably due to the fighting between Konami and Kojima, the game falls a bit short and it’s definitely incomplete. But make no mistake, the game is great, just is a bit disappointing.
The strongest part of the game is, thankfully, the most important one for me: gameplay. The possibilities and polish invested here invites you to try a lot of different tactics, and the game also makes a good job of gradually introducing new stuff for you to play. There’s a lot of weapons and strategies, however the game penalizes you for killing enemies. Because you get rewarded by knocking enemies unconscious and extracting them to be part of your own private military organization, the D-Dogs. Returning and expanded from Peace Walker, this great meta-game allows you to build and expand the D-Dogs facilities, unlocking new weapons for development, field support and intel, and plenty of other stuff to help you on your missions. But for that to work, you’ll need a lot of soldiers, and killing instead of extracting means wasting precious resources. Most of the weapons are also lethal, so if you want to extract a lot of enemies, your options are more limited, but you still have plenty of them. You can also have a buddy to help you, and they’re actually useful if you invest in them. The game is open world, however most of it is empty. In reality, the game feels like a bunch of enemy outposts, where most of the action happens, glued together by boring deserts and jungles. But at least those outposts are varied. The main missions are varied, however they’re not equally good. Between the main story missions, which aren’t many, there’s plenty of filler missions that aren’t as memorable. And I’m not talking about the 157 side ops, because most of them are a chore to complete. However, a few of them unlock good content, especially weapon customization. The story here is good, even if it’s incomplete. Make no mistake, compared to the past Metal Gear Solid games, the Phantom Pain also has lots of cutscenes, but it doesn’t feel that way because they’re spread between the filler main missions. The prologue is awesome, chapter 1 has the main content, telling a full story, but in chapter 2 is where the game feels incomplete. The story missions are just a few, but I found them better than chapter 1. One of them also has a great emotional impact. You can also search online for an additional mission that was cut from the game, that would resolve some story elements. If chapter 2 were as rich as the first, the game would benefit greatly from it. There’s also a lack of bosses, and those that are here are disappointing, except from the last one. It wasn’t great, but way better than the others. There’s also plenty of stuff to do and unlock, from beating all missions with an S-rank, completing all of the optional mission objectives, completing all of the side ops, unlocking all tapes that reveal additional information, music tapes, codenames, capturing all animals, developing all weapons. So, despite everything, the game has plenty of content. So, it’s only natural that we want more when a game is good, even if in this case it isn’t more, but probably the full game that Kojima wanted, before Konami rushed it.
There’s also 2 main multiplayer modes, but I didn’t bother much with them. They’re optional, unlocking extra stuff that is mostly useless in single player. However, if you can, I recommend you to play connected to the internet. It isn’t required, but you will unlock a lot of extra resources that will make your life easier. There’s also microtransactions, but they aren’t that much intrusive, especially for single player. They’re mostly for giving an edge on multiplayer. It doesn’t mean that I approve them, though. Despite everything, I definitely recommend you to buy this game, especially because it isn’t too expensive on sale, and you also get the Ground Zeroes prologue in The Definitive Experience for no additional cost.

As a huge Metal Gear fan since childhood, this game is a huge disappointment. The story has a few good moments, kino even, but for the most part it's really forgettable. Kojima really struck out with this game. It has decent gameplay, but it's nothing special. If you have played Peace Walker, this is just a more fleshed out version of that, with a weak story. The big difference is that in Peace Walker the repetitve side ops were done quickly. Here, that's what you'll be doing for most of your time with the game. You'll extract the highly skilled soldier 20 times, save the prisoner 20 times, and rescue your captured soldier 20 times. It's a downright shame to see what this overall great series became with this game.

This game singlehandedly makes a man question Hideo Kojima and his credibility as a coherent writer. While some characters have amazing voice acting, others are laughable. The main antagonist in particular has so many lines where you just have to wonder what the direction was. If I had to describe how my faith in Kojima is after playing this game, i'd like to use one of the funnier lines from Skull Face himself. "Major, I'M BURNING UP!"

Do yourself a favor and emulate all the older games if you're new to MGS. They're much better than this game and will actually have stories you want to see more of.

review_text:
Best Metal Gear game and anyone who tells you otherwise is dead wrong. Yeah it's a little unfinished and the story doesn't make much sense without the context of the rest of the series but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is it fun to play.

The story of this game gets a bad rap because the average video game enjoyer doesn't understand that plot isn't everything. The Phantom Pain has some of the most interesting themes and messages of any Metal Gear game, but unlike every other Metal Gear game it doesn't spell it out for you. Kojima respects your intelligence and allows you to draw your own conclusions (that is, if you're willing to engage with the material).

The FOX Engine runs like a dream. The game looks fantastic even by today's standards and could probably pull 60fps on a potato. The responsive and tight controls make it feel like a dream to play on both controller and M+KB.

The gameplay is the best it's ever been. I can't say anything that hasn't been said before but I will say that nearly every item and upgrade in the game has hidden uses that aren't immediately obvious. This is a sandbox game and it should be treated as such. Experimentation and improvisation are key to enjoying this game. Do yourself a favor and don't bother save scumming. The action is just as much a part of the intended experience as the sneaking.

In the later game there's some pretty conspicuously cut content. Several early game missions are repeated with extra challenge rules applied. It feels a little lazy but honestly the missions can play out in so many different ways that I didn't mind much. Some of the challenge rules were actually a welcome change of pace. Subsistence Mode specifically felt like a breath of fresh air. But still, Chapter 2 should've been full of original missions and that fact that it isn't is a blight on an otherwise perfect game.

10/10 My only gripe is that there isn't more.

This is a review from a person who never played mgs games before to people who also never played a single mgs game.

Overall, it's a big mehhh.

Plotwise and settingwise, it's a game from kids to kids. Yesyes, I know that the main developer is an old dude, and the game itself is 17+, but oh boy, a sensible adult cannot stand what's happening in the game for more than a couple of hours without throwing up. Not because it's disgusting, but because of untolerable insanity of what's going. ***Imagine an elementary school kid who just read a comic book for the first time and now decided to write his own comic books. Yes, it's that bad*** The game has bad Russians, a nazi villian who is not a nazi (or is he?) but looks 100% like one, huge human-like robots, jumping zombies that are not actually zombies but super soldiers, slow more-zombie-like zombies that are not actually zombies but infected people, ghosts, flying thing which you must know is a boy because if you say it's a girl mgs fans would mount a crusade on you, a flame dude on a flame horse, and other super-natural bs. The main character has a HORN! A freaking HORN! (well, it's not an actual horn - that would be beyond even the author's level of insanity). And I'm just 11 hours into the game. Well, I get it, people love the cutscenes, I get it. The cutscenes are long, awesome if you forget about the content, and there are lots of them. Truly, mgs sets a benchmark for storytelling (not the story, but how to present one), but the story itself is a piecemeal of all blockbuster cliches that exist out there, which is ok and sometimes even enjoyable when it's a 90-min movie in a theater, but hell 50+ hours of this?

Gameplay is kinda ok and might be enjoyable at times when you don't have to deal woith zombies or run from from a huge robot which [spoiler]your copper apparently could have destroyed in a few machine-gun shots but it didn't because you know the plot is written for 8-year-olds[/spoiler]. 
The main selling point of the game, stealth mechanics is ok but lacks depth of other stealth games like splinter cell. You can crouch or crawl, hide behind obstacles, and shoot with suppressed weapons but the suppressor wears off arter a few shots (whaaaaaaaaat?). Not much of a challenge and gets really repetitive, especially once you realize that in any difficult situation you can just get on your belly move to your destination.
The open world feature is somewhat fake, because pretty often you are forced to follow a particular route by visible (aka mountains) and invisible walls (like non-climbable obstacles) to go through a series of cutscenes and scripted events. This is not what I call an open-world game.
And yes, the game is an absolute grind-heaven. Zillions of achievements, challenges, items to collect, items to develop, base modifications to build, side and main missions (that are all the same) to complete over and over again. What for? I have no idea. For me, it's simply a noise between missions that I need to click through: somth buing built, upgraded, arriving here or there, etc - who cares?

Overall, now when I bought it, I think it's an ok game to kill an hour or two occasionally, but I would definitely not spend my money on it in the first place.

UPD after finishing the game:

So, I finished the story part of the game (ironically, only ~30% of the content) and here is my final opinion. It is a casual stealth game worth ~$10:
 - has all the attributes of casual games like timers and lots of grinding. At some point, I was really surprised there were no ads like banners at the bottom of the screen or unskippable ads in between each mission - in so many aspects the game reminds of free smartphone games where you can grind or pay
 - the story is a complete garbage. I thought it was insane at the beginning but it also loses any sense midway and never picks that up. The story in a nutshell: [spoiler]any medic can become a super-comando like the snake[/spoiler]. At times, it might be really hard not to laugh at what's going on in cut-scenes
 - the gameplay is monotonous and relatively easy (well, excluding boss fights; but boss-fights in a stealth game? mehhhhh)

So, if you need to kill time while waiting for a good stealth game to come out and can get this one on sale for cheap, do it. Otherwise, don't waste your time and money.

A weapon to surpass Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is far too uninvitingly long to suggest playing through. Molded around a solid core, MGSV:TPP’s extremities don’t hold up well hours into the game. As my acceptance of its demand my for commitment wore away, I found it harder and harder to enjoy myself as I climbed up the hill, telling myself the end was too close to give up on.


[i]Background:[/i]
My curiosity about the series after playing Metal Gear Rising and after MGSV’s massive media presence during its release a few years ago had me grab a copy given the opportunity during a strange scenario. Thrilled to have a reason to get into series but fearful of the time commitment and not having access to a single PlayStation console, I decided to watch the cutscenes of each game. I ended up enjoying that time and I’d recommend the same procedure to those similarly timid of entering a large series.

My initial impressions of ‘Big Boss’s Balloon and Bioweapon Adventures’ had me blown out of the water. I felt I had been presented with a polished story experience that’d thoroughly engage me and reward my research. Having briefly tried Twin Snakes, I adored the experience of actually learning the controls. The hospital by itself was a curious and mysterious phenomena and added mystery to the direction the game would take after the Ground Zeroes. Cypher appeared as a daunting enemy with the great gameplay and metal-gear-plot craziness potential.

Being both a chaotic and sneaky Snake is enormously gratifying and his moveset has a signature feel. Firing, reloading, throwing, crawling… - with a few exceptions, playing as Snake is a dream. The weapons select and iDroid UI are quick and snappy. Every action has a distinct and excellent sound effect. Going the sleep-only pacifist route is the way to play mostly for that insta-sleep-headshot noise. Pick-ups, even as they become obsolete, are a joy to snatch for that quick swoosh. Praising general aspects like this is tough to expand on, but just know that these fundamentals are a terrific accomplishment.

Outside of these core mechanics, elements like resource management, staff sorting, PF relations and combat deployments quickly became a repetitive, mobile-game style time-suck dedicated to meaningless long-term invested in rewards that require not involvement. Combat deployments are give you loads of free money for clicking menus every 20 minutes. There’s a daily reward for opening the game. The incredibly long wait times for high-level developments feels insulting after working towards or being excited about that new equipment. These distracting features hampered the immersion of role-playing as a war-beaten super soldier with an attractive voice. Despite their plot relevance, many of these features best belong in the PSP game they originated from.

After the first, say, six missions, I had a hard time finding any difficulty between putting a whole base/outpost to sleep from afar and getting repeatedly destroyed by late game ‘bosses’ until I google their anti-climactic weakness. That lovely core gameplay still makes infiltration and combat enjoyable yet it creates a desire for more from everything else.

The weapons and buddies held a lot of potential for alternative playstyles and gameplay mix-ups yet I found myself cozily slipping into one loadout without much inspiration to try out anything new. General guards and their wonky AI barely changed. The occasion shield or helmet was cute but effortlessly countered with better aim. It’s a shame the threatening walker gears did show up more or that the creative potential of the Cypher mutants didn’t expand beyond the miserable boss battles. The panic and excitement of improvising in earlier missions dissipated as your literacy of the game increases. All those buddies and weapons don’t make the game more interesting over time, they make it easier and, when the power-trip wears off, you begin to wonder where the variety went.

I Painfully give it a Solid Five Medals for the Phantom elements that grind my Gears. Pushing through to the end for the sake of the story is something I almost wish I hadn’t done. If MGSV had a more contained and isolated way to move through the story, I believe it’d leave more of an impressive while  avoid losing its limerence. More can be a less.

God bless Hideo Kojima.

I'm investing in this item because I want it now, not SIX DAYS from now (and no, I'm not paying five bucks to speed it up). Although I know this game isn't new, I have had this title on console since release and I lost interest and didn't really get to much into it.

Switching to full time PC gaming a few years ago, I picked it up with intent on forcing myself to get through it, even if it was just to honor the previous titles which I loved in different ways.

At first, having experienced the first few hours previously i wasn't really grabbed. I'm sure i'm not the only metal gear fan to feel like this, the switch from going to the story driven (if not sometimes exhaused) cutscenes and kind of predetermined path to this time be thrown into an open world and a some-what overwhelming mission select, management, map etc. (Idroid). At one point I felt a little let down, I kind of missed the lengthy cut-scenes that metal gear became iconic for, all the Lore (even if some of it was contradicting or confusing) and then I realised that it was all there in the cassette tapes, maybe not visually but just as in-depth and interesting.

Along side that, I think another thing i was alittle disappointed with was the boss'. Another Iconic feature to the franchise, I felt they lacked character. The Skulls although a pain in the Ass, they had nothing really interesting about them apart from abilities, all the previous games the 'boss battles' meant something because of the personalities each boss had. 

Mechanically, the gameplay is amazing and still to this day is stronger than most of the other 'AAA' titles and still has some original idea's that haven't been overused.

The soundtrack is a nice touch, which takes me back to songs not quite from my ERA but definatly songs I grew up hearing through the likes of my family etc. 

I found it to be very slow burning to begin with but once the story grabs you it never lets go, the previous games and characters all start to tie in, all the little side quests that I was planning to stay away from until I had experienced the story became fun, inviting and rewarding. And that Ending, well even if it wasn't fully finished and many people was disappointed with it, I actually thought it wasn't too bad. Or at least it could have been worse.

I'm not going to lie and stay this is the best Metal Gear in the franchise but it is a great game, it stands up to the rest. Maybe not as well as Metal Gear Solid 1 and 3 (Snake eater) in my opinion, perfect games.

All in all, I think I may have been nit-picking a bit too much to begin with because many changes came with this game but you can tell that it's heart and soul is still well and truely ALIVE! This game is amazing when you get through it all and near impossible to stop playing at a certain point. Listen to the tapes, upgrade your base, buddies and weapons. Enjoy!

review_text:
I had planned it all very carefully. There were way too many guards still looking for me, and with sunrise coming shortly, I had almost no chance of making it out to the nearest safe landing zone with an injured prisoner on my shoulders. But I wouldn’t have to. During the night, I planted some C4 on this outpost’s radio communication equipment, the anti-aircraft battery, and most importantly, their AA radar. So I took a deep breath, detonated all three at once, called in a chopper, and watched it all unfold. After a short while, my ride swooped in, blasting an APC to bits with a ferocious rocket barrage, and cutting infantry down with heavy machine gun fire as I scrambled from my hiding place to the main courtyard, prisoner in tow. I hopped in with my precious cargo, and then jumped on the side-mounted minigun to keep the newly arrived reinforcements at bay as my chopper smoked and sputtered its way out of the hotzone.

That’s Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain almost all the time, and what’s truly incredible is that none of this escape  was scripted or directed. My mission was simply to get that prisoner out alive. The rest of it, from the time of day I chose to approach to crippling the base’s ability to deal with an aerial assault was a testament to how perfectly all the pieces of Phantom Pain’s gameplay fit together. It is, unquestionably, my favorite Metal Gear to play, though I do wish its story delivered as many memorable moments as its sandbox empowered me to create for myself.

Right from the moment you’re told to get on your horse and explore the Afghan countryside, Phantom Pain feels intimidating, almost overwhelming in terms of the freedom its open world affords and the number of concepts it expects you to grasp. It’s almost too much, especially given the relative linearity of previous Metal Gears. But what initially appeared to be an overly dense tangle of features to fiddle with instead unraveled into a well integrated set of meaningful gameplay systems that provided me with a wealth of interesting decisions to make.

Let’s take another look at my daring prisoner rescue for instance. Phantom Pain’s day/night cycle and dynamic weather played a big role in my decision to pull the trigger on that C4. While I knew I wouldn’t have the cover of night, I was also fairly certain I wouldn’t have fog, a sandstorm, or even a little rain to make my footsteps harder to hear, because my intelligence team back at my base forecasted the weather in advance. I also knew that I needed a closer extraction point, so I sought out that anti-air radar to open one up. Then there was the comms equipment, which I messed up on. Since I didn’t destroy all of the transmitters, reinforcements from nearby outposts came to complicate things at the end. The number of different factors to consider makes every bad situation you find yourself in a fun puzzle to solve.

More importantly though, you’re free to solve those puzzles your own way because of how flexible Phantom Pain’s core gameplay is. The transition between careful stealth and going loud is a lot more organic than in any previous MGS, and getting aggressive never feels “wrong” the way it often does in stealth games. If someone spots you, you get a few seconds of slow motion (called Reflex Time) to take them down silently and prevent a full combat alert. Not only does this create a lot of tense, sweet-looking movie moments, but it gives you the freedom to take calculated risks with room for exciting mistakes.

Even when things do get out of hand, missions progress accordingly. Your carefully planned sneaking mission might turn into you chasing down a fleeing target on horseback, or a white-knuckle showdown with an enemy gunship instead, but going “off-script” isn’t a one-way ticket to failure and frustration.

The fact that it’s relatively painless to experiment and get a little (or even extremely) aggressive makes playing with the many fun toys Phantom Pain provides a literal blast. I can call in a gunship for close air support, designate targets for a massive sleeping gas bomb, or have a customizable combat walker dropped in for me to wreak havoc with. Gunplay feels responsive, direct, and so very right, and unlike Ground Zeroes, I can use all this stuff guilt-free since it doesn’t completely tank my mission ratings.

That isn’t to say that playing like a trigger-happy maniac doesn’t have ramifications, because it most certainly does, thanks to Phantom Pain’s fantastic base-management layer, Mother Base, which is far deeper and and more detailed than it has any reasonable excuse to be. It’s essentially the full realization of all the good ideas Peace Walker seeded. From Mother Base, you manage the construction, staffing, and R&D needs of your growing mercenary group, the Diamond Dogs. Every soldier I kill and every supply truck I mercilessly blow up in the field is missed potential. In other games, enemy outposts are simply filled with threats to be eliminated, but in Phantom Pain they are opportunities to gain resources and new recruits.

And as it turns out, it takes a whole lot of money, manpower, and materials to run a successful private military corporation. There's an outrageous number of guns, gadgets, and abilities to unlock for yourself, and for the vehicles and sidekicks you’ll employ throughout the story campaign - and many require you to meet several criteria to snag them. You’ll need to keenly assign new recruits to an arm of your infrastructure suited to their talents, send well-rounded combat groups out on side contracts to keep money coming in, and direct research efforts much like you would in an X-COM campaign. The breadth of options to choose from and decisions to make isn’t the most impressive thing though - it’s the fact that all of it has a relevant, meaningful impact when you head out onto the field.

Granted, re-assigning newly conscripted soldiers across different branches of my base sounds about as sexy as balancing my checkbook, but when, for instance, my R&D team threw me a newly modified version of my favorite assault rifle, or when re-routing personnel into support and logistics led to me gaining access to off-map artillery bombardment, I was glad I took the time to sweat the details. The door swings both ways too: just as those back-end decisions become tangible boons in the field, the choices I make during a mission have ramifications for the resource crunch at home as well.

Resource management is, in fact, the blood coursing through the veins of this open world, giving its many interconnected infiltration spaces their reason to be. While Phantom Pain’s thoughtfully structured sandboxes provided the freedom to sneak by smaller outposts on my way to my primary objective, I rarely did. After all, those unsuspecting guards could have vital intel, and they sure aren’t going to interrogate themselves. They might know the location of a supply truck I could steal to drive into the next base unmolested, or they could spill the location of a talented gunsmith for me to rescue. Sure, it’ll take me out of my way, but I’d finally be able to research that sweet new anti-material sniper rifle I’ve been lusting after. This masterfully woven relationship between The Phantom Pain’s many systems, both management and action-based, elevates its gameplay to a wholly different plane than its many open-world action contemporaries.
10/10

Playing this coming off of Nier: Automata definitely struck quite the contrast.  While I'd played none of the previous games in either series, the pacing and story beats in Nier Automata were much more self-contained and steady.  That said, the story here is interesting, if muddled and somewhat incomplete.  The best story content seems to have been shoved into the audio logs, interestingly enough.

Gameplay wise, I enjoyed it, but I don't quite see the masterclass others seem to be seeing.  For better or worse, to me it felt like a third person far cry 3/4 with a base building and mission deployment.  Some of the weapons were pretty cool and feel forceful.  Some of the audio barks trigger too often, and can get annoying.  Minor non-credits related quibbles aside though, the gameplay systems do work well most of the time, and the mission design of the core missions is arguably best in class.  Even the filler is alright, all things considered.

Anyway, I enjoyed my time with this game, and it makes me sad that Kojima is out, such that I imagine we'll never get another game truly in line with the core story of the series.  Here's to hoping they bring MGS4 to steam someday.

TL;DR:  Worth it on deal for sure.

I always loved the Metal Gear saga, every single game since Metal Gear Solid 1 made me feel sad whe reaching the end that it was all over, and the time came to move on to some other game. But with The Phantom Pain I couldn't feel the same way. My major gripe with it is how EMPTY the world feels, I just felt like I was riding through deserts and rocks all the time, eventually coming across an outpost where I got so bored of repeating the same thing over and over it just became an annoyance to avoid the enemies. 
And the big installations felt like nothing more than more desert with a few shacks or more ruins. Overall the maps just felt lacking to me, and maps in an open world are one of the most important aspects to me as I know once I'm done with the story I will be exploring it for most of the time. 

My other major gripe anyway, and the reason why I'm giving it a negative review is the story, particularly when it comes down to the boss fights. I mostly keep MGS1 in mind for this but I fondly remember battling Vulcan Raven, Sniper Wolf, Psycho Mantis and the feels those fights gave me, from the music to the sound effects of Raven with his heavy equipment, gave me shivers to hear him near but not knowing where exactly he was. But aside from the fight itself, I found the enemy characters to be very interesting and even felt sad for them sometimes, while I was happy to kill some others instead. In The Phantom Pain that feeling is completely absent as every boss will feel more like a mindless puppet than anything else. Doesn't really help that they won't utter a word, thus not even giving you a glimpse of personality or feeling or adding anything to the battle more than a cringe moment where you just have to defeat the boss somehow. Ground Zeros (Albeit a cashgrab) contains a lot of extra lore prior to the beginning of the game so if you want that then maybe get that too although it's not a must by any means. Some kind of solution I found to all this is to download a savegame from someone who has finished the game, so I can play all the missions that don't have these supernatural characters. review_text:
This installment in the MGS franchise had the potential to be so much better than it is. I really wanted to like this game, however the repeating missions in the 2nd chapter was enough for me to quit the game. I am aware that you do not have to do these missions, but advancing through side ops is just as much of a chore. Side ops in the game were very random feeling, (clearing mines, extracting animals, extracting more soldiers in exactly the same fashion was just too meaningless to make the effort to complete. Most of these make no impact on the story whatsoever, and feel like they were placed in the game as filler to make the game seem more complete and worth the money.The first chapter had some memorable moments, and I found myself enjoying the game at many points during this portion of my playthrough. However, the pacing of the story was quite poor, many missions felt the same e.g. extract this person, eliminate this person, destroy this etc. Many of which felt as though they did not advance the plot whatsoever. This was especially dissapointing after experiencing the great opening, which sets up the plot brilliantly. However, most of the game falls short of this quality.
Aswell as this, many things included in the game try to play such a vital role but fail in doing so, for example the base development in the game starts to feel rather tedious. The game tries to encourage you to return to mother base often, yet I did not feel inclined to do so enough except for events that advance the plot. Developing equipment isnt great either, the game makes you wait for rather large amounts of time to complete the development process. This can hold you back and can prevent you drom doing some missions e.g. Extracting children with the fulton device requires a seperate dev option?
The world becomes very boring to explore as you have to travel large distances to get to mission areas, whilst trying to avoid outposts so you can accelerate the process.
Other thoughts:
-Boss fights are very lackluster in comparison to the other MGS games. None of which require much thought unlike the other games. There is only one real developed boss fight, the others are not worth a mention in my eyes.
-Outposts can feel almost the same as each other in many instances.
- Not really any facilities with large complex explorable interiors, so most of the game is outside unfortunately.

However, the enjoyment to be had is in the excellent gameplay. Animations are fluid, gunplay is satisfying and you can approach situations in numerous ways, which can make each infiltration different from the other.
- Graphics are really good here no complaints, the fox engine allows this game to shine in that department
-Sound design is very good, really brings what cutscenes there are to life
- Cinematically this game is brilliant, cutscenes look amazing with many effects like the adjustment of light to atmospheric effect, or lens flares.

In conclusion, yes you can have some fun with this game, but if you are aware of the quality of the other Metal gear solid games and how developed their storylines are, it can ruin this exeperience.In My opinion this game does not deserve some of the praise it gets 10/10 (from IGN and gamespot) Which suggests that it has little to no flaws which isnt the case at all.
If you are new to the series perhaps you can find enjoyment in this game, but the bland, repetitive nature of the game especially in the later stages of the game are too much for me to reccomend this personally.
I believe both Kojima and Konami are both to blame for the negatives in this game, Kojima perhaps was just too ambitious and did not stick to the budget set out by Konami. Or Konami should have let Kojima use more resources to finish and perfect the game.This game is unfinished and it can be seen in many aspects of this entry in to the series.

review_text:
The Phantom Pain is a game defined as much by what it is as by what it isn't. It's the final entry in Hideo Kojima’s legendary saga, a farewell drenched in tragedy, not just for the characters we’ve grown to love, but for the creator himself, forcibly separated from his own creation. The result is an open-world stealth masterpiece, stunning in its systems and mechanics, but hauntingly unfinished, echoing with the silence of ideas cut short.

Let’s start with the brilliance. Mechanically, The Phantom Pain is the most fluid, satisfying stealth game ever made. Period. The freedom of approach, the impeccable controls, the vast array of gadgets, weapons, and strategies... it’s unparalleled. No stealth game before or since has given players such refined control over every decision, every encounter, every outcome. Whether you ghost through a base under the cover of darkness or wreak havoc with armored vehicles and supply drops, the game never punishes creativity. Instead, it rewards mastery.

The AI is smart, reactive, and constantly adapting. Enemies begin wearing helmets if you rely on headshots. They deploy searchlights and gas masks if you abuse darkness or gas tactics. It forces you to evolve. Combine that with a dynamic day-night cycle, weather systems, and a responsive open world, and you have a sandbox that, although empty besides the enemy camps, feels nice to explore.

Then there’s the tone. The game is soaked in melancholy. From Snake’s quiet brooding to the desolate Afghan and African landscapes, everything feels like the long shadow of a dream fading into nothing. The base-building and management mechanics, the return of the Fulton system, and the connections with past characters... everything is steeped in themes of memory, loss, and betrayal. Even the title itself is a wound that never heals: The Phantom Pain isn’t just about Snake’s missing limbs, it’s about what’s absent, what’s been taken away.

And here lies the tragedy. As extraordinary as the gameplay is, The Phantom Pain is also an unfinished story. Chapter 2 is abrupt, fragmented, and in many ways, heartbreaking... and not because of its content, but because of its absence. Key characters vanish without closure. Plot threads are raised and dropped. And of course, the infamous Mission 51 (which never made it into the final product) haunts the game like a ghost. It’s clear that Kojima had grander plans, and that those plans were mercilessly cut short by Konami’s internal politics and corporate decisions.

Yet, what remains is still breathtaking. The twist that reframes the entire game (no spoilers here) is bold, meta, and deeply symbolic... less about shock value, and more about identity, legacy, and the myth of the "hero." Kojima doesn’t just end the saga; he questions the very act of storytelling itself, asking us if we’ve really understood what this series was all about.

The score is phenomenal. The use of licensed music like The Man Who Sold the World, Take on Me, or Glorious elevates scenes into unforgettable moments. And let’s not forget the sheer audacity of the cassette system, letting you blast Rebel Yell or Ride of the Valkyries while abducting goats and soldiers from behind enemy lines. It’s both absurd and magnificent.

As for criticisms beyond the story, there’s no denying the repetitive structure of some missions and the underwhelming FOB multiplayer mode. Some design decisions clearly stem from the game’s development turmoil, and a few systems (like base invasions) feel tacked on. But these pale in comparison to the brilliance of its core.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a once-in-a-lifetime contradiction, an unfinished symphony that still delivers some of the most sublime gameplay ever designed. It is both the pinnacle of stealth gaming and a monument to what might have been. That it remains the best stealth experience of all time despite its missing pieces is a testament to Kojima’s vision, his team’s mastery, and the magic that can emerge even from chaos.

Rating: 9.5/10 – A fractured masterpiece that still outshines everything else.

review_text:
This game has a lot going for it, but ultimately it's a variation on a very well-trodden formula (open world stealth shooter with bases to capture) and not an especially good example of it.  

Ultimately this game is a grind, which has you infiltrating the same forts and outposts over and over on a limited number of mission types, all in pursuit of resources or soldiers to build slightly better things. Lack of variety is a bit of a staple of these sorts of games, so it's forgivable on its own, but this game makes it particularly joyless through a number of player-unfriendly decisions:

- it feels like you spend half of your playtime waiting for or in the chopper. You don't, really. But it feels that way, because you have to do this for a couple of minutes every time you deploy, plus a shlep to and from the landing area itself. Everything, in fact, seems designed to waste your time. Want to explore some neat stuff in your base? Guess what, the base is the size of a city with highways in between each section for some reason. You have to either spend several minutes driving, or call the damn chopper just to go between, say, medical and R&D.

- if you want to play it as a non-lethal stealth game -- the way you're seemingly meant to play it -- you are in for a particularly "samey" experience. There's 500 "loud" weapons and explosives to invest in... and like two non-lethal guns. You'll still be using the tranq gun you started with 40 hours in, except with slightly boosted stats. It's the same thing over and over: shoot guy(s) with tranq or body slam them, drag them slightly out of view of the others, balloon them away. (As a side note, the non-lethal approach seems somehow even more sinister than just killing dudes. You end up feeling like some sort of insane serial kidnapper, grabbing randos to be your slaves and research new cardboard box designs.)

- if you want to play it *not* stealthy, the game's clunky controls (two keypresses to bring up iron sights, what?) make it particularly unfun.

- also, even if the only thing you carry on deployment is your tranq gun, you only carry a tiny amount of ammo as well as one rapidly degrading silencer. You can call for resupply drops in-mission, which means screwing around in a menu and, yay, more waiting around.

- CHECKPOINTS. In an open world game. And not good checkpoints. We're talking about the sort where you can do fifty main mission objectives and not trigger a checkpoint. Then you can be approaching a tricky fight and have one trigger right in the middle of it, and nanoseconds before something kills you. Effectively you're best off assuming any unrecoverable screwup means restarting the entire mission -- and they are sometimes very long.

Overall, it's a massive experience that draws you in initially and then exhausts you with pointless nonsense.

Update: After returning to this game, I've had a change of heart. I decided to return to this game because I'm literally running out of things to play, so I thought "what the heck, maybe I might like it".

This game to me is a bit of a flawed gem. This game takes hours and hours and hours to actually get interesting, and this is how the game failed me before, because I feel 10 hours should be more than enough to grab you. But what's funny is that the game's more interesting parts started not long after I gave up, so I've missed out on so much. 

The stealth mechanics are fun, and I absolutely love the buddy mechanics between D-Dog and Quiet, they are what saved this game for me. Before getting the extra buddies, all you have is the horse, and that gets boring fast because so many damn games have a horse. But now after experiencing how fun the game is to play with D-Dog, I can understand why people believe this dog puts Dogmeat from Fallout 4 to shame, because he really does. This buddy system was handled perfectly. 

The story, while not perfect was still fun for me, I found myself playing hours and hours and hours just to see how it all played out, and I love it when I get so caught up in a story.

The gameplay is very polished, and the open world does function well like I said before. However, there are some aspects to the gameplay I really don't like. Army helmets for example are a nightmare. Their hitboxes are insanely large, they cover most of the head, when you can physically see they are only on top of the head, I've shot at soulder's necks only to hear the cling sound from the helmet, it's absolutely ridiculous... Also, the game doesn't make it clear what it wants you to do half of the time. There are many times I had to google search how to even use Quiet as a buddy because not much is ever made clear here. Tanks are also a nightmare, especially in Mission 45 which is a mission from hell. They have almost "too perfect" reflexes for a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tank! Damn, this game frustrated the hell out of me sometimes. Stealth, while addictive can be annoying over the smallest of things, and this is why I wish there were more polish in those areas that really pissed me off.

2/5.   So this game can't decide what it's supposed to be: sneak/combat mission game, a settlement sim, a psych/horror game, a movie with playable parts - and it suffers from not knowing.  

This is the first time I've almost quit a game before it even really started.  The beginning/tutorial is too long, too full of inadequate control, too many overly dramatic, cinematic cut scenes, and too little story-making sense.  It also takes over an hour to do the prologue, nearly all of which you don't control, and if you're playing this for the first time skipping cut scenes isn't usually what you want to do.  I would recommend, if you are going to play this, SKIP ALL CUTSCENES IN THE PROLOGUE/TUTORIAL "AWAKENING".  It doesn't make any sense anyway.

Another big knock against it is that you don't get a full list of mission perameters.  You're supposed to guess what they are; they appear as a question mark on your iDroid/helper list.  There are usually six per mission and can range from helping others escape, to finding specific people to extract, to collecting crap, to blowing stuff up.  There is no rhyme or reason to it, unless you happen to chance seeing something and pressing Intel at the right thing while scoping the place out.  

Another terrible thing is that there is no relaible save.  There's an autosave, which puts you at the beginning of any mission you're doing.  So when you spend over two hours conquering something and the internet suddenly goes out, the game resets you to the beginning of your mission with a big, ol' FU.

Some of the controls are janky, too.  Climb/Jump is an executable rather than pressing jump.  If you go into cover mode, you get stuck a lot trying to unglue yourself from the wall.  Sometimes you end up diving when you want to uncrouch, etc., etc.  It's really irritating when you're attacking or sneaking up on someone.  Also, if you're not in striking distance during reflex, you can't move forward fast enough to hit him.

There's also no difficulty control, and there's a helicopter ride at the beginning of every single mission/side mission that is IAF.  Why can't we start standing next to your ride?

Finally, though mostly fixable, the game is designed to make your eyes cross and your stomach heave from motion sickness with all the blurring, bouncing, shaking, whirling shadows, spastic cinematography.  Within the controls, you can turn off half the stuff making the game less pretty but more viewable, but with the cut scenes you're stuck unless you skip them.  And if you skip them, you miss out on the story.  

I have only played one other MGS game, the one prior to this, and liked it so much I thought I'd give this one a try.  I wish I'd saved my money.  But I still am/will play through to the end.*

It does get one bonus point for the surprise of DD. 

Not recommended for the above reasons.  Buy at your own risk if you are not a prior MGS player further back than the last game.  And don't forget, while you're out killing bad guys, pick some flowers as requested by base.

Let me start by giving a bit of my history with the Metal Gear Solid series.  I started with 2, on the PS2, and I enjoyed it quite a bit.  Then I found a copy of MGS1 the twin snakes for the gamecube, and enjoyed that quite a bit.  MGS3?  I loved it.  The gameplay was great for those 3, and the story was relatively straightforward, if a bit odd, but good.  (except ocelot's "meow" to summon his troops.  I want to forget that.)

Then I got into the later series.  Peace walker was...a nightmare.  I didn't get past the first mission, I disliked it so much.  4 was...OK.  Pretty good mechanically, but the story got....very weird.  And it started to over explain everything, which was unneeded.  


Now we can get into MGSV.  And wow.  Booting up the game for the first time, I was treated to....a 5 minute unskippable cutscene about laying in a bed.  Then I actully got the start the game.  And yay!  More cutscenes.  Note, I'm playing with keyboard and mouse, no controllers connected.  The first prompt the game gives me?  "move (right stick) to look around."  That's not a huge red flag or anything.  Then I got treated to an hour long intro with a nauseating "single shaking camera" angle that actually gave me motion sickness.  (I found out that this shaking was pretty much exclusive to the intro, but that doesn't help the game's case)   Multiple prompts that were, again, for controller, not KB/M.  

I finally got open control of my character, and you know what I discovered?  The open world is an empty, boring world that somehow manages to still be linear.  The gameplay is alright, but since there's so much space in between points of action, it feels like you spend more time running from point A to B than actually sneaking.  

Then I heard "snake" talk.  And it isn't the voice of snake.  That might have saved the game, with snake's trademark dry wit and charm, but from what I heard and saw?  None of that remains.  And I already know all the big spoilers for the game, and I can say for certain that the story is unsalvagable.  

TL;DR The mechanics and open world aren't fun, the story is somehow worse than 4's, Snake is essentially not in the game, and the support for keyboard and mouse is simply terrible.  I actually can't find anything positive to say about this game.

review_text:
Hi, first-time reviewer here.

Of the games in my library, I decided that MGSV was more than worthy of a review.  I will try to cover what I think makes this game worth your money and your time.

OPEN-WORLD ENVIRONMENT:
The open-world environment is by far one of the best I have seen in more recent games.  The world is full of unique locations that are constantly replenishing themselves.  I believe you can almost be lost in just the world without completing many of the missions.

STORY:
The story is honestly a little rough at first.  Now I say this from the perspective of a gamer who has barely touched the other MGS games.  However, the interactions and cutscenes are more than compelling enough to keep me interested in the events of the missions and how they affect the game.

PROGRESSION:
A few games wait too long to let players access the more interesting tools in the game.  MGSV is not one of those games.  Players are constantly unlocking new items through the fair research system.  You ever had a trained wolf attack a guard with a stun suit, then send him flying into the air on a hot air balloon ride that he will be sure to never forget?  If that sounds interesting, this game is for you.

ONLINE:
Although this game does have limited online play, it is more than satisfying more me.  If you want, you can participate in raids as an attacker and a defender against other players.  If you do not like interacting online, you can simply play the game without this multiplayer experience with little loss.  You can also still play as an attacker in frequent special events.

Hoo...okay so, after some thought I am honestly going to have to give this a no. I've had it since launch but by 30-40% through the game, I reaaaaallly begin to struggle to care about completing this game and recently I fired up the game again, managed to JUST complete the first half of the game and get to chapter 2...the fire had just completely died by then and I had to uninstall it once more, possibly for good this time. I really hoped I could have completed the game but I die slowly inside trying my hardest to actually give a ♥♥♥♥ anymore. Let me diverge for just a moment and look back...

I've been a long time MGS fan, my first experience was MGS on the PS1, followed by Substance and Snake Eater on PS2 then Guns of the Patriots on PS3. Later I discovered there were older 2-D variations of the game and a whole bunch of handheld ones too, PeaceWalker, Acid to name a few, but I never played those. Instead I sat through playthroughs on YouTube so I didn't miss a thing. Later on, though not technically a SOLID game, I played Rising and had a blast with that too. I loved the living ♥♥♥♥ out of all of those games and I would play through them all again and again in a heartbeat if I could. So when I heard a new Metal Gear on the horizon I was so excited...and by this time I had become an eternal slave to almost anything that was Open World or Sandbox...its my bread and butter, my one true love, my guilty pleasure. "Metal Gear Solid? OPEN WORLD? HAVE I AT LAST STUMBLED UPON THE FOUNTAIN OF YOUTH!? MY HOLY GRAIL!?!?" I went insane and all I could think about was this game.

So first came the taster, Ground Zeroes...I had already become a mindless zealot for metal gear and at the time, completely bypassed the full game price stunt for a 5 minute long mission. I didn't care, I just wanted metal gear again...and again at the time, anything labeled "Metal Gear" was worth any price to me. I played all the variations of missions on that one tiny ass island when I was notified by a friend "Bro, you do abc, youll get xyz in Phantom Pain" I did it...of course I did.

Finally Phantom Pain arrived and I loved every second of it at first, the sneaking, the open world, how you can have a selection of buddies, vehicles, make weapons, spawn them in at a moments notice to change up tactics...the fact that its not David Hayter didn't phase me as much as I thought it would, I personally think Sutherland did an OK job and I'm not the typical type to jump on the bandwagon. I did miss Davids voice though...that been said ***POTENTIAL SPOILER AHEAD STARTS HERE*** the fact that its not ACTUALLY BB gave it that real sense of individuality for Venom ***SPOILER ENDS HERE***

I played missions and did the side-ops religiously, absorbed the story, tried to get the best army together I could, best gear, do the heroic run and try to kill as fewer people as possible...i've always played like that in any game that gives me the moral choice to. I saved, I spared, I do what I and what the majority of humanity may consider "the morally right thing that defines a hero from a mindless killer"...but mostly just to put those sweet sweet skills into my army. However after a short while I begin to find myself playing less and less over time. I'd take a day or two here and there and come back, usually not so jacked about playing it, but still having some level of enjoyment when I got anything above an A rank...now i'm no hardcore gamer, I just like to casually stroll through games at my own pace and sometimes push the boundaries here and there to prove to myself im not a completely incapable gamer. By this time there were several thing that were grating on my nerves a bit. I began to see the open world aspect of that game as a bit of a gimmick...something of a cheap cash in to the rapidly popular growing genre. Having to constantly go back to the ACC to get mission and side-op updates....having to go back to Mother Base to have a shower to keep my mental and physical state intact and run around to keep my mens moral up so they dont leave...you know, ♥♥♥♥ that began to quickly feel like a real chore as opposed to fun. Why can't the side-ops and mission list just be updated while out in the field then and there...why can't I just STAY out in the field, why do I have to suffer these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ loading screens all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ time. I decided to take a bit of that vented aggitation out by equipping lethal instead of non-lethal, thinking maybe I can just kill some of these trash soldiers that are like B rank in their highest abilities. Unfortunately changing my play styles between lethal, non-lethal, silent and deadly, or loud and proud did absolutely nothing to make me feel any different towards the game itself. I'd literally sit and stare at the screen for 5 minutes at a time and sigh with such a look of disappointment as the veil I cast over my own eyes to blind myself to the reality that I did not once even think to want to accept...which is quite simply...

"I think I actually ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate this game."

I'm not going to sit here and say the graphics are out of this world, because they aren't, they are just OK, they hold up and have occasional places where they look good and some where they look awful...yet graphics have never been Metal Gears strong point, its story has. The disappointing lack there in of either makes this a rather lack luster game overall. If anything I would say that it actually feels like instanced missions haphazardly thrown into what now feels like quite a poor excuse for an open world game that actually ends up feeling more linear than your typical DOOM playthrough (not hating on DOOM, love that series, literally just the first example that came to mind)

I'm sad that I have had to make such a negative review, and this is honestly the first against anything to do with Metal Gear..but i'm just been real. My personal experience quickly grew to detesting the game and just not been able to finish it because of the amount of pointless sidetracking I felt like I had to do, missions that shouldn't have been missions but rather side-ops. I didn't have any problems following the story, which is why the dumb unrelated missions were even more frustrating when you were FORCED to do them as opposed to optionally do them. The side-ops which we got there literally just rinse and repeat recycled garbage that was maybe slightly harder each time...but not really. It all just felt so awkward and not fun.

This game turned out to not be so fun for me...but hey this is just a personal opinion and a review of my experiences. You take it as you will.

review_text:
A modern take on the metal gear series. Unlike previous installments, of which I'm aware of, in addition to espionage missions you are in charge of managing a private military force and its base to which you can procure (steal) raw materials and hire (kidnap) personell, thus upgrading and ehancing your stronghold in order to gain access to amazing new weapons and gadgets.

Is it interesting? Does it add to the metal gear experience? Totally! You truly feel like the manager of a military tychoon with access to the deadliest weaponry which no one objects you for using apart from your clandestine rivals. Feel the need to switch strategy to fit your enviroment? No problem, just have your trusty pilot drop in some toys by aeromail.

Good in thought, however in practice: Money becomes so worthless, Miller's warnings about going in the red become a moot point. You can start a research on a lot of expensive stuff but the time it takes for them to complete and the time you do another mission that completely pays for the cost of the development makes the whole idea of the cost pointless. Materials come by like scattered candy in the wilderness; if you have the patience to meticulously collect every scrap you see, you'll have your base in full operation in no less than a few days.

The missions- Sure it's MGS enough, you've got your sneaking into places in a box, questioning the guards, CQC and the new reflex mechanic. It's all fine and dandy, but the whole gameplay seems to be built around the reflex thing. Try a game without it and you run into some annoying crap: Guards spotting you in the dark from behind a screen wall alerting everyone and their babushka to your immediate location, unless like a feeding mother bird you put a bullet in their mouth. And what happened to the camoflauge rating of MGS 3? I've got rocks and red sand here with some grass; am I supposed to wear the tiger stripe, desert fox or tuxedo? Each mission is a guessing game like the night before the prom.

The story is quite interesting in its own way and each mission conveys it to you in mouthfuls. It's not exactly full-on exposition; most of the backstory is presented via tapes you can listen to as well as snippets of paper. I won't go in depth, but I will say the drama will suck you in. With each completed mission you are presented with side missions, known as side ops. Some of these add to the store while most of them are filler for the wide open areas of the game, by which I will come to the worst parts of the game.

Northern Kabul and Angola are vast. Lots of areas to explore and side missions to complete in an enviroment full of NOTHING. My major gripe with this game is how much of the game area is used for copy/paste missions and villages. Your every day PMF outpost consists of a few buildings to a dozen filled with nothing except a blueprint, some building materials, a handful of stationary weapons and a few watchtowers. Apart from the few story progressing side-ops, you will be tasked with performing a plethora of repetative tasks in a repetative enviroment and it goes as follows:

-Capture crazy soldier
-Capture skillful soldier
-Free prisoner in one of said outposts
-Kill a bunch of people
-Kill a bunch of people with tanks and copters
-Mother base shooting challenge

AND ONE, COUNT THEM, ONE MISSION OF: STEAL RESOURCES

That's about it. And you must do each of those at least a dozen times in different places apart from the last allcaps point.
I guess it's nice they give you a way to fast travel by copter or by mailing yourself in a box to various places, but why make an area of a few square kilometers of nothing if you can do that? I find myself just completing these tasks like a chore then hopping in my trusty chopper for the next area to smash to bits. As I racked up the missions, I saw the enemy combatants with no more humanity than blades of grass or a stubborn stain on the toilet floor that is corrected fastest with the proper application of a high-velocity explosive missile.

 What is worse, the game demands you complete a harder version of a story mission you completed earlier to progress the story. Can you spell f-i-l-l-e-r?. Sure, you get extra story elements and some goodies but that's about it.

I'll just say this to sum it up: There are better MGS games. Sure V has a lot of content for you to hop on and some sweet new additions, but quantity does not equate quality. I'd give this 7/10 at best, buy it at a sale.

review_text:
One of the best stealth games I've ever got to play, and a great (at least gameplay-wise) wrap-up of the series.

+Absolute freedom of operations, you can tackle a mission in multiple ways, you're not limited solely to firearms and non-lethal equipment, you can drop various airstrikes, change the weather for your advantage, have an ally to clean out the way for you

+For a supposedly rushed game, it still has a huge amount of content, especially if you're a completionist like myself, side missions, collectable music tapes, animal hunting, additional tasks (which don't interrupt your game and don't pop up at the end screen like "You did great, but..", which is a huge plus for me)

+Good soundtrack, both licensed songs and OST, really fitting to the setting in the 1980s. 

+Graphics and optimization are really top notch, which was already proven in Ground Zeroes, the game could probably run relatively well on my old rig with a 650ti on board.

+I appreciate the silliness of the plot, even if it has a few holes due to being, well, rather unfinished, the bits that are still there are pretty good, so I don't mind the abscense of the final chapter that much.

With that said:

-The game still feels kind of unpolished at times, with kind of a poor closure to the plot, repetitive endgame ops, poor customization (that doesn't really have to shine anywhere with the avatar later), the motherbase being a bit less lively than promised on the first videos on the game

-Forced FOB content is a con to me, since there's no "real" chance of avoiding it, unless you're willing to play offline, as if not plugged to the game's servers.

-FOBs are swarmed with cheaters, and there isn't much involvment in that matter from Konami, which is a real shame for the people trying to reach the nuclear disarmament, supposed game's true ending.

-Afghanistan is relatively empty, in my opinion the open world didn't really need to be in here, bigger hubs for missions would probably work a bit better than that. It's just nice to explore, but there's not much interraction besides that.


I reccomend the game regardless, but mostly if you  already have a hang of the series and played a few titles in it, TPP plot-wise is a kind of poor entrance to the series IMHO.

This is the first Metal Gear game I have ever played so I didn't really know what to expect. What I got was a fun Stealth Action game with some typical Japanese gameplay design choises. By that I mean they love to page hop. Need an item? Open the page and go to that page, and then open that page to go to that page to get to that one page when the stuff is. It's not as annoying as it is in some JRPG's Iäve played but it is noticable.

The game play is fun, the game encourages you to vary up your style and how you approach things by equipping the opposition with countermeasures to your "prefered" play style. So you either have to work around it or change your style. You have a HUGE selections of weapons of all kinds to use. I was kind of sad that you could only do certain combinations, like you can't have a sniper rifle AND a rocket launcher or be decked out in all pistols and revolvers. Sad but it's fine by me. Now, while the selection is huge, you have to spend in-game money you earn from missions on R&D to develop said weapons and gadgets, some of which can get very expencive very quickly. You really have a lot of candy in the store: assault rifles, SMG's, sniper rifles, shotguns, pistols and revolvers, mines of all kinds, grenades, machine guns, leathal, non-leathal, gas, explosives, cardboard boxes, loads and loads.

The story is fun, if slightly confusing at times. Sadly some plot threads were left abandoned since Konami dropped the game before it was completely finished. What is there works and I followed it with great interest. I get now what people mean by "You have to play it to get it" when I asked about MGS's story. While I enjoyed it I think you might get a little bit more out of it if you played a few of the older games.

There's some online components that were all right but skippable, invading other people online bases and such (Your own Mother Base is immune from such attacks). Stealth invasion missions.

I had loads of fun but I stopped playing not long after I finished the story because it got grindy after that. Grinding for money, resrouces, manpower, etc. to develop more stuff to play around online with but that didn't interest me personally. Good recommendation I think. :)
